# 00 — Hello, Dojo (React) Welcome to the React track. This course teaches you React by making you write it — every component, yourself. Nothing here scaffolds an answer or drops in a snippet. You edit a `.tsx` file, you run one command, and an automated gate renders your component, drives it the way a person would, and tells you whether the result was right. That last part is the thing that makes this track different from the others. The TypeScript track can grade a function by calling it. There is no equivalent for a component, because a component's output is not a return value you inspect — it is a piece of a user interface. So every gate in this track does what a user does: it renders your component into a real DOM (jsdom, in-process, no browser and no dev server), it looks for a *button* or a *heading* or a *text box with this label*, it clicks and types, and then it asserts on what a person would now see. That has a consequence worth internalising before you write a line. **The gate can only find what is accessible.** A `
` styled to look like a button is invisible to `getByRole("button")`, and it is invisible to a screen reader for the same reason. An icon-only control with no label announces itself as nothing at all. In this course, accessibility is not a bonus module at the end — it is the API the grader uses, so you get it right on day one or you do not pass. ## The loop Every lesson is a directory under `tracks/react/lessons/`. Inside: - `README.md` — this file. Read it top to bottom before you write anything. - `reading.md` — the theory. Read it *after* you attempt the exercises. - `ex1/`, `ex2/`, … — one directory per exercise. You edit `exN/solution.tsx` and nothing else. - `gate.test.tsx` — the gate. It is quoted verbatim at the bottom of this README, and always will be. You are never graded by a program you have not been shown. The commands you will live in: ``` uv run dojo test react 00_hello_dojo # grade the whole lesson uv run dojo test react 00_hello_dojo ex2 # grade just one exercise uv run dojo hint react 00_hello_dojo ex2 # stuck? reveal the next tier uv run dojo read react 00_hello_dojo ex2 # the theory behind it uv run dojo status react # the progress dashboard uv run dojo next react # what should I do now? ``` Before you write anything, run the gate and watch it fail: ``` uv run dojo test react 00_hello_dojo ``` Three red tests. That is the correct state of a fresh checkout, and reading a failure you *expected* is the cheapest way to learn to read the ones you don't. Notice the shape of the output: a sentence written for you, then vitest's diff showing what the DOM actually contained. When a query finds nothing at all, Testing Library prints the entire rendered HTML plus a list of every accessible role it *did* find. It takes a single argument, the **props object**, which is destructured here into `{ code }`. And it returns **JSX**: markup-shaped syntax that compiles to ordinary function calls, so it can appear anywhere a value can. # Reading — react/00_hello_dojo The loop you just ran — write, grade, read the evidence — is the whole course. This page is the other half of every lesson: the *why* behind the problems you just solved. Read it **after** you attempt a problem, whether the gate went green or red. Failing first and reading second is not a consolation prize; it is the version of studying that sticks. ## Notes **What React actually is.** React is a library for describing what the screen should look like *as a function of data*, plus a runtime that makes the real DOM match that description. You never write "add a list item" or "change this text"; you write "given these props, the UI looks like this", and React works out the smallest set of DOM operations that gets from what is on screen now to what you just described. That process is called **reconciliation**, and almost every React behaviour that surprises people — why keys matter, why a component "loses its state", why an effect runs twice — is reconciliation showing through. You will meet it properly in `04_lists_conditional`. **JSX is not HTML and it is not a template language.** `

` compiles to a plain function call that returns an object describing an element. That is why JSX can be assigned to a variable, returned from a function, put in an array, or passed as a prop — it is just a value. It is also why the attribute names differ from HTML in a few places: they are JavaScript property names, so `class` (a reserved word) is `className` and `for` is `htmlFor`. And it is why a component must return *one* root element or a fragment: a function returns one value. **Props are one-way and read-only.** Data flows down from parent to child, and a child may never write to the props object it was handed. When a child needs to affect the world above it, the parent passes down a *function* — exactly what `onPress` is in ex3. This "props down, events up" shape is the single most important structural idea in React, and it is why the framework scales to large trees without becoming impossible to reason about. **Why the gates are written in roles and names.** Testing Library's guiding principle is that a test should resemble the way software is used. The practical payoff is that gates written this way fail for the same reasons real users get stuck. If `getByRole("button", { name: "Close panel" })` cannot find your control, a keyboard user cannot tab to it and a screen-reader user cannot identify it. The grader and the person are, by construction, asking the same question. ## ex1 — a component is a function The interesting part of this exercise is the part the gate checked that you were not asked to think about: the *element*. Plenty of people would ship a `
` here and every human looking at the page would see a heading. The machine would not, and neither would a screen reader building its list of page landmarks. Headings are the table of contents of a document; the level says where you are in the outline. `getByRole("heading", { level: 1 })` is the gate asking a question a real user has: "what is this page about?" The second thing hiding here is that rendering twice is a real test-design decision. One render can be satisfied by a hard-coded string. Two renders with different inputs can only be satisfied by a function of the input. You will see this pattern in every gate in the track — whenever a check is repeated with different data, the repetition *is* the assertion. ## ex2 — logic lives before the return Pluralisation is a deliberately unglamorous problem, chosen because it splits cleanly into "what React does for you" and "what it does not". React will faithfully render whatever string you produce. It has no opinion whatsoever about whether `0` is plural, and no amount of framework knowledge substitutes for reading your three expected outputs carefully. The classic mistake is `lessons > 1 ? "lessons" : "lesson"`, which is right for 15, right for 1, and wrong for 0. Interviewers use almost exactly this question — usually phrased as "render 1 file / 2 files" — precisely because the zero case separates people who tested their component from people who eyeballed it. The structural lesson is where the decision goes. A component body is an ordinary function body right up to the `return`, so compute your `noun` there, as a `const`, and interpolate the result. Cramming the ternary inline works too and reads worse. Statements — `if`, `for`, `switch` — cannot go inside JSX braces at all, because braces hold an *expression*; when you need one, put it above the `return`, which is where React developers naturally end up. ## ex3 — the accessible name is a separate thing from the text This exercise exists to make one distinction permanent: what an element *contains* and what it is *called* are computed separately, and for icon controls they are deliberately different. The accessible name comes from the first of these that exists: `aria-labelledby`, then `aria-label`, then the element's own text content. An `` with no label is announced as "✕" or, depending on the screen reader, as nothing — one of the most common real accessibility defects on the web, and the reason icon-only toolbars are so often unusable without sight. The other half of the exercise is the function prop. `onPress` arrives as a value and is handed straight to `onClick`, unchanged and uncalled. Writing `onClick={onPress()}` invokes it during render, which in a real app fires your "delete account" handler the instant the button appears; React would then try to use the return value as an event handler. If you ever need to pass an argument, wrap it — `onClick={() => onPress(id)}` — which creates a new function on every render, a fact that stops being harmless in `11_performance_patterns`. Finally, `user-event` rather than `fireEvent`. `fireEvent.click` dispatches one synthetic click. `user-event`'s click reproduces what a browser actually does: hover, pointer down, focus, pointer up, click. That is why it catches a `
` that a plain `fireEvent` would happily "click" — the div never takes focus, is never reachable by keyboard, and is not a button no matter how it is styled. ## Further reading - [react.dev — Your First Component](https://react.dev/learn/your-first-component) — the official on-ramp; twenty minutes and it is written unusually well. - [react.dev — Writing Markup with JSX](https://react.dev/learn/writing-markup-with-jsx) and [JavaScript in JSX with Curly Braces](https://react.dev/learn/javascript-in-jsx-with-curly-braces) — the two pages that answer 90% of "why won't this compile". - [react.dev — Passing Props to a Component](https://react.dev/learn/passing-props-to-a-component) — props, destructuring, defaults, and children. - [Testing Library — Guiding Principles](https://testing-library.com/docs/guiding-principles/) and [About Queries](https://testing-library.com/docs/queries/about/) — why the gates are written the way they are, and the priority order of queries. - [MDN — ARIA: the accessible name](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Attributes/aria-label) — how `aria-label` participates in name computation, and when not to use it.

## Exercise 1 — your first component

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `Greeting` takes a `name` prop and must render a
**level-1 heading** — an `<h1>` — reading:

- with `name="Eli"` → `Hello, Eli! Welcome to the dojo.`
- with `name="Ada"` → `Hello, Ada! Welcome to the dojo.`

Exact text, including the comma, the exclamation mark and the final full stop.
The heading element matters as much as the words: the gate asks for role
`heading` at level 1, so a `<div>` with large text will not be found no matter
what it says.

```
uv run dojo test react 00_hello_dojo ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — a decision the props cannot make for you

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `TrackSummary` takes `track` and `lessons` and renders
a single paragraph:

- `track="react"`, `lessons={15}` → `react: 15 lessons`
- `track="node"`, `lessons={1}` → `node: 1 lesson`
- `track="csharp"`, `lessons={0}` → `csharp: 0 lessons`

Read those three lines again. Two are the same shape and one is not: English
pluralises on "exactly one", so zero is plural. Your component has to make that
decision while it renders — there is no single piece of JSX that produces all
three.

This gate compares the component's entire rendered text, trimmed, so render one
element and nothing else.

```

## Exercise 3 — seen, heard, and clicked

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `IconButton` takes three props — `label`, `glyph` and
`onPress` — and must render a real `<button>` that:

- **shows** the `glyph` (the gate renders it with `glyph="x"`),
- **announces** the `label` as its accessible name (`label="Close panel"`),
- calls `onPress` once per click.

The gate clicks it twice with `user-event`, which drives the real DOM event
sequence a browser produces — pointer down, focus, pointer up, click — rather
than calling your handler directly. If your control is not focusable and
clickable, that fails, which is the point.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Three separate things are being asked for: what a sighted user *sees* (the
glyph), what a screen-reader user *hears* (the label), and what happens when
either of them activates the control (`onPress`). The first is the button's
children; the other two are attributes.

## Hint 2
In JSX, an attribute whose value is in braces takes any expression, including
a prop or a function:

```tsx
<button type="button" aria-label={/* … */} onClick={/* … */}>
  {/* … */}
</button>
```

`onClick` wants the function itself, not a call to it — `onClick={onPress()}`
would run `onPress` while the component renders and hand React the result.

## Hint 3
`aria-label` overrides the visible content when a screen reader computes the
accessible name, which is exactly why the gate can check both independently.
The last decision left is what goes between the tags — and it is one of the
three props, unchanged.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Three separate things are being asked for: what a sighted user *sees* (the
glyph), what a screen-reader user *hears* (the label), and what happens when
either of them activates the control (`onPress`). The first is the button's
children; the other two are attributes.

## Hint 2
In JSX, an attribute whose value is in braces takes any expression, including
a prop or a function:

```tsx
<button type="button" aria-label={/* … */} onClick={/* … */}>
  {/* … */}
</button>
```

`onClick` wants the function itself, not a call to it — `onClick={onPress()}`
would run `onPress` while the component renders and hand React the result.

## Hint 3
`aria-label` overrides the visible content when a screen reader computes the
accessible name, which is exactly why the gate can check both independently.
The last decision left is what goes between the tags — and it is one of the
three props, unchanged.

# 01 — Components and JSX In lesson 00 you wrote three components and the JSX mostly did what it looked like it would do. That is by design: JSX is engineered to be guessable. But "mostly" is where the bugs live, and every one of them comes from the same fact — **JSX is not HTML and it is not a template language. It is JavaScript.** `

hi

` is not markup that gets parsed at runtime. It is syntax that your build step rewrites into a function call, roughly `jsx("p", { children: "hi" })`, which returns a plain object describing an element. That object is a value like any other: you can put it in a `const`, return it from a function, pass it as a prop, or stick it in an array. Everything surprising about JSX follows from that one sentence, and this lesson is the four consequences you meet first. The first: **a function returns one value**, so a component returns one element. The second: **attributes are JavaScript property names**, so `class` (a reserved word) is `className` and `for` is `htmlFor`. The third: **braces hold an expression, not a statement** — a ternary is fine, an `if` is not. The fourth: because the whole thing is code, an attribute's value can be *computed*, which is how one component renders two different things. ## Concept — the four rules, with a worked example Here is a component that uses all of them: ```tsx export function Receipt({ id, items, paid }: { id: string; items: number; paid: boolean }) { const status = paid ? "Paid" : "Unpaid"; return (

{status}

{items} {items === 1 ? "item" : "items"}

); } ``` **One root.** The `

`, a `` or a flex container whose direct children are being laid out — use a **fragment**, which groups children and then renders nothing itself: ```tsx return ( <>
{label}
{value}
); ``` `<>…` is shorthand for `…`. It exists precisely because "wrap it in a div" is not always a legal move: a `
` between `
` and `
` is invalid HTML, and a stray wrapper inside a grid silently breaks the layout. **Attributes are property names.** `className`, `htmlFor`, `tabIndex`, `onClick` — camelCase, because these are keys in a JavaScript object. The exceptions are the `data-*` and `aria-*` families, which keep their dashes (`aria-label`, `data-testid`) because they were always strings, not properties. **Braces hold expressions.** `{status}`, `{items === 1 ? "item" : "items"}`, `` {`Receipt ${id}`} `` are all fine. `{if (paid) …}` is a syntax error. When the logic outgrows a ternary, compute it above the `return` and interpolate the result — that is what `const status` is doing, and it is what experienced React code looks like. **Attributes can be computed.** `aria-label={`Receipt ${id}`}` is the small version. The large version is choosing the attribute's value from a prop: ```tsx

{message}

``` Note the two returns you now have available for "render one thing or another": a ternary *inside* JSX, and an early `return` *before* it. The second is usually clearer when whole elements differ rather than one value. # Reading — react/01_components_jsx ## Notes **What JSX compiles to.** `

hi

` becomes a call to the JSX runtime — with the modern transform, `jsx("p", { className: "x", children: "hi" })` — which returns a frozen object often called an *element*: a description of what you want, not a DOM node. Rendering is the separate step where React reads those descriptions and issues DOM operations. This is why you can build a tree of elements, throw it away, and pay nothing: elements are cheap objects, and until React commits them nothing has touched the document. **Why capitalisation is load-bearing.** The compiler decides between "HTML tag" and "your component" by the first character. `
` compiles to the string `"header"` and produces a real element; `
` compiles to a reference to a variable called `Header` and calls it. A lowercase component name therefore fails silently: React renders a `` element that no browser knows, and nothing appears. If a component renders as literally nothing and there is no error, check the capital letter first. **Fragments and why they exist.** Before fragments, "return two siblings" was solved by wrapping in a `
`, which was fine until the parent cared about its direct children — tables, description lists, flexbox and grid all do. Fragments group children for React's benefit and emit nothing to the DOM. The long form, ``, is the version you need when a fragment is generated in a loop, because the shorthand `<>` cannot take a `key`; that comes up in `04_lists_conditional`. **Expressions, not statements.** The braces in JSX interpolate the value of an *expression*. That rules out `if`, `for`, `switch` and variable declarations, and rules in ternaries, `&&`, function calls, template literals and array methods. The practical consequence is a style: when rendering logic gets past one ternary, hoist it into a `const` above the `return` or into a small helper component. React code that stays readable is almost always code where the `return` is a flat description and the decisions were made above it. **Semantics are not decoration.** Every exercise in this lesson was gradeable because the elements carried meaning: `
` gives you `banner`, `` gives you `link`, `
`/`
` give you `term`/`definition`, `role="alert"` gives you a live region. The gate can only ask questions the platform can answer, which turns out to be the same constraint a screen reader operates under. Write `
` everywhere and both go blind at once. ## ex1 — one root element The rule "a component returns one element" is not a React rule at all — it is the rule that a function returns one value, wearing a costume. Once you see it that way the follow-up questions answer themselves: yes, you can return `null` (render nothing); yes, you can return an array; no, you cannot return two adjacent elements, for the same reason you cannot write `return 1, 2`. The parentheses after `return` deserve a sentence of their own. JavaScript's automatic semicolon insertion will end a statement at a line break if what follows cannot continue it, and `return` on its own line is the classic casualty: the function returns `undefined` and React renders nothing. Wrapping multi-line JSX in `(` … `)` makes the problem structurally impossible, which is why essentially all React code does it. The choice of `
` over `
` is what made the exercise checkable. Landmarks — `banner`, `navigation`, `main`, `contentinfo` — are how a screen-reader user skips around a page instead of reading it linearly, and they come free from `
`, `
`, `
` and `
` when those elements sit at the top level of the document. ## ex2 — the two kinds of braces `href={href}` versus `href="href"` is a one-character-class mistake that survives review because it looks right. It is worth understanding rather than memorising: in attribute position, a quoted value is a *string literal* — the same as HTML — and a braced value is *an expression evaluated now*. So `href="/people/ada"` is fine, `href={"/people/ada"}` is the same thing said noisily, and `href={href}` is the only form that varies with the prop. The accessible-name check is the other half. For a link with no `aria-label`, the accessible name is its text content, which means `Open Ada` had to be assembled from a literal and an interpolation. Watch for the whitespace rule while you do that: JSX preserves spaces *within* a line of text but strips leading and trailing whitespace on each line and collapses line breaks between text and elements. `Open{name}` gives `OpenAda`; putting `Open` and `{name}` on separate lines gives `Open Ada`, because the newline collapses to one space. Finally, an `` without `href` genuinely has no `link` role — the HTML specification calls it a "placeholder link". If you catch yourself writing `` with no href, the element you actually wanted was a `

# Reading — react/01_components_jsx ## Notes **What JSX compiles to.** `

hi

` becomes a call to the JSX runtime — with the modern transform, `jsx("p", { className: "x", children: "hi" })` — which returns a frozen object often called an *element*: a description of what you want, not a DOM node. Rendering is the separate step where React reads those descriptions and issues DOM operations. This is why you can build a tree of elements, throw it away, and pay nothing: elements are cheap objects, and until React commits them nothing has touched the document. **Why capitalisation is load-bearing.** The compiler decides between "HTML tag" and "your component" by the first character. `
` compiles to the string `"header"` and produces a real element; `
` compiles to a reference to a variable called `Header` and calls it. A lowercase component name therefore fails silently: React renders a `` element that no browser knows, and nothing appears. If a component renders as literally nothing and there is no error, check the capital letter first. **Fragments and why they exist.** Before fragments, "return two siblings" was solved by wrapping in a `
`, which was fine until the parent cared about its direct children — tables, description lists, flexbox and grid all do. Fragments group children for React's benefit and emit nothing to the DOM. The long form, ``, is the version you need when a fragment is generated in a loop, because the shorthand `<>` cannot take a `key`; that comes up in `04_lists_conditional`. **Expressions, not statements.** The braces in JSX interpolate the value of an *expression*. That rules out `if`, `for`, `switch` and variable declarations, and rules in ternaries, `&&`, function calls, template literals and array methods. The practical consequence is a style: when rendering logic gets past one ternary, hoist it into a `const` above the `return` or into a small helper component. React code that stays readable is almost always code where the `return` is a flat description and the decisions were made above it. **Semantics are not decoration.** Every exercise in this lesson was gradeable because the elements carried meaning: `
` gives you `banner`, `` gives you `link`, `
`/`
` give you `term`/`definition`, `role="alert"` gives you a live region. The gate can only ask questions the platform can answer, which turns out to be the same constraint a screen reader operates under. Write `
` everywhere and both go blind at once. ## ex1 — one root element The rule "a component returns one element" is not a React rule at all — it is the rule that a function returns one value, wearing a costume. Once you see it that way the follow-up questions answer themselves: yes, you can return `null` (render nothing); yes, you can return an array; no, you cannot return two adjacent elements, for the same reason you cannot write `return 1, 2`. The parentheses after `return` deserve a sentence of their own. JavaScript's automatic semicolon insertion will end a statement at a line break if what follows cannot continue it, and `return` on its own line is the classic casualty: the function returns `undefined` and React renders nothing. Wrapping multi-line JSX in `(` … `)` makes the problem structurally impossible, which is why essentially all React code does it. The choice of `
` over `
` is what made the exercise checkable. Landmarks — `banner`, `navigation`, `main`, `contentinfo` — are how a screen-reader user skips around a page instead of reading it linearly, and they come free from `
`, `
`, `
` and `
` when those elements sit at the top level of the document. ## ex2 — the two kinds of braces `href={href}` versus `href="href"` is a one-character-class mistake that survives review because it looks right. It is worth understanding rather than memorising: in attribute position, a quoted value is a *string literal* — the same as HTML — and a braced value is *an expression evaluated now*. So `href="/people/ada"` is fine, `href={"/people/ada"}` is the same thing said noisily, and `href={href}` is the only form that varies with the prop. The accessible-name check is the other half. For a link with no `aria-label`, the accessible name is its text content, which means `Open Ada` had to be assembled from a literal and an interpolation. Watch for the whitespace rule while you do that: JSX preserves spaces *within* a line of text but strips leading and trailing whitespace on each line and collapses line breaks between text and elements. `Open{name}` gives `OpenAda`; putting `Open` and `{name}` on separate lines gives `Open Ada`, because the newline collapses to one space. Finally, an `` without `href` genuinely has no `link` role — the HTML specification calls it a "placeholder link". ## Challenge — the same component, two different elements

Edit `challenge/solution.tsx`. A breadcrumb trail is a row of links ending in
the page you are currently on, and that last one **must not be a link** —
linking to the page you are already viewing is a trap for keyboard and
screen-reader users, who tab to it, activate it, and go nowhere.

`Crumb({ label, href, current })` renders:

- when `current` is `false`: an anchor whose text is the `label` and whose
  `href` is the `href`;
- when `current` is `true`: **not a link** — an element carrying the label as
  its text and the attribute `aria-current="page"`.

Honest difficulty note: this previews conditional rendering, which
`04_lists_conditional` covers properly. The hints teach you the one form you
need, and the form is small.

```
uv run dojo test react 01_components_jsx challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Do not try to make one `<a>` behave two ways. The two cases render *different
elements*: a link when the crumb points somewhere else, and something that is
not a link at all when it points at the page you are already on.

## Hint 2
A component body is a normal function body, so an early return is allowed and
is usually the clearest thing to write:

```tsx
if (/* … */) {
  return …;
}
return …;
```

That is the honest answer to "how do I put an `if` inside JSX": you do not —
you put the JSX inside the `if`.

## Hint 3
The non-link branch still has to be findable by the gate and announced
correctly, which is what `aria-current="page"` is for: it tells assistive
technology "this is the item in the set representing the current page". Pick a
neutral element to hang it on and give it the label as its text.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Do not try to make one `<a>` behave two ways. The two cases render *different
elements*: a link when the crumb points somewhere else, and something that is
not a link at all when it points at the page you are already on.

## Hint 2
A component body is a normal function body, so an early return is allowed and
is usually the clearest thing to write:

```tsx
if (/* … */) {
  return …;
}
return …;
```

That is the honest answer to "how do I put an `if` inside JSX": you do not —
you put the JSX inside the `if`.

## Hint 3
The non-link branch still has to be findable by the gate and announced
correctly, which is what `aria-current="page"` is for: it tells assistive
technology "this is the item in the set representing the current page". Pick a
neutral element to hang it on and give it the label as its text.

## Exercise 2 — text braces and attribute braces

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `ProfileLink({ name, href })` renders one anchor whose
visible text is `Open ` followed by the name — with `name="Ada"` that is
`Open Ada` — and whose `href` attribute is the `href` prop, unchanged.

platform rather than a quirk of the gate: a link that goes nowhere is not a
link.

```

exercises.importantHints: ## Hint 1 Two different things are being checked, and they live in two different places in the tag: what the user reads (between the tags) and where the link goes (an attribute). Both need a value from props, and both use braces — but for different reasons. ## Hint 2 In children position, `{name}` splices a value into the text: `Open {name}`. In attribute position, `href={href}` sets the attribute to the *value* of the prop, whereas `href="href"` sets it to the literal five-character string `href`. That second form is the mistake this exercise is here to burn out of you. ## Hint 3 The visible text is `Open ` followed by the name — one literal word, one space, one interpolation. Watch the space: `Open{name}` renders `OpenAda`, because JSX only keeps whitespace that sits between text on the same line.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — two siblings, no wrapper

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `LabelledField({ label, value })` renders the label in
a `<dt>` and the value in a `<dd>` — two sibling elements, and **no wrapper
element around them**.

The gate renders two of your components inside a `<dl>` and then inspects that
`<dl>`'s direct children: it expects exactly `dt, dd, dt, dd`. Anything you
wrap them in shows up there and fails.

```
uv run dojo test react 01_components_jsx ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The gate renders your component inside a `<dl>` and then checks that the
`<dl>`'s direct children are `dt, dd, dt, dd`. So you owe the page two
sibling elements — and, this time, you may not put a `<div>` around them,
because a `<div>` between `<dl>` and `<dt>` is invalid HTML.

## Hint 2
React has an element whose whole job is to group children and then vanish at
render time. It has a long form, `<React.Fragment>…</React.Fragment>`, and a
short form that looks like a tag with no name:

```tsx
return (
  <>
    …
    …
  </>
);
```

## Hint 3
Inside the fragment: the label belongs in a `<dt>` (a description *term*) and
the value in a `<dd>` (its *definition*) — those two elements are where the
`term` and `definition` roles the gate queries for come from. Each holds
exactly one interpolated prop and no extra text.

## Hint 1
The gate renders your component inside a `<dl>` and then checks that the
`<dl>`'s direct children are `dt, dd, dt, dd`. So you owe the page two
sibling elements — and, this time, you may not put a `<div>` around them,
because a `<div>` between `<dl>` and `<dt>` is invalid HTML.

## Hint 2
React has an element whose whole job is to group children and then vanish at
render time. It has a long form, `<React.Fragment>…</React.Fragment>`, and a
short form that looks like a tag with no name:

```tsx
return (
  <>
    …
    …
  </>
);
```

## Hint 3
Inside the fragment: the label belongs in a `<dt>` (a description *term*) and
the value in a `<dd>` (its *definition*) — those two elements are where the
`term` and `definition` roles the gate queries for come from. Each holds
exactly one interpolated prop and no extra text.

inside a live region whose role depends on `tone`:

- `tone="info"` → `role="status"`

present, so a component that always renders both regions does not pass.

## Hint 1
Three sibling elements, no wrapper asked for: a label, a control, and the hint
text. Two invisible wires connect them, and both are made of `id` strings —
one from the label to the input, one from the input to the hint.

## Hint 2
`htmlFor` is JSX's spelling of the HTML `for` attribute (`for` is a reserved
word in JavaScript), and it must equal the input's `id` exactly.
`aria-describedby` goes the other way: it lives on the *input* and holds the
`id` of the element containing the description.

## Hint 3
The hint element needs an id of its own, and the component is only given one
id. Derive a second one from it above the `return` — a template literal is the
usual way — then use it in exactly two places.

## Hint 1
Three sibling elements, no wrapper asked for: a label, a control, and the hint
text. Two invisible wires connect them, and both are made of `id` strings —
one from the label to the input, one from the input to the hint.

## Hint 2
`htmlFor` is JSX's spelling of the HTML `for` attribute (`for` is a reserved
word in JavaScript), and it must equal the input's `id` exactly.
`aria-describedby` goes the other way: it lives on the *input* and holds the
`id` of the element containing the description.

## Hint 3
The hint element needs an id of its own, and the component is only given one
id. Derive a second one from it above the `return` — a template literal is the
usual way — then use it in exactly two places.

# 02 — Props and composition So far every component you have written has been a leaf: props in, markup out, nothing inside it but HTML. Real interfaces are not built that way. A settings page is a card containing a list containing rows containing buttons, and the card knows nothing about the buttons. The mechanism that lets a component contain something it has never heard of is **composition**, and it is the reason React scales past a few hundred lines. The idea is small enough to state in one line: since JSX is a value, a component can be *handed* JSX. Everything in this lesson is a variation on that. `children` is JSX handed in between the tags. A slot prop is JSX handed in by name. Spreading is a whole *bag* of props handed through untouched. And the thing you are avoiding by doing any of this is the alternative — a component with fourteen boolean props, each one adding a branch, none of them ever quite what the next caller needed. There is a name for the two approaches, and it is worth having in your head before an interview. **Configuration** is ``. **Composition** is `Save} />`. The first works until someone wants two buttons and an icon; the second never has that problem, because `Card` was never in the business of describing footers in the first place. ## Concept — four ways to hand a component something **1. `children`.** Anything between a component's tags arrives as a prop called `children`: ```tsx function Bordered({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) { return
{children}
; }

Anything at all.

 ``` `children` is an ordinary prop with syntax sugar — `} />` is legal and means the same thing. It is typed `ReactNode`, which is React's "anything renderable": elements, strings, numbers, arrays of those, `null`, `undefined`, `false`. **2. Named slots.** When there is more than one hole to fill, `children` runs out and you pass JSX by name: ```tsx } main={
} /> ``` Nothing about this is special syntax. `sidebar` is a prop that happens to hold an element, and `Layout` renders it with `{sidebar}` like any other value. **3. Defaults.** Optional props are declared with `?` and defaulted in the destructuring pattern: ```tsx function Avatar({ name, size = 40 }: { name: string; size?: number }) { ``` The default applies when the prop is `undefined` — which includes "not passed at all" — and *only* then. `size={0}` stays `0`. Putting the default in the destructuring rather than writing `const size = props.size || 40` matters for exactly that reason: `||` also swallows `0` and `""`. **4. Rest and spread.** A wrapper component usually cares about two or three props and should pass the rest through untouched: ```tsx function Field({ label, id, ...rest }: FieldProps) { return ( <> ); } ``` `...rest` collects everything not named; `{...rest}` in JSX pours it back out as attributes. Order matters — anything you write after the spread overrides what was in it. The TypeScript idiom for "my props plus every prop a real `` takes" is `{ label: string; id: string } & ComponentProps<"input">`. One rule underneath all of this: **props are read-only**. A component may never assign to the props object it was given. Data flows down; when a child needs to change something above it, the parent passes a *function* down and the child calls it. You did that in lesson 00 with `onPress`, and you will do it in every lesson from here on. ## Exercise 1 — children Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `Card({ title, children })` renders an `

lessons.explanation: # Reading — react/02_props_composition ## Notes **Props are a function's arguments, nothing more.** React calls your component with one object. Destructuring in the parameter list is a JavaScript feature, defaults are a JavaScript feature, rest and spread are JavaScript features. The only React-specific thing in this whole lesson is the `children` convention: the compiler takes whatever sits between a component's opening and closing tags and puts it on the props object under that name. Knowing this stops a whole category of confusion — you cannot "pass props up", for the same reason a function cannot rewrite its caller's variables. **Immutability is a contract, not a suggestion.** Mutating `props.items.push(x)` often *appears* to work and then fails in ways that look like React bugs: another component holding the same array sees the change without re-rendering, or a memoized child skips an update because the array reference did not change. React's model is that rendering is a pure function of props and state, and every optimisation it ships — bailouts, memoization, concurrent rendering — is licensed by that purity. Break it and you are outside the contract. **Composition instead of inheritance.** React has no component inheritance and does not want any. Anything you would reach for a base class to do — shared layout, shared behaviour, shared defaults — is done by containing components inside other components, or by extracting a custom hook (lesson 10). The official guidance is blunt about this, and after a few years of it the absence stops feeling like a gap. **`ReactNode` vs `ReactElement`.** `ReactNode` is the type of "anything you can render": elements, strings, numbers, `null`, `undefined`, `false`, and arrays of those. `ReactElement` is specifically the object a JSX tag produces. Type slot props as `ReactNode` — it is what callers expect to be able to pass, and `false` and `null` in particular need to be legal so that `{cond && }` can be passed as a slot. **Prop drilling has a threshold, not a rule.** Passing a prop through two components that do not use it is fine. Passing it through six is a smell, and the fixes in order of preference are: restructure so the data is closer to its consumer, pass JSX down instead of data (composition often deletes the problem outright), then context (lesson 09). Reaching for a global store first is the usual overcorrection. ## ex1 — children is the composition primitive The stub for this exercise rendered everything except `children`, which is exactly how the mistake happens in real code: you write the wrapper, you style it, you forget the one interpolation, and the content silently disappears with no error. React has nothing to warn you about — you asked for a component that renders a heading, and it rendered a heading. Worth noticing is what `Card` does *not* do. It does not know it was given a paragraph. It does not lay the paragraph out, or restrict what may go inside, or take a `bodyText` string. That ignorance is the feature: the same `Card` will hold a form, a chart or another `Card` without a line of change. When you find yourself adding a prop that describes the *shape* of the content rather than a decision about it, `children` was probably the answer. The ordering check exists because it is the one thing `Card` genuinely decides. A composition component's whole API surface is "where do the pieces go". ## ex2 — defaults, and the `||` trap `max = 5` in the destructuring pattern is the correct place for a default, and the reason is narrow but important. The parameter default fires only for `undefined`. The older idiom, `const max = props.max || 5`, fires for every falsy value — `0`, `""`, `false`, `NaN` — which is a real bug the moment a prop can legitimately be zero. `props.max ?? 5` (nullish coalescing) is the equivalent modern fix when you cannot use a parameter default, and it is a common interview question in exactly this form: "what is the difference between `||` and `??`, and when does it bite?" The `role="img"` half of the exercise is a small lesson in accessible naming that is genuinely used in production. A run of `★★★☆☆` is a picture drawn with characters; without a role and a name a screen reader reads five star characters, or, with some voices, the word "star" five times. Giving the wrapper `role="img"` plus `aria-label` makes it announce as one image called "3 out of 5 stars" — and, because `role="img"` tells assistive technology to treat the subtree as opaque, the individual characters are no longer visited. ## ex3 — slots, and when to prefer them over children `children` handles one hole. The moment there are two — header and footer, list and detail, trigger and content — you need names, and a prop holding JSX is the whole mechanism. There is no separate "slot API" in React because there does not need to be one. The thing to resist is inspecting what you were handed. React has `React.Children` utilities that can map over or count children, and `cloneElement` can inject props into an element you were passed. Both exist, both are legacy, and both couple your component to the exact shape of what callers pass — the component stops working the moment someone wraps their button in a fragment or a conditional. Modern React's answer is: if you need to influence what is inside, pass the influence down another way (context, lesson 09) rather than rewriting the JSX. The other honest trade-off: a slot prop is *evaluated at the call site*, before your component decides whether to render it. `} />` builds the element object either way — cheap, since elements are just objects — but any code you run *while building it* runs regardless. For genuinely expensive or conditional content, pass a function instead of an element. ## ex4 — forwarding what you do not own Every wrapper component you write is a small API, and the most common defect in those APIs is swallowing. ## Challenge — an accessible dialog

Edit `challenge/solution.tsx`. `Modal({ title, children, onClose })` renders:

- an element with `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`;

id. `useId()` is a hook — your first — and the hints tell you the one line you
need. Hooks proper start in lesson 03.

```

## Exercise 2 — an optional prop with a default

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `Rating({ value, max })` renders a run of star
characters as a single labelled image:

- the element carries `role="img"` and an `aria-label` reading exactly
  `3 out of 5 stars` (for `value={3}` with no `max`);
- `max` defaults to `5` when it is not passed;
- a sighted user sees one filled star (`★`) per point of `value` — whether you
  also draw the unfilled `☆` remainder is up to you.

Why `role="img"`? Because `★★★` read out character by character is noise. Text
that is really a picture should announce itself as a picture with a name.

```
uv run dojo test react 02_props_composition ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Two separate problems. One is the default: when the caller omits `max`, the
prop arrives as `undefined`, and `undefined out of stars` is what your label
will say unless you supply a fallback. The other is that a row of star
characters is a *picture*, and pictures need a name.

## Hint 2
Defaults go in the destructuring pattern, not in the type:

```tsx
export function Rating({ value, max = 5 }: { value: number; max?: number }) {
```

That fires only when the prop is `undefined`, which is what you want — passing
`max={0}` explicitly should mean zero, not five.

## Hint 3
Give the wrapper `role="img"` and an `aria-label` built with a template
literal, so the whole run of characters is announced as one image with the name
`3 out of 5 stars`. For the visible content, `"x".repeat(n)` builds a repeated
string; the gate only requires that a sighted user sees one filled star per
point, so whether you also draw the empty ones is your call.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Two separate problems. One is the default: when the caller omits `max`, the
prop arrives as `undefined`, and `undefined out of stars` is what your label
will say unless you supply a fallback. The other is that a row of star
characters is a *picture*, and pictures need a name.

## Hint 2
Defaults go in the destructuring pattern, not in the type:

```tsx
export function Rating({ value, max = 5 }: { value: number; max?: number }) {
```

That fires only when the prop is `undefined`, which is what you want — passing
`max={0}` explicitly should mean zero, not five.

## Hint 3
Give the wrapper `role="img"` and an `aria-label` built with a template
literal, so the whole run of characters is announced as one image with the name
`3 out of 5 stars`. For the visible content, `"x".repeat(n)` builds a repeated
string; the gate only requires that a sighted user sees one filled star per
point, so whether you also draw the empty ones is your call.

lessons.summary: Everything you have written so far is a pure function of its props. lessons.briefing:
# 03 — State and events

Everything you have written so far is a pure function of its props. Give it the
same input twice and you get the same markup twice, which is lovely and also
means nothing on the page can ever *change*. A counter has to remember its
count between clicks. A toggle has to remember it is on. That memory is
**state**, and this is the lesson where components come alive.

The instinct almost everyone has first is to reach for a variable:

```tsx
function Counter() {
  let count = 0;                                  // this does not work
  return <button onClick={() => count++}>{count}</button>;
}
```

Two separate things are wrong. The variable is recreated every time React calls
the function, so it forgets. And even if it did not, incrementing it tells
React nothing — React re-renders when you *ask* it to, not when a variable
somewhere changes value. `useState` fixes both at once: it stores a value
outside the function call, and its setter is the request to render again.

The subtle part — the part that generates interview questions and production
bugs in equal measure — is what happens to that value *during* a render. It is
a snapshot. It does not change under your feet, even inside an async callback
that runs much later. Once you have that, `setCount(count + 1)` twice giving
`+1` stops being a mystery and becomes obvious.

## Concept — state is a snapshot, and updates are queued

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";

function Seat() {
  const [taken, setTaken] = useState(false);

  return (
    <button type="button" aria-pressed={taken} onClick={() => setTaken(!taken)}>
      Seat 4B
    </button>
  );
}
```

`useState(initial)` returns exactly two things: **the value for this render**,
and a **setter**. The initial value is used only on the first render of that
component instance; after that React hands back whatever it is holding.

Now the important half. Consider:

```tsx
function handleClick() {
  setCount(count + 1);
  setCount(count + 1);
}
```

If `count` is `0`, this is `setCount(1)` followed by `setCount(1)`. Both calls
read the same `count`, because `count` is a `const` belonging to *this* render
and nothing that happens in the handler can change it. React queues two
identical instructions and the counter moves by one.

The fix is the **updater form** — pass a function, and React calls it with the
value the previous queued update produced:

```tsx
function handleClick() {
  setCount((previous) => previous + 1);
  setCount((previous) => previous + 1);
}
```

Now the queue reads "add one, add one" instead of "become 1, become 1". The
rule of thumb: **if the next state is computed from the current state, use the
updater form.** It costs nothing and it is right in the cases where the direct
form is wrong — multiple updates in one handler, updates from a timeout or a
promise, updates from an event that fired while a render was in flight.

**Batching** is the other side of the same coin. React does not re-render
between your setter calls. It collects every update produced by one event,
applies them together, and renders once — so three `useState` values changing
in one handler cost one render, not three. Since React 18 this applies to
updates from promises, `setTimeout` and native event handlers too, not only
React's own events.

**State must be replaced, never mutated.** React decides whether to re-render
by comparing the new value with the old using `Object.is`. Push onto an array
you are already holding and the reference is unchanged, so React concludes
nothing happened:

```tsx
setItems((previous) => [...previous, item]);       // yes
items.push(item); setItems(items);                 // renders nothing
```

Finally, a small accessibility habit the gates enforce. A number that changes
because the user did something should live in a **live region** so screen-reader
users hear the result of their click. The `<output>` element has `role="status"`
built in, which is why it shows up throughout this lesson.

## Exercise 1 — your first state

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `Counter` renders a button whose accessible name is
`Increment` and a live region showing the current count, starting at `0`. Each
click adds one.

```
uv run dojo test react 03_state_events ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — two updates, one click

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `DoubleTap` renders a button named `Add two` and a
live region. **One click must add two.**

The stub already does the obvious thing — it calls the setter twice — and gets
`1`. Do not fix it by calling `setCount(count + 2)`; the requirement is that
the handler makes two separate increments and that both of them land. That
constraint is artificial here and completely real the moment two different
pieces of code both want to bump the same counter during one event.

```
uv run dojo test react 03_state_events ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — a toggle that announces itself

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `LikeButton` renders one button whose accessible name
is always `Like` and which carries `aria-pressed="false"` initially,
`aria-pressed="true"` after a click, and back again after another.

Note what is *not* asked for: changing the label to "Unlike". A toggle button
keeps its name and reports its state separately — swapping the name makes a
screen reader announce what sounds like a different control appearing where the
old one was.

```
uv run dojo test react 03_state_events ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — three states, one render

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `BatchProbe` holds three counters and renders them as
`a-b-c`. Write the click handler so that one press of `Bump all` moves all
three.

The component also takes an `onRender` prop and calls it while rendering. That
is a **probe**: the gate counts the calls to find out how many times your
component rendered. It is already wired up — leave it alone, do not add another
call, and do not copy the trick into real code, where calling a prop during
render is a side effect and therefore a bug.

The gate asserts that one click produces exactly **one** extra render. Write
the obvious three lines, watch it pass, and then read the assertion again —
that number is the lesson.

```
uv run dojo test react 03_state_events ex4
```

## Challenge — undo

Edit `challenge/solution.tsx`. `UndoableCounter` renders a live region and
three buttons: `Increment`, `Decrement` and `Undo`. Undo steps the displayed
value back to what it was before the last change, repeatedly, all the way to
the starting `0`. When there is nothing left to undo, the Undo button is
`disabled`.

Honest difficulty note: no new API is involved — this is entirely a question of
choosing what to store. If you find yourself wanting a second `useState` for
"the previous value", keep going; that only buys you one step.

```
uv run dojo test react 03_state_events challenge
```

## Review — clamping

`review1/solution.tsx`. `Thermostat({ min, max })` starts at `min` and renders
buttons `Warmer` and `Cooler` that move the temperature by one degree, never
leaving the range. The live region shows the temperature followed by `°C`.

```
uv run dojo test react 03_state_events review1
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading — react/03_state_events

## Notes

**Where state actually lives.** Not in your variable — in React. Each component
instance has a list of hook "slots", and `useState` reads and writes the next
one in order. That is the entire reason for the rules of hooks: React matches
the call to the slot by *call order*, so a `useState` inside an `if` shifts
every later hook by one and produces the famous "rendered fewer hooks than
expected" crash. Lesson 10 makes you fix one.

**A render is a snapshot.** When React calls your component it produces the JSX
for one particular set of props and state, and every function created during
that call closes over *those* values, permanently. An `onClick` created during
render #3 will always see render #3's `count`, even if it runs a minute later.
This is a feature — handlers see a consistent world — but it is also the source
of every stale-value bug in React, and the reason the same problem reappears in
`06_effects` with sharper teeth.

**The update queue.** Setter calls do not change state; they enqueue an
instruction. A value enqueues "replace with this", a function enqueues "compute
from whatever comes before you". At the end of the event React drains the queue
in order, producing the next state, and re-renders once. If the result is
`Object.is`-equal to the current state, React may skip the re-render entirely —
which is why `setCount(0)` on a counter already at `0` costs nothing, and why
mutating an array in place and setting it back renders nothing at all.

**Batching.** React 18 made batching universal — updates from promises,
`setTimeout` and native event listeners are batched just like React events. The
practical consequence is that you cannot observe intermediate state, and should
not try; `flushSync` exists to force a synchronous render and is a last resort
for things like measuring the DOM between two updates.

**Choosing state.** Three questions, in order. Does it change over time? If
not, it is a constant. Can it be computed from props or other state? If so,
compute it during render — derived values that are stored go stale. Is it
needed by more than one component? Then it belongs to their nearest common
ancestor, which is *lifting state up* (lesson 11 puts a name and a cost on it).

## ex1 — the smallest possible piece of memory

The two-line version of this exercise hides a decision worth naming: `count` is
a `const`, and that is deliberate. You never write to state; you ask for a new
render with a new value. Coming from imperative UI code — where you find the
label and set its text — this inversion is the single biggest adjustment, and
it is what makes React code auditable: the only way the screen changes is a new
render, and the only way a new render happens is a setter call.

`<output>` was chosen over `<span>` for the display because it carries
`role="status"`, which makes it a polite live region. Sighted users see the
number change; without a live region, screen-reader users get nothing at all
after clicking, because focus never moved and no text they are pointed at
changed. This is one of the most common gaps in otherwise careful UI work, and
it costs one element to avoid.

## ex2 — the exercise that explains the updater form

Almost everyone reads `setCount(count + 1); setCount(count + 1);` and expects
`+2`. Understanding why it is `+1` is understanding React's model. `count` is
not a live reading of some cell React owns; it is a value baked into this
render. Both calls therefore enqueue "become 1", and the second one wins by
doing exactly the same thing as the first.

The updater form changes what is enqueued from a value to a *recipe*. React
applies the recipes in order against the accumulating result, so "add one, add
one" composes. The rule to internalise — use the updater whenever the next
state depends on the current state — costs nothing when it was not needed and
saves you in three situations that are hard to see coming: two updates in one
handler, an update inside a `setTimeout` or `.then()` that captured an old
render's state, and an update fired from an event that arrived while another
render was pending.

This exact scenario is a top-five React interview question, usually phrased as
"what does this print?" The answer they are listening for is not "1" but
"because state is a snapshot of that render".

## ex3 — toggles, and why the label does not change

`useState(false)` and `setLiked((was) => !was)` are the mechanical part. The
interesting part is the ARIA. A *toggle button* is a single control with an
on/off state, and the pattern is: keep the accessible name constant, express
the state in `aria-pressed`. Swapping the name from "Like" to "Unlike" means
that after activation a screen reader announces a control that, as far as the
user can tell, is a different button — and it makes the button's name describe
the *action available* rather than the *thing it controls*, which reads
backwards when the state is announced too ("Unlike, pressed").

The related decision, which comes up constantly in real work, is toggle button
versus checkbox versus switch. A checkbox belongs in a form and is submitted; a
toggle button takes effect immediately; `role="switch"` is a toggle whose
states are on/off rather than pressed/not-pressed. Any of the three can be
right, but picking one and implementing it fully beats inventing a fourth.

Note also that `aria-pressed={liked}` renders `"false"` when `liked` is false —
React only drops `false` values for its own boolean DOM properties (`disabled`,
`checked`), not for `aria-*` and `data-*` attributes, which are strings all the
way down. That asymmetry catches people; `aria-hidden={false}` really does
render `aria-hidden="false"`.

## ex4 — measuring batching

The probe deserves a warning label, and the stub carries one: calling a prop
during render is a side effect, which React explicitly forbids. It is used here
because it is the only way to count renders without reaching into React's
internals, and because in `11_performance_patterns` the same technique becomes
the way you *prove* a memoization worked instead of guessing. In production
code, side effects go in event handlers or effects, never in the render body.

What the number tells you: three state updates in one handler produce one
render. React does not re-render between setter calls, so you cannot observe
`a` updated and `b` not. That guarantee is what makes it safe to split state
into several `useState` calls instead of one object — a common beginner worry
with no basis. Split state by what changes together, not by what renders
together.

The historical footnote is worth having for interviews. Before React 18,
batching only applied inside React's own event handlers; an update inside
`setTimeout` or a `.then()` rendered immediately, so two of them rendered
twice. React 18 made batching automatic everywhere, and `flushSync` is the
escape hatch for the rare case where you need a render *now*.

## challenge — modelling state instead of storing the display

The trap this exercise is built around is storing the answer instead of the
question. `count` is what the user sees, so it feels like the state; but undo
needs history, and history cannot be recovered from a number. Once you store
the array, the count stops being state at all — it is `history[history.length - 1]`,
computed fresh on every render, and therefore incapable of disagreeing with the
history.

That is the generalisable move: **keep the source, derive the view**. It also
generalises upward — the same reasoning gets you from "store the filtered list"
to "store the filter", and from "store the selected item" to "store the
selected id". Every derived value you store is a second copy that can go stale.

The immutability details matter here too. `previous.push(next)` mutates and
returns a length, so `setHistory(previous.push(next))` sets state to a number;
`[...previous, next]` builds a new array. `slice(0, -1)` returns a copy without
the last element, where `pop()` mutates and returns the element. If undo
"works" in your first attempt but the display does not update until you click
something else, mutation is the reason.

Finally, `disabled` on the Undo button is not just polish. A control that is
present, focusable and does nothing is worse than one that announces itself as
unavailable — and `disabled` is announced.

## review1 — clamping in the right place

Two buttons that differ by a sign is a hint that they should share one
function, and passing the step as an argument is the smallest way to do it.
The real content is *where* the clamp goes. Computing
`Math.min(max, temperature + 1)` outside the setter reads the snapshot, so two
clicks that land in the same batch both clamp against the same starting value.
Inside the updater you are handed the value the previous queued update
produced, so the clamp is applied to the truth.

This is the same lesson as ex2 wearing different clothes, which is why it is
the review exercise: any rule that reads current state to produce next state —
increment, clamp, toggle, append, "at most five" — belongs inside the updater.

## Further reading

- [react.dev — State: A Component's Memory](https://react.dev/learn/state-a-components-memory) — what `useState` actually gives you.
- [react.dev — State as a Snapshot](https://react.dev/learn/state-as-a-snapshot) and [Queueing a Series of State Updates](https://react.dev/learn/queueing-a-series-of-state-updates) — ex2 and ex4, explained by the people who built it.
- [react.dev — Updating Objects](https://react.dev/learn/updating-objects-in-state) and [Updating Arrays in State](https://react.dev/learn/updating-arrays-in-state) — the immutability cheat sheet the challenge needed.
- [react.dev — Choosing the State Structure](https://react.dev/learn/choosing-the-state-structure) — "keep the source, derive the view", at length.
- [MDN — `<output>`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/output) — the element with `role="status"` built in.
- [MDN — `aria-pressed`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Attributes/aria-pressed) — toggle buttons, and how they differ from checkboxes and switches.

`setTimeout` and native event listeners are batched just like React events. The
practical consequence is that you cannot observe intermediate state, and should
not try; `flushSync` exists to force a synchronous render and is a last resort
for things like measuring the DOM between two updates.

**Choosing state.** Three questions, in order. Does it change over time? If
not, it is a constant. Can it be computed from props or other state? If so,
compute it during render — derived values that are stored go stale. Is it
needed by more than one component? Then it belongs to their nearest common
ancestor, which is *lifting state up* (lesson 11 puts a name and a cost on it).

## ex1 — the smallest possible piece of memory

The two-line version of this exercise hides a decision worth naming: `count` is
a `const`, and that is deliberate. You never write to state; you ask for a new
render with a new value. Coming from imperative UI code — where you find the
label and set its text — this inversion is the single biggest adjustment, and
it is what makes React code auditable: the only way the screen changes is a new
render, and the only way a new render happens is a setter call.

`<output>` was chosen over `<span>` for the display because it carries
`role="status"`, which makes it a polite live region. Sighted users see the
number change; without a live region, screen-reader users get nothing at all
after clicking, because focus never moved and no text they are pointed at
changed. This is one of the most common gaps in otherwise careful UI work, and
it costs one element to avoid.

## ex2 — the exercise that explains the updater form

Almost everyone reads `setCount(count + 1); setCount(count + 1);` and expects
`+2`. Understanding why it is `+1` is understanding React's model. `count` is
not a live reading of some cell React owns; it is a value baked into this
render. Both calls therefore enqueue "become 1", and the second one wins by
doing exactly the same thing as the first.

The updater form changes what is enqueued from a value to a *recipe*. React
applies the recipes in order against the accumulating result, so "add one, add
one" composes. The rule to internalise — use the updater whenever the next
state depends on the current state — costs nothing when it was not needed and
saves you in three situations that are hard to see coming: two updates in one
handler, an update inside a `setTimeout` or `.then()` that captured an old
render's state, and an update fired from an event that arrived while another
render was pending.

This exact scenario is a top-five React interview question, usually phrased as
"what does this print?" The answer they are listening for is not "1" but
"because state is a snapshot of that render".

## ex3 — toggles, and why the label does not change

`useState(false)` and `setLiked((was) => !was)` are the mechanical part. The
interesting part is the ARIA. A *toggle button* is a single control with an
on/off state, and the pattern is: keep the accessible name constant, express
the state in `aria-pressed`. Swapping the name from "Like" to "Unlike" means
that after activation a screen reader announces a control that, as far as the
user can tell, is a different button — and it makes the button's name describe
the *action available* rather than the *thing it controls*, which reads
backwards when the state is announced too ("Unlike, pressed").

The related decision, which comes up constantly in real work, is toggle button
versus checkbox versus switch. A checkbox belongs in a form and is submitted; a
toggle button takes effect immediately; `role="switch"` is a toggle whose
states are on/off rather than pressed/not-pressed. Any of the three can be
right, but picking one and implementing it fully beats inventing a fourth.

Note also that `aria-pressed={liked}` renders `"false"` when `liked` is false —
React only drops `false` values for its own boolean DOM properties (`disabled`,
`checked`), not for `aria-*` and `data-*` attributes, which are strings all the
way down. That asymmetry catches people; `aria-hidden={false}` really does
render `aria-hidden="false"`.

## ex4 — measuring batching

The probe deserves a warning label, and the stub carries one: calling a prop
during render is a side effect, which React explicitly forbids. It is used here
because it is the only way to count renders without reaching into React's
internals, and because in `11_performance_patterns` the same technique becomes
the way you *prove* a memoization worked instead of guessing. In production
code, side effects go in event handlers or effects, never in the render body.

What the number tells you: three state updates in one handler produce one
render. React does not re-render between setter calls, so you cannot observe
`a` updated and `b` not. That guarantee is what makes it safe to split state
into several `useState` calls instead of one object — a common beginner worry
with no basis. Split state by what changes together, not by what renders
together.

The historical footnote is worth having for interviews. Before React 18,
batching only applied inside React's own event handlers; an update inside
`setTimeout` or a `.then()` rendered immediately, so two of them rendered
twice. React 18 made batching automatic everywhere, and `flushSync` is the
escape hatch for the rare case where you need a render *now*.

## challenge — modelling state instead of storing the display

The trap this exercise is built around is storing the answer instead of the
question. `count` is what the user sees, so it feels like the state; but undo
needs history, and history cannot be recovered from a number. Once you store
the array, the count stops being state at all — it is `history[history.length - 1]`,
computed fresh on every render, and therefore incapable of disagreeing with the
history.

That is the generalisable move: **keep the source, derive the view**. It also
generalises upward — the same reasoning gets you from "store the filtered list"
to "store the filter", and from "store the selected item" to "store the
selected id". Every derived value you store is a second copy that can go stale.

The immutability details matter here too. `previous.push(next)` mutates and
returns a length, so `setHistory(previous.push(next))` sets state to a number;
`[...previous, next]` builds a new array. `slice(0, -1)` returns a copy without
the last element, where `pop()` mutates and returns the element. If undo
"works" in your first attempt but the display does not update until you click
something else, mutation is the reason.

Finally, `disabled` on the Undo button is not just polish. A control that is
present, focusable and does nothing is worse than one that announces itself as
unavailable — and `disabled` is announced.

## review1 — clamping in the right place

Two buttons that differ by a sign is a hint that they should share one
function, and passing the step as an argument is the smallest way to do it.
The real content is *where* the clamp goes. Computing
`Math.min(max, temperature + 1)` outside the setter reads the snapshot, so two
clicks that land in the same batch both clamp against the same starting value.
Inside the updater you are handed the value the previous queued update
produced, so the clamp is applied to the truth.

This is the same lesson as ex2 wearing different clothes, which is why it is
the review exercise: any rule that reads current state to produce next state —
increment, clamp, toggle, append, "at most five" — belongs inside the updater.

- [react.dev — State: A Component's Memory](https://react.dev/learn/state-a-components-memory) — what `useState` actually gives you.
- [react.dev — State as a Snapshot](https://react.dev/learn/state-as-a-snapshot) and [Queueing a Series of State Updates](https://react.dev/learn/queueing-a-series-of-state-updates) — ex2 and ex4, explained by the people who built it.
- [react.dev — Updating Objects](https://react.dev/learn/updating-objects-in-state) and [Updating Arrays in State](https://react.dev/learn/updating-arrays-in-state) — the immutability cheat sheet the challenge needed.

- [MDN — `<output>`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/output) — the element with `role="status"` built in.
- [MDN — `aria-pressed`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Attributes/aria-pressed) — toggle buttons, and how they differ from checkboxes and switches.

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — undo

Edit `challenge/solution.tsx`. `UndoableCounter` renders a live region and
three buttons: `Increment`, `Decrement` and `Undo`. Undo steps the displayed
value back to what it was before the last change, repeatedly, all the way to
the starting `0`. When there is nothing left to undo, the Undo button is
`disabled`.

Honest difficulty note: no new API is involved — this is entirely a question of
choosing what to store. If you find yourself wanting a second `useState` for
"the previous value", keep going; that only buys you one step.

```
uv run dojo test react 03_state_events challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
A single number cannot be undone — once you overwrite it, the previous value is
gone. Ask what the *smallest* piece of information is that makes Undo possible,
and store that instead. The displayed count then stops being state and becomes
something you compute.

## Hint 2
Keep an array of every value the counter has had, starting `[0]`. The current
count is its last element. Increment and decrement *append*; Undo *removes the
last element*. Undo is disabled exactly when the array has one element left.

Remember state must be replaced, never mutated: `[...previous, next]` for the
append, `previous.slice(0, -1)` for the undo — `push` and `pop` change the array
in place and React will not notice.

## Hint 3
Both Increment and Decrement do the same thing to the history, differing only
in how they compute the next number from the last one, so a small helper that
takes that function keeps it to one place:

```tsx
function push(next: (current: number) => number) { … }
```

The remaining decision is where the clamp on Undo lives — as a `disabled`
attribute, as a guard inside the handler, or both — and what you want a
keyboard user to experience when there is nothing left to undo.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
A single number cannot be undone — once you overwrite it, the previous value is
gone. Ask what the *smallest* piece of information is that makes Undo possible,
and store that instead. The displayed count then stops being state and becomes
something you compute.

## Hint 2
Keep an array of every value the counter has had, starting `[0]`. The current
count is its last element. Increment and decrement *append*; Undo *removes the
last element*. Undo is disabled exactly when the array has one element left.

Remember state must be replaced, never mutated: `[...previous, next]` for the
append, `previous.slice(0, -1)` for the undo — `push` and `pop` change the array
in place and React will not notice.

## Hint 3
Both Increment and Decrement do the same thing to the history, differing only
in how they compute the next number from the last one, so a small helper that
takes that function keeps it to one place:

```tsx
function push(next: (current: number) => number) { … }
```

The remaining decision is where the clamp on Undo lives — as a `disabled`
attribute, as a guard inside the handler, or both — and what you want a
keyboard user to experience when there is nothing left to undo.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
A plain `let count = 0` inside the component does not survive: React calls the
function again on every render and the variable is created from scratch. You
need a value React holds on to *between* renders, and a way to tell React the
value changed so it re-renders.

## Hint 2
```tsx
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
```

`useState` returns a pair: the value for this render, and a setter. Call the
setter from an event handler and React schedules a re-render with the new
value. Never assign to `count` directly — it is a `const` for a reason.

## Hint 3
Wire the setter to the button's `onClick`. `onClick` wants a function, so
`onClick={setCount(count + 1)}` is wrong twice over — it runs during render and
hands React a return value. Wrap it: `onClick={() => …}`. The `<output>`
element already in the stub gives you the `status` role for free; it just needs
the real value interpolated into it.

## Exercise 3 — a toggle that announces itself

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `LikeButton` renders one button whose accessible name
is always `Like` and which carries `aria-pressed="false"` initially,

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
A like button is a *toggle button*: one control with two states, not two
controls. Its label never changes — what changes is an attribute that says
whether it is currently pressed. Start from `useState(false)`.

## Hint 2
`aria-pressed` takes a boolean in JSX and React renders it as the string
`"true"` or `"false"`:

```tsx
<button type="button" aria-pressed={liked} …>
```

Note that this is one of the few attributes where rendering `false` is
meaningful — React only drops `false` for *its own* boolean DOM properties, not
for `aria-*`, which are always strings.

## Hint 3
For the handler, "the opposite of what it was" is exactly the situation the
updater form is for. Writing `setLiked(!liked)` happens to work here, but the
updater version is right for the same reason it was right in ex2, and costs
nothing.

## Hint 1
A like button is a *toggle button*: one control with two states, not two
controls. Its label never changes — what changes is an attribute that says
whether it is currently pressed. Start from `useState(false)`.

## Hint 2
`aria-pressed` takes a boolean in JSX and React renders it as the string
`"true"` or `"false"`:

```tsx
<button type="button" aria-pressed={liked} …>
```

Note that this is one of the few attributes where rendering `false` is
meaningful — React only drops `false` for *its own* boolean DOM properties, not
for `aria-*`, which are always strings.

## Hint 3
For the handler, "the opposite of what it was" is exactly the situation the
updater form is for. Writing `setLiked(!liked)` happens to work here, but the
updater version is right for the same reason it was right in ex2, and costs
nothing.

## Exercise 4 — three states, one render

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `BatchProbe` holds three counters and renders them as
`a-b-c`. Write the click handler so that one press of `Bump all` moves all
three.

is a **probe**: the gate counts the calls to find out how many times your
component rendered. It is already wired up — leave it alone, do not add another
call, and do not copy the trick into real code, where calling a prop during
render is a side effect and therefore a bug.

the obvious three lines, watch it pass, and then read the assertion again —
that number is the lesson.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Two buttons that differ only by a sign, and a rule that the value may never
leave `[min, max]`. Write one function that takes the step and does the work;
the buttons just call it with `1` and `-1`.

## Hint 2
The clamp has to see the value it is about to write, which means it belongs
*inside* the updater rather than outside it:

```tsx
setTemperature((previous) => /* clamp(previous + by) */);
```

`Math.min` and `Math.max` compose into a clamp: the smaller of `max` and (the
larger of `min` and the candidate).

## Hint 3
Clamping outside the updater — computing the next value from `temperature` and
then calling the setter — happens to work when clicks arrive one at a time, and
stops working the moment two updates land in the same batch. The remaining
decision is whether to also disable a button at the end of the range; the gate
does not require it, but ask yourself what a user learns from a button that
does nothing.
