## Hint 1
Two buttons that differ only by a sign, and a rule that the value may never
leave `[min, max]`. Write one function that takes the step and does the work;
the buttons just call it with `1` and `-1`.

## Hint 2
The clamp has to see the value it is about to write, which means it belongs
*inside* the updater rather than outside it:

```tsx
setTemperature((previous) => /* clamp(previous + by) */);
```

`Math.min` and `Math.max` compose into a clamp: the smaller of `max` and (the
larger of `min` and the candidate).

Clamping outside the updater — computing the next value from `temperature` and
then calling the setter — happens to work when clicks arrive one at a time, and
stops working the moment two updates land in the same batch. The remaining
decision is whether to also disable a button at the end of the range; the gate
does not require it, but ask yourself what a user learns from a button that
does nothing.

# 04 — Lists, keys and conditionals Almost everything on a screen is a list. A table of orders, a row of tags, a feed, a set of radio buttons, the options in a dropdown — all lists, all rendered from arrays, all subject to the same rule. And that rule, `key`, is the most consequential prop in React and the one most often got wrong. Here is the situation React is in. It rendered three rows last time. It is about to render four. Some of the new rows are the old rows moved, some are genuinely new, and its job is to work out which is which so it can reuse the DOM it already built — and, crucially, so it knows which *component instances* survive. Component instances hold state. Uncontrolled inputs hold what the user typed. Focus lives on one specific element. If React guesses wrong about which row is which, all three end up attached to the wrong data. React does not guess. It asks you, and `key` is your answer. When you leave it out, React falls back to position, warns you in the console, and behaves correctly right up until the list changes order — at which point it produces one of the most confusing bug classes in the framework. Exercise 2 makes it happen to you on purpose, because reading about it does not stick. The other half of this lesson is conditional rendering, which is easy except for one trap that everybody falls into exactly once. It involves the number zero. ## Concept — mapping, keying, and choosing not to render **Arrays are renderable.** React renders each element of an array in turn, so turning data into UI is `.map()`: ```tsx

    • ))}

# Reading — react/04_lists_conditional

## Notes

**Reconciliation, concretely.** When React re-renders a component it produces a
new tree of element descriptions and compares it with the previous one. The
comparison is deliberately shallow and fast, and it runs on two rules. First,
if the element *type* changed at a position — `<div>` became `<span>`, `Profile`
became `Settings` — React throws away that whole subtree and builds a new one,
state and all. Second, within a list of children it matches items up by `key`.
Everything about keys follows from that second rule.

**What "reuse" actually means.** When React decides two elements are the same
item, it keeps the existing DOM node and the existing component instance, and
updates only what changed. That means `useState` inside the row keeps its
value, the DOM node keeps its uncontrolled input value, its focus and its
scroll offset, and any running CSS transition continues. Those are exactly the
things that go wrong with a bad key, and they are also exactly the things a
naive test never checks — which is why the bug reaches production.

**When index keys are fine, honestly.** If the list is never reordered, never
filtered, never inserted into except at the end, and the items hold no state of
their own, an index key is harmless. That is a real set of conditions and a lot
of lists meet it. The reason the advice is stated as an absolute is that the
conditions are invisible at the call site and get violated a year later by
somebody adding a sort. Use the id when there is one; use an index knowingly,
and expect to be asked about it in an interview.

**The `key` is not a prop.** `key` is consumed by React and never appears in
`props`. If a component also needs the identifier — and it usually does — pass
it twice: `<Row key={row.id} id={row.id} />`. That surprises people; it follows
from `key` being part of how React addresses the element rather than part of
what the element is.

**Falsy is not the same as blank.** React's render rules treat `false`, `null`
and `undefined` as "nothing", and everything else as a value to display. So
`0`, `""` (invisible but present) and `NaN` all render. `&&` returns its
left operand when that operand is falsy, which is how the number `0` ends up on
the page. Reaching for a ternary (`cond ? <X/> : null`) sidesteps it entirely
and is the safer default when the condition is not obviously boolean.

## ex1 — `map`, and the warning nobody reads

Two things happen here that are worth separating. Rendering an array is not a
special React feature — an array of elements is a legal child, so any expression
that produces one works, including `.map()`, `Array.from`, or a literal.

The `key` requirement is React's, and its warning is one of the most-ignored
messages in front-end development because the app looks fine without it. The
gate checks for it deliberately: a warning you can see going red is a warning
you fix. Using the tag string itself as the key is correct here *because tags in
a tag list are unique* — that is a fact about the data, not a general licence to
key by content. Two people named Ada in a list of people would collide, and
React would render only one of them.

The other detail worth noticing: `key` goes on the outermost element returned
by the map callback, not on some element inside it. If your callback returns a
fragment and you need a key, the shorthand `<>` cannot take one; use
`<Fragment key={id}>`.

## ex2 — the exercise you will remember

This is the canonical demonstration, and the reason it works as a demonstration
is that the buggy version is *indistinguishable from the correct one* until the
list changes. The rows render, the labels are right, React logs no warning —
index keys satisfy the "you must supply a key" rule perfectly. What breaks is
identity.

Walk through it precisely. Before: keys `0 → Ada`, `1 → Lin`. The DOM node for
key `0` contains an input whose *DOM value* is `hello` (uncontrolled inputs are
owned by the browser, not by React). After prepending Zoe: keys `0 → Zoe`,
`1 → Ada`, `2 → Lin`. React matches key `0` to key `0`, decides that row simply
changed its name, and updates the label text and the input's `id` attribute in
place. It has no reason to touch `input.value` — nothing React manages changed
about it. So the text you typed is now sitting in Zoe's row, and Ada's row is a
freshly created node with an empty box.

With `key={person.id}`, React sees `zoe` has no counterpart (create it), and
`ada` and `lin` exist but have moved (move the nodes). Ada's DOM node — with
`hello` still inside it — moves down one position, and everything is where the
user left it.

The same mechanism destroys `useState` inside row components, kills focus while
someone is typing in a filtered list, and restarts animations. This exact
scenario, usually phrased "why shouldn't you use the array index as a key?", is
one of the two or three most common React interview questions, and the answer
that lands is the mechanical one above rather than "because it's bad practice".

## ex3 — three shapes of conditional, one trap

The early return is the right tool when the *whole component* has two modes,
and it keeps the main path un-nested. The ternary is right when two branches
both render something. `&&` is right when the choice is "render this or render
nothing" — and is where the trap lives.

`unreadCount && <Badge/>` is an expression whose value is `0` when
`unreadCount` is `0`, because `&&` returns the left operand rather than a
boolean. React then renders `0`, because `0` is a renderable value. The
canonical bug report is "a random zero appears next to my icon", and the fixes
in order of preference are: compare explicitly (`unreadCount > 0 &&`), coerce
(`Boolean(unreadCount) &&`), or use a ternary with `null`. `array.length &&` is
the same bug with a different variable name and is even more common.

Worth also noticing what the empty state is *for*. Rendering an empty `<ul>` is
technically correct and tells the user nothing — did it load? is it broken? An
empty state is a UI requirement, not a nicety, and it is where you say what
happened and what to do next.

## ex4 — deriving, and the mutation you did not intend

Sorting during render is the right instinct: the sorted list is a view of the
data, and storing it in state would create a second copy that can drift. The
danger is that JavaScript's two most useful array methods for this — `sort` and
`reverse` — are the two that mutate. `players.sort(...)` reorders the caller's
array and returns *the same array*, which means a component that "just
displays" data has quietly rewritten its parent's state. React will not warn;
the parent will simply start rendering in a different order for no visible
reason, and if the parent memoized on that array reference, it will not re-render
at all.

`[...players].sort(...)` copies first. (Modern JavaScript also offers
`toSorted()` and `toReversed()`, which return new arrays; they are available in
Node 20+ and every current browser, and they are worth knowing about.)

The comparator chain — `b.score - a.score || a.name.localeCompare(b.name)` — is
a small idiom worth having: a comparator returns `0` for "equal", `0` is falsy,
so `||` falls through to the tiebreaker. Deterministic tie-breaking is not
pedantry; without it, a leaderboard can render two orderings for the same data
depending on the engine's sort stability, and users notice things jumping
around.

## challenge — iterate the groups, not the items

The instinct is to loop over tasks and bucket them; the cleaner shape is to
loop over the *output structure* — the ordered list of groups — and ask the
data for each group's contents. That is what makes "always in this order" and
"skip empty groups" fall out for free instead of needing a sort afterwards.

Returning `null` from a `map` callback is legal and renders nothing, which is
how a group vanishes. An alternative is to `filter` the groups before mapping;
both are fine, and the second reads better once there is more than one reason
to skip.

Two nested maps means two key decisions, and they are independent: sibling keys
only need to be unique *among their own siblings*, so the inner lists never
collide with each other even if two groups contained tasks with the same title.
This is also the point where `filter(...).sort(...)` is safe without copying —
`filter` already handed you a new array.

## review1 — remove by identity

Everything in this exercise is a restatement of ex2 in a different register.
The handler is created inside the map, so it closes over the chip it belongs to
and can name it precisely; `filter` produces a new array so React sees a new
reference and re-renders; and removing by id rather than index means the
component keeps working when the list is sorted or filtered upstream.

The one new detail is `onClick={() => remove(chip.id)}`. That arrow creates a
new function on every render for every row, which is fine — creating a closure
is cheap, and this is the normal way to write it. It becomes worth thinking
about only when the row is a memoized component, which is exactly the situation
`11_performance_patterns` builds around.

## Further reading

- [react.dev — Rendering Lists](https://react.dev/learn/rendering-lists) — the map, the key rules, and the "where do I get an id" question.
- [react.dev — Preserving and Resetting State](https://react.dev/learn/preserving-and-resetting-state) — the best explanation anywhere of what reconciliation actually preserves, and how to reset state deliberately with a key.
- [react.dev — Conditional Rendering](https://react.dev/learn/conditional-rendering) — including the `&&` trap, in the official words.
- [MDN — `Array.prototype.sort`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array/sort) — "sorts in place", stability, and the comparator contract.
- [MDN — `Array.prototype.toSorted`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array/toSorted) — the non-mutating version, and where it is available.
- [MDN — Logical AND (`&&`)](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/Logical_AND) — why it returns an operand rather than a boolean.

**The `key` is not a prop.** `key` is consumed by React and never appears in
`props`. If a component also needs the identifier — and it usually does — pass
it twice: `<Row key={row.id} id={row.id} />`. That surprises people; it follows
from `key` being part of how React addresses the element rather than part of
what the element is.

**Falsy is not the same as blank.** React's render rules treat `false`, `null`
and `undefined` as "nothing", and everything else as a value to display. So
`0`, `""` (invisible but present) and `NaN` all render. `&&` returns its
left operand when that operand is falsy, which is how the number `0` ends up on
the page. Reaching for a ternary (`cond ? <X/> : null`) sidesteps it entirely
and is the safer default when the condition is not obviously boolean.

## ex1 — `map`, and the warning nobody reads

Two things happen here that are worth separating. Rendering an array is not a
special React feature — an array of elements is a legal child, so any expression
that produces one works, including `.map()`, `Array.from`, or a literal.

The `key` requirement is React's, and its warning is one of the most-ignored
messages in front-end development because the app looks fine without it. The
gate checks for it deliberately: a warning you can see going red is a warning
you fix. Using the tag string itself as the key is correct here *because tags in
a tag list are unique* — that is a fact about the data, not a general licence to
key by content. Two people named Ada in a list of people would collide, and
React would render only one of them.

The other detail worth noticing: `key` goes on the outermost element returned
by the map callback, not on some element inside it. If your callback returns a
fragment and you need a key, the shorthand `<>` cannot take one; use
`<Fragment key={id}>`.

## ex2 — the exercise you will remember

This is the canonical demonstration, and the reason it works as a demonstration
is that the buggy version is *indistinguishable from the correct one* until the
list changes. The rows render, the labels are right, React logs no warning —
index keys satisfy the "you must supply a key" rule perfectly. What breaks is
identity.

Walk through it precisely. Before: keys `0 → Ada`, `1 → Lin`. The DOM node for
key `0` contains an input whose *DOM value* is `hello` (uncontrolled inputs are
owned by the browser, not by React). After prepending Zoe: keys `0 → Zoe`,
`1 → Ada`, `2 → Lin`. React matches key `0` to key `0`, decides that row simply
changed its name, and updates the label text and the input's `id` attribute in
place. It has no reason to touch `input.value` — nothing React manages changed
about it. So the text you typed is now sitting in Zoe's row, and Ada's row is a
freshly created node with an empty box.

With `key={person.id}`, React sees `zoe` has no counterpart (create it), and
`ada` and `lin` exist but have moved (move the nodes). Ada's DOM node — with
`hello` still inside it — moves down one position, and everything is where the
user left it.

The same mechanism destroys `useState` inside row components, kills focus while
someone is typing in a filtered list, and restarts animations. This exact
scenario, usually phrased "why shouldn't you use the array index as a key?", is
one of the two or three most common React interview questions, and the answer
that lands is the mechanical one above rather than "because it's bad practice".

## ex3 — three shapes of conditional, one trap

The early return is the right tool when the *whole component* has two modes,
and it keeps the main path un-nested. The ternary is right when two branches
both render something. `&&` is right when the choice is "render this or render
nothing" — and is where the trap lives.

`unreadCount && <Badge/>` is an expression whose value is `0` when
`unreadCount` is `0`, because `&&` returns the left operand rather than a
boolean. React then renders `0`, because `0` is a renderable value. The
canonical bug report is "a random zero appears next to my icon", and the fixes
in order of preference are: compare explicitly (`unreadCount > 0 &&`), coerce
(`Boolean(unreadCount) &&`), or use a ternary with `null`. `array.length &&` is
the same bug with a different variable name and is even more common.

Worth also noticing what the empty state is *for*. Rendering an empty `<ul>` is
technically correct and tells the user nothing — did it load? is it broken? An
empty state is a UI requirement, not a nicety, and it is where you say what
happened and what to do next.

## ex4 — deriving, and the mutation you did not intend

Sorting during render is the right instinct: the sorted list is a view of the
data, and storing it in state would create a second copy that can drift. The
danger is that JavaScript's two most useful array methods for this — `sort` and
`reverse` — are the two that mutate. `players.sort(...)` reorders the caller's
array and returns *the same array*, which means a component that "just
displays" data has quietly rewritten its parent's state. React will not warn;
the parent will simply start rendering in a different order for no visible
reason, and if the parent memoized on that array reference, it will not re-render
at all.

`[...players].sort(...)` copies first. (Modern JavaScript also offers
`toSorted()` and `toReversed()`, which return new arrays; they are available in
Node 20+ and every current browser, and they are worth knowing about.)

The comparator chain — `b.score - a.score || a.name.localeCompare(b.name)` — is
a small idiom worth having: a comparator returns `0` for "equal", `0` is falsy,
so `||` falls through to the tiebreaker. Deterministic tie-breaking is not
pedantry; without it, a leaderboard can render two orderings for the same data
depending on the engine's sort stability, and users notice things jumping
around.

## challenge — iterate the groups, not the items

The instinct is to loop over tasks and bucket them; the cleaner shape is to
loop over the *output structure* — the ordered list of groups — and ask the
data for each group's contents. That is what makes "always in this order" and
"skip empty groups" fall out for free instead of needing a sort afterwards.

Returning `null` from a `map` callback is legal and renders nothing, which is
how a group vanishes. An alternative is to `filter` the groups before mapping;
both are fine, and the second reads better once there is more than one reason
to skip.

Two nested maps means two key decisions, and they are independent: sibling keys
only need to be unique *among their own siblings*, so the inner lists never
collide with each other even if two groups contained tasks with the same title.
This is also the point where `filter(...).sort(...)` is safe without copying —
`filter` already handed you a new array.

## review1 — remove by identity

Everything in this exercise is a restatement of ex2 in a different register.
The handler is created inside the map, so it closes over the chip it belongs to
and can name it precisely; `filter` produces a new array so React sees a new
reference and re-renders; and removing by id rather than index means the
component keeps working when the list is sorted or filtered upstream.

The one new detail is `onClick={() => remove(chip.id)}`. That arrow creates a
new function on every render for every row, which is fine — creating a closure
is cheap, and this is the normal way to write it. It becomes worth thinking
about only when the row is a memoized component, which is exactly the situation
`11_performance_patterns` builds around.

## Further reading

- [react.dev — Rendering Lists](https://react.dev/learn/rendering-lists) — the map, the key rules, and the "where do I get an id" question.
- [react.dev — Preserving and Resetting State](https://react.dev/learn/preserving-and-resetting-state) — the best explanation anywhere of what reconciliation actually preserves, and how to reset state deliberately with a key.
- [react.dev — Conditional Rendering](https://react.dev/learn/conditional-rendering) — including the `&&` trap, in the official words.
- [MDN — `Array.prototype.sort`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array/sort) — "sorts in place", stability, and the comparator contract.
- [MDN — `Array.prototype.toSorted`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array/toSorted) — the non-mutating version, and where it is available.
- [MDN — Logical AND (`&&`)](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/Logical_AND) — why it returns an operand rather than a boolean.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — grouping

Edit `challenge/solution.tsx`. `GroupedTasks({ tasks })` renders the tasks
grouped by status. The file already exports `GROUPS`, which gives you the three
statuses in display order along with their labels. For each group **that has at
least one task**, render a level-3 heading with the label and a list of that
group's task titles, sorted A–Z. Groups with no tasks must not appear at all —
not as an empty heading, not as an empty list.

Honest difficulty note: no new API, but two nested maps, two sets of keys, and
a `null` returned from inside a `map`. Take it in the order the hints suggest.

```
uv run dojo test react 04_lists_conditional challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Do not iterate the tasks. Iterate the **groups** — they are already in the
order the output needs, and they are already in the file as `GROUPS`. For each
one, ask the task list which tasks belong to it.

## Hint 2
Inside that outer map, per group: filter the tasks down to this status, sort
the survivors by title, and if there are none left, render nothing. Returning
`null` from inside a `map` is legal and renders nothing at all — which is
exactly how you skip an empty group.

Note that `filter` already returns a fresh array, so sorting it in place here
is safe. That is not true of the `tasks` prop itself.

## Hint 3
Two nested maps means two sets of keys: the outer elements are keyed by
something stable per group, the inner ones by something stable per task. Both
groups and tasks carry a natural identifier. The remaining decision is what
element wraps each group — the gate only requires a level-3 heading and a list
per group, so the semantics of the container are yours to choose.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Do not iterate the tasks. Iterate the **groups** — they are already in the
order the output needs, and they are already in the file as `GROUPS`. For each
one, ask the task list which tasks belong to it.

## Hint 2
Inside that outer map, per group: filter the tasks down to this status, sort
the survivors by title, and if there are none left, render nothing. Returning
`null` from inside a `map` is legal and renders nothing at all — which is
exactly how you skip an empty group.

Note that `filter` already returns a fresh array, so sorting it in place here
is safe. That is not true of the `tasks` prop itself.

## Hint 3
Two nested maps means two sets of keys: the outer elements are keyed by
something stable per group, the inner ones by something stable per task. Both
groups and tasks carry a natural identifier. The remaining decision is what
element wraps each group — the gate only requires a level-3 heading and a list
per group, so the semantics of the container are yours to choose.

## Hint 1
The component compiles, renders the right rows, and React logs no warning —
the map does have a `key`. Run the gate and read what it says happened to the
text you typed. Then ask: after the newcomer is prepended, what does the key of
the *first* row say?

## Hint 2
A key is React's answer to "is this the same item I rendered last time?" With
`key={index}`, the row at position 0 is always key `0`, so when a new person
arrives at the front React concludes that row 0 is the *same row* with a
different name — and reuses its DOM node, uncontrolled input value and all.
Everything React re-renders (the label, the id) is updated; everything the DOM
owns (what the user typed, focus, scroll position) stays behind.

## Hint 3
The fix is one expression. Key by something that belongs to the item and does
not change when the list is reordered — these people already carry exactly such
a field. The remaining decision is what you would do in a list where items have
no id of their own; think about where that id should come from before you look
it up.

## Exercise 3 — the empty state, and the zero

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `Inbox({ messages, unreadCount })`:

- when `messages` is empty, render the text `No messages` and **no list at
  all**;
- otherwise render a `<ul>` with one `<li>` per message showing its `subject`;
- show a badge reading `<count> unread` — for example `2 unread` — but only
  when `unreadCount` is above zero, and with **no stray `0`** anywhere in the
  output when it is not.

The stub renders the badge unconditionally, so start there.

```
uv run dojo test react 04_lists_conditional ex3
```
exercises.hints: ## Hint 1 Two independent conditions. One decides between a list and an empty state; the other decides whether the unread badge exists at all. Handle them separately — trying to express both in one piece of JSX is what makes conditional rendering feel hard. ## Hint 2 For the whole-component case, an early return is clearest: ```tsx if (messages.length === 0) { return …; } ``` For the badge, `{condition && …}` renders the element when the condition is true and nothing when it is false — because React skips `false`, `null` and `undefined`. ## Hint 3 That word *skips* is doing a lot of work. React skips `false`, `null` and `undefined` — it does **not** skip `0`, `""` or `NaN`, which are falsy in JavaScript but perfectly renderable. So `{unreadCount && }` evaluates to the number `0` when there is nothing unread, and React dutifully prints it. exercises.importantHints: ## Hint 1 Two independent conditions. One decides between a list and an empty state; the other decides whether the unread badge exists at all. Handle them separately — trying to express both in one piece of JSX is what makes conditional rendering feel hard. ## Hint 2 For the whole-component case, an early return is clearest: ```tsx if (messages.length === 0) { return …; } ``` For the badge, `{condition && …}` renders the element when the condition is true and nothing when it is false — because React skips `false`, `null` and `undefined`. ## Hint 3 That word *skips* is doing a lot of work. React skips `false`, `null` and `undefined` — it does **not** skip `0`, `""` or `NaN`, which are falsy in JavaScript but perfectly renderable. So `{unreadCount && }` evaluates to the number `0` when there is nothing unread, and React dutifully prints it. Make the left-hand side an actual boolean and the problem disappears.

## Hint 1
Each button already knows which chip it belongs to — it was created inside the
map, so the chip is in scope. The only missing pieces are a handler that takes
that chip's identity and a state update that produces a list without it.

## Hint 2
`onClick` wants a function taking no arguments, so wrap the call:

```tsx
onClick={() => remove(chip.id)}
```

and remove by producing a new array:

```tsx
setChips((previous) => previous.filter((chip) => /* … */));
```

`filter` returns a copy; `splice` edits the array you are holding, which leaves
the state reference unchanged and renders nothing.

## Hint 3
Remove by **id**, not by index. Removing by index works right up until the list
is sorted, filtered or re-fetched between the render and the click — the same
identity-versus-position mistake as ex2, wearing different clothes. The last
decision is what the list should look like once it is empty.

## Hint 1
Each button already knows which chip it belongs to — it was created inside the
map, so the chip is in scope. The only missing pieces are a handler that takes
that chip's identity and a state update that produces a list without it.

## Hint 2
`onClick` wants a function taking no arguments, so wrap the call:

```tsx
onClick={() => remove(chip.id)}
```

and remove by producing a new array:

```tsx
setChips((previous) => previous.filter((chip) => /* … */));
```

`filter` returns a copy; `splice` edits the array you are holding, which leaves
the state reference unchanged and renders nothing.

## Hint 3
Remove by **id**, not by index. Removing by index works right up until the list
is sorted, filtered or re-fetched between the render and the click — the same
identity-versus-position mistake as ex2, wearing different clothes. The last
decision is what the list should look like once it is empty.

# 05 — Forms A text input is the one HTML element with a mind of its own. Render `` and the browser gives it a value, updates that value as the user types, and keeps it — without telling React anything. That is fine until you want to uppercase the text, disable a button while the field is empty, validate before submitting, or show a live preview. At that point there are two sources of truth for the same string, and they will disagree. React's answer is to take the field over. A **controlled** input renders its value from state and reports every change back through `onChange`, so state and screen cannot drift: what the user sees *is* your state, one render behind nothing. The alternative — an **uncontrolled** input, where the DOM keeps the value and you read it when you need it — is not wrong, and you have already used it in lesson 04's key demonstration. But controlled is the default, and it is what interviewers mean when they ask you the difference. This lesson also covers the part of forms that is not about React at all: telling somebody what went wrong. An error message that a sighted user can see floating next to a field is invisible to a screen-reader user unless it is *wired* to that field. Two attributes fix that, and the challenge makes you use them. ## Concept — value in, change out ```tsx function Search() { const [query, setQuery] = useState(""); return ( <> setQuery(event.target.value)} />

Searching for: {query}

); } ``` `value` and `onChange` travel together. `value` with no `onChange` gives a box that cannot be typed into (and a React warning saying so); `onChange` with no `value` leaves the browser in charge and your state as a stale copy. # Reading — react/05_forms

## Notes

**Controlled vs uncontrolled, precisely.** A controlled component renders its
value from React state and reports changes upward; React is the source of
truth. An uncontrolled component lets the DOM keep the value — you seed it with
`defaultValue`/`defaultChecked` and read it later, usually through a ref or by
reading the submitted `FormData`. Neither is deprecated. Controlled is the
default because it makes the value available *while* the user is typing, which
is what live validation, character counters, dependent fields and disabled
submit buttons all need. Uncontrolled is genuinely better for large forms where
per-keystroke re-rendering is wasteful, and for integrating a non-React widget.

**React's `onChange` is not the DOM's `change`.** The DOM fires `change` on
blur for text inputs; React's `onChange` is wired to the `input` event and
fires on every keystroke. That difference trips people coming from plain
JavaScript, and it is why controlled inputs feel live without any extra work.

**Every input needs a label, and `placeholder` is not one.** A placeholder
disappears the moment the user types, fails contrast guidelines in most
implementations, and is not reliably announced. `<label htmlFor>` or a wrapping
`<label>` gives the control an accessible name permanently — which is also why
`getByLabelText` is the first query you should reach for in a form test.

**Submit belongs on the form.** Handling submission on the button's `onClick`
breaks pressing Enter inside a field, breaks screen-reader submit affordances,
and misses submissions triggered any other way. `<form onSubmit>` plus
`<button type="submit">` covers all of them — and note `type="submit"` is the
default for a button inside a form, which is why a stray `<button>Cancel</button>`
submits the form. Always be explicit.

**Validation happens at least twice.** Client-side validation is a courtesy to
the user and nothing more; it can be bypassed by anybody with a devtools
window, so the server validates again. The client's job is to be fast, specific
and kind: say which field, say what is wrong, say what "right" looks like, and
do not clear what the user typed.

## ex1 — the loop, seen from the inside

The most useful thing to take from this exercise is what the keystroke actually
does. It does *not* change the input. The sequence is: browser fires `input`,
React calls your `onChange`, you call `setName`, React re-renders, React sets
the DOM node's `value` property from your state. Every character on screen came
from React, which is why transforming the value in the handler changes what is
displayed, and why an `onChange` that forgets to call the setter produces a box
you cannot type in at all.

That also explains the React warning "You provided a `value` prop to a form
field without an `onChange` handler." React is telling you that you have made
the field read-only by accident. The fixes are to add the handler, or — if you
meant it — to add `readOnly`.

One subtlety about the uppercase transform: because the state is uppercased,
the cursor stays put and everything behaves. Transforms that *change the length*
of the string — inserting spaces into a card number, stripping characters — move
the caret to the end on every keystroke, and fixing that requires manual
selection handling. It is a well-known rough edge worth knowing exists before
you promise a formatted input to a designer.

## ex2 — the three control shapes

Selects and text inputs are the same story: `value` in, `event.target.value`
out. The checkbox is the exception that generates bugs — its `value` attribute
is for form submission (`"on"` by default) and its state is `checked`. A
component written with `value={agreed}` on a checkbox silently does nothing
useful, and it looks right.

React's handling of `<select>` is worth one more sentence because it comes up in
interviews. In HTML the selected option is marked on the `<option>`; React
moves it to the `<select>`'s `value` prop, so that the control has one place
that decides. Multi-select works the same way with an array. Radio groups are
the remaining shape: several inputs sharing a `name`, each with its own `value`,
each `checked` when the state equals its value.

## ex3 — one handler, and the spread that keeps the rest

Two techniques combine here, and both are worth having by reflex. The first is
using the `name` attribute as the bridge from DOM to state, which is what lets
a single handler serve any number of fields — and, incidentally, is exactly how
`FormData` names things when you submit uncontrolled forms, so the naming stays
useful either way.

The second is `{ ...previous, [name]: value }`. The broken stub replaces the
object, which deletes every key it did not mention; React does not merge state
objects for you (class components' `setState` did, which is a genuine source of
confusion for people who learned React before hooks). The computed-key syntax
`[name]:` is plain JavaScript and is what makes the update generic.

Using the updater form here is not decoration either. Two changes landing in
the same batch — which happens with autofill, paste handlers, or programmatic
updates — would both spread the *same* stale `form` and one would be lost.

The remaining design question, which has no single right answer: one object or
one `useState` per field? Split state by what changes together. Fields that are
submitted as a unit and validated as a unit belong together; a field that
drives an unrelated piece of UI does not.

## ex4 — validating without lying to the user

The structural move is to keep validation as a **pure function** of the values,
separate from the component. It becomes readable, unit-testable, and reusable
on the server; and the component's job shrinks to "run it, store the result,
decide whether to submit".

`preventDefault()` is not optional. A form's default action is a navigation,
which in a single-page app unmounts everything and loses all state — and in a
test environment produces a confusing "not implemented" message from jsdom.
Calling it first, before any branching, is the habit that never bites.

`role="alert"` on the error region matters because of *when* the user finds
out. Without a live region, a sighted user sees red text appear and a
screen-reader user hears nothing at all — they pressed the button and, as far
as they can tell, nothing happened. `alert` interrupts and reads the new
content. The other half of a really good implementation, which the gate does
not require but real forms should do, is moving focus to the first invalid
field or to the summary.

Note also what the gate checks about the *absence* of the alert. An error region
that is always in the DOM and merely empty is announced as an empty region and
gives assistive technology nothing to work with; rendering it conditionally
means its appearance is itself the signal.

## challenge — errors that know which field they belong to

The shape of the state is the exercise. An array of messages cannot answer
"which field is broken", so every attempt to wire it per-field turns into
string matching. An object keyed by field name answers it directly, and it also
makes "is the form valid" a one-liner (`Object.keys(errors).length === 0`).

`aria-invalid` and `aria-describedby` are the two attributes that make an error
message real for somebody using a screen reader. Without `describedby`, the
message is a floating piece of text with no relationship to the field —
perfectly visible on screen, completely disconnected in the accessibility tree.
With it, tabbing into the field announces "Postcode, edit text, invalid entry,
Postcode must be four digits".

The gate insists on `aria-invalid="false"` rather than an absent attribute for
valid fields, which is a slightly stricter rule than the spec requires; the
reason is that it lets a test — and a screen reader — distinguish "checked and
fine" from "not checked yet". In production either is acceptable; being able to
explain the difference is the point.

The design question the exercise deliberately leaves open is *when* to
validate. Validating on every keystroke tells people their email is invalid
while they are still typing it, which is hostile. The usual answer is: validate
a field on blur once it has been touched, validate everything on submit, and
after a failed submit switch to validating as they type so the error clears as
soon as it is fixed.

## review1 — derived enablement

`disabled={!ready}` where `ready` is computed during render is the small,
important habit: the button's state is not a fact to be stored, it is a
consequence of two facts already stored. Every extra piece of state is another
thing that can disagree with reality — set `ready` in one handler and forget it
in another and you have a form that never unlocks.

`trim()` before deciding is the kind of detail that separates a demo from a
product: a field containing three spaces is not filled in. And the broader
question the hint raises is a real UX debate. A disabled submit button is easy
to implement and leaves users who cannot work out what is missing with nowhere
to go; the increasingly common alternative is to keep the button enabled and
explain on submit. Either is defensible if you chose it.

## Further reading

- [react.dev — `<input>`](https://react.dev/reference/react-dom/components/input) — the controlled/uncontrolled contract, plus every gotcha React has documented.
- [react.dev — `<select>`](https://react.dev/reference/react-dom/components/select) and [`<form>`](https://react.dev/reference/react-dom/components/form) — why `value` moved to the select, and what React 19 added to forms.
- [react.dev — Updating Objects in State](https://react.dev/learn/updating-objects-in-state) — the spread pattern from ex3, including nested objects.
- [MDN — Client-side form validation](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn_web_development/Extensions/Forms/Form_validation) — the native constraint API you are deliberately not using here, and when to use it.
- [MDN — `aria-invalid`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Attributes/aria-invalid) and [`aria-describedby`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Attributes/aria-describedby) — the two attributes from the challenge.
- [Testing Library — `getByLabelText`](https://testing-library.com/docs/queries/bylabeltext/) — why it is the first query to reach for in a form.

which in a single-page app unmounts everything and loses all state — and in a
test environment produces a confusing "not implemented" message from jsdom.
Calling it first, before any branching, is the habit that never bites.

`role="alert"` on the error region matters because of *when* the user finds
out. Without a live region, a sighted user sees red text appear and a
screen-reader user hears nothing at all — they pressed the button and, as far
as they can tell, nothing happened. `alert` interrupts and reads the new
content. The other half of a really good implementation, which the gate does
not require but real forms should do, is moving focus to the first invalid
field or to the summary.

Note also what the gate checks about the *absence* of the alert. An error region
that is always in the DOM and merely empty is announced as an empty region and
gives assistive technology nothing to work with; rendering it conditionally
means its appearance is itself the signal.

## challenge — errors that know which field they belong to

The shape of the state is the exercise. An array of messages cannot answer
"which field is broken", so every attempt to wire it per-field turns into
string matching. An object keyed by field name answers it directly, and it also
makes "is the form valid" a one-liner (`Object.keys(errors).length === 0`).

`aria-invalid` and `aria-describedby` are the two attributes that make an error
message real for somebody using a screen reader. Without `describedby`, the
message is a floating piece of text with no relationship to the field —
perfectly visible on screen, completely disconnected in the accessibility tree.
With it, tabbing into the field announces "Postcode, edit text, invalid entry,
Postcode must be four digits".

The gate insists on `aria-invalid="false"` rather than an absent attribute for
valid fields, which is a slightly stricter rule than the spec requires; the
reason is that it lets a test — and a screen reader — distinguish "checked and
fine" from "not checked yet". In production either is acceptable; being able to
explain the difference is the point.

The design question the exercise deliberately leaves open is *when* to
validate. Validating on every keystroke tells people their email is invalid
while they are still typing it, which is hostile. The usual answer is: validate
a field on blur once it has been touched, validate everything on submit, and
after a failed submit switch to validating as they type so the error clears as
soon as it is fixed.

## review1 — derived enablement

`disabled={!ready}` where `ready` is computed during render is the small,
important habit: the button's state is not a fact to be stored, it is a
consequence of two facts already stored. Every extra piece of state is another
thing that can disagree with reality — set `ready` in one handler and forget it
in another and you have a form that never unlocks.

`trim()` before deciding is the kind of detail that separates a demo from a
product: a field containing three spaces is not filled in. And the broader
question the hint raises is a real UX debate. A disabled submit button is easy
to implement and leaves users who cannot work out what is missing with nowhere
to go; the increasingly common alternative is to keep the button enabled and
explain on submit. Either is defensible if you chose it.

## Challenge — errors that belong to fields

Edit `challenge/solution.tsx`. `AddressForm({ onSubmit })` has controlled
`Street` and `Postcode` fields and a `Save address` button. Street is required;
postcode must be exactly four digits. On an invalid submit, **each broken field**
carries:

- `aria-invalid="true"` (and `aria-invalid="false"` when it is fine — the
  attribute must be present either way, so the gate can tell "valid" from
  "never checked");
- an accessible description equal to its message: `Street is required` or
  `Postcode must be four digits`.

`onSubmit` is called with `{ street, postcode }` only when both are valid.

Honest difficulty note: the shape of the error state is the whole exercise. A
flat array cannot say which field a message belongs to.

```
uv run dojo test react 05_forms challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Ex4 collected problems into a flat list, which is fine when they are shown
together at the top. Here each message has to belong to a *field*, so the shape
of the error state changes: an object keyed by field name, holding one message
per broken field and nothing for the fields that are fine.

## Hint 2
Validation still lives in a plain function, now returning that object:

```tsx
type Errors = { street?: string; postcode?: string };
function validate(street: string, postcode: string): Errors { … }
```

`/^\d{4}$/.test(postcode)` is the four-digit check. The form submits only when
the object has no keys — `Object.keys(found).length === 0`.

## Hint 3
Each input then needs two attributes driven by that object: `aria-invalid`,
which must be `"false"` (not absent) when the field is fine, and
`aria-describedby` pointing at the id of the element rendering that field's
message — and pointing at nothing when there is no message. Rendering
`aria-describedby` as `undefined` omits the attribute entirely, which is what
you want. The remaining decisions are what element carries the message and
whether you also validate as the user types.

## Hint 1
Ex4 collected problems into a flat list, which is fine when they are shown
together at the top. Here each message has to belong to a *field*, so the shape
of the error state changes: an object keyed by field name, holding one message
per broken field and nothing for the fields that are fine.

## Hint 2
Validation still lives in a plain function, now returning that object:

```tsx
type Errors = { street?: string; postcode?: string };
function validate(street: string, postcode: string): Errors { … }
```

`/^\d{4}$/.test(postcode)` is the four-digit check. The form submits only when
the object has no keys — `Object.keys(found).length === 0`.

## Hint 3
Each input then needs two attributes driven by that object: `aria-invalid`,
which must be `"false"` (not absent) when the field is fine, and
`aria-describedby` pointing at the id of the element rendering that field's
message — and pointing at nothing when there is no message. Rendering
`aria-describedby` as `undefined` omits the attribute entirely, which is what
you want. The remaining decisions are what element carries the message and
whether you also validate as the user types.

## Hint 1
Right now the browser owns what is in the box and React has no idea what it
says — which is why the counter cannot move. Make React the owner: hold the
text in state, render that state as the input's `value`, and update the state

## Hint 2
```tsx
const [name, setName] = useState("");
…
<input id="full-name" value={name} onChange={(event) => setName(/* … */)} />
```

Those two attributes always travel together. `value` without `onChange` gives

you already have, and deciding whether to count before or after the transform
is a question worth two seconds of thought.

## Hint 1
Two more controls, two more pieces of state, and one difference worth
memorising: a text box and a `<select>` are controlled through `value`, but a
checkbox is controlled through `checked`. Its `value` is the string `"on"`
whether it is ticked or not.

## Hint 2
```tsx
<select id="theme" value={theme} onChange={(event) => setTheme(event.target.value)}>
<input id="emails" type="checkbox" checked={emails} onChange={(event) => setEmails(/* … */)} />
```

In React you put `value` on the `<select>` itself rather than marking an
`<option selected>` — that is a deliberate departure from plain HTML, and it
keeps the whole control in one place.

## Hint 3
The summary reads exactly `Theme: dark, emails on`, with the theme being the
option's `value` (lower case) rather than its visible label. The on/off word is
a decision made from the boolean, the same shape as the plural in lesson 00.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
One handler serves both inputs, so it has to work out *which* field fired.
Every event carries the element that produced it as `event.target`, and each of
these inputs already has a `name` attribute — that is the connection.

## Hint 2
The other half is that state objects are replaced, not edited. Writing
`setForm({ email: value })` produces an object with no `name` key at all, which
is why the first field goes blank. Copy what was there and override one key:

```tsx
setForm((previous) => ({ ...previous, /* … */ }));
```

Note the parentheses around the object literal — without them the arrow
function body is read as a block.

## Hint 3
A computed key lets you name the property at runtime:
`{ ...previous, [someString]: value }`. Pull both `name` and `value` off
`event.target` first; that leaves you one decision, which is whether to reach
for the updater form here and why it matters when two changes land in the same
batch.

## Hint 1
The email box is already controlled; the checkbox is not. Give the checkbox
state of its own, remembering that a checkbox is driven by `checked` and
reports through `event.target.checked`.

## Hint 2
Whether the button is enabled is not a third piece of state — it is a fact
about the other two, so compute it during render:

```tsx
const ready = /* … */;
…
<button type="submit" disabled={!ready}>
```

Storing `ready` in state would give you two sources of truth that have to be
kept in step by hand, and they eventually will not be.

## Hint 3
"Filled in" should mean more than "not empty string" — a space is not an email
address, so `trim()` before you decide. What counts as a valid address beyond
that is a judgement call: the gate only requires the button to unlock, but ask
yourself whether a disabled button or an error message is kinder to somebody
who cannot work out why nothing happens.

## Hint 1
The email box is already controlled; the checkbox is not. Give the checkbox
state of its own, remembering that a checkbox is driven by `checked` and
reports through `event.target.checked`.

## Hint 2
Whether the button is enabled is not a third piece of state — it is a fact
about the other two, so compute it during render:

```tsx
const ready = /* … */;
…
<button type="submit" disabled={!ready}>
```

Storing `ready` in state would give you two sources of truth that have to be
kept in step by hand, and they eventually will not be.

## Hint 3
"Filled in" should mean more than "not empty string" — a space is not an email
address, so `trim()` before you decide. What counts as a valid address beyond
that is a judgement call: the gate only requires the button to unlock, but ask
yourself whether a disabled button or an error message is kinder to somebody
who cannot work out why nothing happens.

lessons.briefing:
# 06 — Effects

Everything you have written so far lives entirely inside React. Props come in,
markup goes out, clicks change state, React updates the DOM. Nothing in that
loop touches the world.

But real applications do touch the world. They set the document title, listen
for a key press on `document`, open a WebSocket, start a timer, or ask a server
for something. Those are **side effects**: work that happens *because* a
component rendered, but is not part of producing the markup. They cannot go in
the render body — rendering has to be pure, must be safe to run twice, and must
not do anything the user can observe. So React gives them their own place:
`useEffect`.

`useEffect` is also, by a wide margin, the most misused hook in React. Two
things go wrong. People put things in it that were never side effects — deriving
a value, responding to a click — and end up with an extra render and a bug
where the UI is briefly inconsistent. And people get the dependency array wrong,
which produces either an effect that never re-runs (stale data) or one that
re-runs forever (a loop that hammers an API).

This lesson teaches the dependency array honestly. It is not a performance knob
and it is not a list you tune until the warnings stop. It is a **claim you are
making**: "this effect reads exactly these values, and if none of them changed,
running it again would produce the same result." When that claim is false, the
consequences are the two failure modes above.

## Concept — synchronise, do not react

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  // 1. the effect: run after React has updated the DOM
  const socket = connect(roomId);

  // 2. the cleanup: undo the effect
  return () => socket.close();
}, [roomId]);   // 3. the dependencies
```

React runs the effect after the render is committed. Before running it again —
and once more when the component unmounts — it runs whatever the previous run
returned. So the sequence on a changed `roomId` is: *close the old socket, open
the new one.* Cleanup first, always.

**The dependency array.** React compares each entry with `Object.is` against
the previous run:

- **omitted entirely** — run after every render;
- **`[]`** — run once after mount, clean up on unmount, never in between;
- **`[a, b]`** — run again whenever `a` or `b` changed.

The rule for filling it in is mechanical, and it is the rule the
`react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` lint rule applies: **every value from inside the
component that the effect reads goes in the array.** Props, state, and anything
computed from them. Not `document`, not an imported function, not a `setState`
setter (React guarantees those are stable).

That rule exists because of a fact you already met in lesson 03: **a function
created during a render closes over that render's values, permanently.** An
effect body is such a function. If it reads `count` and `count` is not in the
deps, the effect that is still running was created in an older render and is
looking at an older `count` — a **stale closure**. It does not go stale
gradually; it was never anything else.

Here is the classic, and you will fix it in the challenge:

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  const id = setInterval(() => setSeconds(seconds + 1), 1000);
  return () => clearInterval(id);
}, [running]);
```

`seconds` is read but not listed. The interval callback captured `seconds` at
`0` and every tick computes `0 + 1`. The counter sticks at 1 forever. There are
two ways out — add `seconds` to the deps (and tear down and recreate the
interval every second, which drifts), or stop reading `seconds` at all by using
the updater form. The second is almost always right, and the general principle
behind it is: **if you find yourself fighting the dependency array, the effect
is usually reading something it should have been describing instead.**

**Effects you should not write.** Before reaching for `useEffect`, ask:

- *Can I compute this during render?* Then do — a filtered list, a total, a
  validity flag. An effect that sets state from props renders twice and flickers.
- *Did this happen because of a specific user action?* Then it belongs in the
  event handler. Sending an analytics event or a POST when a button is clicked
  is not a synchronisation problem, and putting it in an effect makes it fire
  in situations you did not intend.

`useEffect` is for **synchronising with something outside React** — the
document, a subscription, a timer, a server. That framing answers most "should
this be an effect" questions on its own.

## Exercise 1 — an effect with a cleanup

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `PageTitle({ title })` renders nothing and sets
`document.title` to the `title` prop. When the prop changes the document must
follow, and when the component unmounts the title must be restored to whatever
it was before the component mounted.

```
uv run dojo test react 06_effects ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — the dependency array is a claim

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `ThemeSync({ theme, onSync, label })` renders the
`label` in a paragraph and calls `onSync(theme)` **once per theme**, not once
per render. The gate re-renders with a changed `label` and an unchanged
`theme`, and requires that no sync happened.

The stub's effect has no dependency array at all.

```
uv run dojo test react 06_effects ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — subscribe, and unsubscribe

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `EscapeToClose({ onClose })` listens for `keydown` on
`document` and calls `onClose` when the pressed key is `Escape` — and only
then. When the component unmounts it must stop listening.

The gate presses Escape after unmounting. A component that is still listening
after it is gone fails, which is exactly what a leak looks like in production.

```
uv run dojo test react 06_effects ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — fetching on mount

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `UserBadge({ userId, fetchUser })` calls
`fetchUser(userId)` and renders the resulting `name` in a paragraph. Before the
promise settles it renders nothing.

`fetchUser` is a **prop**, not an import. Every data-fetching exercise in this
track works that way: the function that talks to the network is injected, so
the gate can hand you a deterministic fake and there is never a real request.
That is also good production design — a component that takes its data source as
a prop is testable, mockable and reusable.

The gate re-renders with the same `userId` and requires that no second request
happens. Getting that wrong is an infinite fetch loop.

```
uv run dojo test react 06_effects ex4
```

## Challenge — the stale closure

Edit `challenge/solution.tsx`. `Stopwatch` is written, compiles, and is wrong.
It renders a live region and `Start` / `Stop` buttons, and while running it
should add one second every second.

Run the gate first and read the failure. Then fix it so that:

- three seconds after Start, the display reads `3`;
- after Stop, time may pass and the display does not move;
- Start again resumes from where it stopped.

Honest difficulty note: the fix is one word. Understanding *why* that word fixes
it is the reason this is the challenge, and the same bug returns as an interview
drill in `i2_interview_drills`.

```
uv run dojo test react 06_effects challenge
```

## Review — cleanup ordering

`review1/solution.tsx`. `AnnounceOnChange({ message, onAnnounce, onClear })`
renders the message in a live region, calls `onAnnounce(message)` when the
message changes, and calls `onClear(message)` to retract it — on the way to the
next message and on unmount.

The gate checks that when the message changes from `Saved` to `Deleted`, the
clear call carries `Saved`.

```
uv run dojo test react 06_effects review1
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading — react/06_effects

## Notes

**When effects run.** React renders (calls your function), commits (updates the
DOM), the browser paints, and then `useEffect` callbacks fire. That ordering is
why an effect can safely read the DOM and why it never blocks the first paint.
`useLayoutEffect` is the same hook moved earlier — it runs after the commit but
*before* the browser paints — and exists for the narrow case where you must
measure and adjust the DOM without the user seeing a flash. Reach for
`useEffect` by default; if something visibly flickers, that is the signal to try
the other one.

**Strict Mode double-invokes effects on purpose.** In development, React mounts
a component, runs its effects, runs its cleanups, and runs the effects again.
This is not a bug and is not something to work around: it is a test that your
effect is *resilient to being run twice*, which is the same property that makes
it correct when a dependency changes. An effect that opens a connection and
never closes it survives one mount and breaks under the double invoke — which
is the point. The gates in this course do not enable Strict Mode, but the
production apps you write should.

**Cleanup runs before every re-run, not only on unmount.** The lifecycle of one
effect is: run, later clean up, and that pair always belongs to a single render.
That is what makes `onClear("Saved")` in review1 fall out for free — the
cleanup closes over its own render's props. People are surprised by this because
they think of the cleanup as "the unmount handler"; it is better described as
"the undo for this particular run".

**Effects you should delete.** The official guidance list, worth memorising
because it is also an interview topic: do not use an effect to transform data
for rendering (compute during render), to reset state when a prop changes (use
a `key` instead), to handle a user event (put it in the handler), or to notify a
parent about a state change (call the parent's callback in the same handler that
changed the state). Each of these produces an extra render pass and a moment
where the UI is showing something stale.

**Racing and ordering.** Any effect that starts something asynchronous has to
consider what happens if it is superseded before it finishes. The `cancelled`
flag pattern — set a local `let cancelled = false`, check it before setting
state, flip it in the cleanup — is the smallest complete answer, and lesson 07
is entirely about the failure it prevents.

## ex1 — an effect and its exact undo

`document.title` is the smallest possible "outside React" system, which makes it
a clean first effect: something to set, something to restore, and a dependency
that decides when to redo it.

The detail that matters is *where* the previous title is captured. Reading it
inside the effect body means each run of the effect captures the value that was
true when it ran, and the cleanup closes over that same `const`. Hoisting it to
a `useRef` or module variable seems tidier and quietly breaks: two components
doing this at once would overwrite each other's idea of "previous".

The honest caveat about this pattern in production: two components each setting
`document.title` will fight, and the last one to render wins. Title management
usually belongs to a single owner — a router, a layout component, or a small
library that keeps a stack. That is a good illustration of the general rule that
effects mutating shared global state need an owner, not a convention.

## ex2 — what the dependency array actually claims

The stub's effect had no array, so it ran after every render, and the outside
world was told the theme changed when only a label had. That is the least
dangerous of the three failure modes — it is merely wasteful — but wasteful
effects become real bugs the moment the effect does something non-idempotent:
sending an analytics event, appending to a log, opening a connection.

The mechanical rule for filling the array in: every value the effect body reads
that comes from inside the component. `theme` obviously; `onSync` because it is
a prop that could be a different function next render. People routinely leave
function props out because "it's always the same function" — and it is, right
up until the parent stops memoizing it, at which point either the effect runs
too often or, if you also lied about a value, calls a stale callback forever.

The `react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` lint rule implements exactly this analysis and
is essentially never wrong about what an effect reads. It can be wrong about
what you *want*, and the honest response to that is to change the code so that
the deps you want are the deps you need — not to silence the rule. Every
codebase with `// eslint-disable-next-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps`
scattered through it has at least one stale-closure bug nobody has found yet.

## ex3 — subscriptions, and the identity of a function

Two things make this exercise more than boilerplate.

The first is that `removeEventListener` compares function references. Passing a
freshly created arrow to both `add` and `remove` removes nothing and leaks a
listener on every effect run. Declaring the handler *inside* the effect
guarantees both calls see the same reference — which is why the idiom looks the
way it does.

The second is what "leak" means here. After unmount, a listener still attached
to `document` holds a reference to your component's closure, which holds its
props and state, which holds whatever those reference — so the whole subtree
stays in memory. Worse, if the handler calls a state setter, React used to warn
about setting state on an unmounted component; the warning was removed because
it produced too many false positives, which means the leak is now silent. The
cleanup is the only thing standing between you and it.

The dependency on `onClose` deserves a thought. Listing it means the listener is
removed and re-added whenever the parent passes a new function — which, if the
parent creates it inline, is every render. That is cheap for a DOM listener and
expensive for a WebSocket, and it is one of the situations that motivates
`useCallback` in lesson 11 and the `useEffectEvent` API React has been
developing for effects that need to "read the latest" without re-subscribing.

## ex4 — fetching, and why the fetcher is a prop

Injecting `fetchUser` rather than importing it or calling `fetch` directly is
the single most useful testing decision in this whole track, and it is not a
testing trick — it is dependency inversion. The component states what it needs
("something that turns an id into a promise of a user") instead of naming a
specific implementation. The gate can then hand it a fake with no network, no
mock-server, no timing, and no flakiness.

The dependency array is the whole difficulty. Omit it and you get the canonical
React disaster: fetch → setState → render → fetch → setState → render, forever,
several times a second, against somebody's API. Every experienced React
developer has shipped this once. The reason it is so easy to write is that the
loop is invisible in the code; you have to reason about it.

Two more points about `fetchUser` in the deps. It is correct to include it, and
it is safe here because the gate passes the same function every render. If a
parent created it inline, the effect would refetch on every render — the same
infinite loop through a different door — and the fix belongs in the parent
(`useCallback`, or defining the function outside the component), not in a
shortened dependency array.

Finally, the `cancelled` flag. Even with correct deps, a promise in flight when
the component unmounts will still resolve, and its `.then` will call `setUser`
on something that no longer exists. React tolerates this without complaint
these days, but the work is wasted and — if the component is still mounted with
a *different* id — the answer to a question nobody is asking anymore can
overwrite the answer to the question they are. That is lesson 07.

## challenge — the stale closure, in the wild

This is the bug this lesson exists for. Write out the sequence precisely,
because the precision is what makes it stop being mysterious:

1. `running` becomes `true`, so the effect runs. At that moment `seconds` is
   `0`, and the arrow function passed to `setInterval` closes over that `0`.
2. One second later, the callback runs and calls `setSeconds(0 + 1)`. State
   becomes `1`, the component re-renders.
3. `running` did not change, so the effect does **not** re-run. The interval is
   the same interval, holding the same callback, still closed over `0`.
4. Two seconds later it calls `setSeconds(0 + 1)` again. State is already `1`,
   `Object.is(1, 1)` is true, React bails out. The clock is frozen at 1 forever.

Adding `seconds` to the dependency array does fix the number — the effect now
re-runs after each tick with a fresh closure — but look at what it costs:
`clearInterval` and `setInterval` every second, so the timer restarts from zero
each time and the cadence drifts. That is a real technique for some problems and
the wrong one here.

`setSeconds((previous) => previous + 1)` fixes it properly because the callback
stops reading state altogether. It no longer says "set it to one more than the
value I remember" but "increase whatever it is by one" — a description of a
change rather than a captured value. The effect's dependency list shrinks
honestly to `[running]`, the interval survives, and the deps are now telling the
truth.

The generalisation is worth carrying: **when the dependency array feels like a
fight, the effect is usually reading a value it should have been describing.**
Updater functions, refs, and reducers are all ways of describing a change
without capturing the current state.

## review1 — whose values does a cleanup see?

The gate asserts on the *argument* of `onClear`, which is the only way to
observe the answer. When the message changes from `Saved` to `Deleted`, React
runs the cleanup created by the `Saved` render — which closed over `Saved` — and
only then runs the new effect. So the sequence is announce("Saved"),
clear("Saved"), announce("Deleted"), and on unmount clear("Deleted").

Once you have seen it once, a lot of effect code stops being surprising. A
cleanup that closes a socket closes *the socket its own run opened*, not the
current one. A cleanup that cancels a request cancels *its own* request. That
pairing is what makes effects composable at all, and it is why the `cancelled`
flag in ex4 works: the flag is a fresh `let` per effect run.

## Further reading

- [react.dev — Synchronizing with Effects](https://react.dev/learn/synchronizing-with-effects) — the model this lesson teaches, including the double-invoke rationale.
- [react.dev — You Might Not Need an Effect](https://react.dev/learn/you-might-not-need-an-effect) — the single most valuable React page on the internet; read it twice.
- [react.dev — Lifecycle of Reactive Effects](https://react.dev/learn/lifecycle-of-reactive-effects) and [Removing Effect Dependencies](https://react.dev/learn/removing-effect-dependencies) — the dependency array, honestly.
- [react.dev — `useEffect` reference](https://react.dev/reference/react/useEffect) — the parameter contract, plus a long list of "I'm having trouble with…" cases.
- [MDN — `EventTarget.removeEventListener`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/EventTarget/removeEventListener) — why the function identity in ex3 matters.
- [MDN — `setInterval`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/setInterval) — including the drift the challenge's alternative fix would introduce.

Two more points about `fetchUser` in the deps. It is correct to include it, and
it is safe here because the gate passes the same function every render. If a
parent created it inline, the effect would refetch on every render — the same
infinite loop through a different door — and the fix belongs in the parent
(`useCallback`, or defining the function outside the component), not in a
shortened dependency array.

Finally, the `cancelled` flag. Even with correct deps, a promise in flight when
the component unmounts will still resolve, and its `.then` will call `setUser`
on something that no longer exists. React tolerates this without complaint
these days, but the work is wasted and — if the component is still mounted with
a *different* id — the answer to a question nobody is asking anymore can
overwrite the answer to the question they are. That is lesson 07.

## challenge — the stale closure, in the wild

This is the bug this lesson exists for. Write out the sequence precisely,
because the precision is what makes it stop being mysterious:

1. `running` becomes `true`, so the effect runs. At that moment `seconds` is
   `0`, and the arrow function passed to `setInterval` closes over that `0`.
2. One second later, the callback runs and calls `setSeconds(0 + 1)`. State
   becomes `1`, the component re-renders.
3. `running` did not change, so the effect does **not** re-run. The interval is
   the same interval, holding the same callback, still closed over `0`.
4. Two seconds later it calls `setSeconds(0 + 1)` again. State is already `1`,
   `Object.is(1, 1)` is true, React bails out. The clock is frozen at 1 forever.

Adding `seconds` to the dependency array does fix the number — the effect now
re-runs after each tick with a fresh closure — but look at what it costs:
`clearInterval` and `setInterval` every second, so the timer restarts from zero
each time and the cadence drifts. That is a real technique for some problems and
the wrong one here.

`setSeconds((previous) => previous + 1)` fixes it properly because the callback
stops reading state altogether. It no longer says "set it to one more than the
value I remember" but "increase whatever it is by one" — a description of a
change rather than a captured value. The effect's dependency list shrinks
honestly to `[running]`, the interval survives, and the deps are now telling the
truth.

The generalisation is worth carrying: **when the dependency array feels like a
fight, the effect is usually reading a value it should have been describing.**
Updater functions, refs, and reducers are all ways of describing a change
without capturing the current state.

## review1 — whose values does a cleanup see?

The gate asserts on the *argument* of `onClear`, which is the only way to
observe the answer. When the message changes from `Saved` to `Deleted`, React
runs the cleanup created by the `Saved` render — which closed over `Saved` — and
only then runs the new effect. So the sequence is announce("Saved"),
clear("Saved"), announce("Deleted"), and on unmount clear("Deleted").

Once you have seen it once, a lot of effect code stops being surprising. A
cleanup that closes a socket closes *the socket its own run opened*, not the
current one. A cleanup that cancels a request cancels *its own* request. That
pairing is what makes effects composable at all, and it is why the `cancelled`
flag in ex4 works: the flag is a fresh `let` per effect run.

## Challenge — the stale closure

Edit `challenge/solution.tsx`. `Stopwatch` is written, compiles, and is wrong.
It renders a live region and `Start` / `Stop` buttons, and while running it
should add one second every second.

Run the gate first and read the failure. Then fix it so that:

- three seconds after Start, the display reads `3`;
- after Stop, time may pass and the display does not move;
- Start again resumes from where it stopped.

Honest difficulty note: the fix is one word. Understanding *why* that word fixes
it is the reason this is the challenge, and the same bug returns as an interview
drill in `i2_interview_drills`.

```
uv run dojo test react 06_effects challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The component is complete and looks right. Run the gate and read what happens
after three seconds. Then ask: the function passed to `setInterval` was created
during one particular render — what is `seconds` worth inside it, three seconds
later?

## Hint 2
It is whatever it was when that render happened, forever. The effect only
re-runs when `running` changes, so the interval callback captured `seconds` at
`0` and every tick computes `0 + 1`. This is a **stale closure**, and it is the
single most common React bug involving timers.

There are two families of fix. One is to stop reading `seconds` at all. The
other is to make the effect re-run whenever `seconds` changes, by adding it to
the dependency array.

## Hint 3
Try the second fix and watch what it costs: the interval is torn down and
recreated every single second, so the clock drifts and the timing is no longer
a clean one-second cadence. The first fix is one word long, uses something you
learned in lesson 03, and needs no new dependency — because the callback stops
reading state and starts describing a change to it. Deciding whether `running`
is still the right dependency after that is the last thing to check.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
The component is complete and looks right. Run the gate and read what happens
after three seconds. Then ask: the function passed to `setInterval` was created
during one particular render — what is `seconds` worth inside it, three seconds
later?

## Hint 2
It is whatever it was when that render happened, forever. The effect only
re-runs when `running` changes, so the interval callback captured `seconds` at
`0` and every tick computes `0 + 1`. This is a **stale closure**, and it is the
single most common React bug involving timers.

There are two families of fix. One is to stop reading `seconds` at all. The
other is to make the effect re-run whenever `seconds` changes, by adding it to
the dependency array.

## Hint 3
Try the second fix and watch what it costs: the interval is torn down and
recreated every single second, so the clock drifts and the timing is no longer
a clean one-second cadence. The first fix is one word long, uses something you
learned in lesson 03, and needs no new dependency — because the callback stops
reading state and starts describing a change to it. Deciding whether `running`
is still the right dependency after that is the last thing to check.

## Exercise 1 — an effect with a cleanup

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `PageTitle({ title })` renders nothing and sets
`document.title` to the `title` prop. When the prop changes the document must
follow, and when the component unmounts the title must be restored to whatever
it was before the component mounted.

```
uv run dojo test react 06_effects ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
`document.title` is not part of React's tree, so setting it is a *side effect* —
something that reaches outside the component. Side effects do not belong in the
render body; they belong in `useEffect`, which React runs after the DOM has
been updated.

## Hint 2
```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  // set it
  return () => {
    // put it back
  };
}, [/* what this effect reads */]);
```

Three parts, all required here: the body, the cleanup it returns, and the
dependency list saying when to run again.

## Hint 3
The cleanup has to restore *the title as it was before this effect ran*, so
capture it inside the effect body before overwriting — a `const` at the top of
the effect closes over exactly the right value, because each run of the effect
gets its own. The remaining decision is the dependency array; the gate
re-renders with a new title and expects the document to follow.
