exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — the dependency array is a claim

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `ThemeSync({ theme, onSync, label })` renders the
`label` in a paragraph and calls `onSync(theme)` **once per theme**, not once
per render. The gate re-renders with a changed `label` and an unchanged
`theme`, and requires that no sync happened.

The stub's effect has no dependency array at all.

```
uv run dojo test react 06_effects ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The stub's effect has no second argument at all, which means "run after every
render". Changing an unrelated prop re-renders the component, so the effect
fires again — and the outside world is told the theme changed when it did not.

## Hint 2
The second argument is an array of the values the effect *reads from the
render*. React compares each one with `Object.is` against the previous run and
skips the effect when they are all the same.

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  onSync(theme);
}, [/* … */]);
```

## Hint 3
Read the effect body and list everything in it that comes from props, state or
anything else defined inside the component. There are two such values here, not
one — and including the second is not paranoia: if the parent passed a
different function next time, an effect that skipped would call the wrong one
forever. Whether you can get away with omitting it, and what it would cost, is
worth thinking through before you decide.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
The stub's effect has no second argument at all, which means "run after every
render". Changing an unrelated prop re-renders the component, so the effect
fires again — and the outside world is told the theme changed when it did not.

## Hint 2
The second argument is an array of the values the effect *reads from the
render*. React compares each one with `Object.is` against the previous run and
skips the effect when they are all the same.

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  onSync(theme);
}, [/* … */]);
```

## Hint 3
Read the effect body and list everything in it that comes from props, state or
anything else defined inside the component. There are two such values here, not
one — and including the second is not paranoia: if the parent passed a
different function next time, an effect that skipped would call the wrong one
forever. Whether you can get away with omitting it, and what it would cost, is
worth thinking through before you decide.

## Exercise 3 — subscribe, and unsubscribe

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `EscapeToClose({ onClose })` listens for `keydown` on
`document` and calls `onClose` when the pressed key is `Escape` — and only
then. When the component unmounts it must stop listening.

The gate presses Escape after unmounting. A component that is still listening
after it is gone fails, which is exactly what a leak looks like in production.

```
uv run dojo test react 06_effects ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The key press can happen anywhere on the page, not just inside this component,
so a React `onKeyDown` prop will not see it. You need a real DOM listener on
`document` — which is outside React's tree, which means an effect.

## Hint 2
```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  function handleKeyDown(event: KeyboardEvent) { … }
  document.addEventListener("keydown", handleKeyDown);
  return () => { … };
}, [/* … */]);
```

Declare the handler *inside* the effect. `removeEventListener` only removes a
listener if you pass it the exact same function reference, and a handler
defined inside the effect is guaranteed to be the same one both times.

## Hint 3
`event.key` is the string `"Escape"` for that key — check it before calling
`onClose`, or every keystroke on the page closes the dialog. The dependency
array should list what the effect reads; think about what happens to the
subscription each time that value changes, and whether re-subscribing is a
problem or exactly right.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — fetching on mount

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `UserBadge({ userId, fetchUser })` calls
`fetchUser(userId)` and renders the resulting `name` in a paragraph. Before the
promise settles it renders nothing.

`fetchUser` is a **prop**, not an import. Every data-fetching exercise in this
track works that way: the function that talks to the network is injected, so
the gate can hand you a deterministic fake and there is never a real request.
That is also good production design — a component that takes its data source as
a prop is testable, mockable and reusable.

The gate re-renders with the same `userId` and requires that no second request
happens. Getting that wrong is an infinite fetch loop.

```
uv run dojo test react 06_effects ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
`fetchUser` returns a promise, so this cannot happen during render — rendering
must be synchronous and must not have side effects. Kick the request off in an
effect and put the result in state; the state change is what re-renders the
name into view.

## Hint 2
```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  fetchUser(userId).then((result) => setUser(result));
}, [/* … */]);
```

The dependency array is the whole exercise. Leave it out and every render
fetches, every fetch sets state, every state change renders — an infinite loop
that will hammer a real API. List the values the effect reads.

## Hint 3
There is one more thing worth adding even though the gate does not force it

## Hint 1
`fetchUser` returns a promise, so this cannot happen during render — rendering
must be synchronous and must not have side effects. Kick the request off in an
effect and put the result in state; the state change is what re-renders the
name into view.

## Hint 2
```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  fetchUser(userId).then((result) => setUser(result));
}, [/* … */]);
```

The dependency array is the whole exercise. Leave it out and every render
fetches, every fetch sets state, every state change renders — an infinite loop
that will hammer a real API. List the values the effect reads.

## Hint 3
There is one more thing worth adding even though the gate does not force it
here: if the component unmounts (or the id changes) while a request is in
flight, the `.then` still runs and calls `setUser` on a component that has
moved on. A cleanup that flips a local `cancelled` flag, checked before setting
state, is the standard guard — and lesson 07 turns that idea into a full race
condition you have to defeat.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
One effect, one cleanup, and a dependency array. The announcement happens in
the effect body; the retraction happens in the cleanup it returns. Both are
handed the message they are about.

## Hint 2
The interesting question is *which* message the cleanup should pass. Look at
the gate: when the message changes from `Saved` to `Deleted`, it expects
`onClear("Saved")` — the old one. You do not have to arrange that; it falls out
of how closures work, as long as the cleanup reads the same `message` variable
its own effect run did.

## Hint 3
React's order on an update is: run the previous cleanup, then run the new
effect. Each effect run and its cleanup belong to the same render and therefore
see the same props. The last decision is the dependency array — list everything
the effect and its cleanup read between them.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
One effect, one cleanup, and a dependency array. The announcement happens in
the effect body; the retraction happens in the cleanup it returns. Both are
handed the message they are about.

## Hint 2
The interesting question is *which* message the cleanup should pass. Look at
the gate: when the message changes from `Saved` to `Deleted`, it expects
`onClear("Saved")` — the old one. You do not have to arrange that; it falls out
of how closures work, as long as the cleanup reads the same `message` variable
its own effect run did.

## Hint 3
React's order on an update is: run the previous cleanup, then run the new
effect. Each effect run and its cleanup belong to the same render and therefore
see the same props. The last decision is the dependency array — list everything
the effect and its cleanup read between them.

# 07 — Data fetching Lesson 06 ended with a component that fetched a user and rendered the name. That component is a demo, not a feature, and this lesson is the difference. A real request has three outcomes, not one. It can still be running, it can succeed, and it can fail — and every one of those is a thing the user has to be able to see. A component that only renders the success case shows a blank rectangle while the network is slow and shows the same blank rectangle forever when the server returns a 500, with the actual error visible only to whoever opens the console. That is not an edge case; it is the ordinary experience of using a slow connection. Then there is the problem that makes data fetching genuinely hard, and it is not about React at all. **Requests do not come back in the order you sent them.** Type `re` into a search box and then `react`, and the server may well answer `react` in 40ms and `re` in 300ms. The second answer to arrive is for a query nobody is looking at, and unless you do something about it, it wins — because it wrote to state last. Exercise 3 makes exactly this happen, and the fix is three lines you will use for the rest of your career. One convention for the whole lesson: **the fetcher is always a prop.** No component here imports `fetch` or calls an API module directly; each takes a function like `fetchUser: (id) => Promise` and calls that. It makes the gates deterministic — they hand you promises they control by hand — and it makes the components honest about what they depend on. ## Concept — three states, and the answer you no longer want **The three states.** The minimum viable shape: ```tsx const [data, setData] = useState(null); const [error, setError] = useState(null); const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true); useEffect(() => { setLoading(true); setError(null); fetchThing(id) .then((result) => setData(result)) .catch((problem: unknown) => setError(String(problem))) .finally(() => setLoading(false)); }, [id, fetchThing]); if (loading) return

Loading

; if (error) return

{error}

; return ; ``` Three things in there are deliberate. `loading` starts `true`, because the first render happens before the effect ever runs. `.finally` stops the spinner on both paths, so there is no way to forget one. And the error is announced in a `role="alert"` region while the wait is announced in a `role="status"` one — a spinner nobody can see is not a loading state. **The race.** Now the hard part. Picture two renders in quick succession: ``` render(userId="1") → effect starts request A render(userId="2") → cleanup, then effect starts request B B resolves → setUser(second) ✓ correct A resolves → setUser(first) ✗ and it wins ``` React did nothing wrong. The `.then` attached to request A is a closure that outlived the effect that created it, and promises have no cancel button — once `fetchUser("1")` is in flight, its `.then` *will* run. The fix is to make the result irrelevant rather than to prevent it: ```tsx useEffect(() => { let current = true; fetchUser(userId).then((result) => { if (!current) return; // this effect has been superseded setUser(result); }); return () => { current = false; // …and this is where that happened }; }, [userId, fetchUser]); ``` `current` is declared **inside the effect body**, so every run gets its own, and the cleanup that runs when the id changes flips exactly the flag belonging to the request it is retiring. A `useRef` or a module-level variable would be shared between runs and would not work. The stronger version cancels the request for real: ```tsx const controller = new AbortController(); fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal }); return () => controller.abort(); ``` That saves the bandwidth as well as the confusion, and is what you want once the fetcher is really `fetch`. The flag is the version that works with *any* promise, including the injected fakes here. **Where this goes in real work.** Everything above is what a data-fetching library — TanStack Query, SWR, a framework's loader — does for you, along with caching, deduplication and retries. You are writing it by hand once so that when you adopt one of those you know what it is protecting you from, and so that you can answer the interview question about it. ## Exercise 1 — loading, then data Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `UserCard({ userId, fetchUser })`: - while the request is in flight, render a live region (`role="status"`) containing the word `Loading`; - once it resolves, render the user's `name` in a level-2 heading and no loading region. ``` uv run dojo test react 07_data_fetching ex1 ``` ## Exercise 2 — and failure Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `Profile({ userId, fetchUser })` does everything `UserCard` does, plus: when the promise rejects, render the error's `message` inside a `role="alert"` region, and stop loading. The gate rejects with `new Error("User not found")` and expects that string on screen. ``` uv run dojo test react 07_data_fetching ex2 ``` ## Exercise 3 — the race Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `ProfileViewer` is written and looks correct. The gate renders it with `userId="1"`, immediately re-renders with `userId="2"`, then resolves the **second** request, then resolves the **first** one. After all that, the screen must show the second user. Run it before changing anything and watch the stale answer win. ``` uv run dojo test react 07_data_fetching ex3 ``` ## Exercise 4 — try again Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `RetryableUser({ userId, fetchUser })` renders the error case with a button reading `Try again` that re-runs the same request. After a successful retry the error region is gone and the name is shown. The gate's fetcher fails the first time and succeeds the second, and checks it was called exactly twice. ``` uv run dojo test react 07_data_fetching ex4 ``` ## Challenge — pagination Edit `challenge/solution.tsx`. `PaginatedList({ fetchPage })` where `fetchPage(page)` resolves to `{ items: string[], hasMore: boolean }`: - loads page 1 on mount and renders its items as a list; - has buttons `Previous` and `Next` that move one page at a time; - `Previous` is disabled on page 1; `Next` is disabled when the last response said `hasMore: false`; - shows **only** the current page's items. Honest difficulty note: the trap is deciding what is state. If you find yourself storing the items *and* a page number *and* a "can I go forward" flag, step back and ask which of those the server already tells you. ``` uv run dojo test react 07_data_fetching challenge ``` ## Review — the search box race `review1/solution.tsx`. `SearchResults({ query, fetchResults })` renders the results as a list. The gate races two queries against each other the same way ex3 does; the current query's results must survive. ``` uv run dojo test react 07_data_fetching review1 ```

# Reading — react/07_data_fetching

## Notes

**Why fetching in an effect is awkward at all.** Rendering is synchronous and
must be pure, so a component cannot wait for data while it renders. That leaves
"render nothing useful, start a request, render again when it arrives", which is
what every one of these exercises does. The awkwardness is real and React knows
it: `Suspense`, server components and framework loaders all exist to move the
waiting somewhere better. Understanding the manual version is still the
foundation, because the failure modes are the same wherever the fetch lives.

**Injected dependencies are not a testing hack.** Taking `fetchUser` as a prop
is dependency inversion: the component declares the *shape* of what it needs
rather than naming an implementation. The payoff in this course is deterministic
gates with no network and no mocking library. The payoff in production is a
component you can reuse against a different backend, a cached client, or a
Storybook fixture without touching it.

**Promises cannot be cancelled.** This is the fact everything else follows from.
`promise.then(f)` schedules `f`; there is no API to unschedule it. `AbortController`
does not cancel the promise either — it aborts the *underlying operation* and
causes the promise to reject with an `AbortError`, which the `fetch` API opts
into. For any promise you did not create, the only defence is to ignore its
result.

**Every asynchronous update needs an owner check.** The general pattern is: when
an async operation completes, ask "is this still the operation the component
wants?" before writing state. A boolean flag scoped to the effect run answers
that question for the common case. Libraries answer it with request keys and a
cache, which is the same idea generalised.

**Four states, not three.** The honest enumeration of a request is idle,
loading, success, error — and "idle" matters as soon as the request is triggered
by something other than mounting. Modelling them as separate booleans lets you
express impossible combinations (`loading && error`); modelling them as one
discriminated union (`{ status: "loading" } | { status: "error", message } | …`)
makes those unrepresentable. The TypeScript track's `04_unions_narrowing` is the
same idea from the other end.

## ex1 — why `loading` starts `true`

The first render happens before any effect runs. If `loading` starts `false`,
that render says "not loading, no data" and produces an empty card, which is
then replaced by the spinner one tick later — a flash of nothing that looks like
a bug on a fast connection and looks like a broken layout on a slow one.
Starting at `true` says the truthful thing: we have not asked yet, so we are
certainly not done.

The choice of `role="status"` for the spinner is the accessibility half. A
visual spinner communicates nothing to a screen reader; a polite live region
containing the word "Loading" is announced when it appears. The refinement real
applications add is `aria-busy` on the region being replaced, and not
announcing anything at all for waits under a few hundred milliseconds — a
spinner that flashes for 80ms is worse than no spinner.

The dependency array is the same discipline as lesson 06: `[userId, fetchUser]`,
because both are read. `fetchUser` being a stable reference is the caller's
responsibility, and if the caller gets it wrong, the symptom is an infinite
fetch loop — which is exactly why it belongs in the array rather than being
quietly omitted.

## ex2 — the failure path, and `unknown`

`.finally` is the small structural win here: the spinner stops on both paths
with one line, and there is no branch left in which you can forget it.

The TypeScript detail is worth its own paragraph because it comes up in
interviews. In a `catch`, the caught value is typed `unknown`, not `Error` —
JavaScript lets you `throw` anything, including a string or `undefined`, and
`useUnknownInCatchVariables` (part of `strict`) makes TypeScript admit it. So
you narrow: `problem instanceof Error ? problem.message : "Something went wrong"`.
Writing `catch (e: any) { setError(e.message) }` produces `undefined` on screen
the day something throws a string.

A design question the exercise raises without answering: should the error be
the raw message from the server? Usually not. `Failed to fetch` and
`Unexpected token < in JSON at position 0` mean nothing to a user; a real
implementation maps known failures to sentences a person can act on and keeps
the raw text for the log. The gate asks for `error.message` because that is what
is checkable, not because it is what you would ship.

Also notice `setError(null)` at the *start* of each request. Without it, a
failed load followed by a successful one leaves the old error on screen next to
fresh data — a specific, common, extremely confusing bug.

## ex3 — the race, in detail

The sequence the gate performs is the whole lesson:

1. Render with `userId="1"`. Effect starts request A.
2. Re-render with `userId="2"`. React runs the previous effect's cleanup, then
   the new effect, which starts request B. **Request A is still in flight.**
3. B resolves. `setUser(second)`. Correct.
4. A resolves. Its `.then` — a closure created back in step 1 — runs and calls
   `setUser(first)`. The screen now shows a user the component stopped caring
   about two steps ago.

Nothing here is a React bug, and no dependency array fixes it. The `.then`
callback was scheduled before the cleanup ran, and there is no mechanism to
unschedule it.

The `let current = true` inside the effect works because of scoping. Each run of
the effect body creates a fresh binding; the `.then` closure and the cleanup
closure both capture *that* binding. When the id changes, the cleanup for run 1
sets run 1's `current` to `false`, and run 2's `current` is untouched. Hoisting
the flag to a `useRef` breaks this immediately — there would be one flag shared
by every run, and retiring the old request would also retire the new one.

The `AbortController` version is strictly better when the transport supports it,
because it stops the work rather than discarding it: less bandwidth, less server
load, and the promise rejects with an `AbortError` you then have to remember not
to display as an error. The two techniques compose — abort what you can, ignore
what you cannot.

Why this is *the* interview question: it is invisible in code review, never
reproduces locally, and the correct answer demonstrates that you understand
closures, effect cleanup, and promise semantics at once. If you can narrate the
four steps above, you have answered it.

## ex4 — making the request callable from two places

The structural move — hoist the request into a named function that both the
effect and a handler call — is one you will make constantly, and it exposes a
tension worth understanding. A function declared in a component body is a new
value on every render. Put it in the effect's dependency array and the effect
re-runs every render, which is an infinite fetch loop. Leave it out and the
linter is right that you are lying.

`useCallback(fn, deps)` resolves it by returning the *same* function object
until its dependencies change, so `[load]` becomes an honest dependency that
changes exactly when `userId` or `fetchUser` does. This is the one situation
where `useCallback` is not a performance optimisation but a correctness tool —
it makes a dependency array truthful — and it is worth separating from the
memoization use in lesson 11.

The alternative shapes, both legitimate: move the fetching function outside the
component so it is never recreated, or give the retry a "nonce" piece of state
(`const [attempt, setAttempt] = useState(0)`) and put `attempt` in the effect's
dependency array so clicking Try again just increments it. The second is
delightfully simple and worth knowing.

## challenge — what is state and what is an answer

The design pressure in this exercise is real and shows up in every list UI. It
is tempting to store `items`, `page`, `hasMore`, `loading`, and maybe
`canGoNext` — five pieces of state, several of which restate each other. Ask
which one the *user* changes: the page number. Everything else either arrives
from the server as a unit (`items`, `hasMore`) or is computed during render
(`disabled`).

Replacing rather than appending is what the "no items from page 1" assertion is
about. Appending is the correct behaviour for an infinite scroll and the wrong
behaviour for pagination, and the bug where a "load more" implementation gets
reused for pages is common enough to be worth naming.

The race applies here too, and more visibly than anywhere else: click Next
twice quickly and two page requests are running. Without the guard, the slower
one wins and you land on a page whose number does not match its contents. Real
pagination also has to decide what to show *while* loading — the old page
greyed out, a skeleton, or nothing — and each choice has a different feel. There
is no correct answer, only a decided one.

## review1 — the same bug, where users actually meet it

Search-as-you-type is where the race stops being theoretical: the query changes
several times a second, every keystroke starts a request, and the results
flicker between queries as answers arrive out of order. Users describe this as
"the search is broken", and they are right.

The fix is identical to ex3, which is the point of it being the review
exercise: one technique, two places, and the shape is now familiar enough to
write without thinking. The natural next question — should you be firing a
request per keystroke at all? — is answered by debouncing, which you build from
scratch as a custom hook in `10_custom_hooks` and use in the interview drills.
Debouncing reduces the number of races; it does not eliminate them, so you want
both.

## Further reading

- [react.dev — Synchronizing with Effects: "Fetching data"](https://react.dev/learn/synchronizing-with-effects#fetching-data) — the race, the cleanup flag, and React's own advice about using a framework or library instead.
- [react.dev — You Might Not Need an Effect](https://react.dev/learn/you-might-not-need-an-effect) — worth rereading now that you have written four effects that genuinely needed to exist.
- [MDN — `AbortController`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortController) — real cancellation, and the `AbortError` you have to handle afterwards.
- [MDN — `Promise.prototype.finally`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Promise/finally) — the one-line "always stop the spinner".
- [MDN — Using the Fetch API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Fetch_API/Using_Fetch) — including the detail that a 404 does not reject.
- [Testing Library — Async methods](https://testing-library.com/docs/dom-testing-library/api-async/) — `findBy*` and `waitFor`, and why you should not `waitFor` an assertion that can pass at the wrong time.

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — pagination

Edit `challenge/solution.tsx`. `PaginatedList({ fetchPage })` where
`fetchPage(page)` resolves to `{ items: string[], hasMore: boolean }`:

- loads page 1 on mount and renders its items as a list;
- has buttons `Previous` and `Next` that move one page at a time;
- `Previous` is disabled on page 1; `Next` is disabled when the last response
  said `hasMore: false`;
- shows **only** the current page's items.

Honest difficulty note: the trap is deciding what is state. If you find
yourself storing the items *and* a page number *and* a "can I go forward" flag,
step back and ask which of those the server already tells you.

```
uv run dojo test react 07_data_fetching challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Only one thing is really state here: the page number. The items and the
`hasMore` flag are the *answer* for that page — they arrive from the server and
get replaced wholesale when the page changes. Buttons do not fetch; buttons
change the page number, and the effect notices.

## Hint 2
That gives you the shape:

```tsx
const [page, setPage] = useState(1);
const [data, setData] = useState<Page | null>(null);

useEffect(() => {
  // fetch this page, store the result
}, [page, fetchPage]);
```

`Previous` and `Next` are one line each — they only move `page`. Both buttons'
`disabled` values are derived during render, not stored: `page === 1` for one,
and something about the last response for the other.

## Hint 3
Two details decide whether this is production quality. Replacing `data` rather
than appending is what stops page 1 and page 2 being on screen together. And
the same race you fixed in ex3 applies here — click Next twice quickly and two
requests are in flight — so carry the cleanup guard across. What to show while
a page is loading (the spinner, the previous page, both) is a real product
decision the gate leaves to you.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Only one thing is really state here: the page number. The items and the
`hasMore` flag are the *answer* for that page — they arrive from the server and
get replaced wholesale when the page changes. Buttons do not fetch; buttons
change the page number, and the effect notices.

## Hint 2
That gives you the shape:

```tsx
const [page, setPage] = useState(1);
const [data, setData] = useState<Page | null>(null);

useEffect(() => {
  // fetch this page, store the result
}, [page, fetchPage]);
```

`Previous` and `Next` are one line each — they only move `page`. Both buttons'
`disabled` values are derived during render, not stored: `page === 1` for one,
and something about the last response for the other.

## Hint 3
Two details decide whether this is production quality. Replacing `data` rather
than appending is what stops page 1 and page 2 being on screen together. And
the same race you fixed in ex3 applies here — click Next twice quickly and two
requests are in flight — so carry the cleanup guard across. What to show while
a page is loading (the spinner, the previous page, both) is a real product
decision the gate leaves to you.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — and failure

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `Profile({ userId, fetchUser })` does everything
`UserCard` does, plus: when the promise rejects, render the error's `message`
inside a `role="alert"` region, and stop loading.

The gate rejects with `new Error("User not found")` and expects that string on
screen.

```
uv run dojo test react 07_data_fetching ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The stub only handles the happy path, so a rejected promise leaves `loading`
stuck at `true` forever and the user stares at a spinner that will never stop.
Add the third piece of state, and make sure loading stops on *both* outcomes.

## Hint 2
```tsx
fetchUser(userId)
  .then((result) => setUser(result))
  .catch((problem: unknown) => /* … */)
  .finally(() => setLoading(false));
```

`.finally` runs either way, which is exactly the guarantee "the spinner always
stops" needs. Doing it in both branches by hand works too, and is one more
place to forget.

## Hint 3
The gate wants the error's own message on screen, so pull it out of what you
caught — and note that in TypeScript a caught value is `unknown`, not `Error`,
because anything can be thrown. `problem instanceof Error ? problem.message : …`
narrows it safely. Render the error in a `role="alert"` region, and think about
what should happen to a *previous* error when the id changes and a new request
starts.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
The stub only handles the happy path, so a rejected promise leaves `loading`
stuck at `true` forever and the user stares at a spinner that will never stop.
Add the third piece of state, and make sure loading stops on *both* outcomes.

## Hint 2
```tsx
fetchUser(userId)
  .then((result) => setUser(result))
  .catch((problem: unknown) => /* … */)
  .finally(() => setLoading(false));
```

`.finally` runs either way, which is exactly the guarantee "the spinner always
stops" needs. Doing it in both branches by hand works too, and is one more
place to forget.

## Hint 3
The gate wants the error's own message on screen, so pull it out of what you
caught — and note that in TypeScript a caught value is `unknown`, not `Error`,
because anything can be thrown. `problem instanceof Error ? problem.message : …`
narrows it safely. Render the error in a `role="alert"` region, and think about
what should happen to a *previous* error when the id changes and a new request
starts.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Run the gate and read the sequence it describes. Two requests are in flight at
once, the second one answers first, and then the first one answers — and wins,
because it wrote to state last. Nothing about the code is wrong in isolation;
the problem is that a `.then` from an effect that has already been cleaned up
still runs.

## Hint 2
When the id changes, React runs the previous effect's cleanup before starting
the new one. That cleanup is your chance to mark the old request as no longer
interesting. A variable declared *inside the effect body* is perfect for this:
each run of the effect gets its own, and the cleanup closes over exactly the
one that belongs to it.

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  let current = true;
  …
  return () => {
    current = false;
  };
}, [/* … */]);
```

## Hint 3
Check that flag in the `.then` before touching any state, and return early when
it is false. Note that this does not *cancel* the request — the promise still
settles and the network traffic still happened — it makes the answer
irrelevant. Cancelling for real needs `AbortController`, which is worth reading
about; deciding whether this component needs it is your call.

## Hint 1
Right now the fetching lives inside the effect, and an effect cannot be called
from a click handler. So the first move is structural: lift the whole "start a
request and record what happens" routine into a function that both the effect
and the button can call.

## Hint 2
```tsx
function load() {
  setLoading(true);
  setError(null);
  fetchUser(userId).then(…).catch(…).finally(…);
}

useEffect(() => {
  load();
}, [/* … */]);
…
<button type="button" onClick={load}>Try again</button>
```

Clearing the previous error at the *start* of `load` is what makes the alert
disappear when the retry succeeds.

## Hint 3
There is a wrinkle. A plain `function load()` is a brand-new function on every
render, so putting it in the effect's dependency array would refetch forever,
and leaving it out is the lie the linter warns about. `useCallback(fn, [deps])`
hands back the same function until its own dependencies change, which makes the
dependency array honest. It is properly taught in lesson 11 — for now, wrap
`load` in it and list what `load` reads.

## Hint 1
This is a search box, so the query changes on almost every keystroke and
several requests are always in flight. The one that answers last wins the
screen, and "last" has nothing to do with which query the user is actually
looking at.

## Hint 2
Same shape as ex3: a flag local to each effect run, flipped by that run's
cleanup, checked before the state update.

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  let current = true;
  …
  return () => { current = false; };
}, [query, fetchResults]);
```

## Hint 3
Note what the flag has to be: a `let` declared *inside* the effect body, not a
`useRef` and not a module variable. Each effect run needs its own, so that the
cleanup for the `re` request can retire that request without touching the one
for `react`. Whether you would also debounce the query before fetching at all
is the next question — and it is exactly what lesson 10 builds.

# 08 — Refs and the DOM

Everything so far has been declarative: you describe the UI, React makes the
DOM match. That covers most of what a UI needs, and then there is the residue.
You cannot describe "this input is focused". You cannot describe "scroll this
element into view", "play this video", "measure how tall that is", or "select
the text in that box". Those are **imperative** operations on a real node, and
for them you need the node.

`useRef` is how you get it. It is a small hook with two quite different jobs,
and confusing them is where most ref bugs come from.

The first job is the one everybody meets first: a ref attached to a JSX element
gives you that element's DOM node. The second is subtler and just as useful: a
ref is **a box that survives re-renders and does not cause them**. State that
nobody looks at — the id of a timer you need to cancel, a count you only read in
a handler, the previous value of a prop — belongs in a ref, because putting it
in state would render the component for no visible reason.

The rule that keeps both jobs straight: **if changing it should change what is
on screen, it is state. If it should not, it is a ref.**

## Concept — a box, and sometimes a node

```tsx
const field = useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null);
const timerId = useRef<number | null>(null);
```

`useRef(initial)` returns `{ current: initial }` — the *same object* on every
render, so writing `field.current = x` persists, and writing it never schedules
a render. That is the whole API.

**As a DOM handle.** Pass the ref to an element's `ref` attribute and React
fills it in when it commits the node, and sets it back to `null` when the node
is removed:

```tsx
<input ref={field} />
```

Two consequences follow. During render `field.current` is still whatever it was
*before* this render committed, so reading it while rendering is meaningless —
which is why every DOM operation goes in an effect or an event handler. And the
node can be gone, so `field.current?.focus()` rather than `field.current.focus()`.

**As a mutable box.** No element, no `ref` attribute, just persistence:

```tsx
const renders = useRef(0);
renders.current += 1;             // no re-render, ever
```

Compare the alternatives: a module-level `let` would be shared by every
instance of the component, and a `let` inside the body would reset on every
render. A ref is per-instance and persistent, which is exactly the gap.

**Passing a ref through your own component.** In React 19, `ref` is an ordinary
prop for function components, so a wrapper forwards it by handing it on:

```tsx
function FancyInput({ label, ref }: { label: string; ref?: Ref<HTMLInputElement> }) {
  return <input ref={ref} />;
}
```

Before React 19 this required `forwardRef`, which you will still meet in
existing code; it does the same thing with more ceremony.

**Choosing what the parent gets.** Sometimes the DOM node is the wrong thing to
hand over — the parent would then be able to do *anything* to it, including
things that fight with React. `useImperativeHandle` lets you expose a small
object of your own design instead:

```tsx
useImperativeHandle(ref, () => ({
  focus: () => field.current?.focus(),
  clear: () => setText(""),
}), []);
```

Now `ref.current` is that object and nothing else. Use this sparingly: it is an
escape hatch from one-way data flow, and every method you expose is a promise
you have to keep. But for "focus me", "reset me", "scroll to me" it is the
right tool, and it is what real component libraries do.

**A word on when *not* to reach for refs.** Do not read or write DOM state that
React is managing — setting `input.value` directly on a controlled input, adding
a class React will overwrite, removing a node React thinks it owns. Refs are for
things React has no opinion about.

## Exercise 1 — a DOM handle

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `AutoFocusInput({ label })` renders a labelled input
and focuses it when it first appears.

```
uv run dojo test react 08_refs_dom ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — memory without renders

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `ClickTracker({ onRender })` has two buttons:

- `Tap` — increments a count that **must not** cause a re-render;
- `Show total` — reveals the count in a live region reading `3 taps`, which
  **must** cause exactly one re-render.

The `onRender` probe is already wired up, as in lesson 03. Before `Show total`
is pressed, nothing with `role="status"` may exist.

```
uv run dojo test react 08_refs_dom ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — passing a ref through

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `FancyInput({ label, ref })` renders a labelled input
and forwards the `ref` it was given to that input, so a parent holding the ref
can focus it.

```
uv run dojo test react 08_refs_dom ex3
```

## Challenge — an imperative handle

Edit `challenge/solution.tsx`. `Editor({ label, ref })` renders a labelled
`<textarea>` whose text is controlled state. A parent holding a ref to it must
get an object with exactly two methods:

- `focus()` — focuses the textarea;
- `clear()` — empties it.

Forwarding the ref to the textarea will not do, because `clear` has to change
React state and a DOM node cannot.

The gate renders **two** editors, one with a ref and one without, and checks
that clearing one does not touch the other.

Honest difficulty note: `useImperativeHandle` is new here, and the hints give
you its shape. The `useId` already in the stub is there because two instances
are on screen.

```
uv run dojo test react 08_refs_dom challenge
```

## Review — focus management

`review1/solution.tsx`. `FocusOnOpen` renders a button reading `Open`. Clicking
it shows a `role="dialog"` containing a `Close` button, and **focus moves to
that Close button**. Clicking Close removes the dialog and **returns focus to
the Open button**.

This is the single most-skipped piece of dialog behaviour in real applications,
and it is the difference between a modal a keyboard user can use and one that
strands them.

```
uv run dojo test react 08_refs_dom review1
```

# Reading — react/08_refs_dom

## Notes

**A ref is a mutable box, and that is the whole implementation.** `useRef(x)`
allocates `{ current: x }` once per component instance and hands back the same
object forever. It is `useState` minus the render — literally, in that React
implements it with the same slot mechanism. Everything else about refs follows
from that: writes are invisible to React, reads during render are unreliable,
and the object identity is stable so it never needs to appear in a dependency
array.

**When React fills a DOM ref.** During the commit phase, after the DOM has been
mutated and before `useLayoutEffect` runs, React sets `ref.current` for every
attached node — and sets it to `null` for nodes it is removing. So by the time
any effect runs, refs are populated. During render they hold the *previous*
value, which is why reading them there is a bug even when it appears to work.

**State versus ref, decided in one question.** Does the value appear on screen,
directly or indirectly? Then it is state. Timer ids, "have I already scrolled",
the previous value of a prop, a mutable cache, a subscription object — none of
those are rendered, so they are refs. The failure mode of getting it wrong in
one direction is a stale screen; in the other, a component that re-renders on
every mouse move.

**`ref` is not `key`, and neither is a normal prop — except now it is.** React
19 made `ref` a regular prop for function components, so `forwardRef` is no
longer needed (it still works and is not being removed imminently). `key`
remains special and is still never visible in props.

**Imperative handles are an escape hatch with a cost.** Exposing methods
inverts React's data flow — the parent now *commands* the child rather than
describing what it wants — and that makes the interaction invisible to anyone
reading the JSX. The cases where it is genuinely right are small and
well-known: focus, scroll, select, play/pause, and resetting an uncontrolled
subtree. Anything you could express as a prop should be a prop.

## ex1 — the two-step that every DOM operation needs

The pattern — declare a ref, attach it, act on it in an effect — is the whole
of DOM access in React, and the reason it is two steps rather than one is worth
holding on to. Render describes what should exist; it does not create anything.
The node exists only after React commits, so the earliest moment you can touch
it is an effect.

Autofocus itself deserves a caveat that the exercise cannot express: it is a
usability decision, not a default. Focusing a field on page load moves a
screen-reader user past whatever came before it, and on mobile it opens the
keyboard and hides half the screen. The right places for it are narrow — a
search overlay the user just opened, the first field of a dialog, an inline edit
they just triggered — and they share the property that the user *asked* to be
put there.

`field.current?.focus()` rather than `field.current.focus()` is not defensive
noise. `current` is genuinely `HTMLInputElement | null` in the type system,
because React nulls it when the node unmounts, and the optional chain is the
honest way to say "if it is still there".

## ex2 — the other job of `useRef`

The render probe makes something visible that is normally invisible: the tap
count changes three times and the component does not render. That is the
distinction the exercise exists for. State is "the screen depends on this"; a
ref is "I need to remember this, and nothing on screen cares yet".

Notice which piece of the exercise is which. The count is a ref because nothing
displays it. The *revealed* total is state because something does. And the
moment you press Show total, the ref's value is copied into state — which is
the normal way these two cooperate.

The rule about not reading refs during render is worth understanding rather than
memorising. React reserves the right to render a component without committing
it (concurrent rendering does this — it can start a render, abandon it, and
start again), so a render that reads `taps.current` may be reading a value from
a render that never happened, or may be about to be thrown away. Event handlers
and effects run after a commit, so they see reality.

The classic production uses of a mutable ref: holding the id returned by
`setInterval` so a cleanup can clear it, holding the previous value of a prop to
compare against, holding an instance of a non-React library (a map, a chart, an
editor), and holding "has this already run" flags. All invisible, all persistent.

## ex3 — forwarding, and what React 19 changed

The fix was one attribute, which is the point: the machinery is now boring. It
is worth knowing what it replaced, because you will read code that uses it.
Before React 19:

```tsx
const FancyInput = forwardRef<HTMLInputElement, Props>(function FancyInput(props, ref) {
  return <input ref={ref} />;
});
```

`forwardRef` existed because `ref` was stripped from props before your component
saw them, so a wrapper had no way to receive one. React 19 removed that special
case for function components. Class components still have the old behaviour, and
`forwardRef` still works, so both forms will coexist in real codebases for
years.

The design point underneath is more durable than the API. Any component that
wraps a form control should let a ref through. Form libraries need it to focus
the first invalid field; design systems need it for tooltips and popovers to
position against; test code needs it for the occasional escape. A wrapper that
swallows refs gets forked, in exactly the same way as one that swallows
`className`.

## challenge — designing what the parent may do

The exercise is constructed so that forwarding the DOM node cannot work.
`focus()` is a DOM operation, but `clear()` has to set React state — the
textarea is controlled, so writing `node.value = ""` would be overwritten by the
next render, and would not update `text`. The only thing that can offer both is
an object that closes over the component's internals, which is exactly what
`useImperativeHandle` publishes.

Two details in the reference are deliberate. The internal `field` ref still
exists, because `focus` needs a real node — the imperative handle sits *beside*
the DOM ref, not instead of it. And the dependency array is `[]` because the
returned object's methods only close over things that are stable (the setter and
the ref object), so there is no reason to rebuild it. If a method closed over a
prop, that prop would belong in the array, and forgetting it would give the
parent a handle that calls yesterday's version — a stale closure with a new
face.

The larger judgement: two methods is a good handle, ten is a component that has
been turned inside out. Every method is API surface, and imperative API is
harder to change than props because callers invoke it from arbitrary places. If
you find the handle growing, the state it manipulates probably wants to be
lifted into the parent instead.

## review1 — focus is the keyboard user's cursor

The two directions fail differently, and both fail silently for anyone using a
mouse.

Opening without moving focus leaves a keyboard user parked on the trigger
button, behind the dialog they just opened; they have no idea it exists and
tabbing walks them through the page underneath it. Closing without restoring
focus is worse: the focused element is removed from the document, so the browser
resets focus to `<body>`, and the next Tab starts from the very top of the page.
Users experience this as "it jumped".

The mechanics show the two timings from ex1 in one component. Focusing the close
button has to wait for it to exist, so it goes in an effect keyed on `open`.
Restoring focus to the opener can happen right in the handler, because that
button never left the document. If you tried both in effects, or both in
handlers, one of them would be reaching for a `null` ref.

Everything a real dialog owes its users beyond this: trapping Tab inside it
while it is open, closing on Escape, marking the rest of the page inert, and
labelling the dialog. That is why the honest recommendation is the native
`<dialog>` element or a maintained library — but knowing what those are doing
for you is what lets you tell a good one from a bad one.

## Further reading

- [react.dev — Referencing Values with Refs](https://react.dev/learn/referencing-values-with-refs) — the mutable-box job, and when to prefer state.
- [react.dev — Manipulating the DOM with Refs](https://react.dev/learn/manipulating-the-dom-with-refs) — the DOM job, including refs to a list of nodes.
- [react.dev — `useImperativeHandle`](https://react.dev/reference/react/useImperativeHandle) and [`forwardRef`](https://react.dev/reference/react/forwardRef) — the challenge, and the API React 19 made unnecessary.
- [MDN — `HTMLElement.focus()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/HTMLElement/focus) — including `preventScroll`, which you will eventually need.
- [MDN — `document.activeElement`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Document/activeElement) — what `toHaveFocus()` is really checking.
- [WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices — Dialog (Modal): keyboard interaction](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/dialog-modal/) — the full focus contract the review exercise starts.

// Gate for react/08_refs_dom. Quoted verbatim in README.md.
import { render, screen } from "@testing-library/react";
import userEvent from "@testing-library/user-event";
import { useRef } from "react";
import { describe, expect, test, vi } from "vitest";

import { AutoFocusInput } from "./ex1/solution";
import { ClickTracker } from "./ex2/solution";
import { FancyInput } from "./ex3/solution";
import { Editor, type EditorHandle } from "./challenge/solution";
import { FocusOnOpen } from "./review1/solution";

describe("08_refs_dom", () => {
  test("ex1 - AutoFocusInput takes focus as soon as it appears", () => {
    render(<AutoFocusInput label="Email" />);

    expect(
      screen.getByLabelText("Email"),
      "the field is on screen but nothing is focused, so a keyboard user has " +
        "to tab to it. Point a ref at the input and call .focus() from an " +
        "effect, once the DOM exists (README ex1)",
    ).toHaveFocus();
  });

  test("ex2 - ClickTracker remembers without re-rendering", async () => {
    const user = userEvent.setup();
    const onRender = vi.fn();
    render(<ClickTracker onRender={onRender} />);

    const before = onRender.mock.calls.length;
    const tap = screen.getByRole("button", { name: "Tap" });
    await user.click(tap);
    await user.click(tap);
    await user.click(tap);

    expect(
      onRender.mock.calls.length - before,
      "counting the taps must not re-render anything - nothing on screen has " +
        "changed yet. Writing to a ref does not schedule a render, which is " +
        "the entire reason to use one here (README ex2)",
    ).toBe(0);

      screen.queryByRole("status"),
      "and the total stays hidden until it is asked for",
    ).toBeNull();

    await user.click(screen.getByRole("button", { name: "Show total" }));
    expect(
      screen.queryByRole("status"),
      "revealing the total does need a render, so that part is state - expect: 3 taps",
    ).toHaveTextContent("3 taps");
    expect(
      onRender.mock.calls.length - before,
      "exactly one render, caused by the reveal",
    ).toBe(1);
  }, 20000);

  test("ex3 - FancyInput lets its parent reach the real input", async () => {

    const user = userEvent.setup();
    render(<FocusOnOpen />);

    const open = screen.getByRole("button", { name: "Open" });
    await user.click(open);

    const close = screen.getByRole("button", { name: "Close" });

      close,
      "when a dialog opens, focus has to move into it - otherwise a keyboard " +
        "user is still standing outside a dialog they cannot see",

In plain English:

- **ex1** simply asks whether the input has focus after rendering.
  `toHaveFocus()` compares against `document.activeElement`.
- **ex2** counts renders around three taps and requires the difference to be
  zero, checks nothing is revealed yet, then reveals and requires exactly one
  more render and the right total.
- **ex3** defines a little `Harness` component inside the test that creates a
  ref, hands it to your component, and has a button that calls
  `ref.current?.focus()`. If your component drops the ref, `current` is `null`
  and the click does nothing.
- **challenge** renders two editors, types into one, clears it through the
  handle, checks both, then focuses through the handle. The type
  `EditorHandle` is imported from your file, so the shape you expose is part
  of the contract.
- **review1** clicks Open and asserts focus landed on Close, then clicks Close
  and asserts the dialog is gone and focus is back on Open.

## The teaching point

Refs are the escape hatch, and the useful discipline is to notice when you are
using them as one. Reaching for a ref to focus something, measure something or
integrate a chart library is the tool working as intended. Reaching for a ref
because a piece of state was "causing too many re-renders" is usually a sign the
state was in the wrong place — and the ref version will be quietly wrong later,
because a value nobody renders from can drift out of sync with what is on
screen.

The focus work in the review exercise is worth more than it looks. Focus is the
keyboard user's cursor: if you show them something and do not move focus to it,
they do not know it exists; if you remove the thing they were standing on and do
not put them somewhere sensible, the browser drops them at the top of the
document. Every dialog, drawer, menu and toast has this obligation, and almost
none of them meet it.

# Reading — react/08_refs_dom

## Notes

**A ref is a mutable box, and that is the whole implementation.** `useRef(x)`
allocates `{ current: x }` once per component instance and hands back the same
object forever. It is `useState` minus the render — literally, in that React
implements it with the same slot mechanism. Everything else about refs follows
from that: writes are invisible to React, reads during render are unreliable,
and the object identity is stable so it never needs to appear in a dependency
array.

**When React fills a DOM ref.** During the commit phase, after the DOM has been
mutated and before `useLayoutEffect` runs, React sets `ref.current` for every
attached node — and sets it to `null` for nodes it is removing. So by the time
any effect runs, refs are populated. During render they hold the *previous*
value, which is why reading them there is a bug even when it appears to work.

**State versus ref, decided in one question.** Does the value appear on screen,
directly or indirectly? Then it is state. Timer ids, "have I already scrolled",
the previous value of a prop, a mutable cache, a subscription object — none of
those are rendered, so they are refs. The failure mode of getting it wrong in
one direction is a stale screen; in the other, a component that re-renders on
every mouse move.

**`ref` is not `key`, and neither is a normal prop — except now it is.** React
19 made `ref` a regular prop for function components, so `forwardRef` is no
longer needed (it still works and is not being removed imminently). `key`
remains special and is still never visible in props.

**Imperative handles are an escape hatch with a cost.** Exposing methods
inverts React's data flow — the parent now *commands* the child rather than
describing what it wants — and that makes the interaction invisible to anyone
reading the JSX. The cases where it is genuinely right are small and
well-known: focus, scroll, select, play/pause, and resetting an uncontrolled
subtree. Anything you could express as a prop should be a prop.

## ex1 — the two-step that every DOM operation needs

The pattern — declare a ref, attach it, act on it in an effect — is the whole
of DOM access in React, and the reason it is two steps rather than one is worth
holding on to. Render describes what should exist; it does not create anything.
The node exists only after React commits, so the earliest moment you can touch
it is an effect.

Autofocus itself deserves a caveat that the exercise cannot express: it is a
usability decision, not a default. Focusing a field on page load moves a
screen-reader user past whatever came before it, and on mobile it opens the
keyboard and hides half the screen. The right places for it are narrow — a
search overlay the user just opened, the first field of a dialog, an inline edit
they just triggered — and they share the property that the user *asked* to be
put there.

`field.current?.focus()` rather than `field.current.focus()` is not defensive
noise. `current` is genuinely `HTMLInputElement | null` in the type system,
because React nulls it when the node unmounts, and the optional chain is the
honest way to say "if it is still there".

## ex2 — the other job of `useRef`

The render probe makes something visible that is normally invisible: the tap
count changes three times and the component does not render. That is the
distinction the exercise exists for. State is "the screen depends on this"; a
ref is "I need to remember this, and nothing on screen cares yet".

Notice which piece of the exercise is which. The count is a ref because nothing
displays it. The *revealed* total is state because something does. And the
moment you press Show total, the ref's value is copied into state — which is
the normal way these two cooperate.

The rule about not reading refs during render is worth understanding rather than
memorising. React reserves the right to render a component without committing
it (concurrent rendering does this — it can start a render, abandon it, and
start again), so a render that reads `taps.current` may be reading a value from
a render that never happened, or may be about to be thrown away. Event handlers
and effects run after a commit, so they see reality.

The classic production uses of a mutable ref: holding the id returned by
`setInterval` so a cleanup can clear it, holding the previous value of a prop to
compare against, holding an instance of a non-React library (a map, a chart, an
editor), and holding "has this already run" flags. All invisible, all persistent.

## ex3 — forwarding, and what React 19 changed

The fix was one attribute, which is the point: the machinery is now boring. It
is worth knowing what it replaced, because you will read code that uses it.
Before React 19:

```tsx
const FancyInput = forwardRef<HTMLInputElement, Props>(function FancyInput(props, ref) {
  return <input ref={ref} />;
});
```

`forwardRef` existed because `ref` was stripped from props before your component
saw them, so a wrapper had no way to receive one. React 19 removed that special
case for function components. Class components still have the old behaviour, and
`forwardRef` still works, so both forms will coexist in real codebases for
years.

The design point underneath is more durable than the API. Any component that
wraps a form control should let a ref through. Form libraries need it to focus
the first invalid field; design systems need it for tooltips and popovers to
position against; test code needs it for the occasional escape. A wrapper that
swallows refs gets forked, in exactly the same way as one that swallows
`className`.

## challenge — designing what the parent may do

The exercise is constructed so that forwarding the DOM node cannot work.
`focus()` is a DOM operation, but `clear()` has to set React state — the
textarea is controlled, so writing `node.value = ""` would be overwritten by the
next render, and would not update `text`. The only thing that can offer both is
an object that closes over the component's internals, which is exactly what
`useImperativeHandle` publishes.

Two details in the reference are deliberate. The internal `field` ref still
exists, because `focus` needs a real node — the imperative handle sits *beside*
the DOM ref, not instead of it. And the dependency array is `[]` because the
returned object's methods only close over things that are stable (the setter and
the ref object), so there is no reason to rebuild it. If a method closed over a
prop, that prop would belong in the array, and forgetting it would give the
parent a handle that calls yesterday's version — a stale closure with a new
face.

The larger judgement: two methods is a good handle, ten is a component that has
been turned inside out. Every method is API surface, and imperative API is
harder to change than props because callers invoke it from arbitrary places. If
you find the handle growing, the state it manipulates probably wants to be
lifted into the parent instead.

## review1 — focus is the keyboard user's cursor

The two directions fail differently, and both fail silently for anyone using a
mouse.

Opening without moving focus leaves a keyboard user parked on the trigger
button, behind the dialog they just opened; they have no idea it exists and
tabbing walks them through the page underneath it. Closing without restoring
focus is worse: the focused element is removed from the document, so the browser
resets focus to `<body>`, and the next Tab starts from the very top of the page.
Users experience this as "it jumped".

The mechanics show the two timings from ex1 in one component. Focusing the close
button has to wait for it to exist, so it goes in an effect keyed on `open`.
Restoring focus to the opener can happen right in the handler, because that
button never left the document. If you tried both in effects, or both in
handlers, one of them would be reaching for a `null` ref.

Everything a real dialog owes its users beyond this: trapping Tab inside it
while it is open, closing on Escape, marking the rest of the page inert, and
labelling the dialog. That is why the honest recommendation is the native
`<dialog>` element or a maintained library — but knowing what those are doing
for you is what lets you tell a good one from a bad one.

## Further reading

- [react.dev — Referencing Values with Refs](https://react.dev/learn/referencing-values-with-refs) — the mutable-box job, and when to prefer state.
- [react.dev — Manipulating the DOM with Refs](https://react.dev/learn/manipulating-the-dom-with-refs) — the DOM job, including refs to a list of nodes.
- [react.dev — `useImperativeHandle`](https://react.dev/reference/react/useImperativeHandle) and [`forwardRef`](https://react.dev/reference/react/forwardRef) — the challenge, and the API React 19 made unnecessary.
- [MDN — `HTMLElement.focus()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/HTMLElement/focus) — including `preventScroll`, which you will eventually need.
- [MDN — `document.activeElement`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Document/activeElement) — what `toHaveFocus()` is really checking.
- [WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices — Dialog (Modal): keyboard interaction](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/dialog-modal/) — the full focus contract the review exercise starts.

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — an imperative handle

Edit `challenge/solution.tsx`. `Editor({ label, ref })` renders a labelled
`<textarea>` whose text is controlled state. A parent holding a ref to it must
get an object with exactly two methods:

- `focus()` — focuses the textarea;
- `clear()` — empties it.

Forwarding the ref to the textarea will not do, because `clear` has to change
React state and a DOM node cannot.

The gate renders **two** editors, one with a ref and one without, and checks
that clearing one does not touch the other.

Honest difficulty note: `useImperativeHandle` is new here, and the hints give
you its shape. The `useId` already in the stub is there because two instances
are on screen.

```
uv run dojo test react 08_refs_dom challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Forwarding the ref straight to the `<textarea>`, as you did in ex3, would give
the parent `focus()` — but not `clear()`, because clearing this editor means
changing React state, and the DOM node knows nothing about that. So the parent
should not receive the DOM node at all. It should receive an object you design.

## Hint 2
`useImperativeHandle(ref, () => ({ … }), [deps])` decides what `ref.current`
becomes:

```tsx
useImperativeHandle(ref, () => ({
  focus: () => { … },
  clear: () => { … },
}), []);
```

You will still want an internal ref pointing at the real `<textarea>`, because
`focus` has to reach it.

## Hint 3
`clear` calls the state setter; `focus` calls `.focus()` on the internal ref.
Two Editors are rendered and only one has a ref, so nothing here may reach for
anything global — `useId` is already in the stub for the same reason. The
remaining decision is the dependency array on `useImperativeHandle`, and it is
worth reasoning about rather than copying: what would change about the object
you are returning?

## Hint 1
Forwarding the ref straight to the `<textarea>`, as you did in ex3, would give
the parent `focus()` — but not `clear()`, because clearing this editor means
changing React state, and the DOM node knows nothing about that. So the parent
should not receive the DOM node at all. It should receive an object you design.

## Hint 2
`useImperativeHandle(ref, () => ({ … }), [deps])` decides what `ref.current`
becomes:

```tsx
useImperativeHandle(ref, () => ({
  focus: () => { … },
  clear: () => { … },
}), []);
```

You will still want an internal ref pointing at the real `<textarea>`, because
`focus` has to reach it.

## Hint 3
`clear` calls the state setter; `focus` calls `.focus()` on the internal ref.
Two Editors are rendered and only one has a ref, so nothing here may reach for
anything global — `useId` is already in the stub for the same reason. The
remaining decision is the dependency array on `useImperativeHandle`, and it is
worth reasoning about rather than copying: what would change about the object
you are returning?

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Two different kinds of memory are needed here. The tap count has to survive
between renders but nothing on screen depends on it, so changing it should not
render anything. The revealed total *is* on screen, so changing it must.

## Hint 2
`useState` is for the second kind. `useRef` is for the first: it holds a value
across renders in `.current`, and writing to it does **not** schedule a render.

```tsx
const taps = useRef(0);
…
onClick={() => { taps.current += 1; }}
```

A plain `let` outside the component would be shared by every instance; a plain
`let` inside would reset on every render. A ref is per-instance and persistent.

## Hint 3
Reading `taps.current` while rendering is a bad habit — React makes no promise
about when a ref is up to date relative to a render — but reading it inside an
event handler is exactly what refs are for. That is where "Show total" should
get its number from. The last decision is what the display should do if the
user taps again after revealing the total.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Two different kinds of memory are needed here. The tap count has to survive
between renders but nothing on screen depends on it, so changing it should not
render anything. The revealed total *is* on screen, so changing it must.

## Hint 2
`useState` is for the second kind. `useRef` is for the first: it holds a value
across renders in `.current`, and writing to it does **not** schedule a render.

```tsx
const taps = useRef(0);
…
onClick={() => { taps.current += 1; }}
```

A plain `let` outside the component would be shared by every instance; a plain
`let` inside would reset on every render. A ref is per-instance and persistent.

## Hint 3
Reading `taps.current` while rendering is a bad habit — React makes no promise
about when a ref is up to date relative to a render — but reading it inside an
event handler is exactly what refs are for. That is where "Show total" should
get its number from. The last decision is what the display should do if the
user taps again after revealing the total.

exercises.prompt: ## Review — focus management\n\n
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Two moves of focus, in opposite directions. Opening has to put focus on
something inside the dialog; closing has to put it back on the control that
opened it. That means two refs — one for each button — and both of them must
be attached before you try to use them.

## Hint 2
Focusing the close button cannot happen in the click handler that opens the
dialog: at that moment the button does not exist yet, so its ref is still
`null`. It has to happen after React has rendered the dialog, which is an
effect that runs when `open` changes:

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  if (open) { … }
}, [open]);
```

## Hint 3
Closing is the easier direction — the Open button is already in the document,
so its ref is live and you can focus it directly in the handler that sets
`open` to false. Whether you also restore focus from an effect, and what should
happen if the dialog is closed by pressing Escape rather than the button, are
the questions a production implementation has to answer next.

## Hint 1
Two moves of focus, in opposite directions. Opening has to put focus on
something inside the dialog; closing has to put it back on the control that
opened it. That means two refs — one for each button — and both of them must
be attached before you try to use them.

## Hint 2
Focusing the close button cannot happen in the click handler that opens the
dialog: at that moment the button does not exist yet, so its ref is still
`null`. It has to happen after React has rendered the dialog, which is an
effect that runs when `open` changes:

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  if (open) { … }
}, [open]);
```

## Hint 3
Closing is the easier direction — the Open button is already in the document,
so its ref is live and you can focus it directly in the handler that sets
`open` to false. Whether you also restore focus from an effect, and what should
happen if the dialog is closed by pressing Escape rather than the button, are
the questions a production implementation has to answer next.
