lessons.briefing:
# 09 — Context and reducers

Two problems show up at the same moment in a growing application, and this
lesson is one answer to each.

The first is **prop drilling**. The theme is chosen at the top of the app and
needed by a button nine levels down, so nine components take a `theme` prop
they do not use, pass it on, and now cannot be moved or reused without dragging
it along. Context fixes that: a value published at one level of the tree and
read at any depth below, skipping everything in between.

The second is that **`useState` stops scaling** once a single interaction has to
change several related things at once. Adding an item to a cart touches the
line, the quantity, maybe the total; adding a task assigns an id and appends;
and the logic ends up smeared across four event handlers that each have to
remember the same rules. `useReducer` gathers all of it into one pure function
that takes the current state and a description of what happened, and returns the
next state.

They are independent tools and they combine beautifully — a reducer holds the
state, a context publishes it and the `dispatch` to everyone who needs them,
which is the challenge at the end of this lesson and roughly how every state
management library works underneath.

A warning before you enjoy it too much. Context is not a state manager and it is
not free: every component that reads a context re-renders when that context's
value changes, and a value that is a fresh object each render changes every
time. Reach for context for things that are genuinely tree-wide and change
rarely — theme, locale, the current user, a dispatch function. Reach for it as
"a global variable that React knows about" and you will build something slow.

## Concept — publish a value, and describe what happened

**Context, in three pieces:**

```tsx
// 1. the channel, created once at module scope
const ThemeContext = createContext<string | null>(null);

// 2. the publisher
function ThemeProvider({ theme, children }) {
  return <ThemeContext.Provider value={theme}>{children}</ThemeContext.Provider>;
}

// 3. the subscriber, at any depth
function ThemedButton() {
  const theme = useContext(ThemeContext);
  return <button type="button">Theme: {theme}</button>;
}
```

`useContext` walks up the tree and takes the value from the nearest matching
provider. If there is none, it returns the default you passed to
`createContext` — and that default is a trap worth designing around. A
plausible-looking default (`"light"`) means a component rendered outside its
provider works *incorrectly and silently*. A default of `null`, plus a custom
hook that throws, turns a wiring mistake into an error message with the
provider's name in it:

```tsx
export function useTheme() {
  const value = useContext(ThemeContext);
  if (value === null) throw new Error("useTheme must be used inside a ThemeProvider");
  return value;
}
```

That hook is also the right place to hide the context object entirely, so
consumers import `useTheme` and never `ThemeContext`.

**A reducer** is a pure function — no React, no side effects, testable by
calling it:

```tsx
function reducer(state, action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case "added":   return [...state, action.item];
    case "removed": return state.filter((x) => x.id !== action.id);
    default:        return state;
  }
}
```

Same inputs, same output, and it never modifies the state it was handed — it
returns a new one, because React decides whether anything changed by comparing
references.

`useReducer` connects it to a component:

```tsx
const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, initialState);
…
<button onClick={() => dispatch({ type: "removed", id })}>Remove</button>
```

Handlers stop computing new state and start *describing events*. Name actions
after what happened (`added`, `toggled`, `quantitySet`) rather than after what
you want done (`setItems`) — it keeps the reducer the only place that knows the
rules.

Two practical notes. `dispatch` is **guaranteed stable** across renders, so it
never needs to be in a dependency array — a real advantage over passing setter
functions around. And a reducer must tolerate being called twice with the same
arguments, which is why purity is not optional.

## Exercise 1 — context

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. Export `ThemeProvider({ theme, children })` and
`ThemedButton()`. The button renders `Theme: dark` when the provider above it
was given `theme="dark"`, and gets **no props** — the gate renders it three
levels deep inside a wrapper it defines itself.

```
uv run dojo test react 09_context_reducer ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — a context that fails loudly

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. It already exports `SettingsProvider`, `useSettings`
and `Density`. As written, rendering `Density` with no provider quietly shows
the default. Change it so that `useSettings()` **throws** an error whose message
contains `SettingsProvider`, while still working normally inside one.

```
uv run dojo test react 09_context_reducer ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — a reducer, on its own

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. Implement `cartReducer(state, action)` over an array of
`{ id, name, price, quantity }`:

- `{ type: "added", id, name, price }` — if that id is already in the cart,
  increase its `quantity` by one; otherwise append a new line with
  `quantity: 1`.
- `{ type: "removed", id }` — drop that line.
- `{ type: "quantitySet", id, quantity }` — set the quantity; if it is `0` or
  less, the line is removed instead.
- `{ type: "cleared" }` — an empty cart.

No component and no hooks: the gate calls this function directly, and it also
checks that the state you were handed comes back unmodified.

```
uv run dojo test react 09_context_reducer ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — `useReducer` in a component

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `tasksReducer` and `initialTasks` are **already
written**; the work is the component. `TaskList` renders:

- a controlled input labelled `New task` and a button reading `Add`, which adds
  the task and clears the box;
- a `<ul>` with one `<li>` per task, each containing a checkbox whose label is
  the task's text, checked when the task is done, and toggling that one task;
- a live region reading `1 of 2 done`.

```
uv run dojo test react 09_context_reducer ex4
```

## Challenge — both at once

Edit `challenge/solution.tsx`. `paletteReducer` is written for you. Build:

- `PaletteProvider({ children })` — holds the palette in a `useReducer`
  starting at `"day"` and publishes both the value and the `dispatch`;
- `PaletteLabel()` — a live region reading `Palette: day`;
- `PaletteToggle()` — a button reading `Toggle palette` that flips it.

The gate puts the toggle inside a `<header>` and the label inside a
`<main><section>`, so they are in different branches of the tree and **neither
takes props**.

Honest difficulty note: the design decision is what to put in the context
value. If you get it working, read hint 3 anyway — there is a performance bug
that passes the gate.

```
uv run dojo test react 09_context_reducer challenge
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading — react/09_context_reducer

## Notes

**Context is a lookup, not a store.** `useContext(C)` walks up the fibre tree
from the calling component and returns the `value` of the nearest
`<C.Provider>` above it. It holds nothing itself; the state lives in whatever
component renders the provider, in ordinary `useState` or `useReducer`. That is
why "context re-rendered my whole app" is really "the component holding the
state re-rendered, and so did everything reading its context value".

**Every consumer re-renders when the value changes**, and `React.memo` does not
save them — memo compares props, and context is not a prop. Two consequences
follow. Keep context values stable: an inline `value={{ user, logout }}` is a
new object every render, so every consumer re-renders whenever the provider
does, even if `user` never changed. And split contexts by change frequency —
one for the rarely-changing data and one for the stable `dispatch` is the
standard trick, since a component that only dispatches then never re-renders at
all.

**Context is not a state manager.** It has no selectors, so consumers cannot
subscribe to part of a value; no devtools; no middleware; no caching. For
server data, a data library (TanStack Query, SWR) is the right answer, not
context. For large, frequently-changing client state read by many components,
a store with selector-based subscriptions (Zustand, Redux Toolkit, Jotai) exists
precisely because context re-renders everything. Context is excellent for
theme, locale, auth identity, feature flags and dispatch — things that are
tree-wide and calm.

**A reducer is the Gang-of-Four command pattern with a fresh coat of paint.**
State plus an action in, new state out, no side effects. That purity is what
makes it testable without React, replayable, loggable, and safe for React to
call twice during a development double-render. Every rule about immutability
from lesson 03 applies with full force: return new arrays and objects, never
edit the ones you were handed.

**`useReducer` versus `useState`.** Not a question of how many fields. Use a
reducer when the *transitions* have rules — when "add this item" means different
things depending on what is already there, when two fields must move together,
when the same change is triggered from several places. A single boolean with one
toggle is a `useState`; a wizard with steps, validation and a back button is a
reducer.

## ex1 — the mechanism, and the default that lies

The exercise is deliberately small so that the shape is visible: a context
created at module scope (once per module, not per render), a provider that sets
a value, and a consumer at arbitrary depth. The `Deep` wrapper in the gate is
there to make the point that the value did not travel by props — no component
between the provider and the button mentions the theme.

The detail that generates bugs is that `createContext(default)` is a *fallback
for having no provider*, not an initial value. It is used only when no matching
provider exists above the consumer. Beginners read it as "the starting value"
and then wonder why setting it has no effect.

Worth knowing for React 19: `<ThemeContext>` can now be used directly as the
provider, with `<ThemeContext.Provider>` kept for compatibility. And
`use(Context)` is a new way to read a context that, unlike `useContext`, may be
called conditionally. Both forms appear in modern code; neither changes the
model.

## ex2 — turning a wiring mistake into an error

This is a small change with a large payoff, and it is the pattern every good
codebase uses. The failure it prevents is specific: a component rendered outside
its provider — because someone moved it, or rendered it in a test, or added a
new route that forgot the wrapper — silently receives the default and displays
plausible-looking wrong data. Nobody notices for weeks.

Three things happen at once when you switch the default to `null` and throw in
a custom hook. The mistake becomes loud and names the missing provider. The
context object stops being exported, so consumers cannot bypass your hook. And
TypeScript narrows: after `if (value === null) throw`, the return type is
`string` rather than `string | null`, so no consumer has to handle a case that
cannot happen.

The `console.error` spy in the gate is worth understanding rather than copying.
React logs a render error to the console before rethrowing it, so a test that
deliberately renders a throwing component fills the output with a stack trace
that looks like a failure. Silencing it keeps the signal readable — and it is
the same reason production apps put an error boundary above anything that can
throw.

## ex3 — the reducer as a pure function

Testing this by calling it is the point. A reducer has no dependencies, no
timing, and no DOM, so its tests are as fast and as boring as tests get — and
they cover the part of your application where the actual rules live. If you take
one habit from this exercise, take that one: push rules into pure functions and
the hard-to-test surface shrinks to wiring.

The immutability assertion is the one people fail. `state.push(...)` returns a
length, `state.sort()` reorders in place, and `item.quantity += 1` edits an
object that some other render may still be holding. All three "work" in the
sense that the data is right; all three break React, because `Object.is(prev,
next)` is `true` and React concludes nothing happened. The symptom is a UI that
updates only when something *else* forces a render, which is maddening to debug
if you have not seen it before.

The `quantitySet` rule — zero means remove — is there because reducers are where
this kind of business rule belongs. Put it in the click handler and you have to
remember it in the keyboard handler, the "apply coupon" path, and the sync code.
Put it in the reducer and it is true by construction.

The `default` branch returning state unchanged is a convention worth keeping.
With a discriminated union and `switch` on `action.type`, TypeScript can prove
you handled every case — the TypeScript track's exhaustiveness checking with
`never` is the same idea from the other side.

## ex4 — describing events instead of computing state

The shift in how handlers read is the thing to notice. Before:
`setTasks([...tasks, { id: nextId, text: draft, done: false }]); setNextId(nextId + 1);`
— the handler knows the data shape, the id scheme and the ordering. After:
`dispatch({ type: "added", text: draft })` — the handler knows what the user
did. Every rule moved to one function, and adding a task from a second place
(a keyboard shortcut, a paste handler, an import) is now one line that cannot
get the rules wrong.

Notice what stayed in `useState`: the draft text in the input. It is transient,
belongs to one control, and has no rules — putting it through the reducer would
add an action type for every keystroke and gain nothing. Mixing the two hooks in
one component is normal and correct.

`doneCount` needs updating in the add path, the toggle path, and every future
path somebody adds.

loses the click-the-label-to-toggle behaviour sighted users expect.

it is the one every real implementation makes: consumers that read and consumers
that write both need something, and only the provider has both.

# Reading — react/09_context_reducer

## Notes

**Context is a lookup, not a store.** `useContext(C)` walks up the fibre tree
from the calling component and returns the `value` of the nearest
`<C.Provider>` above it. It holds nothing itself; the state lives in whatever
component renders the provider, in ordinary `useState` or `useReducer`. That is
why "context re-rendered my whole app" is really "the component holding the
state re-rendered, and so did everything reading its context value".

**Every consumer re-renders when the value changes**, and `React.memo` does not
save them — memo compares props, and context is not a prop. Two consequences
follow. Keep context values stable: an inline `value={{ user, logout }}` is a
new object every render, so every consumer re-renders whenever the provider
does, even if `user` never changed. And split contexts by change frequency —
one for the rarely-changing data and one for the stable `dispatch` is the
standard trick, since a component that only dispatches then never re-renders at
all.

**Context is not a state manager.** It has no selectors, so consumers cannot
subscribe to part of a value; no devtools; no middleware; no caching. For
server data, a data library (TanStack Query, SWR) is the right answer, not
context. For large, frequently-changing client state read by many components,
a store with selector-based subscriptions (Zustand, Redux Toolkit, Jotai) exists
precisely because context re-renders everything. Context is excellent for
theme, locale, auth identity, feature flags and dispatch — things that are
tree-wide and calm.

**A reducer is the Gang-of-Four command pattern with a fresh coat of paint.**
State plus an action in, new state out, no side effects. That purity is what
makes it testable without React, replayable, loggable, and safe for React to
call twice during a development double-render. Every rule about immutability
from lesson 03 applies with full force: return new arrays and objects, never
edit the ones you were handed.

**`useReducer` versus `useState`.** Not a question of how many fields. Use a
reducer when the *transitions* have rules — when "add this item" means different
things depending on what is already there, when two fields must move together,
when the same change is triggered from several places. A single boolean with one
toggle is a `useState`; a wizard with steps, validation and a back button is a
reducer.

## ex1 — the mechanism, and the default that lies

The exercise is deliberately small so that the shape is visible: a context
created at module scope (once per module, not per render), a provider that sets
a value, and a consumer at arbitrary depth. The `Deep` wrapper in the gate is
there to make the point that the value did not travel by props — no component
between the provider and the button mentions the theme.

The detail that generates bugs is that `createContext(default)` is a *fallback
for having no provider*, not an initial value. It is used only when no matching
provider exists above the consumer. Beginners read it as "the starting value"
and then wonder why setting it has no effect.

Worth knowing for React 19: `<ThemeContext>` can now be used directly as the
provider, with `<ThemeContext.Provider>` kept for compatibility. And
`use(Context)` is a new way to read a context that, unlike `useContext`, may be
called conditionally. Both forms appear in modern code; neither changes the
model.

This is a small change with a large payoff, and it is the pattern every good
codebase uses. The failure it prevents is specific: a component rendered outside
its provider — because someone moved it, or rendered it in a test, or added a
new route that forgot the wrapper — silently receives the default and displays
plausible-looking wrong data. Nobody notices for weeks.

Three things happen at once when you switch the default to `null` and throw in
a custom hook. The mistake becomes loud and names the missing provider. The
context object stops being exported, so consumers cannot bypass your hook. And
TypeScript narrows: after `if (value === null) throw`, the return type is
`string` rather than `string | null`, so no consumer has to handle a case that
cannot happen.

The `console.error` spy in the gate is worth understanding rather than copying.
React logs a render error to the console before rethrowing it, so a test that
deliberately renders a throwing component fills the output with a stack trace
that looks like a failure. Silencing it keeps the signal readable — and it is
the same reason production apps put an error boundary above anything that can
throw.

## ex3 — the reducer as a pure function

Testing this by calling it is the point. A reducer has no dependencies, no
timing, and no DOM, so its tests are as fast and as boring as tests get — and
they cover the part of your application where the actual rules live. If you take
one habit from this exercise, take that one: push rules into pure functions and
the hard-to-test surface shrinks to wiring.

The immutability assertion is the one people fail. `state.push(...)` returns a
length, `state.sort()` reorders in place, and `item.quantity += 1` edits an
object that some other render may still be holding. All three "work" in the
sense that the data is right; all three break React, because `Object.is(prev,
next)` is `true` and React concludes nothing happened. The symptom is a UI that
updates only when something *else* forces a render, which is maddening to debug
if you have not seen it before.

The `quantitySet` rule — zero means remove — is there because reducers are where
this kind of business rule belongs. Put it in the click handler and you have to
remember it in the keyboard handler, the "apply coupon" path, and the sync code.
Put it in the reducer and it is true by construction.

The `default` branch returning state unchanged is a convention worth keeping.
With a discriminated union and `switch` on `action.type`, TypeScript can prove
you handled every case — the TypeScript track's exhaustiveness checking with
`never` is the same idea from the other side.

## ex4 — describing events instead of computing state

The shift in how handlers read is the thing to notice. Before:
`setTasks([...tasks, { id: nextId, text: draft, done: false }]); setNextId(nextId + 1);`
— the handler knows the data shape, the id scheme and the ordering. After:
`dispatch({ type: "added", text: draft })` — the handler knows what the user
did. Every rule moved to one function, and adding a task from a second place

get the rules wrong.

belongs to one control, and has no rules — putting it through the reducer would

one component is normal and correct.

## Challenge — both at once

Edit `challenge/solution.tsx`. `paletteReducer` is written for you. Build:

- `PaletteProvider({ children })` — holds the palette in a `useReducer`
  starting at `"day"` and publishes both the value and the `dispatch`;
- `PaletteLabel()` — a live region reading `Palette: day`;
- `PaletteToggle()` — a button reading `Toggle palette` that flips it.

The gate puts the toggle inside a `<header>` and the label inside a
`<main><section>`, so they are in different branches of the tree and **neither
takes props**.

Honest difficulty note: the design decision is what to put in the context
value. If you get it working, read hint 3 anyway — there is a performance bug
that passes the gate.

uv run dojo test react 09_context_reducer challenge

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The two consumers need different things: the label needs the current palette,
the toggle needs a way to change it. Neither takes props, so **both** have to
come down through the context — which means the context value is an object, not
a string.

## Hint 2
The provider owns the state and puts both halves in the value:

```tsx

## Hint 1
Three pieces, and they live at three different levels of the file. A **context
object** created once at module scope; a **provider** that puts a value into it;
and a **consumer** that reads whatever the nearest provider above it supplied.

```tsx
const ThemeContext = createContext("light");

```

`createContext` goes outside the components — it is created once for the module,
not once per render.

provider above it, which is a default, not an initial value. The button then
renders that value in its text; note the gate re-renders the provider with a
different theme, so the button must read the context on every render rather
than capturing it once.

Three pieces, and they live at three different levels of the file. A **context
object** created once at module scope; a **provider** that puts a value into it;

```tsx
const ThemeContext = createContext("light");
…

…

not once per render.

## Exercise 3 — a reducer, on its own

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. Implement `cartReducer(state, action)` over an array of
`{ id, name, price, quantity }`:

- `{ type: "added", id, name, price }` — if that id is already in the cart,
  increase its `quantity` by one; otherwise append a new line with
  `quantity: 1`.
- `{ type: "removed", id }` — drop that line.
- `{ type: "quantitySet", id, quantity }` — set the quantity; if it is `0` or
  less, the line is removed instead.
- `{ type: "cleared" }` — an empty cart.

No component and no hooks: the gate calls this function directly, and it also
checks that the state you were handed comes back unmodified.

```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
No React here at all: `cartReducer(state, action)` takes the current cart and a
description of something that happened, and returns the cart afterwards. Same
inputs, same output, no side effects — which is why you can test it by calling
it, and why React can call it twice without consequence.

## Hint 2
Every branch has to build a **new array**. The three tools:

- `state.filter(…)` — removal;
- `state.map((item) => condition ? { ...item, changed } : item)` — edit one line
  and keep the others;
- `[...state, newItem]` — append.

`push`, `splice` and assigning to `item.quantity` all mutate, and the gate
checks the state it handed you afterwards.

## Hint 3
Two branches need thought. `added` has to notice whether the item is already
there — one line's quantity goes up, or a new line appears with quantity 1.
And `quantitySet` has a rule hiding in the gate: setting a quantity to zero or
below is not a line showing 0, it is a line that is gone. Whether you express
that by reusing the removal logic or by repeating the filter is your call.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
No React here at all: `cartReducer(state, action)` takes the current cart and a
description of something that happened, and returns the cart afterwards. Same
inputs, same output, no side effects — which is why you can test it by calling
it, and why React can call it twice without consequence.

## Hint 2
Every branch has to build a **new array**. The three tools:

- `state.filter(…)` — removal;
- `state.map((item) => condition ? { ...item, changed } : item)` — edit one line
  and keep the others;
- `[...state, newItem]` — append.

`push`, `splice` and assigning to `item.quantity` all mutate, and the gate
checks the state it handed you afterwards.

## Hint 3
Two branches need thought. `added` has to notice whether the item is already
there — one line's quantity goes up, or a new line appears with quantity 1.
And `quantitySet` has a rule hiding in the gate: setting a quantity to zero or
below is not a line showing 0, it is a line that is gone. Whether you express
that by reusing the removal logic or by repeating the filter is your call.

## Exercise 4 — `useReducer` in a component

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `tasksReducer` and `initialTasks` are **already
written**; the work is the component. `TaskList` renders:

- a controlled input labelled `New task` and a button reading `Add`, which adds
  the task and clears the box;
- a `<ul>` with one `<li>` per task, each containing a checkbox whose label is
  the task's text, checked when the task is done, and toggling that one task;
- a live region reading `1 of 2 done`.

uv run dojo test react 09_context_reducer ex4

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
`useReducer` is `useState`'s bigger sibling: instead of a value and a setter you
get a value and a `dispatch`, and every change goes through the reducer that is
already written at the top of the file.

```tsx
const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(tasksReducer, initialTasks);
```

The draft text in the box stays ordinary `useState` — it is not part of the task
list, and it is not something the reducer should know about.

## Hint 2
Handlers no longer compute the next state; they *describe what happened*:

```tsx
dispatch({ type: "added", text: draft });
dispatch({ type: "toggled", id: task.id });
```

Each task needs a checkbox joined to a label whose text is the task, so the gate
(and a screen reader) can find it by name — `id={`task-${task.id}`}` and a
matching `htmlFor`.

## Hint 3
The summary is not state. Count the done tasks during render from the list you
already have — storing a `doneCount` gives you two things that have to agree and
eventually will not. Two smaller decisions are left to you: clearing the draft
after adding, and what should happen when somebody clicks Add with an empty box.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
`useReducer` is `useState`'s bigger sibling: instead of a value and a setter you
get a value and a `dispatch`, and every change goes through the reducer that is
already written at the top of the file.

```tsx
const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(tasksReducer, initialTasks);
```

The draft text in the box stays ordinary `useState` — it is not part of the task
list, and it is not something the reducer should know about.

## Hint 2
Handlers no longer compute the next state; they *describe what happened*:

```tsx
dispatch({ type: "added", text: draft });
dispatch({ type: "toggled", id: task.id });
```

Each task needs a checkbox joined to a label whose text is the task, so the gate
(and a screen reader) can find it by name — `id={`task-${task.id}`}` and a
matching `htmlFor`.

## Hint 3
The summary is not state. Count the done tasks during render from the list you
already have — storing a `doneCount` gives you two things that have to agree and
eventually will not. Two smaller decisions are left to you: clearing the draft
after adding, and what should happen when somebody clicks Add with an empty box.

lessons.briefing:
# 10 — Custom hooks You have now written the same three lines four times: a piece of state, an effect that keeps it in step with something, and a cleanup. Debouncing a search box, reading from storage, subscribing to an event, fetching and tracking loading — all the same shape, all repeated in every component that needs them. The fix is startlingly small. **A custom hook is just a function that calls hooks.** No registration, no base class, no API to learn. If you move that state-plus-effect into a function whose name begins with `use`, you can call it from any component and each caller gets its own independent copy of the state. That last part is the bit people get wrong when they first meet it. A custom hook is not a shared value; it is shared *logic*. Two components calling `useToggle()` have two separate toggles, exactly as if they had each written `useState` themselves — because that is literally what happened. If you want a shared value, that is context (lesson 09). The `use` prefix is not decoration either. It is how the linter knows to apply the rules of hooks to your function, and how a reader knows the function may contain state and therefore may not be called conditionally. Which brings us to the rules themselves, and to exercise 4, where you fix a component that breaks them. ## Concept — extract the shape, keep the independence Here is a component with logic worth extracting: ```tsx function Widget() { const [online, setOnline] = useState(navigator.onLine); useEffect(() => { const goOnline = () => setOnline(true); window.addEventListener("online", goOnline); return () => window.removeEventListener("online", goOnline); }, []); return

{online ? "Connected" : "Offline"}

; } ``` And here it is extracted — the same lines, moved: ```tsx function useOnlineStatus() { const [online, setOnline] = useState(navigator.onLine); useEffect(() => { const goOnline = () => setOnline(true); window.addEventListener("online", goOnline); return () => window.removeEventListener("online", goOnline); }, []); return online; } function Widget() { const online = useOnlineStatus(); return

{online ? "Connected" : "Offline"}

; } ``` Nothing clever happened. The state still belongs to `Widget` — the hook has no storage of its own — and a second component calling `useOnlineStatus()` gets its own `useState` slot with its own value. **What to return.** A single value if there is one (`useOnlineStatus`), a tuple if there are exactly two and their order is obvious (`useState`'s own shape, which is why `const [on, toggle] = useToggle()` reads naturally), and an object once there are three or more — nobody wants to remember what the fourth element of a tuple means. **Return stable functions.** This is the one piece of extra care an extracted hook needs. A function created fresh in the hook body is a new object every render, so a consumer who puts it in a dependency array re-runs their effect every render. `useCallback(fn, deps)` returns the same function until its dependencies change: ```tsx const toggle = useCallback(() => setOn((previous) => !previous), []); ``` State setters from `useState` and `dispatch` from `useReducer` are already stable — React guarantees it — so those can be returned as they are. **The rules of hooks**, and the reason for them. React stores hook state in a list per component instance and matches each call to a slot **by call order**. So: - **Only call hooks at the top level.** Not in `if`, not in loops, not after an early `return`, not inside a callback. - **Only call hooks from components or other hooks.** If a component calls `useState` on some renders and not others, the lists stop lining up and React throws. That is not a stylistic rule with an escape hatch; it is the mechanism showing through, and exercise 4 makes it fail in front of you. **When to extract.** When the same state-and-effect appears twice, or when the logic has a name — `useDebouncedValue`, `useLocalStorage`, `useOnlineStatus`. Name it after *what it gives you*, not after when it runs (`useOnMount` is a bad name because it describes the mechanism rather than the meaning). ## Exercise 1 — a hook of your own Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `useToggle(initial = false)` returns a tuple: ```tsx const [on, toggle, setOn] = useToggle(); ``` `toggle` flips the value, `setOn` sets it explicitly, and the gate also checks that **`toggle` is the same function object across renders**. ``` uv run dojo test react 10_custom_hooks ex1 ``` ## Exercise 2 — state that survives a reload Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `useLocalStorage(key, initialValue)` returns `[value, setValue]`, where: - the initial value comes from `localStorage` when that key exists, and from `initialValue` when it does not — **on the first render**, not after an effect; - calling the setter updates React *and* writes to `localStorage`; - values are stored as JSON, so objects and numbers survive the round trip. ``` uv run dojo test react 10_custom_hooks ex2 ``` ## Exercise 3 — debouncing Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `useDebouncedValue(value, delay)` returns a value that follows its argument only after `delay` milliseconds have passed **since the last change**. Values that are superseded before the delay elapses are never returned at all. This is the hook that stops a search box firing a request per keystroke, and you will use it again in the interview drills. ``` uv run dojo test react 10_custom_hooks ex3 ``` ## Exercise 4 — the rules of hooks Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `VisitorPanel({ signedIn })` shows `Please sign in` when signed out and a clap counter when signed in. It compiles, and it throws the moment `signedIn` changes. Run the gate, read React's error, then fix it so that switching in both directions works and the counter still counts. ``` uv run dojo test react 10_custom_hooks ex4 ``` ## Challenge — one hook for all your data fetching Edit `challenge/solution.tsx`. `useAsync(run)` takes a function returning a promise and returns: ```tsx { status: "loading" | "success" | "error", data, error, reload } ``` - `status` starts at `"loading"` and the effect runs `run()` on mount; - on success, `data` holds the value and `status` is `"success"`; - on failure, `error` holds the `Error`'s **message** and `status` is `"error"`; - `reload()` runs it again; - a result from a run that has been superseded is **ignored** — the gate resolves an abandoned run last and checks it did not win. `run` is required to be stable across renders (the caller wraps it in `useCallback`). Everything else is the lesson-07 material, packaged. Honest difficulty note: this is the biggest single piece of code in the track so far, but every part of it is something you have already written once. ``` uv run dojo test react 10_custom_hooks challenge ```

# Reading — react/10_custom_hooks

## Notes

**A custom hook is inlined, conceptually.** When `Widget` calls
`useOnlineStatus()`, the `useState` inside it takes a slot in *Widget's* hook
list. The hook function has no identity of its own at runtime — it is not an
object, not an instance, and it holds nothing between calls. That single fact
answers most beginner questions: two components do not share a hook's state,
calling a hook twice in one component gives two independent copies, and a hook
cannot be called outside a render.

**The `use` prefix is a contract with tooling.** ESLint's rules-of-hooks plugin
decides whether a function may contain hook calls by looking at its name, and
whether a call site is legal by the same rule. Naming a hook `getOnlineStatus`
disables all of that checking silently. React 19 added a separate `use()` API
for reading promises and contexts, which — unusually — *may* be called
conditionally; it is a built-in, not a naming convention, and does not change
the rules for your own hooks.

**Extract for meaning, not for line count.** The good reasons to make a custom
hook: the logic appears in more than one component, the logic has a name, or a
component has become a pile of unrelated effects that would each be clearer
alone. The bad reason is "this component is long" — a hook that exists only to
move lines elsewhere leaves you with two places to look and no new concept.

**Return stable identities.** Anything a consumer might put in a dependency
array — functions, objects, arrays — should be memoized inside the hook, because
the consumer has no way to fix it from outside. `useState` setters and
`useReducer` dispatchers are stable by guarantee; everything you build yourself
is not, until you say so.

**Hooks and testing.** `renderHook` is the honest way to test a hook: it renders
a minimal component, calls the hook, and exposes the return value. That is not
"testing implementation details" — the return value is the hook's entire public
API, in the same way a function's return value is. What *would* be
implementation-testing is asserting on how many `useState` calls it made.

## ex1 — the smallest possible extraction

`useToggle` is barely worth extracting for its own sake — its whole body is one
`useState` and one updater — but it is exactly the right size to isolate the two
decisions that matter in every hook you will write.

The first is **the shape of the return value**. A tuple works here because the
convention is already established by `useState`, and because tuples let callers
rename freely: `const [isOpen, toggleOpen] = useToggle()` reads better than
destructuring an object and aliasing. Once you get to three or four values,
switch to an object; positional arguments stop being memorable somewhere around
three.

The second is **function stability**, and it is the one that catches people. A
consumer writing `useEffect(() => { … }, [toggle])` is doing the right thing —
the linter told them to — and if your hook hands back a new `toggle` on every
render, their effect runs on every render forever. They cannot fix it from their
side. This is why library hooks are so careful about identity, and why
`useCallback` in a *hook* is a correctness concern rather than the performance
tweak it usually is inside a component.

Note that the empty dependency array is only correct because the body uses the
updater form. A `toggle` written as `() => setOn(!on)` reads `on` from the
render, so it would need `[on]` in the array and would change identity on every
flip — the same "describe the change rather than capture the value" move from
lesson 03, now paying a second dividend.

## ex2 — lazy initial state, and the flash you avoid

The interesting line is `useState(() => …)`. Passing a *function* to `useState`
makes React call it only on the first render of that component instance;
passing a value evaluates that expression on every render and throws the result
away. For `useState(0)` the waste is nothing. For
`useState(JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(key)))` it is a synchronous storage
read and a parse on every keystroke of an unrelated field.

Reading during initial state rather than in an effect also removes a visible
defect. The effect version renders once with the default, then re-renders with
the stored value — so a user with dark mode saved sees a white flash on every
page load. Storage is synchronous, so there is no reason to pay that.

Two failure modes the reference handles that people usually forget.
`localStorage.getItem` returns `null` for a missing key, and `JSON.parse(null)`
returns `null` rather than throwing — so without an explicit check you get
`null` where you wanted your default. And stored data can be corrupt (a schema
change, a half-written value, a user editing devtools), so the `try/catch` is
not paranoia; a thrown error during initial state takes the whole app down.

What this hook deliberately does not do, and what a production version needs:
listen for the `storage` event so two tabs stay in sync, handle
`localStorage` being unavailable (Safari private mode used to throw on write,
and some corporate policies block it), and cope with server-side rendering,
where `localStorage` does not exist at all.

## ex3 — the cleanup *is* the debounce

Nearly everyone writes the `setTimeout` and forgets the `clearTimeout`, and the
result is not "no debounce" but something stranger: every intermediate value
arrives, each one 300ms late, in order. The box appears to work and then floods
the network on the next slow connection.

The mechanism is worth stating precisely. React runs the previous effect's
cleanup before running the next effect. So when `value` changes: cancel the
timer scheduled by the previous value, schedule a new one. A value that changes
faster than `delay` never gets its timer to fire, which is exactly the
definition of debouncing. You are not implementing a queue or comparing
timestamps; the effect lifecycle already has the semantics.

Debounce versus throttle is a standard interview follow-up. Debounce waits for a
pause and fires once at the end — right for search-as-you-type, autosave and
validation. Throttle fires at most once per interval regardless of pauses —
right for scroll and resize handlers, where you want steady updates rather than
one at the end. Both are two lines with `setTimeout`; knowing which you want is
the skill.

Note also what debouncing does *not* solve: requests still race. A debounced
search can still have two requests in flight if the user pauses, types, and
pauses again, and the first can still answer last. Debounce reduces the number
of races; the cleanup guard from lesson 07 eliminates the damage. Real search
boxes use both.

## ex4 — why the rules exist

React does not know your state is called `claps`. Internally, each component
instance holds a linked list of hook records, and each `useState`/`useEffect`
call consumes the next one in order. Render one: the early return fires before
the `useState`, so zero hooks are consumed. Render two: `signedIn` is true, the
`useState` runs, and React finds one more hook than the previous render had.
There is no way to reconcile that — is this new state, or state that belonged to
something else? — so it throws.

That framing tells you what the legal moves are:

- To do work conditionally, put the condition *inside* the hook: an effect that
  returns early, a `useMemo` whose body branches.
- To reset state when something changes, give the component a different `key`
  so React unmounts the old instance and mounts a fresh one — the cleanest
  answer, and the one people reach for last.
- To genuinely vary the number of hooks, split into two components and choose
  between them in the parent. Each component gets its own hook list.

Also worth knowing: `eslint-plugin-react-hooks` catches this statically and the
React Compiler (now shipping) refuses to optimise components that break the
rules. Both are reasons the rules are getting stricter rather than looser.

## challenge — the shape of every data-fetching library

Writing `useAsync` is worth the effort mainly because of what it reveals when
you then read the documentation for TanStack Query or SWR: the surface is the
same — status, data, error, a way to refetch — and everything *else* those
libraries offer is the part you did not build. Caching by key so two components
asking for the same thing make one request. Deduplication. Retries with
backoff. Revalidation on focus and reconnect. Pagination helpers. Optimistic
updates and rollback.

That is the honest conclusion of this whole thread of the course: hand-rolled
fetching is correct and it is not enough at scale, and knowing precisely which
parts you are missing is what makes the choice to adopt a library an engineering
decision instead of a fashion.

Two implementation notes. The `attempt` counter is a neat and widely used idiom
for "run this effect again on demand" — the effect depends on a number nobody
renders, and incrementing it is a refetch. And checking `current` in the
`.catch` as well as the `.then` matters more than it looks: without it, a stale
*failure* can overwrite a fresh success, which is the worst possible version of
the race because the screen shows an error for a request that succeeded.

The contract that `run` must be stable is a real API design decision with a real
cost — a caller who passes an inline arrow gets an infinite loop. The
alternatives are to keep `run` in a ref and drop it from the deps (which
silently uses a stale function), or to take a dependency array parameter the way
`useEffect` does (which is what most libraries end up doing, via a query key).
There is no free option; being able to name the trade-off is the point.

## Further reading

- [react.dev — Reusing Logic with Custom Hooks](https://react.dev/learn/reusing-logic-with-custom-hooks) — the whole lesson, including when *not* to extract.
- [react.dev — Rules of Hooks](https://react.dev/reference/rules/rules-of-hooks) — the rules, with the reasoning.
- [react.dev — `useState`: avoiding recreating the initial state](https://react.dev/reference/react/useState#avoiding-recreating-the-initial-state) — the lazy initialiser from ex2.
- [react.dev — `useCallback`](https://react.dev/reference/react/useCallback) — including the "should I add it to every function?" answer.
- [MDN — `Window.localStorage`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/localStorage) and the [`storage` event](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/storage_event) — what a production `useLocalStorage` owes you.
- [MDN — `clearTimeout`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/clearTimeout) — the one line that turns a delay into a debounce.
- [Testing Library — `renderHook`](https://testing-library.com/docs/react-testing-library/api/#renderhook) — the API these gates are written in.

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — one hook for all your data fetching

Edit `challenge/solution.tsx`. `useAsync(run)` takes a function returning a
promise and returns:

```tsx
{ status: "loading" | "success" | "error", data, error, reload }
```

- `status` starts at `"loading"` and the effect runs `run()` on mount;
- on success, `data` holds the value and `status` is `"success"`;
- on failure, `error` holds the `Error`'s **message** and `status` is
  `"error"`;
- `reload()` runs it again;
- a result from a run that has been superseded is **ignored** — the gate
  resolves an abandoned run last and checks it did not win.

`run` is required to be stable across renders (the caller wraps it in
`useCallback`). Everything else is the lesson-07 material, packaged.

Honest difficulty note: this is the biggest single piece of code in the track so
far, but every part of it is something you have already written once.

```
uv run dojo test react 10_custom_hooks challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Everything in this hook is something you have already written — lesson 07's
three states, lesson 07's cleanup guard, lesson 07's "callable from two places"
problem. The new part is that it is a *hook*, so nothing here renders anything
and the return value is the whole API.

## Hint 2
Start with the effect: set the status to loading, call `run()`, and record
either the data or the error's message.

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  let current = true;
  …
  return () => { current = false; };
}, [run, attempt]);
```

The `attempt` in that array is the trick for `reload`. Keep a counter in state
and have `reload` increment it; the effect is watching, so it runs again.

## Hint 3
Three details separate a working version from a good one. Check the `current`
flag in both the `.then` **and** the `.catch`, or a stale failure can still
overwrite a fresh success. Wrap `reload` in `useCallback` so consumers can put
it in their own dependency arrays. And note the contract in the file header:
`run` goes in the dependency array, so a caller who passes an inline arrow gets
an infinite loop — worth deciding whether you would document that, assert it, or
design around it.

## Hint 1
Everything in this hook is something you have already written — lesson 07's
three states, lesson 07's cleanup guard, lesson 07's "callable from two places"
problem. The new part is that it is a *hook*, so nothing here renders anything
and the return value is the whole API.

## Hint 2
Start with the effect: set the status to loading, call `run()`, and record
either the data or the error's message.

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  let current = true;
  …
  return () => { current = false; };
}, [run, attempt]);
```

The `attempt` in that array is the trick for `reload`. Keep a counter in state
and have `reload` increment it; the effect is watching, so it runs again.

## Hint 3
Three details separate a working version from a good one. Check the `current`
flag in both the `.then` **and** the `.catch`, or a stale failure can still
overwrite a fresh success. Wrap `reload` in `useCallback` so consumers can put
it in their own dependency arrays. And note the contract in the file header:
`run` goes in the dependency array, so a caller who passes an inline arrow gets
an infinite loop — worth deciding whether you would document that, assert it, or
design around it.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — state that survives a reload

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `useLocalStorage(key, initialValue)` returns
`[value, setValue]`, where:

- the initial value comes from `localStorage` when that key exists, and from
  `initialValue` when it does not — **on the first render**, not after an
  effect;
- calling the setter updates React *and* writes to `localStorage`;
- values are stored as JSON, so objects and numbers survive the round trip.

```
uv run dojo test react 10_custom_hooks ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Two halves. On the way in, the stored value has to be found *before the first
render paints*, or the user sees the default flash and then the real value. On
the way out, every write has to reach both React and storage.

## Hint 2
`useState` accepts a **function** as its argument, and calls it only on the
first render:

```tsx
const [value, setValue] = useState<T>(() => {
  const stored = localStorage.getItem(key);
  …
});
```

That is the lazy initialiser, and it is the right tool for anything expensive
or side-effecting. `useState(localStorage.getItem(key))` would read storage on
every single render and throw the result away.

## Hint 3
Storage holds strings, so `JSON.stringify` on the way out and `JSON.parse` on
the way in — that is what makes the hook work for objects and numbers, not just
strings. Two failure cases are worth a thought: `getItem` returns `null` when
the key is absent (and `JSON.parse(null)` is not an error, which makes it a
nasty one), and stored JSON can be corrupt. Wrap the setter in `useCallback` for
the same reason as ex1, and decide for yourself what its dependencies are.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Two halves. On the way in, the stored value has to be found *before the first
render paints*, or the user sees the default flash and then the real value. On
the way out, every write has to reach both React and storage.

## Hint 2
`useState` accepts a **function** as its argument, and calls it only on the
first render:

```tsx
const [value, setValue] = useState<T>(() => {
  const stored = localStorage.getItem(key);
  …
});
```

That is the lazy initialiser, and it is the right tool for anything expensive
or side-effecting. `useState(localStorage.getItem(key))` would read storage on
every single render and throw the result away.

## Hint 3
Storage holds strings, so `JSON.stringify` on the way out and `JSON.parse` on
the way in — that is what makes the hook work for objects and numbers, not just
strings. Two failure cases are worth a thought: `getItem` returns `null` when
the key is absent (and `JSON.parse(null)` is not an error, which makes it a
nasty one), and stored JSON can be corrupt. Wrap the setter in `useCallback` for
the same reason as ex1, and decide for yourself what its dependencies are.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — debouncing

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `useDebouncedValue(value, delay)` returns a value that
follows its argument only after `delay` milliseconds have passed **since the
last change**. Values that are superseded before the delay elapses are never
returned at all.

This is the hook that stops a search box firing a request per keystroke, and
you will use it again in the interview drills.

```
uv run dojo test react 10_custom_hooks ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The hook returns a value that *lags* behind its argument. So there are two
values in play: the live one it is given, and the delayed one it hands back —
which means the delayed one is state.

## Hint 2
When the live value changes, start a timer that will copy it across:

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  const id = setTimeout(() => setDebounced(value), delay);
  return () => { … };
}, [value, delay]);
```

## Hint 3
The cleanup is the entire debounce. Because React runs the previous cleanup
before the next effect, a value that changes again before the timer fires
cancels the pending `setTimeout` and schedules a new one — so only a pause
longer than `delay` ever lets a value through. Without `clearTimeout` you do not
have a debounce; you have every intermediate value arriving late, in order. The
last thing to decide is what the very first render should return.

## Hint 1
The hook returns a value that *lags* behind its argument. So there are two
values in play: the live one it is given, and the delayed one it hands back —
which means the delayed one is state.

## Hint 2
When the live value changes, start a timer that will copy it across:

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  const id = setTimeout(() => setDebounced(value), delay);
  return () => { … };
}, [value, delay]);
```

## Hint 3
The cleanup is the entire debounce. Because React runs the previous cleanup
before the next effect, a value that changes again before the timer fires
cancels the pending `setTimeout` and schedules a new one — so only a pause
longer than `delay` ever lets a value through. Without `clearTimeout` you do not
have a debounce; you have every intermediate value arriving late, in order. The
last thing to decide is what the very first render should return.

lessons.briefing:
# 11 — Performance patterns Here is the default behaviour, and it surprises people: **when a component re-renders, React re-renders every component below it**, whether or not their props changed. Not the DOM — React still only touches the parts of the document that actually differ — but your component functions all run again, and all the work inside them runs again with them. That is usually fine. Rendering a function that returns some JSX is cheap, and React is very good at the diffing that follows. It stops being fine in two situations: when a component does something genuinely expensive during render, and when a large subtree re-renders because of a state change that had nothing to do with it — a keystroke in a search box redrawing a thousand-row table. React gives you three tools for that, and this lesson is as much about when *not* to reach for them. `memo` lets a component skip a render whose props are unchanged. `useMemo` remembers a computed value between renders. `useCallback` remembers a function. All three have the same shape — "keep the previous one unless something changed" — and all three cost something: a comparison on every render, memory, and a dependency array you now have to keep honest. The most important idea in the lesson is exercise 4, where the fix is not memoization at all. Moving state to where it belongs deletes the problem outright, costs nothing, and cannot rot. Reach for structure first. ## Concept — three tools, one idea **`memo` — skip a component.** ```tsx const Row = memo(function Row({ product }) { return
  • {product.name}
    • ; }); ``` `memo` returns a component that compares its new props with the old ones and skips rendering when they are shallowly equal — each prop compared with `Object.is`. Strings and numbers behave the way you expect. **Objects, arrays and functions are compared by identity**, so a prop rebuilt on every render makes `memo` a comparison that always fails, plus a wasted render. That failure mode is exercise 2, and it is the single most common reason memo "does nothing". **`useMemo` — remember a value.** ```tsx const visible = useMemo(() => filterAndSort(products, filter), [products, filter]); ``` The factory runs on the first render and again whenever a dependency changes; otherwise React hands back the value it already has. Note the shape — a function that *returns* the value, not the value. `useMemo` has a second job that is not about speed at all: keeping an object or array **identity-stable** so that a memoized child, or an effect's dependency array, sees it as unchanged. That use is a correctness tool, not an optimisation. **`useCallback` — remember a function.** `useCallback(fn, deps)` is exactly `useMemo(() => fn, deps)`, with nicer syntax. It matters only when the function is a dependency of something: a prop to a memoized child, or an entry in an effect's dependency array (which is why it turned up in lesson 07). **What is already stable and needs none of this:** `useState` setters, `useReducer`'s `dispatch`, refs from `useRef`, and anything defined outside the component. ### When not to - **Do not memoize by default.** Every `memo` is a comparison on every render and a dependency array that can go stale. A wrong dependency array does not make things slow, it makes them *wrong* — the classic symptom is a handler that keeps calling yesterday's callback. - **Measure first.** React DevTools' Profiler shows you which components rendered and why. "This feels slow" is not a finding. - **Prefer structure.** Moving state down (exercise 4), lifting content up as `children` so it does not re-render with its parent, or splitting a component in two are all free and permanent. - **React Compiler.** React now ships a compiler that inserts this memoization automatically, which is a strong signal about how much of it is mechanical bookkeeping. It does not remove the need to understand what it is doing, and it only works on code that follows the rules of hooks. ## Exercise 1 — `memo` Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `ExpensiveRow({ label, onRender })` renders the label in an `
  • `. Make it skip rendering when its props have not changed, while still updating when `label` really does change. The `onRender` probe counts renders, as in lesson 03. ``` uv run dojo test react 11_performance_patterns ex1 ``` ## Exercise 2 — `useCallback` Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `Child` is **already memoized** and you should not change it. `Parent` has its own click counter, and every click of `Bump` re-renders the child even though nothing the child cares about changed. Fix `Parent` so that clicking `Bump` three times leaves the child rendered exactly once, and clicking `Pick` still sets the picked value. ``` uv run dojo test react 11_performance_patterns ex2 ``` ## Exercise 3 — `useMemo` Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `Report({ rows, compute })` shows `Total: 6` and has a `Toggle details` button. `compute` is expensive; pretend it takes 200ms. Make it run once per distinct `rows`, not once per render. ``` uv run dojo test react 11_performance_patterns ex3 ``` ## Exercise 4 — the fix that is not memoization Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `Dashboard` has a note field and an `ExpensiveList` that has nothing to do with it. Every keystroke re-renders the list. Make five keystrokes produce exactly **one** render of `ExpensiveList`, while the note is still echoed in the live region. `ExpensiveList` is not memoized and must stay that way — **solve this without `memo`**. There is a structural change that removes the problem entirely, and finding it is the exercise. ``` uv run dojo test react 11_performance_patterns ex4 ``` ## Challenge — the capstone Edit `challenge/solution.tsx`. `ProductTable({ products, onRowRender })` already works: it filters by a text box labelled `Filter`, sorts A–Z, renders each product in an `
  • `, and reports `1 of 4 shown`. What it does badly is re-render every visible row on every keystroke. Fix that so a row which was on screen before the filter changed, and is still on screen after, does not render again — without changing any visible behaviour. Honest difficulty note: two of this lesson's three tools apply, and one of them does not. Working out which is which is the point. ``` uv run dojo test react 11_performance_patterns challenge ```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading — react/11_performance_patterns

## Notes

**Rendering is not painting.** A React "render" is calling your component
function and producing element objects; the commit that follows touches only
the DOM nodes that actually differ. So a component re-rendering is usually
cheap — the expensive parts are whatever *you* do during render (sorting ten
thousand rows, formatting dates in a loop) and the sheer number of components
when a large subtree re-renders. Both of those are what the three tools in this
lesson target, and neither is "the DOM is slow".

**Why React re-renders children by default.** Comparing props costs time and
memory, and for the overwhelming majority of components the comparison is more
expensive than just rendering. React's designers chose the default that is right
most often and made the opt-in explicit. That is the honest answer to "why isn't
memo the default", and it is a good interview answer.

**Shallow equality, and the identity trap.** `memo`'s comparison is one level
deep, per prop, with `Object.is`. Primitives compare by value; objects, arrays
and functions compare by reference. Since JSX creates a new object literal every
time it is evaluated, `style={{}}`, `items={[]}`, `onClick={() => …}` and
`config={{ a: 1 }}` are all new on every render. A memoized child receiving any
of them never skips anything.

**Dependency arrays are the maintenance cost.** A wrong dependency array on
`useMemo` or `useCallback` does not degrade performance — it produces a stale
value or a stale closure, which is a correctness bug that reproduces
intermittently. That asymmetry is the real argument against memoizing "just in
case": the downside of not memoizing is some wasted work, and the downside of
memoizing wrong is a bug.

**Measure with the Profiler.** React DevTools' Profiler records a session,
shows which components rendered in each commit, how long they took, and — with
"record why each component rendered" enabled — which prop or state caused it.
Almost every real performance investigation ends somewhere surprising, which is
why guessing is a poor use of a day.

**The React Compiler.** React now ships a compiler that automatically inserts
the equivalent of `memo`, `useMemo` and `useCallback` where it can prove they
are safe. It is a strong statement about how much of this is mechanical. It also
raises the value of understanding the model rather than the API: the compiler
can only work on components that obey the rules of hooks and do not mutate their
props or state.

## ex1 — what `memo` actually compares

The mechanics are simple; the useful part is the boundary. `memo` compares
props, and props only. It does **not** stop a re-render caused by the
component's own state changing, and it does **not** stop one caused by a context
the component reads. A memoized component that consumes `ThemeContext`
re-renders whenever that context value changes, no matter what its props say —
which is the interaction that surprises people, and the reason lesson 09 was
fussy about stable context values.

almost always a mistake: it is easy to write one that ignores a prop that
matters, producing a component that silently shows stale data. If shallow

every bump, and the memoization would be back to doing nothing — at which point
the right move is to restructure (updater form, a ref, or a reducer) rather than

callers it cannot control. Being able to say that out loud is a senior-level

challenge, an options object passed to a memoized child, a dependency of an

every keystroke re-rendered a component that had no interest in it. Moving the
state into the smallest component that needs it means `Dashboard` holds no
state at all and therefore never re-renders — and no comparison, no wrapper and
no dependency array had to be introduced to achieve it.

somebody passes an inline arrow. Moving the state adds nothing and cannot rot.

function and producing element objects; the commit that follows touches only

cheap — the expensive parts are whatever *you* do during render (sorting ten
thousand rows, formatting dates in a loop) and the sheer number of components
when a large subtree re-renders. Both of those are what the three tools in this
lesson target, and neither is "the DOM is slow".

**Why React re-renders children by default.** Comparing props costs time and
memory, and for the overwhelming majority of components the comparison is more
expensive than just rendering. React's designers chose the default that is right
most often and made the opt-in explicit. That is the honest answer to "why isn't
memo the default", and it is a good interview answer.

**Shallow equality, and the identity trap.** `memo`'s comparison is one level
deep, per prop, with `Object.is`. Primitives compare by value; objects, arrays
and functions compare by reference. Since JSX creates a new object literal every
time it is evaluated, `style={{}}`, `items={[]}`, `onClick={() => …}` and

of them never skips anything.

value or a stale closure, which is a correctness bug that reproduces
intermittently. That asymmetry is the real argument against memoizing "just in

shows which components rendered in each commit, how long they took, and — with
"record why each component rendered" enabled — which prop or state caused it.

why guessing is a poor use of a day.

## Challenge — the capstone

Edit `challenge/solution.tsx`. `ProductTable({ products, onRowRender })` already
works: it filters by a text box labelled `Filter`, sorts A–Z, renders each
product in an `<li>`, and reports `1 of 4 shown`.

What it does badly is re-render every visible row on every keystroke. Fix that
so a row which was on screen before the filter changed, and is still on screen
after, does not render again — without changing any visible behaviour.

Honest difficulty note: two of this lesson's three tools apply, and one of them
does not. Working out which is which is the point.

```
uv run dojo test react 11_performance_patterns challenge
```

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `ExpensiveRow({ label, onRender })` renders the label
in an `<li>`. Make it skip rendering when its props have not changed, while

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
By default, when a parent re-renders, React re-renders every child — it does
not compare props, because comparing is not free and is usually a waste. You
can opt one component into that comparison.

## Hint 2
`memo` wraps a component and returns a new one that skips rendering when its
props are shallowly equal to last time:

```tsx
export const ExpensiveRow = memo(function ExpensiveRow({ label, onRender }) {
  …
});
```

Naming the inner function is not required, but it is what shows up in stack
traces and the React DevTools, so it is worth the seven characters.

## Hint 3
"Shallowly equal" means each prop compared with `Object.is`. Strings and
numbers behave the way you expect; objects, arrays and functions are compared
by identity, so a prop rebuilt on every render defeats the whole thing. The gate
passes the same spy every time, which is why this one works — and exercise 2 is
what happens when it does not.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
By default, when a parent re-renders, React re-renders every child — it does
not compare props, because comparing is not free and is usually a waste. You
can opt one component into that comparison.

## Hint 2
`memo` wraps a component and returns a new one that skips rendering when its
props are shallowly equal to last time:

```tsx
export const ExpensiveRow = memo(function ExpensiveRow({ label, onRender }) {
  …
});
```

Naming the inner function is not required, but it is what shows up in stack
traces and the React DevTools, so it is worth the seven characters.

## Hint 3
"Shallowly equal" means each prop compared with `Object.is`. Strings and
numbers behave the way you expect; objects, arrays and functions are compared
by identity, so a prop rebuilt on every render defeats the whole thing. The gate
passes the same spy every time, which is why this one works — and exercise 2 is
what happens when it does not.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
`compute(rows)` runs during every render, including the renders caused by
opening and closing the details — which have nothing to do with the numbers.
Pretend `compute` takes 200ms and the problem becomes obvious.

## Hint 2
`useMemo(factory, deps)` calls the factory on the first render and then only
again when a dependency changes; in between it hands back the value it already
had:

```tsx
const total = useMemo(() => compute(rows), [/* … */]);
```

Note the shape: `useMemo` takes a *function that returns the value*, not the
value. `useMemo(compute(rows), […])` calls it immediately every render, which
is exactly what you are trying to avoid.

## Hint 3
List everything the factory reads from this render — there are two things, not
one. Then note the sharp edge: `rows` is an array, compared by identity, so a
parent that writes `<Report rows={[1, 2, 3]} …/>` inline gets a new array every
render and no memoization at all. Deciding whose problem that is — the parent's
or `Report`'s — is a real API design question.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
`compute(rows)` runs during every render, including the renders caused by
opening and closing the details — which have nothing to do with the numbers.
Pretend `compute` takes 200ms and the problem becomes obvious.

## Hint 2
`useMemo(factory, deps)` calls the factory on the first render and then only
again when a dependency changes; in between it hands back the value it already
had:

```tsx
const total = useMemo(() => compute(rows), [/* … */]);
```

Note the shape: `useMemo` takes a *function that returns the value*, not the
value. `useMemo(compute(rows), […])` calls it immediately every render, which
is exactly what you are trying to avoid.

## Hint 3
List everything the factory reads from this render — there are two things, not
one. Then note the sharp edge: `rows` is an array, compared by identity, so a
parent that writes `<Report rows={[1, 2, 3]} …/>` inline gets a new array every
render and no memoization at all. Deciding whose problem that is — the parent's
or `Report`'s — is a real API design question.

## Exercise 4 — the fix that is not memoization

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `Dashboard` has a note field and an `ExpensiveList`
that has nothing to do with it. Every keystroke re-renders the list.

Make five keystrokes produce exactly **one** render of `ExpensiveList`, while
the note is still echoed in the live region.

`ExpensiveList` is not memoized and must stay that way — **solve this without
`memo`**. There is a structural change that removes the problem entirely, and
finding it is the exercise.

```
uv run dojo test react 11_performance_patterns ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Ask who actually needs `note`. Two elements: the input and the `<output>` that
echoes it. `ExpensiveList` does not, and never will — yet it re-renders on every
keystroke, because a state change re-renders the component that owns the state
and everything below it.

## Hint 2
So move the state down to the smallest component that can hold it. Pull the
label, the input and the output into a component of their own, put the
`useState` in there, and let `Dashboard` render it as a sibling of the list.

```tsx
function NoteField() {
  const [note, setNote] = useState("");
  return ( … );
}
```

`Dashboard` then holds no state at all, so nothing makes it re-render.

## Hint 3
You could also have reached for `memo` on `ExpensiveList`, and the gate would
go green. Do it the structural way anyway, and notice what it costs: nothing.
No wrapper, no comparison on every render, no prop that has to stay stable
forever, nothing to break the day somebody passes an inline arrow. The remaining
question — worth answering before you move on — is when moving state down is
*not* available, and what you would do then.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Ask who actually needs `note`. Two elements: the input and the `<output>` that
echoes it. `ExpensiveList` does not, and never will — yet it re-renders on every
keystroke, because a state change re-renders the component that owns the state
and everything below it.

## Hint 2
So move the state down to the smallest component that can hold it. Pull the
label, the input and the output into a component of their own, put the
`useState` in there, and let `Dashboard` render it as a sibling of the list.

```tsx
function NoteField() {
  const [note, setNote] = useState("");
  return ( … );
}
```

`Dashboard` then holds no state at all, so nothing makes it re-render.

## Hint 3
You could also have reached for `memo` on `ExpensiveList`, and the gate would
go green. Do it the structural way anyway, and notice what it costs: nothing.
No wrapper, no comparison on every render, no prop that has to stay stable
forever, nothing to break the day somebody passes an inline arrow. The remaining
question — worth answering before you move on — is when moving state down is
*not* available, and what you would do then.

# Reading — react/d01_jsx_rendering ## Notes Every problem in this set is the same shape: props in, one element tree out, no state anywhere. What varies is where the trap sits. Three of them are about the boundary between JavaScript and markup — braces hold an expression, and that expression is evaluated to a *value*, which React then inserts as text. Three are about attributes: which ones are camelCase props (`dateTime`, `className`), which ones keep their hyphens (`aria-*`, `data-*`), and what React does with an attribute whose value is `undefined`. The last two are about the accessibility tree, which is the only DOM the gates can see — a component that renders beautifully and announces nothing is, to these tests and to a screen-reader user, not finished. ## ex1 Tests whether you can keep a computation inside the render output instead of smuggling it into a variable you then forget to use. The classic mistake is `{cents}` — shipping the raw storage unit to the user, which is how you get a coffee priced at 350 dollars. The model answer computes `cents / 100` and calls `.toFixed(2)` at the point of use, because the formatted string has no reason to exist anywhere else in the component. ## ex2 Tests whether you reach for the elements that carry meaning rather than the ones that carry styles. The classic mistake is a `
` with an `` and a `

`: it looks identical and says nothing, so `getByRole("figure")` finds nothing. The second trap is `alt=""`, which is a deliberate claim that the image is decorative — it removes the image from the accessibility tree entirely, and with it the `img` role the gate queries by. The model answer uses `figure` + `figcaption` and puts the real description in `alt`. ## ex3 Tests two things at once: that a component returning several siblings returns a fragment, and that you know which JSX attribute names differ from their HTML spelling. The classic mistake is wrapping the pair in a `

` — invisible in the browser, fatal inside a `

` or a `

` where only certain children are legal. The second is writing `datetime` in JSX and getting a React warning about an unknown prop. The model answer returns `<>...` and spells the prop `dateTime`, letting React lowercase it on the way to the DOM. ## ex4 Tests whether you can say the same fact twice — once visually, once to the accessibility tree — from one computed value. The classic mistake is a progress-shaped `
` with no role, which announces nothing at all; the second is `done / total` with a total of zero, which renders the string `NaN%` in front of the user. The model answer computes the percentage once, above the return, with a guard for the empty case, then spends it in two places. ## ex5 Tests the boring correctness that interviews actually probe: the comparison, the slice length, and the trailing space. The classic mistake is `>=` instead of `>`, which truncates a string that fits perfectly and adds three dots to hide it. The second is `slice(0, limit) + "..."` with no trim, which produces `Coffee is a ...` whenever the cut lands on a space. The model answer decides the string in a `const` where both cases are visible side by side. ## ex6 Tests whether you understand what JSX interpolation actually does. The classic mistake is the one the stub makes: reaching for `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` because the string "contains HTML". It does not contain HTML; it contains angle brackets, and turning them into markup is precisely how a notice string from a database becomes a cross-site scripting hole. The model answer is `{text}` — React escapes it, which is the default you should have to argue your way out of, not into. ## ex7 Tests the two-audience problem. A rating drawn with characters is a picture: it needs `role="img"` and a label that says what the picture shows, and the characters themselves need to disappear from the accessibility tree or the user hears the sentence and then a mouthful of punctuation. The classic mistake is putting `aria-label` on the element and forgetting `aria-hidden` on the glyphs — or the reverse, hiding the wrapper so the whole widget vanishes from the tree. The model answer nests them: labelled outer element, hidden inner element. ## ex8 Tests three independent details spread over two elements. The `` is what carries the sort state, and `aria-sort` must be *absent* — not `"none"`, not `"ascending"` by default — when the column is not sorted, because those are different claims to a screen-reader user scanning a table. The classic mistake is a ternary with two branches, which asserts a direction the component was never given; the model answer computes the value with three cases and hands React `undefined`, which it omits. The other two details are the arrow, which is decoration next to a real label and so must stay out of the accessible name, and `type="button"` on a control whose parent form this component cannot see. ## Further reading - [Writing markup with JSX](https://react.dev/learn/writing-markup-with-jsx) - [JavaScript in JSX with curly braces](https://react.dev/learn/javascript-in-jsx-with-curly-braces) - [Common components: props and attributes](https://react.dev/reference/react-dom/components/common) - [Fragment (`<>...`)](https://react.dev/reference/react/Fragment) - [MDN: the `
