## Exercise 1 — cents into a price line

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `PriceTag({ label, cents })` renders one paragraph
reading exactly `<label> - $<amount>`, where the amount is `cents / 100` with two
decimal places: `PriceTag({ label: "Flat white", cents: 350 })` renders
`Flat white - $3.50`, and `cents: 0` renders `$0.00`.

```
uv run dojo test react d01_jsx_rendering ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Everything between `{` and `}` in JSX is a JavaScript expression, evaluated
once per render. The price is not a prop you were given; it is a value you
compute from `cents` at the moment you render it.

## Hint 2
Two decimal places is `toFixed(2)`, which returns a string. Watch the literal
text around the braces: the dash, the spaces and the dollar sign are ordinary
JSX text, and JSX keeps the spaces you type on a single line.

## Exercise 4 — one percentage, two audiences

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `ProgressMeter({ label, done, total })` renders a `<div>`
with `role="progressbar"`, named by `label`, carrying `aria-valuemin="0"`,
`aria-valuemax="100"` and an `aria-valuenow` holding the rounded percentage —
and showing that same percentage as text, as `38%`. A `total` of `0` is not an
error: the percentage is `0`.

```
uv run dojo test react d01_jsx_rendering ex4
```

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Two jobs. Compute one percentage - rounded, and safe when there is nothing to
do - and then say it twice: once as text for the reader, once as ARIA
attributes for everyone else.

## Hint 2
`role`, `aria-label`, `aria-valuenow`, `aria-valuemin` and `aria-valuemax` are
written in JSX exactly as they are in HTML, hyphens and all - they are the
exception to camelCase. Numbers in braces are fine; React stringifies them.

## Hint 3
`done / total` with a total of zero is `NaN`, and `NaN%` is what your users
would read. Decide the percentage before the JSX, in a `const`, where a guard
is one ternary rather than three.

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. `Excerpt({ text, limit })` renders a paragraph. Text
whose length is `limit` or less is shown unchanged. Longer text is shown as its
first `limit` characters, with any trailing whitespace removed, followed by three
dots: `Coffee is a brewed drink` at `limit: 12` renders `Coffee is a...`.

```
uv run dojo test react d01_jsx_rendering ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Work out the string first and render it second. A `const` above the `return`
keeps the JSX readable and gives you somewhere to put the two cases.

## Hint 2
Three details decide this one: the comparison is strictly greater than the
limit, `slice(0, limit)` takes exactly that many characters, and a slice that
ends mid-space needs its end trimmed before the dots are appended.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — text that stays text

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. `LiteralNotice({ text })` renders a paragraph showing
`text` exactly as given — including any angle brackets in it. The gate passes a
string containing an `<a>` tag and then asserts that the document contains no
link. The stub does the wrong thing on purpose.

```
uv run dojo test react d01_jsx_rendering ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The stub reaches for the escape hatch. Ask what the plain version does with a
string that happens to contain angle brackets - JSX has a rule about that, and
the rule is the whole answer.

## Hint 2
A value interpolated into JSX is inserted as a text node, never parsed as
markup. That is React's built-in defence against injected HTML, and the fix
here is to delete code rather than write it.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — the sortable column header

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. `SortHeader({ label, direction })` renders a
`<th scope="col">` holding a `<button>`, and:

- the button's **accessible name is exactly `label`** — an arrow next to it is
  hidden from assistive technology, and the button carries `type="button"`;
- the arrow is `^` when `direction` is `"asc"` and `v` when it is `"desc"`, and
  there is no arrow at all when `direction` was not passed;
- the `<th>` carries `aria-sort="ascending"` or `aria-sort="descending"` to
  match — and **no `aria-sort` attribute at all** when `direction` was not
  passed.

The gate renders it inside a `<table>`, because a `<th>` outside one is not a
column header.

```
uv run dojo test react d01_jsx_rendering ex8
```

The arrow is decoration sitting beside a real text label, so it gets the same
treatment the stars got in ex7 - and check the button's `type` while you are
there. A header button inside a filter form is the classic place where a
missing type reloads the page on the first click.

lessons.explanation:
# Reading — react/d02_components_props

## Notes

A props interface is an API, and these eight problems drill the parts of it that
callers actually get wrong. Half of them turn on the difference between three
absences: a prop that was never passed (`undefined`), one passed as an explicit
nothing (`null`), and one passed as an empty value (`""`, `0`, `false`). Default
parameters fire for exactly the first; `||` fires for all of them; `??` fires
for the first two. The other half are about who owns a value. A component that
copies a prop into state has forked the truth, and every bug after that is a
synchronisation bug. The pattern that unites the set: decide during render, from
props, and hand decisions the component cannot make back to the caller through
a callback.

## ex1

Tests the most basic form of an optional prop, and whether you put the fallback
in the parameter list rather than in the JSX. The classic mistake is
`{salutation ?? "Hello"}` scattered at each use site, which works until there
are three of them and one drifts. The model answer defaults in the destructuring
pattern, so the rest of the component can treat `salutation` as a plain string.

## ex2

Tests two ideas at once: that `alt` is not a nice-to-have but the image's
accessible name, and that one prop can feed several attributes. The classic
mistake is `alt=""`, which is a deliberate claim that the image is decorative
and removes it from the accessibility tree — the gate cannot even find it by
role afterwards. The model answer defaults `size` to 40 in the parameter list
and spends it twice.

## ex3

Tests conditional attributes. The classic mistake is applying `target="_blank"`
to every link because one of them needed it, which hijacks internal navigation;
the second is adding the new-tab warning as a `title` or an `aria-label`, both
of which replace or duplicate the name rather than extending it. The model
answer yields `undefined` for the attributes in the internal case — React omits
an attribute whose value is `undefined` — and adds real text inside the anchor
for the external one, because a warning that only screen readers get is a
warning sighted users deserve too.

## ex4

Tests whether you can write a component that owns nothing. The gate clicks
`Increase` twice without changing the `value` prop; a component holding its own
`useState` answers 6 and then 7, and that second 7 is the moment the component's
idea of the number and the parent's idea of it part company. The classic mistake
is `useState(value)`, which reads as harmless because it initialises correctly
and is wrong ever after. The model answer has no state at all: the display is
the prop, and the buttons only ask.

## ex5

Tests a variant map plus the honest empty case. Roles are not decoration:
`status` is a polite live region and `alert` interrupts, so choosing between
them is a product decision about how loudly a failure should shout. The classic
mistake is an if-chain that falls through to a default pill for unknown input,
inventing UI for data the component does not understand. The model answer looks
the label up in one object and returns `null` when there is no entry.

## ex6

Tests derived values and the off-by-one that always comes with them. The classic
mistake is `last = page * pageSize`, which reads `Showing 51-60 of 57` on the
final page and is the single most common pagination bug in production. The model
answer clamps with `Math.min` and gives the empty case its own sentence rather
than rendering `Showing 1-0 of 0`.

## ex7

Tests the distinction between an accessible *name* and an accessible
*description*. Text placed inside the button joins the name, so a helpful
sentence rendered there silently renames the control from `Email alerts` to
`Email alerts We send at most one message a day` — the stub does exactly this,
and it is what happens in real code when a hint is dropped inside a label. The
model answer renders the description in its own element with a `useId` id and
points `aria-describedby` at it, leaving the attribute off entirely when there
is no description so nothing dangles.

## ex8

Tests all three absences in one component. `footer={null}` is a caller saying
"there is deliberately no footer", and both `||` and a naive default parameter
that the caller never triggers will talk over that instruction. The second half
tests optional callbacks: a Dismiss button that calls `undefined` looks fine
until someone clicks it, so the button should not exist unless the handler does.
The model answer defaults `footer` in the parameter list, tests `footer === null`
explicitly for the deliberate-nothing case, and renders the button only when
`onDismiss` was passed.

## Further reading

- [Passing props to a component](https://react.dev/learn/passing-props-to-a-component)
- [Sharing state between components (controlled components)](https://react.dev/learn/sharing-state-between-components)
- [Conditional rendering](https://react.dev/learn/conditional-rendering)
- [MDN: default parameters](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Functions/Default_parameters)
- [MDN: the switch role](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Roles/switch_role)
- [MDN: aria-describedby](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Attributes/aria-describedby)

## Exercise 3 — the external link

anchor with that `href`.

  `<label> (opens in a new tab)`.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — the switch and its description

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. `ToggleRow({ label, checked, onChange, description,
disabled })` renders a control with `role="switch"`:

- its accessible name is exactly `label`, and `aria-checked` follows `checked`;
- clicking it calls `onChange(!checked)` once — it stores nothing itself;
- when `description` is passed, it becomes the switch's **accessible
  description** (`aria-describedby` pointing at another element, not text inside
  the button);
- when `description` is not passed there is no description and no
  `aria-describedby` attribute at all;
- `disabled` disables the control, and a click on it calls nothing.

```
uv run dojo test react d02_components_props ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
A name and a description are two different things in the accessibility tree.
The name is what the control is called; the description is extra detail read
after it. Text placed inside the button becomes part of the name.

## Hint 2
So the description has to live in its own element outside the button, joined to
it by `aria-describedby`, which takes the *id* of that element. `useId` gives
you an id that is unique even when the component is rendered twice on a page.

## Hint 3
When there is no description there must be no attribute either - a
`aria-describedby` pointing at nothing is a silent bug that survives code
review. You already know how React treats an attribute whose value is
`undefined`; decide where that ternary goes.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
A name and a description are two different things in the accessibility tree.
The name is what the control is called; the description is extra detail read
after it. Text placed inside the button becomes part of the name.

## Hint 2
So the description has to live in its own element outside the button, joined to
it by `aria-describedby`, which takes the *id* of that element. `useId` gives
you an id that is unique even when the component is rendered twice on a page.

## Hint 3
When there is no description there must be no attribute either - a
`aria-describedby` pointing at nothing is a silent bug that survives code
review. You already know how React treats an attribute whose value is
`undefined`; decide where that ternary goes.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — undefined is not null

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. `NoticeBar({ message, footer, onDismiss })` shows
`message`, plus:

- no `footer` prop → the default text `Nothing to do`;
- `footer={null}` → **no footer text at all** (the caller said there is none);
- `footer="…"` → that text;
- `onDismiss` passed → a `type="button"` button named `Dismiss` that calls it
  once; not passed → no button at all.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Three values that all read as "falsy" mean three different things here:
`undefined` is "I did not say", `null` is "I say there is none", and a string is
the answer. Only one of them should reach the default.

## Hint 2
A default parameter fires for `undefined` and for nothing else - not for
`null`, not for `""`, not for `0`. `||` fires for all of them, which is why the
stub loses the difference; `??` fires for `undefined` and `null` together,
which is not what is wanted either.

## Hint 3
The Dismiss button exists only when there is something for it to call. Decide
what your condition tests - the presence of the prop, not its truthiness - and
remember what an unlabelled `<button>` inside a form does by default.

lessons.briefing:
# d03 — Children and composition (drill set)

Eight problems on the prop that is markup. Slots, wrappers, specialisation,
children as a function, reading the children you were handed, and a compound
component that shares one id between three parts that never meet. It drills
`02_props_composition` — go back there if "composition over configuration" is
still a slogan rather than a decision you can make in code.

The rule that runs through the set: a component that accepts children should
know as little as possible about them. Every time one of these components is
tempted to inspect, wrap or rewrite what it was given, ask what it costs the
caller.

## Exercise 1 — a titled section

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `Section({ title, children })` renders a `<section>`
containing exactly two things in order: an `<h2>` holding `title`, then
`children`.

```
uv run dojo test react d03_children_composition ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — a label with no ids

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `FieldWrapper({ label, children })` renders the `label`
text and the children so that the control passed as `children` is genuinely
labelled — `screen.getByLabelText("Email")` must find it. You are not given an
id and must not invent one: the association is structural.

```
uv run dojo test react d03_children_composition ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — a banner with two volumes

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `Banner({ tone, children })` wraps `children` in a live
region: `role="alert"` when `tone` is `urgent`, `role="status"` for any other
tone. The children may be markup, and they go inside the live region.

```
uv run dojo test react d03_children_composition ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — three slots, three landmarks

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `PageLayout({ header, sidebar, children })` renders
`header` inside a `<header>`, `sidebar` inside an `<aside>` and `children`
inside a `<main>`. Those three elements are the banner, complementary and main
landmarks, and the gate finds them by role.

```
uv run dojo test react d03_children_composition ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — specialisation, not duplication

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`, which exports two components.

- `Button({ tone = "default", children, onClick })` renders a `type="button"`
  button showing `children`. When `tone` is `"danger"` it also renders the text
  ` (cannot be undone)` inside the button, so the accessible name becomes
  `<children> (cannot be undone)`.
- `DangerButton({ children, onClick })` renders **`Button`** with the danger
  tone, passing `children` and `onClick` through. It does not render a
  `<button>` of its own.

```
uv run dojo test react d03_children_composition ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — children as a function

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. `Toggler({ children })` owns a boolean that starts
`false` and calls `children({ on, toggle })` to render. `toggle` flips the
boolean. `Toggler` renders no markup of its own — whatever the function returns
is what reaches the page, with nothing wrapped around it.

```
uv run dojo test react d03_children_composition ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — reading the children

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`, which exports two components.

- `Case({ when, children })` — a marker: on its own it renders its children.
- `Switcher({ value, fallback, children })` — walks its children, finds the
  single `Case` whose `when` equals `value`, and renders **that Case's
  children** and nothing else. When no `Case` matches it renders `fallback`.
  Children that are not elements (`false`, `null`, a whitespace string) must be
  skipped without complaint.

```
uv run dojo test react d03_children_composition ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — the compound field

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`, which exports `FormField` with `FormField.Label`,
`FormField.Control` and `FormField.Hint` attached to it. Used like this:

```tsx
<FormField>
  <FormField.Label>Password</FormField.Label>
  <FormField.Control type="password" />
  <FormField.Hint>At least 12 characters</FormField.Hint>
</FormField>
```

- the label labels the control, and the hint is the control's **accessible
  description**;
- ids are generated with `useId`, so two `FormField`s on one page do not collide;
- props given to `FormField.Control` reach the real `<input>`;
- when there is no `FormField.Hint` among the children, the control carries **no**
  `aria-describedby` at all.

```
uv run dojo test react d03_children_composition ex8
```

# Reading — react/d03_children_composition

## Notes

Composition is the answer React gives to the question every UI library has to
answer: how do you write a component that is useful in situations its author
never imagined? The answer is that you do not add another prop. You leave a hole
and let the caller fill it. This set walks the ladder of holes, from the plain
one to the awkward ones: `children` as markup, several named slots, a
specialised component built on a general one, `children` as a *function* so the
caller gets access to state the component owns, and finally children that the
parent inspects rather than merely renders. The higher you climb, the more the
component knows about its children and the less freely it can be reused - which
is why the last two rungs need a real reason.

## ex1

Tests the plain slot and the discipline of not looking inside it. The classic
mistake is a `title` prop that the component renders in a `<div>` styled to look
like a heading, which leaves the document with no outline for a screen-reader
user to navigate. The model answer is three lines: a sectioning element, a real
`<h2>`, and `{children}` rendered untouched.

## ex2

Tests the two ways of associating a label with a control, and which one survives
not knowing what the control is. `htmlFor` needs an id, and this wrapper was
never given one and must not invent one, because the caller may have set an id
already. The classic mistake is a `<span>` holding the label text next to the
input: visually identical, invisible to `getByLabelText` and to every assistive
technology. The model answer wraps the children in a real `<label>`, which
associates implicitly.

## ex3

Tests that the wrapper decides the container and nothing else, with the tone
choosing between two live-region roles. The classic mistake is hard-coding
`role="alert"` because the first case needed it - which means every draft-saved
message interrupts whatever the user was reading. The model answer computes the
role from the prop and puts the children inside the region, so an announcement
carries the link it came with.

## ex4

Tests named slots. Once a component has more than one hole, only one of them can
be `children`, and the rest arrive as props whose values are markup. The classic
mistake is rendering all three slots into anonymous `<div>`s, which produces a
page with no landmarks at all: keyboard users lose the "skip to main content"
target, and screen-reader users lose the ability to jump between regions. The
model answer maps each slot to the element that already carries the right role.

## ex5

Tests specialisation. `DangerButton` is not a new button; it is `Button` with
one decision taken, and the way you can tell is that it does not contain the
word `<button>` anywhere. The classic mistake is copying the markup so the two
diverge the first time someone adds a loading state to one of them. The model
answer renders `Button` with `tone="danger"` and forwards `children` and
`onClick` - about four lines, none of them markup.

## ex6

Tests the render prop, which is the first pattern in this set where the caller
gets something back. `Toggler` owns the state and knows nothing about the UI;
the function it calls owns the UI and knows nothing about how the state is
kept. The classic mistake is wrapping the result in a `<div>`, which quietly
imposes a layout decision on every caller, and the second is a `toggle` that
sets state from a captured value rather than the updater form. The model answer
returns a fragment and flips with `setOn((current) => !current)`.

## ex7

Tests the `Children` API, which exists precisely because `props.children` is not
an array. It might be a single element, a string, `false`, or a nested array,
and `Children.toArray` flattens all of that while dropping the empty slots.
`isValidElement` is the guard that makes `child.type` and `child.props` safe to
read at all. The classic mistake is `children.map(...)`, which throws the moment
someone passes one child; the second is comparing `child.type.name`, which does
not survive minification. The model answer compares `child.type === Case` by
reference and renders that Case's own children.

## ex8

Tests the compound component: three parts, one shared identity, no props passed
between them. Context is what carries the id down, `useId` is what makes it
unique per instance, and `Object.assign` is what puts `Label`, `Control` and
`Hint` on `FormField` so the caller writes them as a set. The classic mistake is a
hard-coded id string, which works perfectly in a demo with one field and breaks
in production the moment there are two - both labels then point at the first
input. The second is an unconditional `aria-describedby`, which leaves a
dangling reference no browser reports; the model answer asks whether a `Hint`
is among the children before deciding what the context carries.

## Further reading

- [Passing JSX as children](https://react.dev/learn/passing-props-to-a-component#passing-jsx-as-children)
- [Extracting state logic and sharing behaviour with render props](https://react.dev/reference/react/Children)
- [`useId`](https://react.dev/reference/react/useId)
- [`createContext` and `useContext`](https://react.dev/reference/react/useContext)
- [MDN: the `<label>` element](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/label)
- [MDN: ARIA landmark roles](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Roles#landmark_roles)

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
There are two ways to join a label to a control: `htmlFor` pointing at an id,
and putting the control inside the label. Only one of them works when you have
never seen the control and cannot give it an id.

## Hint 2
A `<label>` element that contains a form control labels it implicitly - no ids,
no `useId`, nothing for the caller to remember. That is what makes this wrapper
work for an input it was handed as `children`.

## Hint 1
There are two ways to join a label to a control: `htmlFor` pointing at an id,
and putting the control inside the label. Only one of them works when you have
never seen the control and cannot give it an id.

A `<label>` element that contains a form control labels it implicitly - no ids,
no `useId`, nothing for the caller to remember. That is what makes this wrapper
work for an input it was handed as `children`.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
A slot is just a prop whose value is markup. This component has three of them -
two named, one called `children` - and its whole job is deciding what element
each one lands in.

## Hint 2
Landmarks are elements, not attributes: `<header>`, `<aside>` and `<main>` come
with the banner, complementary and main roles already attached, as long as they
are not nested inside another sectioning element that would change what they
mean.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — specialisation, not duplication

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`, which exports two components.

- `Button({ tone = "default", children, onClick })` renders a `type="button"`
  button showing `children`. When `tone` is `"danger"` it also renders the text
  ` (cannot be undone)` inside the button, so the accessible name becomes
  `<children> (cannot be undone)`.
- `DangerButton({ children, onClick })` renders **`Button`** with the danger
  tone, passing `children` and `onClick` through. It does not render a
  `<button>` of its own.

```
uv run dojo test react d03_children_composition ex5
```

## Hint 1
Two exports, but only one of them renders a `<button>`. The other is a
component that renders the first one with one decision already taken, and
forwards everything else it was given.

## Hint 2
The warning is text inside the button, which is why it changes the accessible
name. Add it in `Button`, driven by the tone, and `DangerButton` gets it for
free - that is the whole argument for specialisation over copying.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — reading the children

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`, which exports two components.

- `Case({ when, children })` — a marker: on its own it renders its children.
- `Switcher({ value, fallback, children })` — walks its children, finds the
  single `Case` whose `when` equals `value`, and renders **that Case's
  children** and nothing else. When no `Case` matches it renders `fallback`.
  Children that are not elements (`false`, `null`, a whitespace string) must be
  skipped without complaint.

```
uv run dojo test react d03_children_composition ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
`Switcher` has to look at its children before deciding what to render. Children
are a value - an array-shaped one that may also contain strings, `null` and
`false` - and React ships helpers for walking it safely.

## Hint 2
`Children.toArray(children)` gives you a flat array with the empty slots
already removed; `isValidElement(child)` tells you whether a given entry is an
element at all, which is what makes the `false` and the whitespace harmless.

## Hint 3
An element carries its component in `child.type` and its props in
`child.props`, so "is this a Case for this value" is one comparison of each.
What you render is not the matching element itself - decide what part of it the
user should actually see.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
`Switcher` has to look at its children before deciding what to render. Children
are a value - an array-shaped one that may also contain strings, `null` and
`false` - and React ships helpers for walking it safely.

## Hint 2
`Children.toArray(children)` gives you a flat array with the empty slots
already removed; `isValidElement(child)` tells you whether a given entry is an
element at all, which is what makes the `false` and the whitespace harmless.

## Hint 3
An element carries its component in `child.type` and its props in
`child.props`, so "is this a Case for this value" is one comparison of each.
What you render is not the matching element itself - decide what part of it the
user should actually see.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — the compound field

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`, which exports `FormField` with `FormField.Label`,
`FormField.Control` and `FormField.Hint` attached to it. Used like this:

```tsx
<FormField>
  <FormField.Label>Password</FormField.Label>
  <FormField.Control type="password" />
  <FormField.Hint>At least 12 characters</FormField.Hint>
</FormField>
```

- the label labels the control, and the hint is the control's **accessible
  description**;
- ids are generated with `useId`, so two `FormField`s on one page do not collide;
- props given to `FormField.Control` reach the real `<input>`;
- when there is no `FormField.Hint` among the children, the control carries **no**
  `aria-describedby` at all.

```
uv run dojo test react d03_children_composition ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The three parts never see each other in the JSX, so the shared id cannot travel
as a prop. Something has to make it available to whatever is rendered inside
`FormField`, at any depth.

## Hint 2
That is context: `createContext`, a provider in `FormFieldRoot` holding the ids from
`useId`, and `useContext` in each part. `Object.assign(FormFieldRoot, { Label,
Control, Hint })` is what lets the caller write `FormField.Label`.

## Hint 3
The last requirement is the interesting one: the control may only carry
`aria-describedby` when a hint is actually there. `FormFieldRoot` can see its own
children, and you already know how to ask whether one of them is a particular
component - decide what the context should carry when the answer is no.

lessons.briefing:
# d04 — State basics (drill set)

Eight problems on `useState`: what belongs in state, what does not, how a value
gets replaced rather than edited, and what a click handler actually sees when it
reads one. It drills `03_state_events` — if the difference between
`setCount(count + 1)` and `setCount(c => c + 1)` is still something you decide by
feel, reread that lesson first.

Nothing here fetches anything. Where a problem needs time to pass, the gate uses
fake timers and `fireEvent`, so your solution has to be correct rather than fast.

## Exercise 1 — the count that reaches the screen

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `WaterTracker({ goal })` renders a live region
(`role="status"`) reading `<n> of <goal> glasses`, a `Drink` button that adds one
glass and is **disabled** once the count reaches `goal`, and a `Reset` button
that puts the count back to `0`. The stub keeps the count in a module-level
variable, which is the bug.


while the spoiler is open, a paragraph containing `text`. The button is named
`Show spoiler` while closed and `Hide spoiler` while open. Closed means the text
is **not in the document**.

```

```

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `DraftBox({ makeInitial })` takes a function that
produces the starting draft. The draft is shown in a live region, and an `Append`
button adds one `!` to it. `makeInitial` must be called **exactly once** for the
life of the component, however many renders and updates happen.

```

```

`Add` appends the next unused name from the `names` prop (the one at index
`queue.length`) and is disabled once every name is in; `Remove first` drops the
head and is disabled while the queue is empty. A live region reads
`<n> waiting - Next: <name>`, or `Next: nobody` when it is empty.

```
uv run dojo test react d04_state_basics ex4
```

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. `SearchSummary({ items, query, onRender })` renders a
live region reading `Showing all <n> items` when `query` is empty, and otherwise
`<matches> of <n> items match <query>`, where a match is a case-insensitive
substring. `onRender` is a spy you must call once per render, and the gate
requires that **one prop change costs exactly one render**.

```
uv run dojo test react d04_state_basics ex5
```

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. `NotificationSettings()` starts from
`{ channels: { email: true, sms: false }, quietHours: false }` and renders three
`role="switch"` buttons named `Email`, `SMS` and `Quiet hours`, each reporting
itself with `aria-checked`, plus a `Revert` button that restores the settings the
component started with. Toggling one switch must leave the other two exactly as
they were — and `Revert` has to still work afterwards.

```

```

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. `DelayedCounter()` shows `Count: <n>` in a live region.
`Later` schedules `+1` to be applied 1000ms from now; `Reset` sets the count to
`0` **and cancels every increment still in flight**. Three quick taps followed by
one second of time must land on `3`.

```

```

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. `TitleDraft({ noteId, initialTitle })` renders a text box
labelled `Title`, starting from `initialTitle`, that the user can type into. A
re-render with the **same** `noteId` keeps whatever was typed. A re-render with a
**different** `noteId` shows that note's `initialTitle` instead. Do it without an
effect.

```

```

# Reading — react/d04_state_basics

## Notes

One question runs through all eight problems: what does React actually know?
It does not watch your variables, it does not look inside your objects, and it
does not re-read the arguments you gave a hook on the first render. It knows
that a setter was called, and it compares the value it was handed with the one
it is holding. Everything in this set falls out of that. A count in a plain
variable never reaches the screen; an array edited with `push` is the array
React already has; an initial value you computed yourself is computed again on
every render; and a summary kept in state is a second copy of a fact that is
already in the props. The last two problems are the ones interviewers keep
asking, because both are about *when* a value is read: the updater form reads at
apply time, and adjusting state during render reads at the moment a prop
changed.

## ex1

Tests the most basic claim in React: rendering is a function of state, and only
a state update schedules a render. The classic mistake is the stub's - a
module-level `let`, which happily counts to five while the screen still shows
zero, then jumps when some unrelated update forces a re-render. The model answer
holds the count in `useState` and computes `disabled` from it during render, so
the two can never disagree.

## ex2

Tests deriving several outputs from one boolean. The classic mistake is a second
piece of state for the button label, which then has to be flipped in every place
the first one is - two facts, one truth, and they drift the first time someone
adds a keyboard shortcut. The model answer keeps one `shown` boolean and reads
both the label and the conditional render off it.

## ex3

Tests the lazy initialiser. `useState(makeInitial())` calls the function on every
render and throws the result away every time after the first, which is invisible
until the function is expensive or has a side effect - reading `localStorage`,
parsing a large blob, generating an id. The model answer passes the function
itself, `useState(makeInitial)`, so React calls it exactly once on mount.

## ex4

Tests immutable updates for arrays. The classic mistake is `push` or `shift`
followed by a setter call with the same array: React compares the old and new
values, sees the same object, and skips the work - the screen freezes and the
bug looks like a broken button. The model answer builds a new array with a
spread or `slice` and reads the next name inside the updater callback, where the
length is the one the update is being applied to.

## ex5

Tests the difference between state and a derived value. The classic mistake is
`useState` plus a `useEffect` that recomputes the summary when props change:
correct-looking, one render too slow, and it puts a stale sentence in front of
the user every time. The `onRender` spy is how the gate sees it - one prop
change must cost one render. The model answer computes the string in a `const`
and deletes both hooks.

## ex6

Tests nested immutable updates, and it is rigged so that mutation is actually
visible. Editing `settings.channels.email` in place also edits the object the
component started from, because they are the same object - so `Revert` restores
the mutated values and the bug finally surfaces somewhere the user can see it.
The model answer copies every level it changes, using a computed key so one
function serves both channels.

## ex7

Tests the two things people get wrong about a delayed update. First, a callback
created in one render remembers that render's `count` forever, so three taps
inside one second all compute `0 + 1`; the updater form asks React for the
current value at apply time instead. Second, cancelling: a Reset that does not
clear the pending timers is undone a second later by an increment nobody can see
coming, which is why the timer ids live in a ref.

## ex8

Tests resetting state when a prop changes, which is the problem `useEffect` gets
misused for most often. An effect that syncs `initialTitle` into state renders
the wrong title first and the right one second, and re-runs whenever the
identity of its dependency changes. The classic mistake behind that is
forgetting that `useState` reads its argument only on the first render. The
model answer remembers which note is on screen and adjusts during render when it
differs - React discards that render and immediately re-runs the component, so
nothing stale is ever committed.

## Further reading

- [State: a component memory](https://react.dev/learn/state-a-components-memory)
- [Queueing a series of state updates](https://react.dev/learn/queueing-a-series-of-state-updates)
- [Updating objects in state](https://react.dev/learn/updating-objects-in-state)
- [Updating arrays in state](https://react.dev/learn/updating-arrays-in-state)
- [You might not need an effect](https://react.dev/learn/you-might-not-need-an-effect)
- [useState reference, including the lazy initialiser](https://react.dev/reference/react/useState)
- [MDN: setTimeout and clearTimeout](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/setTimeout)

## Exercise 4 — a queue you replace

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `QueueBoard({ names })` holds a queue that starts empty.
`Add` appends the next unused name from the `names` prop (the one at index
`queue.length`) and is disabled once every name is in; `Remove first` drops the
head and is disabled while the queue is empty. A live region reads
`<n> waiting - Next: <name>`, or `Next: nobody` when it is empty.

```
uv run dojo test react d04_state_basics ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The stub calls `push` and `shift`. Both of those edit the array that is already
sitting in state, and neither of them tells React anything - the screen is
still showing the render that was made before the edit.

## Hint 2
State is replaced, never edited. `[...current, item]` and `current.slice(1)`
both hand back a brand new array; `push`, `shift`, `splice` and `sort` all
change the one you were given. Learn which is which by what they return.

## Hint 3
Which name is added is a question about the queue, not about the props: the
next name is `names[queue.length]`. Reading that inside the updater callback
means you are reading the length React is about to apply the change to, rather
than the length from the render you clicked in.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
The stub calls `push` and `shift`. Both of those edit the array that is already
sitting in state, and neither of them tells React anything - the screen is
still showing the render that was made before the edit.

## Hint 2
State is replaced, never edited. `[...current, item]` and `current.slice(1)`
both hand back a brand new array; `push`, `shift`, `splice` and `sort` all
change the one you were given. Learn which is which by what they return.

## Hint 3
Which name is added is a question about the queue, not about the props: the
next name is `names[queue.length]`. Reading that inside the updater callback
means you are reading the length React is about to apply the change to, rather
than the length from the render you clicked in.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — the summary that is not state

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. `SearchSummary({ items, query, onRender })` renders a
live region reading `Showing all <n> items` when `query` is empty, and otherwise
`<matches> of <n> items match <query>`, where a match is a case-insensitive
substring. `onRender` is a spy you must call once per render, and the gate
requires that **one prop change costs exactly one render**.

```
uv run dojo test react d04_state_basics ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Ask the question that decides every one of these: could this value be worked
out from the props during the render that has them? If yes, it is not state,
and keeping it in state means keeping two copies of one fact in step.

## Hint 2
The gate counts renders with the injected `onRender` spy. An effect that sets
state renders once with the old summary and once with the new one, so the count
is the evidence - delete the state and the effect, and compute the string in a
`const` above the return.

`Later` schedules `+1` to be applied 1000ms from now; `Reset` sets the count to

```
uv run dojo test react d04_state_basics ex7
```

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Two separate bugs live in the stub. The first is arithmetic: three callbacks
created during the same render all remember the same `count`, so they all
compute the same answer. The second is ownership: nobody is holding on to the
timers, so nothing can call them off.

## Hint 2
`setCount(current => current + 1)` asks React for the value at the moment the
update is applied rather than the value from the render that scheduled it. That
alone fixes the count.

## Hint 3
For Reset you need the timer ids to survive re-renders without causing them,
which is what a ref is for. Keep the ids you have not cancelled yet, clear them
all in Reset, and decide what the list should look like afterwards so a later
Reset does not try to cancel timers that already fired.

## Hint 1
Two separate bugs live in the stub. The first is arithmetic: three callbacks
created during the same render all remember the same `count`, so they all
compute the same answer. The second is ownership: nobody is holding on to the
timers, so nothing can call them off.

## Hint 2
`setCount(current => current + 1)` asks React for the value at the moment the
update is applied rather than the value from the render that scheduled it. That
alone fixes the count.

## Hint 3
For Reset you need the timer ids to survive re-renders without causing them,
which is what a ref is for. Keep the ids you have not cancelled yet, clear them
all in Reset, and decide what the list should look like afterwards so a later
Reset does not try to cancel timers that already fired.

labelled `Title`, starting from `initialTitle`, that the user can type into. A
re-render with the **same** `noteId` keeps whatever was typed. A re-render with a


`useState(initialTitle)` reads its argument on the first render of this

lessons.briefing:
# d05 — Events and updates (drill set)

Eight problems on the other half of `03_state_events`: handlers. What a handler
is (a function you hand over, not a call you make), what it receives, how far a
click travels, and what the values it reads are worth by the time it runs. If
`onClick={handle()}` versus `onClick={handle}` is still a coin flip, reread that
lesson before starting.

Two of these are driven by `fireEvent` rather than `user-event` — ex5 because it
needs exact modifier keys, ex8 because it runs on fake timers. ex3 asserts on
what `fireEvent` *returns*, which is `false` exactly when a handler called
`preventDefault`.

## Exercise 1 — hand it over, do not call it

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `DoorBell({ onRing })` renders a button named `Ring`
that calls `onRing` once per click — and never during render. The stub calls it
while rendering, which is the shape `onClick={onRing()}` has once you unpick it.

```
uv run dojo test react d05_events_updates ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — a handler that knows which button it is

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `Keypad({ onPress })` renders four buttons named `1`,
`2`, `3` and `Clear`. The digits call `onPress` with the **number** `1`, `2` or
`3`; `Clear` calls it with the string `clear`. No extra calls.

```
uv run dojo test react d05_events_updates ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — handled here, thank you

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `LinkGuard({ href, onNavigate })` renders a real anchor
named `Settings`, keeping `href` as its `href`, that calls `onNavigate(href)` on
click and **prevents the browser from navigating**. The gate checks the return
value of `fireEvent.click`.

```
uv run dojo test react d05_events_updates ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — a click inside a click

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `NotificationCard({ title, onOpen, onDismiss })` renders
a `role="group"` element named `Notification` that shows `title` and calls
`onOpen` when clicked, containing a `Dismiss` button that calls `onDismiss` —
and only `onDismiss`.

```
uv run dojo test react d05_events_updates ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — Enter sends, Shift and Enter does not

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. `HotkeyBox({ onSubmit })` renders a textarea labelled
`Message` that it controls. Enter on its own calls `onSubmit` with the current
text, prevents the newline, and empties the box. Shift and Enter together submit
nothing. Escape empties the box without submitting.

```
uv run dojo test react d05_events_updates ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — what the handler saw

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. `Basket({ onLog })` shows `<n> in basket` in a live
region and renders an `Add two` button whose handler adds **two** to the count

# Reading — react/d05_events_updates

## Notes

A handler is a value, not an instruction. You write the function, you hand it to
React, and React calls it when something happens - which means every problem in
this set is really a question about *when* something runs and *what it can see
at that moment*. Three of them (ex1, ex2, ex6) are about that gap between
writing a call and scheduling one. Three (ex3, ex4, ex7) are about the DOM event
itself: it travels outwards from the element it started on, it carries a default
action the browser is about to perform, and it knows exactly where it began.
The last two are the ones that separate people who have shipped an input from
people who have not: modifier keys, and the fact that a single tap only becomes
a single tap once you have waited long enough to be sure.

## ex1

Tests the difference between a function and a call. The classic mistake is
`onClick={onRing()}`, which calls the handler during render and hands React
whatever it returned - usually `undefined`, so the button then does nothing at
all when clicked. The stub writes the same bug more plainly, as a bare call in
the body. The model answer passes a function React can hold onto and invoke
later.

## ex2

Tests closing over a value. Each button needs to send something different, and
that difference only exists in the JSX that built it, so each needs its own
small function created there. The classic mistake is one shared handler with no
argument - the stub's - which cannot tell the buttons apart, or
`onClick={onPress(2)}`, which calls immediately for the same reason as ex1. The
model answer wraps the call in an arrow function per button.

## ex3

Tests `preventDefault`. A link that the app handles itself must stay a real link
- real `href`, real `link` role, still openable in a new tab - while cancelling
the navigation the browser was about to perform. The classic mistake is either
forgetting to prevent it, so the SPA does a full page load, or replacing the
anchor with a `<div onClick>`, which destroys the semantics to fix the symptom.
The model answer keeps the anchor and calls `preventDefault` in the handler.

## ex4

Tests bubbling. The Dismiss button sits inside a clickable card, so a click on
it runs both handlers and the user gets the notification dismissed *and* opened.
The classic mistake is to reach for `preventDefault`, which cancels the browser
default and has nothing to do with propagation. The model answer calls
`event.stopPropagation()` in the inner handler, which ends the event where it
is - and is worth being able to describe as "stop travelling" versus "do not do
the browser thing".

## ex5

Tests reading the event before acting on it. A keydown carries the key and the
modifiers, and this component has to consult both: Enter alone submits, Shift
and Enter is a newline the textarea should insert itself. The classic mistake is
checking `event.key === "Enter"` and nothing else, which submits half-written
messages every time someone tries to start a paragraph. The second is forgetting
`preventDefault` on submit, which sends the message and then puts a newline in
the freshly emptied box.

## ex6

Tests the render snapshot. Inside a handler, `count` is a `const` from the
render the click belonged to, so `setCount(count + 1)` twice asks for the same
value twice and adds one. The classic mistake is exactly that, and the classic
follow-up mistake is "fixing" the log with the updater form as well - but the
log genuinely wants the value the user was looking at. The model answer uses the
updater form for the updates and the plain variable for the log, deliberately.

## ex7

Tests event delegation, which is what you fall back on when there are fifty
buttons rather than three, or when the buttons arrive after the listener did.
The classic mistake is the stub's: one listener that always sends the same
command, because reading the target was the part that was skipped. The second is
using `event.target` directly and being surprised when a click lands on an icon
inside the button. The model answer uses `closest("button")` and reads a
`data-command` attribute, and it copes with a click that hit no button at all.

## ex8

Tests deferring a decision. A single tap cannot be reported straight away
because it might still become a double, so the first click starts a timer and
the second one cancels it - the classic mistake being to fire both, which is how
a double click deletes a row twice. The timer id belongs in a ref, since nothing
on screen depends on it, and the model answer also cancels a pending timer on
unmount, because a callback that outlives its component reports a tap on
something that is no longer there.

## Further reading

- [Responding to events](https://react.dev/learn/responding-to-events)
- [State as a snapshot](https://react.dev/learn/state-as-a-snapshot)
- [Queueing a series of state updates](https://react.dev/learn/queueing-a-series-of-state-updates)
- [Referencing values with refs](https://react.dev/reference/react/useRef)
- [MDN: Event.preventDefault](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Event/preventDefault)
- [MDN: Event.stopPropagation](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Event/stopPropagation)
- [MDN: KeyboardEvent.key](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/KeyboardEvent/key)

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Every button needs to send a different value, and the only place that value is
known is the JSX that created the button. So each button needs its own handler,
built where the value is in scope.

## Hint 2
An arrow function in the prop is that handler: `onClick={() => onPress(2)}`
creates a function that, when React eventually calls it, calls yours with the
argument you closed over. Writing `onClick={onPress(2)}` calls it immediately
instead - the parentheses decide which.

argument you closed over. Writing `onClick={onPress(2)}` calls it immediately
instead - the parentheses decide which.

## Exercise 6 — what the handler saw

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. `Basket({ onLog })` shows `<n> in basket` in a live
region and renders an `Add two` button whose handler adds **two** to the count

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Two of the three lines in this handler are wrong in the same way, and the third
is right for the same reason. Work out what the number `count` is worth inside
the handler, and remember that it cannot change while the handler runs.

## Hint 2
`count` is a constant belonging to the render the click came from. Passing a
function to the setter asks React for the value it will be holding when the
update is applied instead - which is how two updates in one handler add two
rather than one. `onLog` genuinely wants the old value, so it stays as it is.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Two of the three lines in this handler are wrong in the same way, and the third
is right for the same reason. Work out what the number `count` is worth inside
the handler, and remember that it cannot change while the handler runs.

## Hint 2
`count` is a constant belonging to the render the click came from. Passing a
function to the setter asks React for the value it will be holding when the
update is applied instead - which is how two updates in one handler add two
rather than one. `onLog` genuinely wants the old value, so it stays as it is.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — one listener for the whole toolbar

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. `EditorToolbar({ onCommand })` renders a `role="toolbar"`
element named `Formatting` containing three buttons — `Bold`, `Italic`, `Link` —
each carrying its command in a `data-command` attribute. There is **one**
`onClick`, on the toolbar itself: it works out which button was clicked and calls
`onCommand` with that command. A click that hits no button calls nothing.

```
uv run dojo test react d05_events_updates ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Only the toolbar gets a listener. Since the click reaches it by travelling
outwards from whatever was actually clicked, the event already knows where it
started - your job is to ask.

## Hint 2
`event.target` is the deepest element the click landed on, which may be
something inside the button rather than the button. `closest("button")` walks
back up from there, and returns `null` when the click was not inside one at all.

## Hint 3
Read the command from the button rather than from a list you keep in parallel:
a `data-command` attribute is available as `button.dataset.command`. Handle the
`null` case deliberately - decide whether an unrecognised click should be
ignored silently or is worth complaining about.

lessons.briefing:
# d06 — Lists and keys (drill set)

Eight problems on turning arrays into markup: mapping, filtering, ordering, the
empty case, and the one thing that goes wrong quietly — keys. It drills
`04_lists_conditional`; if the phrase "key by identity, not by position" does not
already mean something specific to you, reread that lesson first.

Four of these can be passed by code that looks correct and is not. Two of them
mutate data they were handed, and two of them lose a user's typing when the list
moves. That is the point of the set: the bug never appears until the list
changes, and then it appears in production.

## Exercise 1 — the ordered list

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `RecipeSteps({ steps })` renders an `<ol>` with one
`<li>` per step, in the order given, with no missing-key warning in the console.

```
uv run dojo test react d06_lists_keys ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — rank without disturbing

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `HighScores({ scores })` renders a list, highest
`points` first, each item reading `<name> - <points>`. The gate checks the array
you were handed afterwards: it must still be in the order the caller left it in.

```
uv run dojo test react d06_lists_keys ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — only the ones aimed at you

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `Mentions({ messages, me })` lists the `text` of every
message containing `@<me>`, in their original order. When none match, there is no
list at all — just a paragraph reading `No mentions yet`.

```
uv run dojo test react d06_lists_keys ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — the sort that steals a note

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `SortableRoster({ people })` renders one `<li>` per
person, each with a label showing the name and an **uncontrolled** note box
(`defaultValue=""`) wired to that label, plus a `Sort by name` button that puts
the rows in alphabetical order. Type a note into one row, sort, and the note must
still belong to the same person.

```
uv run dojo test react d06_lists_keys ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — two elements, one key

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. `Glossary({ entries })` renders a `<dl>` whose direct
children are `<dt>`, `<dd>`, `<dt>`, `<dd>` — the term then the definition for
each entry, with no wrapper element between the `<dl>` and them, and no
missing-key warning.

```
uv run dojo test react d06_lists_keys ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — the byline

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. `AuthorLine({ names })` renders a paragraph:
`Unknown author` for none, the bare name for one, `Ada and Bo` for two, and
`Ada, Bo and Cy` (commas until the last, which gets the `and`) for three or more.

```
uv run dojo test react d06_lists_keys ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — edit in place, immutably

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. `EditableList({ initialItems })` renders one row per
item, each showing its text and an `Edit <text>` button. Clicking Edit turns that
row — and only that row — into an input named `Item text` holding the current
text, with `Save` and `Cancel` buttons. Opening a second row closes the first.
`Save` shows the new text; `Cancel` restores the old one. The item objects the
caller passed in must never change.

```
uv run dojo test react d06_lists_keys ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — the filter that moves a tick

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. `SearchableChecklist({ items })` renders a text box
labelled `Filter` and one **uncontrolled** checkbox per item, labelled by the
item, showing only items whose label contains the filter text (case-insensitive).
Tick a box, filter the list, and the tick must still be on the item you ticked —
while it is filtered, and after the filter is cleared.

```
uv run dojo test react d06_lists_keys ex8
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading — react/d06_lists_keys

## Notes

Every problem here is one array becoming markup, and the whole set is organised
around the two mistakes that survive code review. The first is mutating what you
were handed: `sort` and `reverse` rearrange in place, and rendering is supposed
to be a pure function of props, so a component that reorders its own props has
changed the caller's world as a side effect of being drawn. The second is keying
by position. An index key is a promise that row three will always be the same
thing, which is true right up until somebody sorts, filters or inserts — and the
damage lands on state that React is not managing: the value of an uncontrolled
input, the ticked state of a checkbox, the scroll position of a row. Both bugs
render perfectly on the first paint. That is why they need drilling rather than
explaining.

## ex1

Tests the two habits that should be automatic before anything harder: choosing
the element that carries the meaning, and keying the output of a `map`. The
classic mistake is `<ul>` for a sequence of steps — visually identical, and a
lie to anyone listening to the page. The model answer uses `<ol>` and keys on the
step text, which is stable and unique in this data; if it were not, the data
would need ids.

## ex2

Tests whether you notice that `reverse()` is as destructive as `sort()`. The stub
renders the right rows in the right order and still fails, because the array the
caller still holds has been rearranged underneath it — the kind of bug that
surfaces three components away as a list that is mysteriously backwards. The
model answer copies with a spread before sorting, and sorts by the field rather
than relying on the input happening to be in ascending order.

## ex3

Tests filter-then-decide, in that order. The classic mistake is rendering the
`<ul>` unconditionally and putting the empty message inside it, which leaves a
screen reader announcing a list of zero items and a sentence that is not a list
item. The model answer filters first, returns the empty-state paragraph early
when nothing survives, and only then maps — so the list element exists precisely
when there is a list.

## ex4

Tests key-by-identity where the evidence is a user's typing. The note box is

# Reading — react/d06_lists_keys

## Notes

Every problem here is one array becoming markup, and the whole set is organised
around the two mistakes that survive code review. The first is mutating what you
were handed: `sort` and `reverse` rearrange in place, and rendering is supposed
to be a pure function of props, so a component that reorders its own props has
changed the caller's world as a side effect of being drawn. The second is keying
by position. An index key is a promise that row three will always be the same
thing, which is true right up until somebody sorts, filters or inserts — and the
damage lands on state that React is not managing: the value of an uncontrolled
input, the ticked state of a checkbox, the scroll position of a row. Both bugs
render perfectly on the first paint. That is why they need drilling rather than
explaining.

## ex1

Tests the two habits that should be automatic before anything harder: choosing
the element that carries the meaning, and keying the output of a `map`. The
classic mistake is `<ul>` for a sequence of steps — visually identical, and a
lie to anyone listening to the page. The model answer uses `<ol>` and keys on the
step text, which is stable and unique in this data; if it were not, the data
would need ids.

## ex2

Tests whether you notice that `reverse()` is as destructive as `sort()`. The stub
renders the right rows in the right order and still fails, because the array the
caller still holds has been rearranged underneath it — the kind of bug that
surfaces three components away as a list that is mysteriously backwards. The

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The sorting works. What breaks is where the typed note ends up, and the only
line that decides that is the one that tells React which row in this render is
the same row as in the last one.

## Hint 2
The note box is uncontrolled: its value lives in the DOM node, not in React
state. So when React decides to reuse a DOM node for a different person, the
old text comes along for the ride. `key` is what makes that decision.

## Hint 3
An index is a description of a position, and after a sort every position holds
somebody new. Key by something that travels with the person. While you are
there, look at the copy in front of `sort` - and decide whether the unsorted
branch needs one too.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
The sorting works. What breaks is where the typed note ends up, and the only
line that decides that is the one that tells React which row in this render is
the same row as in the last one.

## Hint 2
The note box is uncontrolled: its value lives in the DOM node, not in React
state. So when React decides to reuse a DOM node for a different person, the
old text comes along for the ride. `key` is what makes that decision.

## Hint 3
An index is a description of a position, and after a sort every position holds
somebody new. Key by something that travels with the person. While you are
there, look at the copy in front of `sort` - and decide whether the unsorted
branch needs one too.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — edit in place, immutably

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. `EditableList({ initialItems })` renders one row per
item, each showing its text and an `Edit <text>` button. Clicking Edit turns that
row — and only that row — into an input named `Item text` holding the current
text, with `Save` and `Cancel` buttons. Opening a second row closes the first.
`Save` shows the new text; `Cancel` restores the old one. The item objects the
caller passed in must never change.

```
uv run dojo test react d06_lists_keys ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Everything about which row is open lives in one piece of state, and it is not
a boolean. Ask what value answers the question "is this row the one being
edited" for every row at once.

## Hint 2
The draft text is separate state from the list, which is what makes Cancel a
one-liner: throw the draft away and close the editor without touching the
list.

## Hint 3
The stub finds the item and assigns to `item.text`. That object is the one the
caller handed you, so you just edited data you do not own, and React has no
way to tell what changed. Build a new array with `map`, returning a new object
for the row that changed and the original object for every other row.

## Exercise 8 — the filter that moves a tick

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. `SearchableChecklist({ items })` renders a text box
labelled `Filter` and one **uncontrolled** checkbox per item, labelled by the
item, showing only items whose label contains the filter text (case-insensitive).
Tick a box, filter the list, and the tick must still be on the item you ticked —
while it is filtered, and after the filter is cleared.

```
uv run dojo test react d06_lists_keys ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Nothing about the filtering is wrong. Ask instead where a ticked checkbox
keeps the fact that it is ticked, and what happens to that fact when React
decides two rows from two different renders are the same row.

## Hint 2
Filtering does not just shorten the list - it changes which item sits at which
position. Any key derived from the position therefore says that Sourdough and
Milk are the same row, and React reuses the DOM node accordingly.

## Hint 3
Give each row a key that belongs to the item and the DOM node follows the item
in and out of the filter. Worth thinking about afterwards: if the ticks had
been React state instead of DOM state, would this bug have shown up at all -
and where would you have had to put that state?

## Hint 1
Nothing about the filtering is wrong. Ask instead where a ticked checkbox
keeps the fact that it is ticked, and what happens to that fact when React
decides two rows from two different renders are the same row.

## Hint 2
Filtering does not just shorten the list - it changes which item sits at which
position. Any key derived from the position therefore says that Sourdough and
Milk are the same row, and React reuses the DOM node accordingly.

## Hint 3
Give each row a key that belongs to the item and the DOM node follows the item
in and out of the filter. Worth thinking about afterwards: if the ticks had
been React state instead of DOM state, would this bug have shown up at all -
and where would you have had to put that state?

# d07 — Conditional UI (drill set) Eight problems on deciding what to render: ternaries, guard clauses, returning `null`, conditional attributes, and the two traps that outlive every tutorial — the falsy `0` that leaks into the page, and the state that disappears when the branch holding it is unmounted. It drills the conditional half of `04_lists_conditional`. No data fetching here, and no timers. Every component is a pure function of its props except the last one, which is where the interesting question lives. ## Exercise 1 — signed in, or not Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `AuthNav({ user })` renders a `Sign in` button when `user` is `null`, and otherwise the text `Hi, ` plus a `Sign out` button. Never both. ``` uv run dojo test react d07_conditional_ui ex1 ``` ## Exercise 2 — the badge that leaks a zero Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `CartBadge({ count })` renders `{count}` when the count is above zero, and **nothing whatsoever** when it is zero. The gate reads the whole container and fails if a `0` reached the DOM. ``` uv run dojo test react d07_conditional_ui ex2 ``` ## Exercise 3 — rendering nothing Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `MaintenanceBanner({ notice })` renders a `role="status"` element carrying the notice — or, when `notice` is `null`, nothing at all: the gate asserts the container's `innerHTML` is the empty string, so an empty wrapper counts as a failure. ``` uv run dojo test react d07_conditional_ui ex3 ``` ## Exercise 4 — four statuses, four shapes Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `OrderStatus({ order })` takes a discriminated union and renders: - `pending` — the words `Placing order`; - `shipped` — a link named `Track with ` whose `href` is `trackingUrl`; - `delivered` — a `` showing `deliveredOn` with `deliveredAt` in its `datetime` attribute; - `cancelled` — a `role="alert"` containing the `reason`. Exactly one of them at a time. ``` uv run dojo test react d07_conditional_ui ex4 ``` ## Exercise 5 — three answers in priority order Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. `AccessGate({ user, feature, children })` renders `Sign in to continue` when `user` is `null`, `Upgrade to Pro` when the user's `entitlements` do not include `feature`, and the `children` when they do. In the first two cases the children must not be in the document at all. ``` uv run dojo test react d07_conditional_ui ex5 ``` ## Exercise 6 — conditions on attributes Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. `SaveButton({ dirty, saving })` renders one button whose label is `Saving` while saving and `Save` otherwise, which is disabled while saving **and** while nothing has changed, and which carries `aria-busy="true"` only while saving — with no `aria-busy` attribute at all otherwise. ``` uv run dojo test react d07_conditional_ui ex6 ``` ## Exercise 7 — the review queue tab Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. `ReviewQueueTab({ count, snoozed })` renders a button whose accessible name is: - `Reviews snoozed` when snoozed, whatever the count; - `No reviews waiting` at zero; - `1 review waiting` at one, and ` reviews waiting` above that. Inside it, a badge showing the count — capped at `9+` above nine — which is hidden from assistive technology and is not drawn at all when snoozed or at zero. The gate checks that no digit reaches the screen in those two cases. ``` uv run dojo test react d07_conditional_ui ex7 ``` ## Exercise 8 — the draft that must survive Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. `ComposeTabs()` renders `Write` and `Preview` buttons — the current one carrying `aria-pressed="true"`, the other `"false"` — and one panel below them. `Write` shows a textarea labelled `Draft`; `Preview` shows a `
` containing the current draft text and no textarea. Typing, switching to Preview and switching back must not lose a character. ``` uv run dojo test react d07_conditional_ui ex8 ```

# Reading — react/d07_conditional_ui

## Notes

Conditional rendering looks like the easiest thing in React and produces some of
its most durable bugs, because three separate questions hide inside "show this
when that". The first is what JavaScript actually evaluates: `&&` returns an
operand, not a boolean, and React renders every value except `false`, `null`,
`undefined` and the empty string. The second is what "hidden" means — a branch
that is not rendered does not exist, which is what makes conditionals a real
access boundary and also what makes them destroy state. The third is where the
condition belongs: sometimes it swaps an element, and sometimes it should only
change an attribute on an element that stays put. This set walks all three, and
the last problem is the one that separates people who have shipped React from
people who have read about it.

## ex1

Tests whether you treat mutually exclusive states as one decision. The classic
mistake is the stub: three independent conditions that can all be true at once,
so a signed-in user is offered Sign in and Sign out side by side. The model
answer returns early for the signed-out case, which makes the exclusivity a
property of the code rather than something you have to keep true by hand.

## ex2

Tests the falsy-zero leak, which is the single most-seen React bug on earth. The
classic mistake is `{count && <Badge/>}`: when `count` is `0` the expression
evaluates to `0`, React renders it, and a lone zero appears where the badge was
meant to be absent. The model answer compares explicitly and returns `null`,
which also documents the intent - zero is a state, not a falsy accident.

## ex3

Tests that you know a component may render nothing at all. The classic mistake is
returning an empty wrapper, which is invisible in a screenshot and very visible
in a layout with gaps, borders or grid gutters - and which a screen reader still
walks through. The model answer guards at the top and returns `null`, leaving the
rest of the component to deal only with the case that has content.

## ex4

Tests branch selection when the branches differ structurally rather than
cosmetically. The classic mistake is nesting ternaries three deep until nobody
can read them, or - worse - rendering all four and hiding three with CSS. The
model answer switches on the discriminant, which both reads like the
specification and lets TypeScript narrow the union so each arm can reach the
fields that only exist in it.

## ex5

Tests priority ordering and what a gate actually means. The classic mistake is
rendering the children and putting the message over them, or joining the
conditions with `&&` so that "signed out" and "not entitled" can both try to
render. The model answer uses two guard clauses in priority order, so the content
is never even created for a user who may not have it - the markup is not in the
DOM to be found in devtools.

## ex6

Tests knowing when *not* to branch on elements. Everything here is one button
whose word, disabled state and busy state change - so the condition belongs on
the attributes. The classic mistake is two separate `<button>` elements in a
ternary, which loses focus when the branch flips, and `aria-busy={saving}`, which
writes `aria-busy="false"` and tells assistive technology about a wait that is
not happening. The model answer keeps one element and lets `undefined` remove the
attribute.

## ex7

Tests separating what a control says from what it draws. The classic mistakes
come in pairs: the pluralisation that renders `1 reviews waiting`, and the
badge cap that is applied to the accessible name as well, so a screen-reader user
is told there are `9+` reviews when the component knows there are twelve.
The model answer computes the label and the badge as two independent values above
the return, checks the snoozed case first in both, and represents "no badge" as
`null` rather than as a falsy number.

## ex8

Tests the rule that carries the most weight in real applications: state lives at
a position in the tree, and unmounting a subtree destroys everything it held. The
draft is kept in the DOM node of an uncontrolled textarea, so switching to
Preview deletes it - and the same failure mode shows up as a lost scroll position,
a reset accordion or a re-triggered animation. The classic mistake is trying to
fix it by hiding the panel with CSS instead of understanding it. The model answer
lifts the draft into state above the branch and makes the textarea controlled,
which is also what gives the preview something to show.

## Further reading

- [Conditional rendering](https://react.dev/learn/conditional-rendering)
- [Preserving and resetting state](https://react.dev/learn/preserving-and-resetting-state)
- [Sharing state between components](https://react.dev/learn/sharing-state-between-components)
- [MDN: logical AND returns an operand, not a boolean](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/Logical_AND)
- [MDN: aria-busy](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Attributes/aria-busy)

## Exercise 1 — signed in, or not

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `AuthNav({ user })` renders a `Sign in` button when
`user` is `null`, and otherwise the text `Hi, <name>` plus a `Sign out` button.

```
uv run dojo test react d07_conditional_ui ex1
```

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The stub asks the same question twice and answers a third question - whether
to show Sign in - not at all. Signed in and signed out are alternatives, so
they want one decision, not three.

## Hint 2
Either a ternary around the whole thing or an early `return` for the
signed-out case. The early return usually reads better here, because the two
branches have different numbers of elements in them.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The gate checks the container is completely empty - not that it looks empty.
A wrapper with nothing inside it is still an element in the DOM, and it can
still carry margins, borders and a gap in the layout.

`return null` from a component and React renders nothing for it at all. Decide
that at the top of the function, before any markup, and the rest of the
component only ever deals with the case where there is something to say.

The gate checks the container is completely empty - not that it looks empty.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Three answers, in a fixed order of priority: not signed in beats not entitled,
and not entitled beats showing the content. Guard clauses express a priority
order; a chain of `&&` does not.

## Hint 2
Each guard returns immediately, so by the time you reach the last line both
questions are settled and the only thing left to do is render `children`. Note
what that means for the failing cases: the children are never created at all,
which is the difference between a gate and a coat of paint.

## Exercise 6 — conditions on attributes

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. `SaveButton({ dirty, saving })` renders one button
whose label is `Saving` while saving and `Save` otherwise, which is disabled
while saving **and** while nothing has changed, and which carries
`aria-busy="true"` only while saving — with no `aria-busy` attribute at all
otherwise.

```
uv run dojo test react d07_conditional_ui ex6
```

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
There is only one button here in every state. What changes is a word, whether
it is disabled, and whether it is busy - so the conditions belong inside the
element, on its attributes and its text.

## Hint 2
Two separate reasons to be disabled, joined with `||`. And remember that
`aria-busy={false}` still writes `aria-busy="false"` into the DOM, which is a
statement about a thing that is not happening - `undefined` is how you say
nothing at all.

There is only one button here in every state. What changes is a word, whether
it is disabled, and whether it is busy - so the conditions belong inside the
element, on its attributes and its text.

## Hint 2
Two separate reasons to be disabled, joined with `||`. And remember that
`aria-busy={false}` still writes `aria-busy="false"` into the DOM, which is a
statement about a thing that is not happening - `undefined` is how you say
nothing at all.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — the review queue tab

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. `ReviewQueueTab({ count, snoozed })` renders a button
whose accessible name is:

- `Reviews snoozed` when snoozed, whatever the count;
- `No reviews waiting` at zero;
- `1 review waiting` at one, and `<n> reviews waiting` above that.

Inside it, a badge showing the count — capped at `9+` above nine — which is
hidden from assistive technology and is not drawn at all when snoozed or at zero.
The gate checks that no digit reaches the screen in those two cases.

```
uv run dojo test react d07_conditional_ui ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Two independent questions with different answers: what the button is called,
and what is drawn inside it. Work them out as two values above the return and
the JSX stops fighting you.

## Hint 2
Snoozed wins over everything - check it first, in both values. After that the
name has three forms (none, one, many) and the badge has two (the number, or
the cap).

## Hint 3
Watch the badge condition: it has to produce nothing at all for zero and for
snoozed, so a bare `&&` on a number will bite you the same way ex2 did. Decide
what "nothing" is represented by in your badge value, and check for that
exactly.
