exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — the draft that must survive

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. `ComposeTabs()` renders `Write` and `Preview` buttons —
the current one carrying `aria-pressed="true"`, the other `"false"` — and one
panel below them. `Write` shows a textarea labelled `Draft`; `Preview` shows a
`<section aria-label="Preview">` containing the current draft text and no
textarea. Typing, switching to Preview and switching back must not lose a
character.

```
uv run dojo test react d07_conditional_ui ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Ask where the typed text is being kept. In the stub it is kept by the DOM node
of an uncontrolled textarea - and that node only exists while the Write branch
is on screen.

## Hint 2
Anything that has to outlive a branch has to be stored outside it. The draft
belongs in state next to the tab, and the textarea becomes controlled: value
from state, state from `onChange`.

## Hint 3
The preview then has something to show, which is the other half of the point -
one piece of state feeding two different renderings of it. Worth thinking
about: if the requirement had been to keep the scroll position of the textarea
too, would lifting state have been enough?

lessons.briefing:
# d08 — Controlled forms (drill set)

Eight problems on the one idea that makes React forms work: the component owns
the value, the input renders it, and the change handler is where every rule
lives. It drills `05_forms` — if the difference between `value` and
`defaultValue`, or between `event.target.value` and `event.target.checked`, is
still something you look up, reread that lesson first.

Nothing here is validated (that is d09) and nothing here is async. Every problem
is a small widget with an injected callback, and every gate assertion is
something the user could see, type or hear.

## Exercise 1 — the box that says no

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `NicknameField({ maxLength })` renders an input labelled
`Nickname` and a live region (`role="status"`) reading `<length>/<maxLength>`.
The state refuses two kinds of change outright — anything longer than
`maxLength`, and anything containing a space — so those keystrokes leave the box
exactly as it was. The `maxlength` attribute is not the answer here; the change
handler is.

```
uv run dojo test react d08_forms_controlled ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — one question, three answers

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `ShippingChoice({ onChange })` renders a
`role="radiogroup"` named `Shipping` holding three radios labelled `Standard`,
`Express` and `Overnight` (values `standard`, `express`, `overnight`). Nothing is
selected at first. Choosing one calls `onChange` with the value and updates a
`role="status"` line: `Arrives in 5 days`, `Arrives in 2 days` and
`Arrives tomorrow` respectively. Choosing a second option unselects the first.

```
uv run dojo test react d08_forms_controlled ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — select, textarea, submit

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `FeedbackForm({ onSubmit })` renders a form with
`aria-label="Feedback"` containing a `Category` select (`Bug` / `Idea` /
`Praise`, values `bug` / `idea` / `praise`, starting on `bug`), a `Message`
textarea, and a `Send feedback` submit button. Submitting calls
`onSubmit({ category, message })` and calls `preventDefault()` on the event — the
gate checks the return value of `fireEvent.submit`, which is `false` exactly when
the default was prevented.

```
uv run dojo test react d08_forms_controlled ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — three fields, one object

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `AddressBlock({ onChange })` renders inputs labelled
`Street`, `City` and `Postcode` whose values live in **one** state object, driven
by **one** change handler that works out which key to update from the input's
`name` attribute. `onChange` receives the whole address object after every
change. A `Clear` button puts all three fields back to empty — and tells
`onChange` about that too.

```
uv run dojo test react d08_forms_controlled ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — the number that is allowed to be nothing

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. `QuantityBox({ onQuantityChange })` renders an input
labelled `Quantity`:

- only digits are accepted; any other change is ignored entirely, callback
  included;
- the box may be empty while the user is typing, and an empty box reports `null`;
- on blur the value is clamped into `1..99`, and an empty box becomes `1`.

```
uv run dojo test react d08_forms_controlled ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — the second select depends on the first

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. `CountryCity({ catalogue })` — `catalogue` maps a country
name to its cities. Render a `Country` select and a `City` select, each starting
with a placeholder option (`Choose a country`, `Choose a city`) whose value is
`""`. The city options come from the chosen country. Changing the country clears
any chosen city. A `Continue` button is disabled until both have been chosen.

```
uv run dojo test react d08_forms_controlled ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — the tags input

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. `TagsInput({ onChange })` renders an input labelled
`Tags`, a `<ul>` of chips, and a `role="status"` region:

- `Enter` commits the trimmed draft as a chip and empties the box;
- a duplicate is refused: no chip, the text stays in the box, and the status
  region reads `<tag> is already added`;
- `Backspace` in an **empty** box removes the last chip;
- every chip carries a button named `Remove <tag>`;
- `onChange` is called with the full array of tags after every change, and not
  at all when a tag was refused.

```
uv run dojo test react d08_forms_controlled ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — the masked amount

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. `CurrencyField({ onValueChange })` renders an input
labelled `Amount` that shows a grouped number — `1234567` is displayed as
`1,234,567` — while everything that is not a digit is dropped on the way in
(`12ab34` becomes `1,234`). `onValueChange` receives the plain number, or `null`
when the box is empty. Zero is a number, not nothing. The gate drives this one
with `fireEvent.change`, so the whole value arrives at once.

```
uv run dojo test react d08_forms_controlled ex8
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading — react/d08_forms_controlled

## Notes

One sentence unites all eight problems: **the input does not hold the value, the
component does.** Everything else follows. If the state is the truth, then a
keystroke you refuse to store never happened; a field you forget to spread is a
field you deleted; a value the user is halfway through typing has to be
representable, which is why `""` is a legal quantity and `null` is not the same
as `0`. The set also drills the shape of the surrounding markup — a group of
radios is one question and needs to say so, a form needs a name to be findable,
a live region is how a change gets announced — because a form that works with a
mouse and vanishes for a screen reader is half a form.

## ex1

Tests whether you understand that a controlled input is a render of state, so
rejecting a change is simply not calling the setter: React re-renders the box
with the value it already had and the keystroke disappears. The classic mistake
is `defaultValue`, which makes the input uncontrolled — the state then trails
behind the DOM and every rule you write is advisory. The model answer validates
the proposed value first and returns early, which is the same shape every masked
or capped field in the set uses.

## ex2

Tests the difference between three radios and one question. The classic mistake
is omitting the shared `name` attribute, which leaves you with three
independently checkable controls that happen to look like radios, and omitting
`role="radiogroup"`, which leaves a screen-reader user with three unrelated
options and no idea they belong together. The model answer keeps one `chosen`
string in state, starts it at `""` to mean nothing is chosen, and lets each radio
compare itself to it.

## ex3

Tests that selects and textareas are controlled exactly like text boxes, and
that a submit handler owes the event a `preventDefault()`. The classic mistake is
forgetting it: in a browser the page reloads and the state is gone, and in a test
you get a silent pass because jsdom does not navigate. The second is expecting
`getByRole("form")` to work on an unnamed form — the form role only exists once
the element has an accessible name. The model answer names the form and prevents
the default in one handler.

## ex4

Tests the spread. Three fields in one object with one handler is the shape every
real form has, and the handler learns which key to write from the input's `name`,
so adding a fourth field is markup only. The classic mistake is
`setAddress({ [name]: value })`, which does not update the address — it replaces
it, silently emptying the two fields the user filled in first. The model answer
copies the previous object before overriding one key, and routes both the edit
and the reset through one `update` function so the callback can never be
forgotten.

## ex5

Tests whether you can tell the value from its representation. A quantity box has
a state a number cannot express: empty, mid-edit, on the way from 1 to 12. The
classic mistake is `useState(1)` plus `Number(event.target.value)`, which turns
an empty box into `0`, a deleted digit into a jump, and a stray letter into
`NaN`. The model answer keeps the text, reports `null` for empty, and does the
clamping on blur — because clamping during typing rewrites what the user is
still saying.

## ex6

Tests derived state. The city list is a function of the chosen country and
belongs in the render body, not in a second `useState` that some effect has to
keep in step. The classic mistake is exactly that copy, and its twin: leaving the
previously chosen city in place when the country changes, which submits a pair
like Geelong, Japan. The model answer computes `cities` during render and clears
the city in the country handler, so the two states can never disagree.

## ex7

Tests keyboard handling and array updates together, which is why it is an
interview favourite. Three details separate a working tags input from a good one:
`Enter` needs `preventDefault()` or it submits the form the widget is sitting in;
`Backspace` may only eat a chip when the draft is empty; and a refused duplicate
must say why rather than doing nothing. The classic mistake is committing on
`onChange` instead of `onKeyDown` — `onChange` never sees Enter. The model answer
keeps committed tags and the draft as separate state and funnels every mutation
through one `commit` so the callback and the message stay in step.

## ex8

Tests the masked-input pattern: the state is the digits, the displayed value is
derived from them, and the parent gets the plain number. The classic mistake is
storing the formatted string, which means the next keystroke has to be parsed
back out of a value your own formatter produced — commas and all. The second is
`Number("")`, which is `0`: an empty box then reports a price the user never
typed, and the difference between `0` and `null` is a real bug in real checkouts.
The model answer strips to digits on the way in and groups on the way out.

## Further reading

- [Reacting to input with state](https://react.dev/learn/reacting-to-input-with-state)
- [`<input>` — React reference](https://react.dev/reference/react-dom/components/input)
- [`<select>` — React reference](https://react.dev/reference/react-dom/components/select)
- [Choosing the state structure](https://react.dev/learn/choosing-the-state-structure)
- [MDN: `<input type="radio">`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/input/radio)
- [MDN: ARIA live regions](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/ARIA_Live_Regions)

## Hint 1
One question, three answers, one piece of state holding the chosen value. Every
radio compares itself to that state to decide whether it is checked - none of
them owns anything.

## Hint 2
Two attributes do the grouping work. `name` is what makes the browser treat the
radios as mutually exclusive, and `role="radiogroup"` with a name is what tells
a screen reader the same thing. A state of `""` is how you say nothing is
chosen yet.

## Exercise 3 — select, textarea, submit

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `FeedbackForm({ onSubmit })` renders a form with
`aria-label="Feedback"` containing a `Category` select (`Bug` / `Idea` /
`Praise`, values `bug` / `idea` / `praise`, starting on `bug`), a `Message`
textarea, and a `Send feedback` submit button. Submitting calls
`onSubmit({ category, message })` and calls `preventDefault()` on the event — the
gate checks the return value of `fireEvent.submit`, which is `false` exactly when
the default was prevented.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
A `<select>` and a `<textarea>` are controlled the same way a text box is: they
render `value` and report `event.target.value`. The difference is only in the
markup - React gives a textarea a `value` prop rather than children.

## Hint 2
Two details decide this one. The submit handler receives the event and owes it
`preventDefault()`, or the browser posts the form and reloads the page. And a
form is only findable by role once it has an accessible name, which for a form
with no visible heading means `aria-label`.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
A `<select>` and a `<textarea>` are controlled the same way a text box is: they
render `value` and report `event.target.value`. The difference is only in the
markup - React gives a textarea a `value` prop rather than children.

## Hint 2
Two details decide this one. The submit handler receives the event and owes it
`preventDefault()`, or the browser posts the form and reloads the page. And a
form is only findable by role once it has an accessible name, which for a form
with no visible heading means `aria-label`.

## Exercise 5 — the number that is allowed to be nothing

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. `QuantityBox({ onQuantityChange })` renders an input
labelled `Quantity`:

- only digits are accepted; any other change is ignored entirely, callback
  included;

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The state is the text in the box, not the quantity. A number cannot represent
"the user has deleted everything and is about to type something else", and that
is a state the box has to be able to be in.

## Hint 2
Three moments, three jobs. On change: reject anything that is not digits, then
store the text and report `null` for empty or `Number(text)` otherwise. On
blur: clamp. The clamp only belongs on blur, because clamping mid-typing turns
`10` into `1` before the user has finished.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
The state is the text in the box, not the quantity. A number cannot represent
"the user has deleted everything and is about to type something else", and that
is a state the box has to be able to be in.

## Hint 2
Three moments, three jobs. On change: reject anything that is not digits, then
store the text and report `null` for empty or `Number(text)` otherwise. On
blur: clamp. The clamp only belongs on blur, because clamping mid-typing turns
`10` into `1` before the user has finished.

## Hint 1
Two pieces of state that must not be confused: the list of committed tags, and
the draft text in the box. Every rule in the prompt is about moving text from
the second into the first, or about refusing to.

Both key rules live in `onKeyDown`, because `onChange` never sees Enter or
Backspace. Enter also needs `preventDefault()` - inside a real form it would
otherwise submit the whole thing while the user was still adding tags.

Backspace must only remove a chip when the draft is empty, or you delete
someone-s work while they are mid-word. For the duplicate case, decide what
should happen to the text still sitting in the box - the gate says it stays,
and that is a deliberate product decision, not an accident.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Two pieces of state that must not be confused: the list of committed tags, and
the draft text in the box. Every rule in the prompt is about moving text from
the second into the first, or about refusing to.

## Hint 2
Both key rules live in `onKeyDown`, because `onChange` never sees Enter or
Backspace. Enter also needs `preventDefault()` - inside a real form it would
otherwise submit the whole thing while the user was still adding tags.

## Hint 3
Backspace must only remove a chip when the draft is empty, or you delete
someone-s work while they are mid-word. For the duplicate case, decide what
should happen to the text still sitting in the box - the gate says it stays,
and that is a deliberate product decision, not an accident.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — the masked amount

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. `CurrencyField({ onValueChange })` renders an input
labelled `Amount` that shows a grouped number — `1234567` is displayed as
`1,234,567` — while everything that is not a digit is dropped on the way in
(`12ab34` becomes `1,234`). `onValueChange` receives the plain number, or `null`
when the box is empty. Zero is a number, not nothing. The gate drives this one
with `fireEvent.change`, so the whole value arrives at once.

```
uv run dojo test react d08_forms_controlled ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
There are two representations of one amount: the digits the component keeps,
and the grouped string the box shows. Decide which one is the state - the other
is derived from it on every render.

## Hint 2
Strip first, then format. `value.replace(/\D/g, "")` throws away everything the
user should not have been able to type, including the commas your own last
render put there.

## Hint 3
Grouping is `digits.replace(/\B(?=(\d{3})+(?!\d))/g, ",")` if you want it in one
line, or a loop if you would rather read it later. The remaining decision is
what to report when the box is empty: `Number("")` is `0`, and `0` is a real
amount somebody might have typed.

## Hint 1
There are two representations of one amount: the digits the component keeps,
and the grouped string the box shows. Decide which one is the state - the other
is derived from it on every render.

## Hint 2
Strip first, then format. `value.replace(/\D/g, "")` throws away everything the
user should not have been able to type, including the commas your own last
render put there.

## Hint 3
Grouping is `digits.replace(/\B(?=(\d{3})+(?!\d))/g, ",")` if you want it in one
line, or a loop if you would rather read it later. The remaining decision is
what to report when the box is empty: `Number("")` is `0`, and `0` is a real
amount somebody might have typed.

lessons.briefing:
# d09 — Form validation (drill set)

Eight problems on saying no politely: when to check, which field to blame, how to
connect a message to the box it is about, and what a form does while the server
is still thinking. It drills `05_forms` — the second half, the part with
`aria-invalid` and `aria-describedby` in it.

Two rules run through the whole set. **An error message that is not wired to its
field is decoration**: `aria-describedby` is what makes it the field's accessible
description, and the gate reads exactly that. And **a disabled button is not
validation** — a control the user cannot press cannot tell them why.

The last two problems are async. The slow function arrives as a prop and the gate
resolves it by hand, so nothing here waits on a clock.

## Exercise 1 — required, and connected

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `RequiredEmail({ onSubmit })` renders an input labelled
`Email` and a `Continue` submit button. Submitting an empty field must not call
`onSubmit`, must set `aria-invalid="true"` on the input, and must give it the
accessible description `Email is required`. A filled field submits once, with the
address **trimmed**, and leaves no error behind.

```
uv run dojo test react d09_forms_validation ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — complain late, forgive early

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `UsernameField()` renders an input labelled `Username`.
The rule is three characters. While the user is typing for the first time there
is no error at all. When they leave the field, a value that breaks the rule gets
`aria-invalid="true"` and the description
`Username must be at least 3 characters`. From then on the field is judged on
every keystroke, so fixing it clears the error immediately.

```
uv run dojo test react d09_forms_validation ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — which field is wrong

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `PasswordPair({ onSubmit })` renders `Password` and
`Confirm password` inputs and a `Set password` button.

- an empty password is a `Password is required` error **on the password field**;
- a confirmation that does not match is a `Passwords do not match` error **on the
  confirmation field**, and the password field stays valid;
- when they match, `onSubmit` is called once with the password.

```
uv run dojo test react d09_forms_validation ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — the error summary

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `BookingForm({ onSubmit })` renders `Name`, `Email` and
`Guests` inputs and a `Book` button. The rules: name is required
(`Name is required`), email must contain an `@`
(`Enter a valid email address`), guests must be a number from 1 to 8
(`Guests must be between 1 and 8`).

An invalid submit renders a `role="alert"` region listing every current problem
and **moves focus to the first invalid field**, in the order name, email, guests.
A valid submit calls `onSubmit({ name, email, guests })` with `guests` as a
number, and leaves no alert on screen.

```
uv run dojo test react d09_forms_validation ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — normalise before you judge

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. `CouponField({ onApply })` renders an input labelled
`Coupon code` and an `Apply` button. A code is trimmed and upper-cased first,
then tested against three letters, a dash and four digits. A code that fails gets
`aria-invalid="true"` and the description `Coupon codes look like ABC-1234`. A
code that passes calls `onApply` with the **normalised** value.

```
uv run dojo test react d09_forms_validation ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — a rule between two fields

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. `DateRange({ onSubmit })` renders `Start date` and
`End date` inputs (`type="date"`) and a `Check availability` button that is
disabled until both are filled. Pressing it with an end date **before** the start
date attaches `End date cannot be before the start date` to the end field and
calls nothing; the start field stays valid. Equal dates are a legal one-day
range. A valid range calls `onSubmit({ start, end })` with the two ISO strings.

The gate drives the date fields with `fireEvent.change` and the button with
`fireEvent.click`, so the button here is an ordinary `type="button"`.

```
uv run dojo test react d09_forms_validation ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — the rule the server owns

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. `HandleField({ checkAvailable })` renders an input
labelled `Handle`, a `role="status"` region and a `Save` button.
`checkAvailable(handle)` returns a promise of a boolean.

- `Save` is disabled until a check has come back saying the handle is free;
- leaving the field runs the check with the trimmed handle;
- while it is in flight the status region reads `Checking`;
- taken (`false`) becomes the field's error, `That handle is taken`;
- free (`true`) makes the status read `Available` and unlocks `Save`;
- editing the field clears the error, the status and the permission to save,
  because they were all about a value that no longer exists.

```
uv run dojo test react d09_forms_validation ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — the whole loop

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. `ProfileSetup({ onSubmit })` renders `Team name` (at
least 3 characters, `Team name must be at least 3 characters`) and `Website`
(must start with `https://`, `Website must start with https://`), a
`role="status"` region and a `Create profile` submit button.

- no field shows an error before the first submit attempt;
- after one attempt, every field is judged on every keystroke, each error wired
  to its field with `aria-describedby`;
- `onSubmit` returns a promise: while it is pending the button reads `Saving` and
  is disabled, so a second press does nothing at all;
- when it resolves, the status region reads `Saved` and the button says
  `Create profile` again.

```
uv run dojo test react d09_forms_validation ex8
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading — react/d09_forms_validation

## Notes

Validation is three questions, and mixing them up is where most form code goes
wrong. *What is the rule?* — that is a pure function of the values, so it belongs
in the render body, derived, never copied into state. *When may the user be told?*
— that is separate state (`touched`, `attempted`) and it is what stops a form
shouting at somebody who has typed one letter. *Where does the message go?* — on
the field that can fix it, connected with `aria-describedby` so it becomes that
field's accessible description, plus `aria-invalid` so the state is announced
even when the message is out of view. The set ends with the two async cases,
because in real forms half the rules live on a server, and the moment between
asking and knowing is a state your UI has to have a name for.

## ex1

Tests the wiring rather than the rule. Anyone can render a red paragraph; the
question is whether the field and the paragraph know about each other. The
classic mistake is exactly what the stub does — a correct message floating beside
an input that still claims to be valid, which for a screen-reader user is a form
that silently refuses to submit. The model answer computes `aria-invalid` and
`aria-describedby` from the error state, so both appear and disappear with it,
and trims the value before it decides anything.

## ex2

Tests timing. The rule is checkable from the first keystroke, but applying it
then produces a form that calls you wrong before you have finished being right.
The classic mistake is validating in `onChange` from the start; the equally
classic over-correction is validating only on blur, which then makes the user
leave the field again to discover they fixed it. The model answer derives the
error every render and gates the *display* on a `touched` flag set in `onBlur` —
late to complain, quick to forgive.

## ex3

Tests where a cross-field error lives. The mismatch is a fact about two boxes,
but only one of them is worth retyping, and marking both makes the user delete a
password they had right. The classic mistake is the shared banner, which is
announced once and connected to nothing. The second is complaining that the
confirmation does not match when the password is empty, which is technically
true and useless. The model answer orders the rules and attaches each message to
exactly one field.

## ex4

Tests the pattern every long form needs: a summary and a jump. `role="alert"`
gets the list announced, and focusing the first invalid control means the
keyboard user does not have to hunt for the field the summary is talking about.
The classic mistake is a summary in a plain `<div>`, which is announced to nobody,
and the second is leaving focus on the submit button. The model answer validates
into a record keyed by field, keeps one array defining field order, and reads
both the summary and the focus target from it.

## ex5

Tests the order of normalisation and judgement. Users type with caps lock off and
paste with spaces attached; a validator that judges the raw string rejects codes
that are perfectly correct. The classic mistake is validating `value` and then
passing `value.trim().toUpperCase()` to the callback, or the reverse — the two
have to be the same string, computed once. The model answer normalises at the top
of the handler and lets nothing downstream see the raw value.

## ex6

Tests a comparison and a boundary. ISO date strings compare correctly with `<`,
so reaching for `Date` objects here adds timezone bugs and nothing else. The
classic mistake is `<=`, which rejects a one-day booking that every hotel in the
world sells. The second is disabling the button when the range is invalid, which
removes the only way to find out why. The model answer disables only for
incompleteness and reports the ordering rule as an error on the end field.

## ex7

Tests whether you have a name for "asking". A remote rule has three states, not
two — unchecked, checking, judged — and Save is only legal in one of them. The
classic mistake is firing the check on every keystroke, which is a request per
letter; the second is leaving the previous verdict on screen while the user edits
the value it was about, so the form says "taken" about a handle nobody typed. The
model answer checks on blur, clears everything in the change handler, and gates
Save on a verdict rather than on the absence of an error.

## ex8

Tests the whole loop, and in particular the two flags people collapse into one.
`attempted` decides whether errors may be shown; `saving` decides whether the
form may be submitted again. The classic mistake is a single `submitted` boolean
doing both jobs, which either shows errors too early or lets a slow save be
started twice — and a double-submitted checkout is a real charge, twice. The
model answer keeps them separate, disables the button while the promise is in
flight, and clears `saving` in a `finally` so a rejected save cannot strand the
button on "Saving" forever.

## Further reading

- [Reacting to input with state](https://react.dev/learn/reacting-to-input-with-state)
- [Manipulating the DOM with refs](https://react.dev/learn/manipulating-the-dom-with-refs)
- [You might not need an effect](https://react.dev/learn/you-might-not-need-an-effect)
- [MDN: `aria-invalid`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Attributes/aria-invalid)
- [MDN: `aria-describedby`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Attributes/aria-describedby)
- [MDN: client-side form validation](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn/Forms/Form_validation)

## Exercise 2 — complain late, forgive early

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `UsernameField()` renders an input labelled `Username`.
The rule is three characters. While the user is typing for the first time there

`aria-invalid="true"` and the description

every keystroke, so fixing it clears the error immediately.

```

second question - the usual name for it is `touched`, and the moment it becomes
true is `onBlur`. Show the message only when both are true, and notice that
this gives you the forgiving half for free.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Two jobs the stub does not do: announce the problems as a group, and put the
keyboard where the first problem is. Neither is decoration - they are what makes
a long form usable without a mouse.

## Hint 2
`role="alert"` is the announcement. For the focus, you need a handle on the real
DOM node of each input, which is what `useRef` plus the `ref` prop gives you.

## Hint 3
Validate into a record keyed by field name rather than a flat list, and keep one
array that fixes the field order. Then the summary and the field to focus are
both reads of the same record - and you still have to decide when to move focus,
because doing it on every render would trap the user.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Two jobs the stub does not do: announce the problems as a group, and put the
keyboard where the first problem is. Neither is decoration - they are what makes
a long form usable without a mouse.

## Hint 2
`role="alert"` is the announcement. For the focus, you need a handle on the real
DOM node of each input, which is what `useRef` plus the `ref` prop gives you.

## Hint 3
Validate into a record keyed by field name rather than a flat list, and keep one
array that fixes the field order. Then the summary and the field to focus are
both reads of the same record - and you still have to decide when to move focus,
because doing it on every render would trap the user.

## Exercise 6 — a rule between two fields

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. `DateRange({ onSubmit })` renders `Start date` and
`End date` inputs (`type="date"`) and a `Check availability` button that is
disabled until both are filled. Pressing it with an end date **before** the start
date attaches `End date cannot be before the start date` to the end field and
calls nothing; the start field stays valid. Equal dates are a legal one-day
range. A valid range calls `onSubmit({ start, end })` with the two ISO strings.

The gate drives the date fields with `fireEvent.change` and the button with
`fireEvent.click`, so the button here is an ordinary `type="button"`.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Three states, not two. The handle has not been checked, is being checked, or has
been judged - and Save is only possible in one of them. Write down what each
state looks like on screen before you write any code.

## Hint 2
The check belongs on blur, not on change: one request per finished handle rather
than one per keystroke. `checkAvailable` returns a promise, so the handler that
awaits it has to be `async`.

## Hint 3
Every keystroke invalidates the last verdict, so the change handler has to clear
the status, the error and the permission to save. That leaves one decision worth
thinking about: what should happen if the user edits the box while a check is
still in flight, and whether the answer that arrives afterwards is still about
anything.

## Hint 1
Three states, not two. The handle has not been checked, is being checked, or has
been judged - and Save is only possible in one of them. Write down what each
state looks like on screen before you write any code.

## Hint 2
The check belongs on blur, not on change: one request per finished handle rather
than one per keystroke. `checkAvailable` returns a promise, so the handler that
awaits it has to be `async`.

## Hint 3
Every keystroke invalidates the last verdict, so the change handler has to clear
the status, the error and the permission to save. That leaves one decision worth
thinking about: what should happen if the user edits the box while a check is
still in flight, and whether the answer that arrives afterwards is still about
anything.

## Exercise 8 — the whole loop

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. `ProfileSetup({ onSubmit })` renders `Team name` (at
least 3 characters, `Team name must be at least 3 characters`) and `Website`
(must start with `https://`, `Website must start with https://`), a
`role="status"` region and a `Create profile` submit button.

- no field shows an error before the first submit attempt;
- after one attempt, every field is judged on every keystroke, each error wired
  to its field with `aria-describedby`;
- `onSubmit` returns a promise: while it is pending the button reads `Saving` and
  is disabled, so a second press does nothing at all;
- when it resolves, the status region reads `Saved` and the button says
  `Create profile` again.

```
uv run dojo test react d09_forms_validation ex8
```

lessons.briefing:
# d10 — Effects, the basics (drill set)

Eight problems on the two questions every `useEffect` has to answer: *should
this be an effect at all*, and *what does it actually depend on*. It drills
`06_effects` — if the dependency array still feels like a list you tune until
the warnings stop, reread that lesson first, because half of this set is
designed to punish exactly that habit.

Every external system here arrives as a prop — `join`, `save`, `apply`, `load`,
`chart` — so nothing touches the network and every effect is observable as a
spy. Three of the eight are effects that should not exist.

## Exercise 1 — one join per room

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `RoomJoiner({ roomId, label, join })` renders
`In room <roomId>` in one paragraph and `label` in another, and calls
`join(roomId)` after the first render and again whenever `roomId` changes. A
change to `label` alone must join nothing. The stub has no dependency array.

```
uv run dojo test react d10_effects_basics ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — not on the first render

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `SavedIndicator({ value, save })` calls `save(value)`
whenever `value` changes — but **not** for the first render, when nothing has
changed yet. A `role="status"` paragraph reads `Nothing saved yet` until the
first save and `Saved <value>` afterwards.

```
uv run dojo test react d10_effects_basics ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — the total that is not state

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `LiveTotal({ items, onRender })` renders
`Total: <sum>` in a `role="status"` paragraph and calls `onRender()` once per
render (leave that call where the stub has it). The gate rerenders with new
items and requires **one** render for it.

```
uv run dojo test react d10_effects_basics ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — the object that is new every time

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `FilterSync({ filters, apply })` renders
`<status> / <sort>` in a `role="status"` paragraph and calls `apply` with the
current `{ status, sort }` once on mount and once per real change of those two

nothing.

button and `Orders: <n>` in a `role="status"` paragraph. Every click calls

```

`Loading` until the promise resolves, then shows the resolved string in a

```

```

`theme` in a `role="status"` paragraph and keeps an injected chart in step:

`chart.setSize(size)` on mount and whenever `size` changes, and a change of
`theme` alone calls neither.

```
uv run dojo test react d10_effects_basics ex8
```

# Reading — react/d10_effects_basics

## Notes

The set splits into two halves that people usually blur together. Five problems
are about the dependency array as a *claim*: this effect reads exactly these
values, and re-running it when none of them changed would be pointless work — so
the failures here are an effect that runs too often (no array, an object
rebuilt by the parent, a function defined in the parent render) or one that runs
when it should not (the very first render). The other three are about the prior
question nobody asks: whether the code belongs in an effect at all. A total you
can add up during render is not state; a purchase caused by a click is not
synchronisation; and two unrelated calls to an external system are two effects,
not one. Interviewers reach for these because a candidate who reasons from
"what is this synchronising with?" gets all eight right, and a candidate who
reasons from "when do I want this to run?" gets about half.

## ex1

Tests the simplest form of the claim: an effect with no array at all. The classic
mistake is thinking the array is a performance knob, so it gets omitted while
"getting it working" — and then a label change rejoins a chat room, which in a
real app means a duplicate presence event and a flood of join notifications. The
model answer lists the two values the effect reads, `roomId` and `join`, and
nothing that merely happens to be nearby.

## ex2

Tests whether you can distinguish "this value changed" from "this value
arrived". The classic mistake is a correct dependency array with no guard, which
saves a draft the user never edited every time the component mounts — the
autosave bug that fills a table with identical revisions. The model answer keeps
a `useRef` flag, because a ref is memory that survives a render without causing
one, and consuming it inside the effect leaves the array honest.

## ex3

Tests the "you might not need an effect" reflex, measured by counting renders.
The classic mistake is mirroring props into state and syncing them in an effect,
which costs a second render per change and, more importantly, commits a frame
where the visible total does not match the visible items. The model answer
computes the sum in a `const` during render, where it is always consistent with
the props by construction.

## ex4

Tests whether you know how React compares dependencies. The classic mistake is
depending on an object or array prop: `Object.is` says two structurally
identical objects are different, so an effect keyed on one runs after every
parent render — the usual cause of an infinite fetch loop when the effect also
sets state. The model answer destructures the two primitives it actually reads
and depends on those, which is both correct and a more honest description of the
effect.

## ex5

Tests whether you can tell a reaction from an event. The classic mistake is a
`submitted` boolean plus an effect keyed on it: it works once, then silently
does nothing forever, because setting state to the value it already holds is not
a change and does not re-render. Worse, the effect also re-runs when unrelated
props change, so the same flag can buy twice. The model answer puts the call in
the click handler, where the cause lives, and keeps only the count in state.

## ex6

Tests the hardest of the dependency rules: a function prop that is recreated by
the parent on every render. The classic mistakes are opposite errors — leaving
`load` in the array (an infinite refetch) or deleting it from the array (a stale
closure that calls the first render's function forever). The model answer stores
the newest function in a ref updated by its own effect and depends only on `id`,
which is the pattern `useEffectEvent` is being designed to replace.

## ex7

Tests resetting derived state when the thing it derives from changes. The classic
mistake is an effect keyed on the product object: it resets when a parent merely
rebuilt an equal object, throwing away the user's selection, and it resets one
render late, so the UI briefly shows a size the new product does not sell. The
model answer stores the choice together with the id it was made for and derives
the displayed size during render, which makes both bugs unrepresentable.

## ex8

Tests whether "one effect" is a unit of code or a unit of responsibility. The
classic mistake is one effect that pushes data and size together with every prop
in its array, so a theme change redraws a chart that has not changed — cheap in
a test, visible as a flicker on a real canvas. The model answer writes two
effects with two arrays, each naming exactly what its own call reads, and lets
the theme be ordinary markup.

## Further reading

- [Synchronizing with effects](https://react.dev/learn/synchronizing-with-effects)
- [You might not need an effect](https://react.dev/learn/you-might-not-need-an-effect)
- [Removing effect dependencies](https://react.dev/learn/removing-effect-dependencies)
- [`useEffect` reference](https://react.dev/reference/react/useEffect)
- [`useRef` reference](https://react.dev/reference/react/useRef)
- [MDN: `Object.is()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Object/is)

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `RoomJoiner({ roomId, label, join })` renders

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The stub has no dependency array at all, which is the strongest possible claim:
run again after every render, forever. Ask what this effect actually reads, and
say only that.

## Hint 2
The array is a list of the values the effect uses - here that is the room it
joins and the function it joins with. Everything else the component renders is

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The gate hands the component an object literal, so the parent builds a fresh
one on every render. React compares dependencies with `Object.is`, which says
two objects with identical contents are different values.

## Hint 2
You cannot make the parent stop, and you should not compare by hand with
`JSON.stringify`. Depend on the things inside the object instead - pull them
out above the effect and let the array list those.

## Hint 3
Destructuring at the top of the component gives you two stable strings to
depend on, and it also makes the effect honest: those two values really are all
it reads. What it passes onward is up to you, as long as `apply` receives the
current status and sort.

## Hint 1
The gate hands the component an object literal, so the parent builds a fresh
one on every render. React compares dependencies with `Object.is`, which says
two objects with identical contents are different values.

## Hint 2
You cannot make the parent stop, and you should not compare by hand with
`JSON.stringify`. Depend on the things inside the object instead - pull them
out above the effect and let the array list those.

## Hint 3
Destructuring at the top of the component gives you two stable strings to
depend on, and it also makes the effect honest: those two values really are all
it reads. What it passes onward is up to you, as long as `apply` receives the
current status and sort.

## Exercise 6 — the function prop in the array

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. `Loader({ id, load })` calls `load(id)`, shows
`Loading` until the promise resolves, then shows the resolved string in a

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The dependency array in the stub is honest - the effect really does read
`load`. The trouble is that the parent writes a new arrow function every
render, so an honest array refetches forever. That loop is one of the two
classic `useEffect` disasters.

## Hint 2
Deleting `load` from the array without changing anything else leaves the effect
holding the first render-s function forever, which is a stale closure. You need
the latest function *and* a dependency list that does not mention it.

## Hint 3
A ref updated in its own dependency-free effect always holds the newest value,
and reading `.current` inside the fetching effect does not make it a
dependency. Decide for yourself where the read belongs - and keep the guard
that stops a late answer to an abandoned id from winning.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
The dependency array in the stub is honest - the effect really does read
`load`. The trouble is that the parent writes a new arrow function every
render, so an honest array refetches forever. That loop is one of the two
classic `useEffect` disasters.

## Hint 2
Deleting `load` from the array without changing anything else leaves the effect
holding the first render-s function forever, which is a stale closure. You need
the latest function *and* a dependency list that does not mention it.

## Hint 3
A ref updated in its own dependency-free effect always holds the newest value,
and reading `.current` inside the fetching effect does not make it a
dependency. Decide for yourself where the read belongs - and keep the guard
that stops a late answer to an abandoned id from winning.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — a choice that stops applying

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. `ProductPicker({ product, onRender })` renders one
button per entry in `product.sizes` and a `role="status"` paragraph reading
`<product.id>: <size>`. Before any click the size is `product.sizes[0]`; a click
selects that size. When the **product** changes the size falls back to the new
product's first size, in the same render — the gate allows exactly one render
for that change. A parent that rebuilds an equal product object has not changed
the product, and must not throw the user's choice away. Call
`onRender(product.id, size)` once per render, as the stub does.

```
uv run dojo test react d10_effects_basics ex7
```

## Hint 1
Two separate bugs live in the stub. It resets when the product object is
rebuilt but not really changed, and it resets one render too late - after a
commit in which the user could see a mug offered in a bean size.

## Hint 2
The selected size is only meaningful together with the product it was chosen
for. Store both together, and the question "does this choice still apply?"
becomes a comparison you can make during render.

## Hint 3
With the pair in state, the size you display is derived: use the stored size
when the stored id matches the current product, otherwise fall back to the
current product-s first size. No effect, no second render, and nothing to keep
in step. What you store on a click is your decision.

lessons.briefing:
# d11 — Effect cleanup (drill set)

Eight problems on the second half of every effect: the function it returns.
Subscriptions, intervals, timeouts and document listeners all have the same
shape — something is started that will outlive the render unless the component
stops it. It drills `06_effects`; if "React runs the previous cleanup before the
next effect" is not yet a sentence you could say out loud, reread that lesson
first.

Every external system arrives as a prop and every gate counts what is still
open. The timed drills use fake timers and `fireEvent`, because `user-event`
waits on real timers and the two do not mix.

## Exercise 1 — unsubscribe on the way out

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `PresenceList({ subscribe })` calls
`subscribe(callback)`, which returns an unsubscribe function, and renders one
`<li>` per name the callback is given. Unmounting must unsubscribe exactly once.

```
uv run dojo test react d11_effects_cleanup ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — the interval that outlives its component

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `IntervalClock({ tick })` calls `tick()` once per
second and shows `<n> seconds` in a `role="status"` paragraph. After unmounting,
advancing time must call `tick` no more and leave nothing scheduled.

```
uv run dojo test react d11_effects_cleanup ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — leave before you arrive

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `ChannelSwitch({ channel, connect })` calls
`connect(channel)`, which returns a disconnect function, and renders
`Listening to <channel>` in a `role="status"` paragraph. Switching channels must
produce exactly `connect alpha`, `disconnect alpha`, `connect beta`, and
unmounting must disconnect the last one.

```
uv run dojo test react d11_effects_cleanup ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — start, pause, finish

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `Countdown({ from, onDone })` renders `Start` and
`Pause` buttons and `Time left: <n>` in a `role="status"` paragraph. It counts
down one per second **only while running**, pausing stops it where it is,
reaching zero calls `onDone` exactly once and stops the countdown, and no timer
is left scheduled afterwards.

```
uv run dojo test react d11_effects_cleanup ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — clicks that are somewhere else

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. `ClickOutside({ onOutside })` renders a `<div>`
containing a button labelled `Inside`, and listens for clicks on `document`.
Clicks inside its own element call nothing; clicks anywhere else call
`onOutside`. A new `onOutside` prop must replace the old listener, and unmounting
must remove it.

```
uv run dojo test react d11_effects_cleanup ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — save when the typing stops

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. `Autosave({ text, save })` calls `save(text)` 500ms
after the last change to `text`, once. A change inside that window cancels the
pending save; unmounting inside it cancels the save entirely. A `role="status"`
paragraph reads `Unsaved changes` between a change and its save, and
`All changes saved` otherwise — including on the first render, when nothing has
changed yet.

```
uv run dojo test react d11_effects_cleanup ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — set up twice, on purpose

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. `SessionKeeper({ connect })` calls `connect()`, which
returns a close function, and renders `Session open` in a `role="status"`
paragraph. The gate renders it inside `<StrictMode>`, which in development runs
every effect setup–cleanup–setup: afterwards there must be two setups, one
cleanup and **one** live connection, and unmounting must close it.

```
uv run dojo test react d11_effects_cleanup ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — one stream at a time

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. `LiveTicker({ source, paused, subscribe })` calls
`subscribe(source, callback)`, which returns an unsubscribe function, and shows
`<source>: <value>` in a `role="status"` paragraph (`No data` before anything
arrives). It is subscribed only while `paused` is false, resubscribes when
`source` changes, and never has two streams open at once — pausing, resuming,
switching source and unmounting all have to leave the count right. A value that
arrived for one source must never be displayed as another source's.

```
uv run dojo test react d11_effects_cleanup ex8
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading — react/d11_effects_cleanup

## Notes

One rule generates every answer in this set: **an effect synchronises an
external system with your component, and the cleanup un-synchronises it.** If
the effect started something, the cleanup stops that same thing — and React runs
it at two moments, before the next run of the effect and once on unmount. Read
those two moments together and the drills stop being eight different problems.
The pairs here are subscribe/unsubscribe, setInterval/clearInterval,
setTimeout/clearTimeout, addEventListener/removeEventListener and
connect/disconnect, and the failure is always the same shape: the setup ran more
times than the teardown. That imbalance shows up as a leak in production and as
a doubled subscription under StrictMode in development, which is exactly why
StrictMode double-invokes effects — it is a symmetry test you can run before
your users do.

## ex1

Tests whether you recognise a teardown when an API hands you one. The classic
mistake is calling `subscribe(...)` and discarding its return value, which
leaves the source holding a callback into a component that no longer exists —
the leak that later shows up as "setState on an unmounted component". The model
answer returns the unsubscribe function from the effect, which is all React
needs to run it at the right moment.

## ex2

Tests the same rule with a timer, where the symptom is louder: an interval that
is never cleared keeps firing forever and, worse, a component that mounts and
unmounts repeatedly leaves one running per mount. The classic mistake is
forgetting the handle entirely; the second is dropping the updater form in
`setSeconds`, so every tick adds one to the same captured value. The model
answer keeps the id in a `const` and clears it in the cleanup.

builds a log because ordering is the whole point: React runs the previous
cleanup before the next effect, so switching channels reads leave-then-join. The
classic mistake is hand-rolling the teardown in a ref, which usually gets the
ordering right and always forgets the unmount. The model answer returns the
disconnect function and deletes the ref.

effect re-running with a changed dependency, and the previous run's cleanup is
what stops the interval. The classic mistake is starting an interval with no
cleanup, which leaves one running per Start ever pressed — the countdown then
accelerates, which is a bug users describe as "the timer went weird". The model
answer returns early when not running (registering no cleanup for that run) and
handles finishing separately, keeping the updater function pure.

Tests two failures that share one cause: an effect claiming an empty dependency
array while reading a prop. The listener then calls the first render's

adding `onOutside` to the array without adding a cleanup, which turns a stale
listener into a growing pile of them. The model answer declares the handler
inside the effect so the cleanup can remove that exact reference, and depends on
`onOutside`.

Tests the debounce, which is not an algorithm here but a consequence of the
lifecycle. The classic mistake is starting a timeout with no cleanup: every
keystroke schedules a save and they all fire, which is the opposite of what a
debounce is for. The model answer clears the pending timeout in the cleanup, so
a change inside the window cancels the save that was about to go out — and the
unmount case is covered by the same two lines, for free.

## ex7

Tests idempotence, using StrictMode as the instrument. The classic mistake is
reading the doubled setup as a React quirk to be worked around — with a ref
guard, or by disabling StrictMode — rather than as the signal it is: setup ran
twice and teardown zero times, so the pairing is broken and production will leak
one connection per mount. The model answer changes nothing about the structure;
it just returns the close function, after which running setup twice leaves
exactly one connection open.

## ex8

Tests all of it at once, with a second dependency that decides whether the
effect should do anything at all. The classic mistakes are leaving `paused` out
of the dependency array (so pausing does nothing until something else changes),
and returning no cleanup, so resuming and switching source pile streams up
without closing any. The model answer puts every value the effect reads in the
array, returns early while paused, and returns the unsubscribe function
otherwise — one open stream at every point in the sequence, and none at the end.

# Reading — react/d11_effects_cleanup

## Notes

One rule generates every answer in this set: **an effect synchronises an
external system with your component, and the cleanup un-synchronises it.** If
the effect started something, the cleanup stops that same thing — and React runs
it at two moments, before the next run of the effect and once on unmount. Read
those two moments together and the drills stop being eight different problems.
The pairs here are subscribe/unsubscribe, setInterval/clearInterval,
setTimeout/clearTimeout, addEventListener/removeEventListener and
connect/disconnect, and the failure is always the same shape: the setup ran more
times than the teardown. That imbalance shows up as a leak in production and as
a doubled subscription under StrictMode in development, which is exactly why
StrictMode double-invokes effects — it is a symmetry test you can run before
your users do.

## ex1

mistake is calling `subscribe(...)` and discarding its return value, which

answer returns the unsubscribe function from the effect, which is all React
needs to run it at the right moment.

## Hint 1
`subscribe` already hands you everything you need - look at what it returns and
ask who is supposed to call it.

## Hint 2
Whatever an effect returns, React treats as its cleanup and runs before the
next run of that effect and once more on unmount. Note that
`useEffect(() => subscribe(setNames), deps)` returns it by accident, which is
either elegant or too clever depending on who reviews your code.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
`subscribe` already hands you everything you need - look at what it returns and
ask who is supposed to call it.

## Hint 2
Whatever an effect returns, React treats as its cleanup and runs before the
next run of that effect and once more on unmount. Note that
`useEffect(() => subscribe(setNames), deps)` returns it by accident, which is
either elegant or too clever depending on who reviews your code.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Pausing is not a special case in the component - it is the ordinary case of an
effect whose dependency changed. The effect that owns the interval already
re-runs when `running` changes; the question is what it leaves behind when it
does.

## Hint 2
An effect may return early, and returning early means no cleanup is registered
for that run - which is exactly right for the paused case, because the previous
run-s cleanup has already fired by then.

## Hint 3
Finishing is a second, separate concern: something has to notice that the
counter reached zero, stop the countdown and call `onDone` once. Whether that
lives in another effect or somewhere else is your call, but keep it out of the
updater function - updaters must stay pure.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Pausing is not a special case in the component - it is the ordinary case of an
effect whose dependency changed. The effect that owns the interval already
re-runs when `running` changes; the question is what it leaves behind when it
does.

## Hint 2
An effect may return early, and returning early means no cleanup is registered
for that run - which is exactly right for the paused case, because the previous
run-s cleanup has already fired by then.

## Hint 3
Finishing is a second, separate concern: something has to notice that the
counter reached zero, stop the countdown and call `onDone` once. Whether that
lives in another effect or somewhere else is your call, but keep it out of the
updater function - updaters must stay pure.

## Exercise 6 — save when the typing stops

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. `Autosave({ text, save })` calls `save(text)` 500ms
after the last change to `text`, once. A change inside that window cancels the
pending save; unmounting inside it cancels the save entirely. A `role="status"`
paragraph reads `Unsaved changes` between a change and its save, and
`All changes saved` otherwise — including on the first render, when nothing has
changed yet.

```
uv run dojo test react d11_effects_cleanup ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
A debounce is not a queue and it is not a comparison of timestamps. It is one
pending timer that keeps getting thrown away, and the effect lifecycle already
throws things away at exactly the right moments.

## Hint 2
React runs the previous cleanup before the next effect, so a change arriving
inside the window cancels the save that was about to go out - as long as the
cleanup clears the timeout it started. The same cleanup covers the unmount case
for free.

## Hint 1
A debounce is not a queue and it is not a comparison of timestamps. It is one
pending timer that keeps getting thrown away, and the effect lifecycle already
throws things away at exactly the right moments.

## Hint 2
React runs the previous cleanup before the next effect, so a change arriving
inside the window cancels the save that was about to go out - as long as the
cleanup clears the timeout it started. The same cleanup covers the unmount case
for free.

## Exercise 7 — set up twice, on purpose

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. `SessionKeeper({ connect })` calls `connect()`, which
returns a close function, and renders `Session open` in a `role="status"`
paragraph. The gate renders it inside `<StrictMode>`, which in development runs
every effect setup–cleanup–setup: afterwards there must be two setups, one
cleanup and **one** live connection, and unmounting must close it.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — one stream at a time

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. `LiveTicker({ source, paused, subscribe })` calls
`subscribe(source, callback)`, which returns an unsubscribe function, and shows
`<source>: <value>` in a `role="status"` paragraph (`No data` before anything
arrives). It is subscribed only while `paused` is false, resubscribes when
`source` changes, and never has two streams open at once — pausing, resuming,
switching source and unmounting all have to leave the count right. A value that
arrived for one source must never be displayed as another source's.

```
uv run dojo test react d11_effects_cleanup ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Three questions decide the whole exercise: when should this component be
subscribed at all, which values does that answer depend on, and what closes the
stream when the answer changes.

## Hint 2
Pausing is not a separate mechanism from switching source - both are just the
effect re-running with a different dependency, and the cleanup React already
ran is what closed the old stream. `paused` therefore belongs in the array.

## Hint 3
An effect that returns early registers no cleanup for that run, which is what
you want while paused. What the display should show on the way through a
resubscribe is your decision - just make sure a value that arrived for one
source cannot be shown as though it came from another.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Three questions decide the whole exercise: when should this component be
subscribed at all, which values does that answer depend on, and what closes the
stream when the answer changes.

## Hint 2
Pausing is not a separate mechanism from switching source - both are just the
effect re-running with a different dependency, and the cleanup React already
ran is what closed the old stream. `paused` therefore belongs in the array.

## Hint 3
An effect that returns early registers no cleanup for that run, which is what
you want while paused. What the display should show on the way through a
resubscribe is your decision - just make sure a value that arrived for one
source cannot be shown as though it came from another.

# d12 — Fetching and its states (drill set)

Eight problems on the four things a request can be doing — not started, in
flight, failed, answered — and on the fact that the answer can also be empty.
It drills `07_data_fetching`; if the difference between "no results" and "no
answer yet" is not obvious to you yet, go and redo that lesson first.

Nothing here touches the network. Every component takes its request as a prop,
and the gate hands you promises it resolves and rejects by hand, so a run is the
same on every machine. Races between two in-flight requests are the next drill
set (`d13_race_abort`) — none of these problems need a guard.

## Exercise 1 — loading is a state

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `WeatherCard({ city, fetchWeather })` calls
`fetchWeather(city)` once per city. While the promise is pending it renders a
`role="status"` reading `Loading weather for <city>`; once it settles it renders
`<tempC>C, <summary>` — for example `12C, Cloudy` — and the loading message is
gone.

```
uv run dojo test react d12_fetching_states ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — failure is a state too

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `InvoiceView({ invoiceId, load })` shows
`Loading invoice <invoiceId>` in a `role="status"` while `load(invoiceId)` is
pending. If the promise rejects, it shows the rejection's message in a
`role="alert"` and stops claiming to be loading. If it resolves, it shows
`Total: <total>`.

```
uv run dojo test react d12_fetching_states ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — empty is not the same as pending

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `SearchPanel({ query, search })` calls `search(query)`
whenever the query changes and renders:

- `role="status"` with `Searching for <query>` while the promise is pending;
- a paragraph reading `No matches for <query>` when the answer is an empty array;
- a `<ul>` with one `<li>` per result otherwise.

```
uv run dojo test react d12_fetching_states ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — refresh, without stampeding

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `StockLevel({ sku, fetchLevel })` shows
`In stock: <n>` once `fetchLevel(sku)` answers, plus a `Refresh` button that
asks again. While any request is in flight the button is **disabled**, and the
number already on screen **stays on screen** — a refresh never blanks it.

```
uv run dojo test react d12_fetching_states ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — a retry starts clean

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. `TicketView({ ticketId, load })` shows
`Loading ticket <ticketId>` in a `role="status"`, the subject on success, and the
rejection message in a `role="alert"` plus a `Retry` button on failure. Pressing
`Retry` must clear the old error **before** the new request is in flight: while
the retry runs there is a status and no alert.

```
uv run dojo test react d12_fetching_states ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — stale while revalidating

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. `RateBoard({ pair, fetchRate })` renders one
`role="region"` named `Exchange rate` that:

- reads `Loading rates` on the very first request, when there is nothing else to
  show;
- otherwise keeps showing the rate it already has while a new one is fetched;
- carries `aria-busy="true"` exactly while a request is in flight, and
  `aria-busy="false"` when it is not.

A new `pair` prop is a new request.

```
uv run dojo test react d12_fetching_states ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — one request that needs another one's answer

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. `CustomerOrders({ customerId, fetchCustomer, fetchOrders })`
loads the customer, then calls `fetchOrders(customer.id)` with the id the first
answer returned. Until **both** have arrived it renders `role="status"` with
`Loading customer`; then a level-2 heading with the name and a `<ul>` of order
ids. If the first request rejects, the message goes in a `role="alert"` and
`fetchOrders` is never called.

```
uv run dojo test react d12_fetching_states ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — paging that adds up

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. `ActivityFeed({ fetchPage })` calls `fetchPage(n)`,
which resolves to `{ items, hasMore }`. Page 1 loads on mount, and a `Load more`
button (disabled while loading) fetches the next page and **appends** it. If a
page rejects:

- the items already loaded stay on screen;
- the message appears in a `role="alert"`, and `Load more` is replaced by
  `Retry`, which asks for the *same* page again and clears the error;
- when a page answers with `hasMore: false`, the `Load more` button is gone.

```
uv run dojo test react d12_fetching_states ex8
```

# Reading — react/d12_fetching_states

## Notes

One idea unites this set: a request is a little state machine, and every state
it can be in is a screen somebody has to see. Idle, in flight, failed, answered,
answered-with-nothing — five, not two. Almost every fetching bug in a real
codebase is a pair of these states that were collapsed into one boolean: a
spinner that also means "failed", an empty list that also means "loading", an
error that survives its own retry. The drills push you to keep the states
separate and to notice which of them the user is entitled to be told about out
loud, through `role="status"` and `role="alert"`. The one thing deliberately
left out is the race between two in-flight requests — that is the next set, and
none of these problems need the guard.

## ex1

Tests whether the pending state exists at all. The classic mistake is rendering
the data-shaped markup with empty values in it, which flashes a component full
of blanks and tells a screen-reader user nothing whatsoever. The model answer
uses `null` as the "no answer yet" value and returns early with a live region,
which also means the happy-path markup never has to defend itself against
missing data.

## ex2

Tests the rejection branch, which is the branch nobody writes until an interview
or an incident. The classic mistake is `.then(setState)` with no second
argument: the promise rejects, nothing catches it, the spinner runs forever and
the console gets an unhandled rejection. The second mistake is a boolean
`failed` flag that throws away the message the server took the trouble to send.
The model answer stores the message and renders it in an alert, and puts the
error branch *above* the loading branch so the two cannot both be true.

## ex3

Tests whether you can distinguish "the server answered, and the answer is
nothing" from "the server has not answered". The classic mistake is initialising
the results to `[]`, which makes those two states literally the same value —
after which no amount of branching can tell them apart. The model answer starts
at `null` and treats an empty array as a real, successful answer with its own
sentence naming the query.

## ex4

Tests re-fetching on demand, and the etiquette around it. The classic mistake is
leaving the refresh control enabled while a request is in flight, which lets an
impatient user queue five identical requests and guarantees a race. The second
is blanking the value while it refreshes, so the number the user was reading
disappears. The model answer keeps `loading` as its own piece of state, uses it
only for the disabled attribute, and re-runs the effect through a counter it can
bump.

## ex5

Tests the transition between states rather than the states themselves. The
classic mistake is a retry that leaves the previous error on screen, so for one
frame the user sees a failure notice sitting beside a fresh spinner and
reasonably concludes it failed again. The model answer clears the error and the
old result at the top of the effect body — the start of a request is the moment
everything belonging to the last one becomes invalid.

## ex6

Tests stale-while-revalidate, the pattern every data library implements and most
hand-rolled code does not. The classic mistake is deriving "loading" from "data
is null", which forces you to null the data to show a spinner and makes flicker
unavoidable. The model answer keeps the last good value and a separate busy
flag, and moves the "something is happening" signal into `aria-busy` on the
region, where it costs the reader nothing.

## ex7

Tests sequential, dependent requests. The classic mistake is firing both
requests in parallel because it looks faster, which cannot work when the second
call needs an id only the first response carries — in production this is the
request for `/customers/undefined/orders`. The second mistake is two independent
loading flags, which lets a half-loaded screen render. The model answer chains
inside `then`, returns one combined object, and gives both steps a single
rejection handler.

## ex8

Tests accumulating state across requests plus a failure in the middle of it. The
classic mistake is `setItems(result.items)`, which turns pagination into
"replace the list" — the same code works for a first page and is wrong from the
second onwards. The second is emptying the list when a page fails, throwing away
data that was never in question. The model answer appends with the updater form,
keeps the page number stable so the retry asks for the page that failed, and
lets `hasMore` from the server decide when the button disappears.

## Further reading

- [Synchronizing with effects](https://react.dev/learn/synchronizing-with-effects)
- [You might not need an effect](https://react.dev/learn/you-might-not-need-an-effect)
- [Choosing the state structure](https://react.dev/learn/choosing-the-state-structure)
- [MDN: using promises](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Guide/Using_promises)
- [MDN: ARIA live regions](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/ARIA_Live_Regions)

classic mistake is `setItems(result.items)`, which turns pagination into
"replace the list" — the same code works for a first page and is wrong from the
second onwards. The second is emptying the list when a page fails, throwing away
data that was never in question. The model answer appends with the updater form,
keeps the page number stable so the retry asks for the page that failed, and
lets `hasMore` from the server decide when the button disappears.

## Exercise 1 — loading is a state

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `WeatherCard({ city, fetchWeather })` calls
`fetchWeather(city)` once per city. While the promise is pending it renders a
`role="status"` reading `Loading weather for <city>`; once it settles it renders
`<tempC>C, <summary>` — for example `12C, Cloudy` — and the loading message is
gone.

```
uv run dojo test react d12_fetching_states ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
There are two things on screen here, never at the same time: the sentence you
show while the promise is pending, and the data you show once it settles. One
piece of state can express both if you choose its empty value carefully.

## Hint 2
`null` means "no answer yet". Return early while the state is `null`, with a
live region - `role="status"` - so a screen-reader user is told that something
is happening. The dots the stub renders say nothing to anybody.

## Exercise 4 — refresh, without stampeding

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `StockLevel({ sku, fetchLevel })` shows
`In stock: <n>` once `fetchLevel(sku)` answers, plus a `Refresh` button that
asks again. While any request is in flight the button is **disabled**, and the
number already on screen **stays on screen** — a refresh never blanks it.

```
uv run dojo test react d12_fetching_states ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Two problems. The button currently does nothing, and even once it does
something there is no way for the component to know that a request is in
flight - which is the fact the disabled attribute needs.

## Hint 2
An effect re-runs when one of its dependencies changes, so a counter in state
that the button increments is a perfectly good "please run again" signal. Keep
a separate `loading` boolean: it goes true when a request starts and false when
it settles.

## Hint 3
Notice what the gate asserts while the refresh is in flight: the number that is
already on screen has to stay there. That rules out clearing the level when the
new request starts - the only thing that changes at that moment is `loading`.

The stub derives "am I loading?" from "do I have data?", which is why a refresh

busy. Separate the two facts.

Two pieces of state: the rate you last received, and whether a request is in
flight. The second one drives `aria-busy` and nothing else, so the first can be
left alone from the moment it arrives until the moment a better value replaces
it.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — paging that adds up

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. `ActivityFeed({ fetchPage })` calls `fetchPage(n)`,
which resolves to `{ items, hasMore }`. Page 1 loads on mount, and a `Load more`
button (disabled while loading) fetches the next page and **appends** it. If a
page rejects:

- the items already loaded stay on screen;
- the message appears in a `role="alert"`, and `Load more` is replaced by
  `Retry`, which asks for the *same* page again and clears the error;
- when a page answers with `hasMore: false`, the `Load more` button is gone.

```
uv run dojo test react d12_fetching_states ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Three separate bugs live in the stub: a page replaces the list instead of
joining it, a failed page empties the list, and there is no way to ask for the
same page again. Fix them one at a time and rerun the gate between each.

## Hint 2
Appending is the updater form - `setItems((current) => [...current, ...next])` -
because the value you are adding to is the one from the previous state, not the
one this render captured. A failed page should touch the error only; the items
it never received are not evidence about the items you already have.

## Hint 3
Retrying the *same* page means the page number must not change, so the effect
needs a second reason to run. What appears where the Load more button used to
be, while the error is on screen, is a design decision the gate has already
made for you - reread the gate assertions.

## Hint 1
Three separate bugs live in the stub: a page replaces the list instead of
joining it, a failed page empties the list, and there is no way to ask for the
same page again. Fix them one at a time and rerun the gate between each.

## Hint 2
Appending is the updater form - `setItems((current) => [...current, ...next])` -
because the value you are adding to is the one from the previous state, not the
one this render captured. A failed page should touch the error only; the items
it never received are not evidence about the items you already have.

## Hint 3
Retrying the *same* page means the page number must not change, so the effect
needs a second reason to run. What appears where the Load more button used to
be, while the error is on screen, is a design decision the gate has already
made for you - reread the gate assertions.
