lessons.briefing:
# d13 — Races and aborts (drill set)

Eight problems on one fact: a promise you no longer want will still resolve.
It drills `07_data_fetching` — if the picture of request A being started,
superseded, and then answering last is not yet in your head, reread that
lesson's "The race" section before you start, because every problem here is a
variation on it.

Every request is an injected function and the gate resolves the promises **out
of order on purpose**, so nothing depends on timing. Three of the eight cannot
be solved with the flag-in-a-cleanup pattern at all: one wants an
`AbortController`, one wants a request number, and one dissolves the race by
storing answers where they belong.

## Exercise 1 — the answer you walked away from

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `StationBoard({ station, fetchDepartures })` calls
`fetchDepartures(station)`, shows `Loading departures for <station>` in a
`role="status"` paragraph while the promise is pending, and lists the resolved
strings as `<li>`s. A change of `station` starts a new request and goes back to
loading. The gate resolves the **first** station last, and the board must
ignore it.

```
uv run dojo test react d13_race_abort ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — the failure you walked away from

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `ShipmentTracker({ trackingId, fetchStatus })` shows
`Checking <trackingId>` in a `role="status"` while pending, the resolved string
in a paragraph, and a rejection's message in a `role="alert"`. The gate
supersedes the first parcel and then **rejects** it: that failure must reach
nobody. A rejection of the parcel actually on screen must still be announced.

```
uv run dojo test react d13_race_abort ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — stop the work, not just the answer

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `DocumentPane({ docId, fetchDoc })` calls
`fetchDoc(docId, signal)` — the second argument is an `AbortSignal`. It shows
`Loading document <docId>` in a `role="status"`, the text in a paragraph, and a
rejection's message in a `role="alert"`. When `docId` changes, the signal that
went out with the abandoned request must end up **aborted**, and the signal of
the live request must not. The rejection that aborting causes is not an error
the user should see.

```
uv run dojo test react d13_race_abort ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — the race the keyboard starts

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `SymbolSearch({ lookup })` renders an input labelled
`Ticker`. While the box is empty it shows `Type a ticker` in a `role="status"`
and asks nothing. Otherwise it calls `lookup(<value>)` once per change, shows
`Searching for <value>` in a `role="status"` while pending, and shows the
resolved company name in a paragraph. The gate types `AC`, then `ACM`, then
answers `ACM` first.

```
uv run dojo test react d13_race_abort ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — two clicks, no cleanup

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. `AccountBalance({ accountId, fetchBalance })` shows
`Loading balance` in a `role="status"` until it has a number, then
`Balance: <n>` in a paragraph. A `Refresh` button — always enabled — asks
again. The gate clicks it twice in a row and answers the **second** click
first; the older answer must lose, and the refresh after that must still work.
No prop changes here, so no effect re-runs and no cleanup fires.

```
uv run dojo test react d13_race_abort ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — a flag per request

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. `PollenIndex({ city, fetchIndex })` shows
`Checking <city>` in a `role="status"` while pending and
`Pollen in <city>: <index>` in a paragraph once answered. The stub guards its
answer with a `useRef`, which works exactly once and then wedges the component
forever. The gate walks through four cities and abandons one of them mid-flight.

```
uv run dojo test react d13_race_abort ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — abandoning a chain

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. `ItineraryPanel({ tripId, fetchTrip, fetchLegs })`
calls `fetchTrip(tripId)`, then `fetchLegs(trip.id)` with the id the first
answer carried. Until both have arrived it shows `Loading itinerary` in a
`role="status"`; then a level-2 heading with `trip.traveller` and one `<li>`
per leg. When `tripId` changes before the first step has answered, the
abandoned chain must **not** send the second request at all.

```
uv run dojo test react d13_race_abort ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — file it under the question

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. `MetricTabs({ fetchMetric })` renders three buttons —
`Traffic`, `Signups`, `Revenue` — and starts with `Traffic` selected. The
selected metric's value is shown in a paragraph, or `Loading <metric>` in a
`role="status"` while it has none. `fetchMetric(metric)` is called **at most
once per metric, ever**: an answer that arrives after the user has moved on
must still be kept, so that returning to that tab shows it immediately without
a new request — but it must never appear while another tab is selected.

```
uv run dojo test react d13_race_abort ex8
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading — react/d13_race_abort

## Notes

Every problem in this set is the same shape: two requests exist at once and the
one you stopped caring about answers anyway. What changes from problem to
problem is *what the component can hang the answer on*. When the request was
started by an effect, the effect's own cleanup is the hook — a `let` declared
inside the effect body, flipped on the way out, read before any `setState`.
When the request was started by a click, no effect re-ran and no cleanup fired,
so the component has to number its own requests. When the request is real
network traffic, a flag only hides the answer while the bytes keep coming, and
an `AbortController` stops the work itself. And in the last problem the race
stops existing, because answers are stored under the question that produced
them rather than under "the current answer". Interviewers like this material
because the bug never appears on a fast machine or a small dataset: it appears
in production, for the one user on hotel wifi, as a screen that shows somebody
else's data.

## ex1

Tests the base pattern: a flag scoped to one run of the effect. The classic
mistake is assuming React's own cleanup already handles it — it does not; React
has no idea a promise exists, and the `.then` closure outlives the effect that
created it. The model answer declares `let current = true` in the effect body
so the cleanup flips exactly the flag belonging to the run it is retiring, and
the callback returns early rather than calling `setDepartures`.

## ex2

Tests whether the guard covers both branches of the promise. The classic
mistake is guarding `.then` and leaving `.catch` open, which lets a dead
request paint an error alert over a screen that was already correct — and
because errors are usually rendered instead of data, the user loses the good
answer as well. The model answer passes both callbacks to a single `.then(ok,
fail)` with the same check at the top of each, and clears the previous error
when the id changes so an old alert cannot survive into a new request.

## ex3

Tests the difference between ignoring an answer and cancelling the work. The
classic mistake is creating an `AbortController` and never keeping it, so its
signal goes out and nothing ever aborts — the request still downloads, still
costs the user bandwidth, still occupies a connection. The model answer builds
one controller per effect run, aborts it in the cleanup, and treats
`signal.aborted` as the guard, remembering that the abort surfaces as a
rejection it must not report.

## ex4

Tests whether you recognise the race when a keystroke starts it rather than a
prop. The classic mistake is firing the request straight from the change
handler, where there is no cleanup and no way to know a later keystroke has
happened, so the shortest query — which the server answers fastest, or slowest,
depending on the day — wins at random. The model answer keeps the handler down
to `setQuery` and moves the request into an effect that depends on the query,
which turns each keystroke into a retirement of the previous run.

## ex5

Tests the case the flag pattern cannot reach. The classic mistake is
concluding that two clicks with no prop change cannot race — they can, and the
symptom is a balance that flickers back to an older number. The model answer
keeps a monotonically increasing request number in a `useRef`, captures it when
the request goes out, and compares it against the newest number when the answer
returns; a boolean would either wedge the component or fail to distinguish the
two in-flight requests.

## ex6

Tests where the guard lives. The classic mistake is reaching for `useRef`
because "it survives renders", which is true and exactly wrong: one ref is one
box shared by every run of the effect, so the first cleanup sets it to `false`
and no later answer is ever accepted again — the component simply stops
updating, which is far worse than the stale answer it was trying to prevent.
The model answer uses a local `let`, giving each run its own box, and the
cleanup closes over the box belonging to its own run.

## ex7

Tests guarding a chain rather than a single request. The classic mistake is
one check before the final `setState`, which is enough to keep the wrong data
off the screen but still fires the second request for a trip nobody is looking
at any more — a wasted round trip, and a real bug when the second call is a
mutation rather than a read. The model answer asks the same question again at
every point where the chain is about to spend something, using one flag for the
whole run because the cleanup retires both steps at once.

## ex8

Tests the idea that dissolves the whole category. The classic mistake is
storing "the answer" in one slot and cancelling anything that does not belong
there, which throws away a true answer and then pays for it again when the user
comes back. The model answer keys the answers by metric and renders the slot
the selected tab points at, so a late answer lands in its own slot and could
not be displayed by accident; the set of already-requested metrics lives in a
ref, because it never needs to be rendered and putting it in state would put it
in the effect's dependencies.

## Further reading

- [Synchronizing with effects](https://react.dev/learn/synchronizing-with-effects)
- [`useEffect` reference](https://react.dev/reference/react/useEffect)
- [`useRef` reference](https://react.dev/reference/react/useRef)
- [MDN: `AbortController`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortController)
- [MDN: `AbortSignal`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortSignal)
- [MDN: `Promise.prototype.then()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Promise/then)

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `StationBoard({ station, fetchDepartures })` calls
`fetchDepartures(station)`, shows `Loading departures for <station>` in a
`role="status"` paragraph while the promise is pending, and lists the resolved
strings as `<li>`s. A change of `station` starts a new request and goes back to
loading. The gate resolves the **first** station last, and the board must
ignore it.

```
uv run dojo test react d13_race_abort ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two requests are in flight and both will call their `.then` — there is no way
to stop that. The question is not how to cancel a promise; it is how the
callback can tell that nobody wants its answer any more.

The effect already returns nothing. Give it a cleanup, and give it something
for that cleanup to change: a plain `let` declared **inside the effect body**,
which the callback reads before it touches state. One variable per run of the
effect is the whole trick.

## Hint 1

The stub builds an `AbortController`, hands over its signal and then forgets
about it — which is exactly as useful as not building one. Whoever creates the
controller has to keep it long enough to abort it.

## Hint 2

One controller per run of the effect, created in the effect body, aborted in
the cleanup. Once you have it, notice that `controller.signal.aborted` already
answers the question your `let` flag was answering, so you do not need both.

## Hint 3

Aborting makes the request reject. That rejection is your own doing, not a
failure the user needs to hear about — the error branch has to check whether
this request was aborted before it announces anything.

## Hint 1

The stub's guard is not wrong, it is wasteful: it throws away a true answer
because the user moved on, and then pays for that answer again. Ask what the
state should be. `value` means "the answer", singular — which is why a second
answer has nowhere to live.

## Hint 2

Store the answers keyed by the metric they answer, and render the key that is
selected. Once you do, a late answer cannot be shown by accident, because
showing it would mean the user is on that tab — and the race is gone rather
than guarded.

## Hint 3

The other half is not asking twice. Keeping "which metrics have been requested"
in state would put it in the effect's dependencies and start a loop; it never
needs to be rendered, so it does not need to be state.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The stub's guard is not wrong, it is wasteful: it throws away a true answer
because the user moved on, and then pays for that answer again. Ask what the
state should be. `value` means "the answer", singular — which is why a second
answer has nowhere to live.

## Hint 2

Store the answers keyed by the metric they answer, and render the key that is
selected. Once you do, a late answer cannot be shown by accident, because
showing it would mean the user is on that tab — and the race is gone rather
than guarded.

## Hint 3

The other half is not asking twice. Keeping "which metrics have been requested"
in state would put it in the effect's dependencies and start a loop; it never
needs to be rendered, so it does not need to be state.

# Reading — react/d14_refs_dom

## Notes

A ref pointed at a DOM node is React's admission that some things cannot be
described declaratively. You cannot render "this input is focused" or "this
field is empty again" — you have to reach for the node and say so. Three rules
tie the whole set together. First, the node does not exist while the component
is rendering, so every one of these operations lives in an effect or an event
handler and every one of them starts `node?.` because the node can be gone.
Second, the node is only yours to touch where React has no opinion: reading an
uncontrolled input's value is fine, writing to a controlled one is a bug.
Third — and this is what the set actually drills — almost every legitimate use
is about focus, and focus is a property of the whole document. State can say
which entry is "active", but until something calls `.focus()` the browser and
the screen reader do not know, and the keyboard user is somewhere else entirely.

## ex1

Tests the dependency array of an imperative effect. The classic mistakes sit on
either side of the right answer: `[]` focuses the first recipient and never
again, no array at all yanks the cursor back on every render — including the
render caused by the user typing somewhere else. The model answer keys the
effect on the value that defines "this is a different reply", which is the same
question a dependency array always asks.

## ex2

Tests reading and writing a value React does not manage. The classic mistake is
the stub's: `defaultValue` looks like a binding but is a one-time handover, so
the state and the field drift apart immediately and every read returns the
initial value. The model answer deletes the state entirely and treats the node
as the source of truth — `.value` to read on Apply, `.value = ""` plus
`.focus()` to clear — which is exactly the deal an uncontrolled input offers.

## ex3

Tests ref forwarding in its React 19 form. The classic mistake is a wrapper
that quietly keeps the ref for itself, leaving the parent holding `null` and no
error message anywhere; in older code the same bug appears as forgetting
`forwardRef`. The model answer puts the ref prop straight onto the node the
parent means, and drops the internal ref that had no work to do.

## ex4

Tests focus as part of validation. The classic mistake is a loop with no early
exit: it reports every problem in turn, so the message ends up naming the last
one and the cursor ends up at the bottom of the form, below the field the user
actually has to fix. The model answer collects the fields in the order they
appear, uses `find` to stop at the first gap, and both names and focuses that
one.

## ex5

Tests the difference between a highlight and a focus. The classic mistake is
tracking an "active index" in state, styling that entry, and never calling
`.focus()` — the menu looks right, and a screen reader announces nothing while
Enter presses whatever was focused before. The model answer stores the nodes in
a ref-held array via a callback ref, keeps a roving `tabIndex`, and runs an
effect keyed on the active index so the browser's focus follows the state.

## ex6

Tests the form element as a node with its own API. The classic mistake is
treating a form as a bag of inputs and wiring up a ref per field, which is
three times the code and still cannot clear them all at once; the second
mistake is a `<button>` with no `type` next to a submit handler, which submits
the form because that is the HTML default. The model answer keeps one ref on
the `<form>`, reads it with `FormData`, empties it with `.reset()`, and marks
the button that is not a submit.

## ex7

Tests focus management around a modal. The classic mistakes are leaving focus
on the page behind when the dialog opens, letting Tab walk out of the dialog
into content that is visually covered, and destroying the focused node on close
so focus lands on `document.body`. The model answer focuses the first control
in an effect keyed on open, catches Tab at exactly the two ends by comparing
`document.activeElement` against the first and last refs, and sends focus back
to the opener from the close handler while that button is still mounted.

## ex8

Tests the hardest thing on this list: focus across a list mutation. The classic
mistake is removing the row and stopping there, because on screen it looks
perfect — the failure is invisible unless you are using a keyboard, when the
cursor silently returns to the top of the document. The model answer splits the
work in two, because the two halves happen at different times: the handler
decides who inherits the focus while the old list still exists, stores that in
a ref, and an effect keyed on the list does the focusing once the replacement
node has been committed.

## Further reading

- [Manipulating the DOM with refs](https://react.dev/learn/manipulating-the-dom-with-refs)
- [`useRef` reference](https://react.dev/reference/react/useRef)
- [`ref` as a prop, and callback refs](https://react.dev/reference/react-dom/components/common#ref-callback)
- [MDN: `HTMLElement.focus()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/HTMLElement/focus)
- [MDN: `FormData`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/FormData)
- [WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices: keyboard interface and roving tabindex](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/practices/keyboard-interface/)

input labelled `Promo code`, an `Apply` button that calls `onApply` with

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`defaultValue` is a starting value, not a binding — React hands it to the DOM
once and then stops caring. So the `code` state in the stub and the text on
screen are two unrelated things, and `Apply` is reading the one nobody typed
into.

## Exercise 5 — arrow keys move the focus

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. `CommandMenu({ commands, onRun })` renders a
`role="menu"` element containing one `role="menuitem"` button per command. The

```
uv run dojo test react d14_refs_dom ex5
```

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The stub already tracks which entry is active and already moves the tabindex
around. What it never does is tell the browser. Focus is a property of the
document, not of your state, and only a `.focus()` call changes it.

## Hint 2

Collect the button nodes as they mount — a callback ref writing into
`items.current[index]` — and add an effect that focuses `items.current[active]`
whenever `active` changes. Note that such an effect also covers the very first
render, so the mount-only effect in the stub can go.

## Hint 3

Home and End are missing entirely, and every arrow key you handle should call
`event.preventDefault()` so the page does not scroll underneath the menu. The
wrap-around at both ends is arithmetic you should write out rather than guess.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two things are missing, and both are about where focus is allowed to go. Tab
from the last control currently leaves the dialog for the page behind it; and
closing the dialog deletes the focused node, which drops focus on the document
body.

## Hint 2

A `keydown` handler on the dialog element sees every key pressed inside it,
because events bubble. You only have to intercept two cases: Tab while the last
control is focused, and Shift+Tab while the first one is. Both are
`preventDefault()` plus a `.focus()` on the other end.

## Hint 3

For the way out, remember what a ref on the opening button is worth: it is
still mounted when the dialog closes, so the handler that closes can also send
the cursor back to it. `document.activeElement` is how you ask what is focused
right now.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two things are missing, and both are about where focus is allowed to go. Tab
from the last control currently leaves the dialog for the page behind it; and
closing the dialog deletes the focused node, which drops focus on the document
body.

## Hint 2

A `keydown` handler on the dialog element sees every key pressed inside it,
because events bubble. You only have to intercept two cases: Tab while the last
control is focused, and Shift+Tab while the first one is. Both are
`preventDefault()` plus a `.focus()` on the other end.

## Hint 3

For the way out, remember what a ref on the opening button is worth: it is
still mounted when the dialog closes, so the handler that closes can also send
the cursor back to it. `document.activeElement` is how you ask what is focused
right now.

## Exercise 8 — where the focus goes when the row is gone

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. `PlaylistRows({ songs })` renders a level-2 heading
`Playlist` (focusable by script, not by tabbing), then one `<li>` per song
containing the song's name and a button named `Remove <song>`. Removing a row
drops it from the list and moves focus to the **next** row's remove button, or
to the **previous** one when there is no next, or to the heading when the list
is now empty — in which case a `role="status"` paragraph reads `No tracks
left`. The component owns the list after mount; the prop is only its starting
value.

```
uv run dojo test react d14_refs_dom ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The button the user pressed no longer exists after the click, and a browser
does not guess where the cursor should go — it puts it on the document body,
which for a keyboard user means starting again from the top of the page. Work
out the rule in words first: which row takes the place of the one that left?

## Hint 2

The decision has to be made while the old list is still around, because that is
the only moment you can look at the neighbours. The `.focus()` call has to
happen after the new list is on screen, because that is the only moment the
replacement node exists. Two different times, so store the answer in a ref in
the handler and read it in an effect keyed on the list.

## Hint 3

The map of button nodes is already being filled in by a callback ref, so
`buttons.current.get(name)` is your node. A heading is not focusable by
default — `tabIndex={-1}` makes it focusable by script without putting it in
the tab order — and the stub has already done that part for you.

## Hint 1

The button the user pressed no longer exists after the click, and a browser
does not guess where the cursor should go — it puts it on the document body,
which for a keyboard user means starting again from the top of the page. Work
out the rule in words first: which row takes the place of the one that left?

## Hint 2

The decision has to be made while the old list is still around, because that is
the only moment you can look at the neighbours. The `.focus()` call has to
happen after the new list is on screen, because that is the only moment the
replacement node exists. Two different times, so store the answer in a ref in
the handler and read it in an effect keyed on the list.

## Hint 3

The map of button nodes is already being filled in by a callback ref, so
`buttons.current.get(name)` is your node. A heading is not focusable by
default — `tabIndex={-1}` makes it focusable by script without putting it in
the tab order — and the stub has already done that part for you.

# d15 — Ref patterns (drill set)

Eight problems on `useRef`'s **other** job: a box that survives re-renders and
never causes one. Not a single ref in this set points at a DOM node — that was
`d14_refs_dom`. It drills `08_refs_dom`, and the sentence to have in your head
before you start is that lesson's rule: if changing it should change what is on
screen it is state, and if it should not, it is a ref.

Three of the eight are about the sharpest form of that question — a value the
code must read *now*, before the next render can possibly happen. Two are
`useImperativeHandle`: choosing what a parent is allowed to do to you. The rest
are the classic traps, including the one where a ref is exactly the wrong tool.

## Exercise 1 — what it showed a moment ago

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `PressureGauge({ label, reading })` renders
`<label>: now <reading>, was <previous>` in a `role="status"` paragraph, where
`previous` is the reading from the render before this one, or the words
`nothing yet` on the very first render. The gate puts **two** gauges on screen
at once, which the stub's module-level variable cannot survive.

```
uv run dojo test react d15_ref_patterns ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — report it once, ever

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `ImpressionBeacon({ slotId, report })` renders
`Showing <slotId>` in a paragraph and calls `report(slotId)` the first time it
shows a given slot. A slot this component has already reported is never
reported again, even after showing something else and coming back to it.

```
uv run dojo test react d15_ref_patterns ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — three verbs and nothing else

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `MediaScrubber({ label, ref })` renders
`<label>: playing|paused at <position>s` in a `role="status"` paragraph,
starting paused at `0`. A parent holding the ref gets exactly
`{ play(), pause(), seek(seconds) }` — no DOM node — and each method changes
what the component shows. The stub already exposes the three methods; their
bodies are empty.

```
uv run dojo test react d15_ref_patterns ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — one connection, the newest handler

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `PingMonitor({ subscribe, onMessage })` calls
`subscribe(handler)` **once** and returns the unsubscribe function it is given
as the effect's cleanup. It renders `Messages: <n>` in a `role="status"`
paragraph, counting what has arrived, and every message goes to the `onMessage`
the component has *now* — even though the parent passes a new function on every
render and the subscription must not be reopened.

```
uv run dojo test react d15_ref_patterns ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — the second click of a double-click

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. `PayoutRequest({ onSubmit })` renders a
`Request payout` button and a `role="status"` paragraph reading `Ready` or
`Sending`. A click calls `onSubmit()`, which returns a promise; while it is in
flight the button is disabled. The gate dispatches two clicks inside one
`act()`, before React has re-rendered anything, and exactly one payout may go
out — but a click after the first has settled must work normally.

```
uv run dojo test react d15_ref_patterns ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — a ref for them, a ref for you

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. `PassphraseBox({ label, ref })` renders an input
labelled `label` and a button named `Clear <label>` which empties the field and
focuses it. The optional `ref` prop must reach the input, so a parent can focus
it — and `Clear` must work just as well on a box nobody passed a ref to.

```
uv run dojo test react d15_ref_patterns ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — created once, closed once

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. `AnalyticsSession({ label, createSession })` calls
`createSession()` **exactly once per mount**, no matter how many times it
renders, and calls the returned session's `close()` exactly once when it
unmounts. It renders `label` in a paragraph, `Session <id>, Events: <n>` in a
`role="status"` paragraph, and a `Bump` button that adds one to `n`.

```
uv run dojo test react d15_ref_patterns ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — a handle that is not out of date

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. `ScratchPad({ label, ref })` renders a `<textarea>`
labelled `label`, controlled by state. A parent holding the ref gets
`{ read(), insert(extra), clear() }`: `read` returns the text as it is right
now, `insert` appends to it, `clear` empties it. Two pads on one page know
nothing about each other.

```
uv run dojo test react d15_ref_patterns ex8
```

# Reading — react/d15_ref_patterns

## Notes

Everything here follows from one sentence: a ref is per-instance memory that
survives renders and never schedules one. Each half of that does work. "Per
instance" is what a module-level variable is not, which is why the first
problem breaks the moment two gauges share a page. "Survives renders" is what a
`let` in the component body is not. "Never schedules one" is why a ref is the
right home for bookkeeping nobody looks at — what has already been reported,
which request is newest, whether a submit is already in flight — and it is
equally why a ref is the *wrong* home for anything the screen depends on, since
writing it will never update the display. The set also drills the second
meaning of a ref, `useImperativeHandle`: a component choosing a small, named
API for its parent instead of handing over a DOM node it cannot defend. The
recurring interview trap in both halves is time — a ref is readable and
writable *now*, while state is a value that only exists between renders, and
half these problems are decided by which of those two clocks the code needs.

## ex1

Tests where per-instance memory lives. The classic mistake is the stub's:
module scope looks like it works, because with one component on screen it does,
and it fails silently the moment a second instance mounts and starts reading
the first one's numbers. The model answer keeps a ref, reads `.current` during
render to get the old value and writes the new one in an effect with no
dependency array, so the write always lands after the commit that displayed the
previous value.

## ex2

Tests remembering across effect runs rather than between two of them. The
classic mistake is trusting the dependency array to do it: an array compares
this run against the previous one, so returning to a slot looks exactly like
seeing it for the first time, and an analytics backend gets billed twice for
one impression. The model answer keeps a `Set` in a ref — deliberately not
state, because nothing renders from it and putting it in state would put it in
the dependency array and start a loop.

## ex3

Tests the basic shape of an imperative handle. The point the exercise makes by
construction is why a DOM node would not do: `play()` has to flip React state,
and no element can. The classic mistake once people find `useImperativeHandle`
is exposing too much — returning the node, or a method per internal field —
where the discipline is that every method you expose is a promise you have to
keep. The model answer returns three verbs backed by state setters, which are
stable, so an empty dependency array is honest here.

## ex4

Tests the latest-value ref. The classic mistakes are the two obvious dependency
arrays, and each is a real bug: including the callback tears down a live
connection on every parent render, excluding it leaves the subscription calling
the first render's function for ever. The model answer stores the newest
callback in a ref updated by its own tiny effect and reads `ref.current` when a
message arrives — the pattern `useEffectEvent` is being designed to replace,
and worth recognising in existing code either way.

## ex5

Tests the gap between an event and the render that answers it. The classic
mistake is guarding with state and believing the disabled attribute: both
clicks of a double-click are handled before React re-renders, so both read the
same `false` and the DOM button is still enabled when the second one lands.
The model answer keeps both — state for what the user sees, a ref for what the
code tests — and clears the ref in a `finally` so a failed payout does not
leave the button dead.

## ex6

Tests sharing one node between the component and its caller. The classic
mistake is the stub's: using the parent's ref for your own internal work, which
makes the component's behaviour depend on a prop the caller was never obliged
to pass, and breaks in the ordinary case rather than the exotic one. The model
answer attaches a callback ref that writes the node into an internal ref *and*
forwards it to whatever the parent gave — remembering that a `Ref` may be a
function, an object, or absent.

## ex7

Tests lazy initialisation. The classic mistake is `useRef(createSession())`,
which reads as "create it once" and means "create it on every render and throw
all but the first away" — the argument is evaluated before `useRef` is called,
so every keystroke opens a connection. The model answer starts the ref at
`null` and fills it only when it is still `null`, and pairs that with a cleanup
in a mount effect so what was opened once is closed once.

## ex8

Tests the dependency array of a handle. The classic mistake is `[]`, which
freezes the returned object around the first render's state: `read()` answers
with the text as it was then, for ever, and an `insert` that computes from the
old text overwrites whatever has been typed since. The model answer puts the
functional updater form in `insert` and `clear` — which need no dependencies at
all — and lists `text` for the sake of `read`, which genuinely has to see the
present.

## Further reading

- [Referencing values with refs](https://react.dev/learn/referencing-values-with-refs)
- [`useRef` reference](https://react.dev/reference/react/useRef)
- [`useImperativeHandle` reference](https://react.dev/reference/react/useImperativeHandle)
- [Separating events from effects](https://react.dev/learn/separating-events-from-effects)
- [Choosing the state structure](https://react.dev/learn/choosing-the-state-structure)
- [MDN: `Set`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Set)

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `ImpressionBeacon({ slotId, report })` renders
`Showing <slotId>` in a paragraph and calls `report(slotId)` the first time it

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The dependency array is already right: the effect runs when the slot changes,
which is when a new impression *might* have happened. What it cannot tell you
is whether this particular slot has been reported before, because a dependency
array only compares against the previous run, not against every run.

The component needs a memory of every slot it has already reported. Nothing on
screen depends on that memory, so it must not be state — putting it in state
would also put it in the array and start a loop. A `Set` living in a ref is
the whole answer.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The dependency array is already right: the effect runs when the slot changes,
which is when a new impression *might* have happened. What it cannot tell you
is whether this particular slot has been reported before, because a dependency
array only compares against the previous run, not against every run.

## Hint 2

The component needs a memory of every slot it has already reported. Nothing on
screen depends on that memory, so it must not be state — putting it in state
would also put it in the array and start a loop. A `Set` living in a ref is
the whole answer.

## Exercise 7 — created once, closed once

`createSession()` **exactly once per mount**, no matter how many times it

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`useRef` keeps the first value it is given — but the expression you pass it is
evaluated every render, before `useRef` gets a chance to ignore it. Say that
sentence out loud while looking at the stub's first line.

## Hint 2

Start the ref at `null` and fill it in only if it is still `null`. That check
runs during render, which is fine because it is idempotent: after the first
time it does nothing at all.

## Hint 3

The other half is the closing. Something opened on mount has to be closed on
unmount, which is a cleanup returned from an effect with an empty dependency
array — read the ref into a local before you return the cleanup, so the
function closes over the session it was born with.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`useRef` keeps the first value it is given — but the expression you pass it is
evaluated every render, before `useRef` gets a chance to ignore it. Say that
sentence out loud while looking at the stub's first line.

## Hint 2

Start the ref at `null` and fill it in only if it is still `null`. That check
runs during render, which is fine because it is idempotent: after the first
time it does nothing at all.

## Hint 3

The other half is the closing. Something opened on mount has to be closed on
unmount, which is a cleanup returned from an effect with an empty dependency
array — read the ref into a local before you return the cleanup, so the
function closes over the session it was born with.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — a handle that is not out of date

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. `ScratchPad({ label, ref })` renders a `<textarea>`
labelled `label`, controlled by state. A parent holding the ref gets
`{ read(), insert(extra), clear() }`: `read` returns the text as it is right
now, `insert` appends to it, `clear` empties it. Two pads on one page know
nothing about each other.

```
uv run dojo test react d15_ref_patterns ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`useImperativeHandle` takes a dependency array for the same reason `useEffect`
does, and the stub's is empty. The object the parent is holding was built
during the first render and its `read` still closes over the text as it was
then.

## Hint 2

Two independent fixes are needed. `insert` should not read the old text to
compute the new one — the functional updater form removes that question
entirely. `read` genuinely needs the current text, so the array has to say so.

## Hint 3

There is a second way to write `read` that keeps the array empty: mirror the
text into a ref updated on every render and read `ref.current`. Decide which
you prefer and be able to say why — for three methods, the array is plainer.

lessons.briefing:
# d16 — Context (drill set)

Eight problems on `createContext` and `useContext` alone — no reducers here,
they are the next set. It drills the first half of `09_context_reducer`; if
"every component that reads a context re-renders when that context's value
changes" is not a sentence you could have written yourself, reread that lesson
before you start, because three of these problems are about nothing else.

Every consumer in this set is rendered by the gate several levels below its
provider and is given **no props at all**, so the context is the only route a
value can take. Where a problem is about wasted work, the gate counts renders
with an injected `onRender` spy.

## Exercise 1 — publish, then subscribe

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `UnitsProvider({ units, children })` publishes `units`;
`UnitsLabel()` takes no props and renders `Units: <units>` in a `role="status"`
paragraph. The context and the consumer are written; the publisher is not.

```
uv run dojo test react d16_context ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — fail loudly instead of quietly

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `WorkspaceProvider({ name, children })`,
`useWorkspace()` and `WorkspaceName()` are all written, and rendering
`WorkspaceName` with no provider above it currently shows a plausible default.
Change it so `useWorkspace()` **throws** an error whose message contains
`WorkspaceProvider`, while still working normally inside one.

```
uv run dojo test react d16_context ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — the nearest one wins

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `ZoneProvider({ zone, children })` and `ZoneBadge()`,
which renders `Zone: <zone>` in a `role="status"` paragraph. A `ZoneProvider`
nested inside another one overrides the zone **for its own subtree only**: a
badge that comes after the nested section still reads the outer zone. The stub
keeps the zone in a module-level variable, which cannot express that.

```
uv run dojo test react d16_context ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — two audiences, two contexts

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `VolumeProvider({ children })` holds a volume starting
at `5`. `VolumeReadout({ onRender })` renders `Volume: <n>` in a `role="status"`
paragraph; `VolumeButtons({ onRender })` renders `Louder` and `Quieter`
buttons. Changing the volume must re-render the readout and **not** the
buttons, however many times it changes. Leave the `onRender()` calls where the
stub has them.

```
uv run dojo test react d16_context ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — the same account, a new object

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. `AccountProvider({ name, children })` publishes
`{ name, initials }`, and also renders its own `Synced <n> time(s)`
`role="status"` paragraph and a `Refresh` button that adds one to `n`.
`AccountChip({ onRender })` renders `<initials> - <name>` in a paragraph.
Pressing `Refresh` re-renders the provider, changes nothing about the account,
and must not re-render the chip.

```
uv run dojo test react d16_context ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — a value that counts as it goes down

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. `SectionHeading({ children })` renders an `<h1>` when
it is outside every `SectionProvider`, an `<h2>` inside one, an `<h3>` inside
two, and so on — stopping at `<h6>`, because HTML has nothing below it.
`SectionProvider({ children })` is what makes a subtree one level deeper.

```
uv run dojo test react d16_context ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — a context factory

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. `createSafeContext<T>(name)` returns
`{ Provider, useValue }`, where `Provider` takes `{ value, children }` and
`useValue()` returns the published value — or throws an error containing `name`
when there is no provider above. Two calls to the factory must produce two
completely independent contexts.

```
uv run dojo test react d16_context ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — inherit, then override

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. `PrefsProvider({ prefs, children })` takes a
**partial** `{ locale?, density? }` and publishes the full pair;
`PrefsReadout()` renders `<locale> / <density>` in a `role="status"` paragraph.
With no provider at all the answer is `en / cosy`. A nested provider overrides
only the keys it was given and inherits the rest from the provider above it —
not from the defaults.

```
uv run dojo test react d16_context ex8
```

# Reading — react/d16_context

## Notes

Context answers one question — how does a value get from here to a component a
long way below without every component in between having to carry it — and it
answers it by position in the tree rather than by name in a namespace. Three
consequences run through this whole set. The first is that a provider provides
to what is *inside* it, which is why nesting overrides and why a module-level
variable, which has one value at a time, cannot imitate it. The second is that
reading a context is a subscription: when the value changes, every component
that read it re-renders, and React decides "changed" with `Object.is` — so an
object rebuilt during the provider's render is a change even when nothing about
it is different. That single fact is behind exercises 4 and 5 and behind most
"context made my app slow" complaints. The third is that a provider may read
the same context it is about to provide, which turns context from an assignment
into an accumulation and is how heading levels, themes and preference
inheritance are really built.

## ex1

Tests the three pieces of a context and which one the stub is missing. The
classic mistake is a provider component that takes the value as a prop and then
renders `{children}` without wrapping them, so every consumer silently gets the
default — the code reads as though it works because the word "Provider" is in
the component's name. The model answer wraps the children in
`<UnitsContext.Provider value={units}>`, and keeps `createContext` at module
scope, since a context created during render would be a new channel each time.

## ex2

Tests the default value as a design decision. The classic mistake is choosing a
plausible default — `"Untitled"`, `"light"`, `{}` — which means a component
rendered outside its provider works incorrectly and says nothing; the bug then
surfaces days later as data that is subtly wrong. The model answer makes the
default `null` and puts the check in the custom hook, so the failure is
immediate and the message names the provider that is missing.

## ex3

Tests what "nearest provider" means. The classic mistake is thinking of context
as a global variable with a nicer syntax: the stub's module-level `let` gets
the first two badges right by accident of render order and then fails the third,
because a global has one value at a time while a context has one value per
position in the tree. The model answer publishes with a real provider, which is
what makes nesting an override scoped to a subtree rather than an assignment
that leaks to everything rendered afterwards.

## ex4

Tests splitting a context by who reads what. The classic mistake is one context
carrying `{ value, actions }`, which subscribes the buttons to a number they
never display — in a real app that is every toolbar in the tree re-rendering on
every keystroke. The model answer publishes two contexts from one provider and
writes the actions with the functional updater form so they never close over
the current value, which lets a single memoized object serve for the component's
whole lifetime.

## ex5

Tests context value identity. The classic mistake is building the value inline
in the provider's body, where it is a brand new object every time the provider
renders for any reason at all — including reasons that have nothing to do with
the value. The model answer wraps it in `useMemo` keyed on what the value is
actually derived from, which is the same identity discipline a dependency array
asks for, applied to a prop instead of an effect.

## ex6

Tests a provider that consumes its own context. The classic mistake is
publishing a constant, which is correct at exactly one depth and wrong at every
other; the second mistake is forgetting that HTML stops at `h6`, so a deeply
nested page renders `<h7>` elements that have no heading role at all and vanish
from a screen reader's outline. The model answer reads the inherited level, adds
one, clamps it, and publishes that.

## ex7

Tests packaging the pattern. The tell in the stub is the cast in `useValue`: it
promises TypeScript a `T` while the value may be `null`, which is precisely the
lie exercise 2 was about. The model answer replaces the cast with the check and
builds the message from the `name` captured in the closure, so each context
created by the factory gets a private channel, a matching provider, and an error
that names the right component.

## ex8

Tests inheritance, which is exercise 6's idea applied to an object with
defaults. The classic mistake is merging the overrides onto the hard-coded
defaults, so any nested provider silently resets every setting it did not
mention — the bug is invisible until somebody nests two of them, which is the
only reason to have written a partial override in the first place. The model
answer reads the outer value with `useContext`, merges the partial on top of
that, and lists both in the `useMemo` dependencies.

## Further reading

- [Passing data deeply with context](https://react.dev/learn/passing-data-deeply-with-context)
- [`useContext` reference](https://react.dev/reference/react/useContext)
- [`createContext` reference](https://react.dev/reference/react/createContext)
- [Scaling up with reducer and context](https://react.dev/learn/scaling-up-with-reducer-and-context)
- [MDN: heading elements](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/Heading_Elements)
- [MDN: `Object.is()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Object/is)

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Reading a context is a subscription: when its value changes, every component
that read it re-renders. `VolumeButtons` reads a value that contains the
volume, so it is subscribed to the volume — even though it never displays it.

## Hint 2

Two audiences want two different things, so publish two things. One context for
the number, one for the pair of functions, both provided by the same component.

## Hint 3

Splitting alone is not enough: the actions context has to hand out the *same*
object every time, or its consumers are back where they started. Write the two
functions so they never need to know the current volume, and the object can be
built once and kept.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Reading a context is a subscription: when its value changes, every component
that read it re-renders. `VolumeButtons` reads a value that contains the
volume, so it is subscribed to the volume — even though it never displays it.

## Hint 2

Two audiences want two different things, so publish two things. One context for
the number, one for the pair of functions, both provided by the same component.

## Hint 3

Splitting alone is not enough: the actions context has to hand out the *same*
object every time, or its consumers are back where they started. Write the two
functions so they never need to know the current volume, and the object can be
built once and kept.

## Exercise 6 — a value that counts as it goes down

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. `SectionHeading({ children })` renders an `<h1>` when
it is outside every `SectionProvider`, an `<h2>` inside one, an `<h3>` inside
two, and so on — stopping at `<h6>`, because HTML has nothing below it.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The stub publishes the number 2, which is right exactly once — at the first
level of nesting. What a section actually publishes is not a fixed number but a
relationship: one more than whatever it found above it.

A provider may call `useContext` on the very context it is about to provide.
Read the level, add one, publish that. Remember that HTML has no heading below
`h6`, so the number has to stop climbing there — an `<h7>` is not a heading at
all as far as the accessibility tree is concerned.

## Hint 1

The stub publishes the number 2, which is right exactly once — at the first
level of nesting. What a section actually publishes is not a fixed number but a
relationship: one more than whatever it found above it.

## Hint 2

A provider may call `useContext` on the very context it is about to provide.
Read the level, add one, publish that. Remember that HTML has no heading below
`h6`, so the number has to stop climbing there — an `<h7>` is not a heading at
all as far as the accessibility tree is concerned.

## Exercise 7 — a context factory

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. `createSafeContext<T>(name)` returns
`{ Provider, useValue }`, where `Provider` takes `{ value, children }` and
`useValue()` returns the published value — or throws an error containing `name`
when there is no provider above. Two calls to the factory must produce two
completely independent contexts.

```
uv run dojo test react d16_context ex7
```

## Hint 1

Everything exercise 2 asked for by hand, this factory has to do for any type.
Look at what the stub does with its `name` parameter: nothing. That is the
missing half.

The cast in `useValue` is the tell — it promises TypeScript a `T` while the
value may really be `null`. Replace the cast with the check that makes the
promise true, and throw a message built from the captured `name`.

Note what a closure buys you: `Context` and `name` are created once per call to
the factory, and the `Provider` and `useValue` returned both see them. Two
calls make two contexts that cannot see each other, which is exactly what the
gate checks.

lessons.briefing:
# d17 — Reducers (drill set)

Eight problems on the second half of `09_context_reducer`: a reducer as what it
actually is, a pure function of `(state, action)` that you can call from a test
without React anywhere in sight. Five of these are exactly that — the gate
calls your function and checks the state it handed in came back untouched.
Three drive a reducer through a component.

The thread running through the set is that a reducer owns the rules. Whether a
seat may be taken, whether a paused job can make progress, whether an action is
worth remembering for an undo: all of that belongs in one pure function, not
scattered across the handlers that dispatch to it. Watch for the gate's `toBe`
assertions — several of them require that an action which changes nothing hands
back **the very object it was given**, because that is how a reducer tells
React there is nothing to re-render.

## Exercise 1 — moving between steps

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `wizardReducer(state, action)` over
`{ step, total }`, with `next`, `back` and `reset`. The step never goes below
`0` or above `total - 1`, the state you are handed is never modified, and an
action that does not move the step returns that same state object.

```
uv run dojo test react d17_reducers ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — a rule the reducer enforces

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `seatingReducer(state, action)` over
`{ chosen, capacity }`:

- `{ type: "toggled", seat }` — a seat that is already chosen is given up; a
  seat that is not is added at the **end** of `chosen`, unless that would
  exceed `capacity`, in which case nothing happens;
- `{ type: "cleared" }` — no seats chosen.

Nothing happening means returning the state you were given.

```
uv run dojo test react d17_reducers ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — the total that is not state

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `PollPanel({ options })` renders a
`Vote for <option>` button per option, a `Reset` button, a `<ul>` with one
`<li>` per option reading `<option>: <n>`, and a `role="status"` paragraph
reading `<total> votes` — or `1 vote` when the total is one. The stub keeps the
total in the reducer's state, where it goes out of date immediately.

```
uv run dojo test react d17_reducers ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — the initial state, computed once

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `BudgetPlanner({ plan, label, parsePlan })` renders
`label` in a paragraph, `Remaining: <n>` in a `role="status"` paragraph, and a
`Spend 10` button that subtracts ten. The opening balance comes from
`parsePlan(plan)`, which must be called **exactly once**, no matter how many
times the component renders.

```
uv run dojo test react d17_reducers ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — copies all the way down

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. `moderationReducer(state, action)` over
`{ tickets: Ticket[] }`, with `approved`, `rejected` and `escalated`, each
carrying an `id`. The named ticket takes that status; the ticket objects you
were handed are never modified; the rows that did not change come back as **the
same objects**; an id that is not in the queue changes nothing; and an action
type nobody wrote a case for **throws** an error whose message contains that
type.

```
uv run dojo test react d17_reducers ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — a reducer as a state machine

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. `jobReducer(state, action)` over
`{ status, progress }` where status is `idle`, `running`, `paused` or `done`:

- `started` only from `idle`, and starts at progress `0`;
- `paused` only from `running`, `resumed` only from `paused`, both keeping the
  progress they had;
- `progressed` only while `running`, adding `by` and stopping at `100`;
- `finished` only from `running`, leaving `done` at `100`;
- `reset` from anywhere, back to idle at `0`.

Every transition that is not in that list leaves the state exactly as it was.

```
uv run dojo test react d17_reducers ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — undo, for any reducer

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. `withHistory(reducer)` takes a reducer and returns one
over `{ past, present, future }` that also understands `{ type: "undo" }` and
`{ type: "redo" }`. Any other action goes to the wrapped reducer; if the answer
is a new present, the old one is pushed onto `past` and `future` is emptied. If
the wrapped reducer changed nothing, nothing is remembered. Undo with an empty
`past`, or redo with an empty `future`, changes nothing at all.

```
uv run dojo test react d17_reducers ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — one subscription, current state

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. `MonitorPanel({ subscribe })` calls `subscribe(handler)`
**once** and unsubscribes on unmount. It renders the alerts it has received as
`<li>`s, a `role="status"` paragraph reading `<n> hidden while muted`, a button
reading `Mute` or `Unmute` that toggles, and a `Clear` button that empties both.
An alert arriving while muted is counted instead of listed — and the handler
registered on the first render has to know about a mute switched on after it.

```
uv run dojo test react d17_reducers ex8
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading — react/d17_reducers

## Notes

A reducer is a pure function of `(state, action)`, and every property worth
drilling here follows from that one sentence. Because it is pure it cannot edit
what it was given, which is not a style rule: React decides whether to
re-render by comparing the old state with the new one by reference, so a
mutated object is a change React is structurally unable to see. Because it is a
plain function it can be called from a test with no component, wrapped by
another function, or reused in two places — exercise 7 exists to make that
concrete. Because it is the single place that turns an event into the next
state, it is also the natural home for the rules: capacity limits, legal
transitions, what counts as a change worth remembering. The other half of the
set is about what belongs *in* the state — never a value you can compute from
the rest of it — and about the two things `useReducer` gives you that `useState`
does not: a lazy initialiser argument, and a `dispatch` that React guarantees is
stable, which is what makes exercise 8's single subscription possible.

## ex1

Tests immutability in its plainest form, plus the "nothing happened" answer.
The classic mistake is treating the state argument as scratch space —
`state.step += 1; return state` looks harmless and produces a component that
never re-renders, because React compares by reference and gets the same object
back. The model answer clamps the step, returns a fresh object when it moved,
and returns the original when it did not, which is the signal React uses to
skip the render entirely.

## ex2

Tests immutability of a nested array and a rule that refuses. The classic
mistake is `push`, which edits the array the caller still holds and hands back
a new wrapper object around the same stale contents — the state looks new and
its insides are not. The model answer covers the three cases in order — already
chosen, at capacity, otherwise add — using `filter` and spread, and expresses a
refusal by returning the state rather than a copy of it.

## ex3

Tests what belongs in state. The classic mistake is keeping a `total` beside
the counts: it is a second copy of the same fact, every action has to remember
to update it, and the first one that forgets leaves the screen contradicting
itself for ever. The model answer stores only the counts and adds them up while
rendering, where the total cannot be stale by construction — the same reflex as
d10's "a value computable from props is not state".

## ex4

Tests lazy initialisation. The classic mistake is `useReducer(reducer,
parsePlan(plan))`, which reads as "start from the parsed plan" and means "parse
the plan on every render and discard every result but the first" — invisible
when parsing is cheap, and a real cost when the initial state comes from
`localStorage` or a large computation. The model answer uses the third
parameter, `useReducer(reducer, plan, parsePlan)`, which React calls once.

## ex5

Tests immutability one level deeper than exercise 2, and error handling. The
classic mistakes are editing a ticket object found inside the state — a new
array of the same mutated rows — and a `default: return state` that swallows a
misspelled action type so the button silently does nothing. The model answer
maps, copying only the row that changed so that unchanged rows keep their
identity, and throws from the default branch with the offending type in the
message.

## ex6

Tests a reducer as a state machine. The classic mistake is writing one case per
action that always does the action's thing, which makes every impossible
sequence possible: pausing a job that never started, finishing one that is
paused, progress accumulating after it is done. The model answer asks "is this
legal from where we are?" first in every case, and returns the state unchanged
when the answer is no — an illegal transition is not an error, it is nothing
happening.

## ex7

Tests that a reducer is just a function, by wrapping one. The classic mistakes
are recording history for actions that changed nothing (so the user presses
undo and watches nothing happen, twice), and keeping the redo stack after a new
action, which offers a future that is no longer reachable. The model answer
compares the inner reducer's answer with what it was given — the "nothing
happened" convention from exercises 1, 2 and 6, now being consumed rather than
produced — and empties `future` whenever a genuinely new present appears.

## ex8

Tests why `dispatch` being stable matters. The classic mistake is three

# Reading — react/d17_reducers

## Notes

A reducer is a pure function of `(state, action)`, and every property worth
drilling here follows from that one sentence. Because it is pure it cannot edit
what it was given, which is not a style rule: React decides whether to
re-render by comparing the old state with the new one by reference, so a
mutated object is a change React is structurally unable to see. Because it is a
plain function it can be called from a test with no component, wrapped by
another function, or reused in two places — exercise 7 exists to make that
concrete. Because it is the single place that turns an event into the next
state, it is also the natural home for the rules: capacity limits, legal
transitions, what counts as a change worth remembering. The other half of the
set is about what belongs *in* the state — never a value you can compute from
the rest of it — and about the two things `useReducer` gives you that `useState`
does not: a lazy initialiser argument, and a `dispatch` that React guarantees is
stable, which is what makes exercise 8's single subscription possible.

## ex1

Tests immutability in its plainest form, plus the "nothing happened" answer.
The classic mistake is treating the state argument as scratch space —
`state.step += 1; return state` looks harmless and produces a component that
never re-renders, because React compares by reference and gets the same object
back. The model answer clamps the step, returns a fresh object when it moved,
and returns the original when it did not, which is the signal React uses to
skip the render entirely.

## ex2

Tests immutability of a nested array and a rule that refuses. The classic
mistake is `push`, which edits the array the caller still holds and hands back
a new wrapper object around the same stale contents — the state looks new and
its insides are not. The model answer covers the three cases in order — already
chosen, at capacity, otherwise add — using `filter` and spread, and expresses a
refusal by returning the state rather than a copy of it.

## ex3

Tests what belongs in state. The classic mistake is keeping a `total` beside
the counts: it is a second copy of the same fact, every action has to remember
to update it, and the first one that forgets leaves the screen contradicting
itself for ever. The model answer stores only the counts and adds them up while
rendering, where the total cannot be stale by construction — the same reflex as
d10's "a value computable from props is not state".

## ex4

Tests lazy initialisation. The classic mistake is `useReducer(reducer,
parsePlan(plan))`, which reads as "start from the parsed plan" and means "parse
the plan on every render and discard every result but the first" — invisible
when parsing is cheap, and a real cost when the initial state comes from
`localStorage` or a large computation. The model answer uses the third
parameter, `useReducer(reducer, plan, parsePlan)`, which React calls once.

## ex5

Tests immutability one level deeper than exercise 2, and error handling. The
classic mistakes are editing a ticket object found inside the state — a new
array of the same mutated rows — and a `default: return state` that swallows a
misspelled action type so the button silently does nothing. The model answer
maps, copying only the row that changed so that unchanged rows keep their
identity, and throws from the default branch with the offending type in the
message.

## ex6

Tests a reducer as a state machine. The classic mistake is writing one case per
action that always does the action's thing, which makes every impossible
sequence possible: pausing a job that never started, finishing one that is
paused, progress accumulating after it is done. The model answer asks "is this
legal from where we are?" first in every case, and returns the state unchanged
when the answer is no — an illegal transition is not an error, it is nothing
happening.

## ex7

Tests that a reducer is just a function, by wrapping one. The classic mistakes
are recording history for actions that changed nothing (so the user presses
undo and watches nothing happen, twice), and keeping the redo stack after a new
action, which offers a future that is no longer reachable. The model answer
compares the inner reducer's answer with what it was given — the "nothing
happened" convention from exercises 1, 2 and 6, now being consumed rather than
produced — and empties `future` whenever a genuinely new present appears.

## ex8

Tests why `dispatch` being stable matters. The classic mistake is three

and the un-muted flag from the first render, so each alert rebuilds the list
from nothing and the mute is never noticed. Adding those values to the

change, which is a different bug. The model answer moves all three into one
reducer, so the handler only has to say *what happened* and something holding
the current state decides what it means — and because `dispatch` never changes
identity, the effect can depend on it and still subscribe exactly once.

## Exercise 1 — moving between steps

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `wizardReducer(state, action)` over
`{ step, total }`, with `next`, `back` and `reset`. The step never goes below
`0` or above `total - 1`, the state you are handed is never modified, and an

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Every branch of the stub writes to `state` and hands the same object back.
React decides whether anything changed by comparing the old state with the new
one by reference, so a mutated object is a change React cannot see.

## Hint 2

Build a new object with the step you want — and clamp it, because there is no
step below the first or above `total - 1`. All three actions are the same
operation with a different target, so one small helper covers them.

## Hint 3

Read the gate's `toBe` assertions carefully: when the clamp means the step does
not move, the right answer is not a fresh copy that happens to be equal, it is
the very object you were handed.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Every branch of the stub writes to `state` and hands the same object back.
React decides whether anything changed by comparing the old state with the new
one by reference, so a mutated object is a change React cannot see.

## Hint 2

Build a new object with the step you want — and clamp it, because there is no
step below the first or above `total - 1`. All three actions are the same
operation with a different target, so one small helper covers them.

## Hint 3

Read the gate's `toBe` assertions carefully: when the clamp means the step does
not move, the right answer is not a fresh copy that happens to be equal, it is
the very object you were handed.

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `seatingReducer(state, action)` over
`{ chosen, capacity }`:

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Cast a vote and watch the two numbers disagree. The counts went up and the
total did not, because they are two separate copies of the same fact and only
one of them was updated.

## Hint 2

You could patch the `voted` case to keep the total in step — and then you would
have to remember it in every future action too. The better fix is to stop
storing it: a total is something you can add up during render, where it cannot
be out of date.

## Hint 3

The reducer is then only about counts, which also simplifies `reset`. Watch the
wording of the live region: one vote is a vote, not votes.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Cast a vote and watch the two numbers disagree. The counts went up and the
total did not, because they are two separate copies of the same fact and only
one of them was updated.

## Hint 2

You could patch the `voted` case to keep the total in step — and then you would
have to remember it in every future action too. The better fix is to stop
storing it: a total is something you can add up during render, where it cannot
be out of date.

## Hint 3

The reducer is then only about counts, which also simplifies `reset`. Watch the
wording of the live region: one vote is a vote, not votes.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`useReducer` keeps only the first initial state it is given, but the expression
you pass as that argument runs on every render regardless — React never gets a
say in whether it is evaluated.

## Hint 2

`useReducer` takes an optional third argument for exactly this: the value to
start from, and a function to turn it into state. React calls that function
once. Note that the same idea has a `useState` spelling — passing the function
itself rather than calling it.

you pass as that argument runs on every render regardless — React never gets a
say in whether it is evaluated.

once. Note that the same idea has a `useState` spelling — passing the function
itself rather than calling it.

## Hint 1

The stub answers "what does this action do?" for every action. The missing
question is "may this action happen from here?" — a job that has not started
cannot be paused, and a paused job makes no progress.

## Hint 2

Draw the four statuses and the arrows between them before you write anything.
Every case then becomes: check `state.status`, and if the arrow does not exist,
return the state unchanged.

## Hint 3

Two details hide in the arrows. Progress is capped at 100 rather than allowed
to run past it, and pausing keeps the progress the job already had — only
`started`, `finished` and `reset` set a progress of their own.

The stub answers "what does this action do?" for every action. The missing
question is "may this action happen from here?" — a job that has not started
cannot be paused, and a paused job makes no progress.

Draw the four statuses and the arrows between them before you write anything.

return the state unchanged.

to run past it, and pausing keeps the progress the job already had — only
`started`, `finished` and `reset` set a progress of their own.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — undo, for any reducer

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. `withHistory(reducer)` takes a reducer and returns one
over `{ past, present, future }` that also understands `{ type: "undo" }` and
`{ type: "redo" }`. Any other action goes to the wrapped reducer; if the answer
is a new present, the old one is pushed onto `past` and `future` is emptied. If
the wrapped reducer changed nothing, nothing is remembered. Undo with an empty
`past`, or redo with an empty `future`, changes nothing at all.

```
uv run dojo test react d17_reducers ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — one subscription, current state

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. `MonitorPanel({ subscribe })` calls `subscribe(handler)`
**once** and unsubscribes on unmount. It renders the alerts it has received as
`<li>`s, a `role="status"` paragraph reading `<n> hidden while muted`, a button
reading `Mute` or `Unmute` that toggles, and a `Clear` button that empties both.
An alert arriving while muted is counted instead of listed — and the handler
registered on the first render has to know about a mute switched on after it.

```
uv run dojo test react d17_reducers ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The subscription is opened once, and the function handed to it was created
during the first render — so `alerts` inside it is `[]` and `muted` is `false`,
for ever. Every alert rebuilds the list from that empty array.

## Hint 2

Adding the three values to the dependency array would fix the staleness by
reopening the connection every time anything changes, which the gate forbids.
What you want is a handler that does not need to remember anything: one that
describes what happened and lets something else, holding the current state,
decide what that means.

## Hint 3

`dispatch` from `useReducer` is guaranteed stable, so an effect that depends on
it never re-runs. Put all three values in one reducer state — whether an alert
is listed or counted is a decision about the mute, and a reducer is where a
decision like that belongs.

## Hint 1

The subscription is opened once, and the function handed to it was created
during the first render — so `alerts` inside it is `[]` and `muted` is `false`,
for ever. Every alert rebuilds the list from that empty array.

## Hint 2

Adding the three values to the dependency array would fix the staleness by
reopening the connection every time anything changes, which the gate forbids.
What you want is a handler that does not need to remember anything: one that
describes what happened and lets something else, holding the current state,
decide what that means.

## Hint 3

`dispatch` from `useReducer` is guaranteed stable, so an effect that depends on
it never re-runs. Put all three values in one reducer state — whether an alert
is listed or counted is a decision about the mute, and a reducer is where a
decision like that belongs.

lessons.briefing:
# d18 — Context and reducers together (drill set)

Eight small applications. Each one is a provider holding a `useReducer`, plus
two or three components the gate scatters through the tree — and not one of
those components is given a prop that carries state, so the context is the only
wiring there is. It drills `09_context_reducer` as a whole, and leans on
`d16_context` and `d17_reducers`; if either of those is still shaky, do it
first.

What is being drilled is the join. A reducer owns the rules, a provider
publishes the state and the way to change it, and the consumers stay dumb —
which means every one of these bugs is a component that decided to remember
something it should have asked about, or a provider that published half of what
its consumers needed.

## Exercise 1 — an id that stays unique

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `ToastProvider({ children })`,
`ToastTrigger({ message })` — a button reading `Notify <message>` that adds a
toast — and `ToastList()`, a `<ul>` with one `<li>` per toast containing the
message and a button reading `Dismiss <message>`. Dismissing a toast removes
that toast and no other, however many have come and gone.

```
uv run dojo test react d18_context_reducer_apps ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — one item, one answer

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `WishlistProvider({ children })`,
`WishlistToggle({ item })` — a button reading `Save <item>` or `Saved <item>`,
which toggles it — and `WishlistCount()`, a `role="status"` paragraph reading
`<n> saved`. The gate puts two toggles for the same item in different branches;
they must always say the same thing.

```
uv run dojo test react d18_context_reducer_apps ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — a step you cannot leave yet

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `FlowProvider({ children })`, `FlowSteps()` and
`FlowNav()`. The flow has three steps: an input labelled `Email`, then a
`role="status"` reading `Confirm <email>`, then one reading `Done`. `FlowNav`
renders `Back` and `Next`. `Back` is disabled on the first step, `Next` on the
last — and also on the first step while the email is empty.

```
uv run dojo test react d18_context_reducer_apps ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — none, some, all

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `SelectionProvider({ ids, children })`,
`RowBox({ id })` — a checkbox labelled with the id — and `SelectAllBox()`, a
checkbox labelled `All`. `All` is checked when every row is, **partially
checked** when some but not all are, and unchecked otherwise. Clicking it when
it is fully checked clears the selection; clicking it in either other state
selects everything.

```
uv run dojo test react d18_context_reducer_apps ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — four states of a request

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. `AuthProvider({ signIn, children })`, `SignInForm()` —
an input labelled `Email` and a `Sign in` button — and `AuthStatus()`. The
status is `Signed out`, then `Signing in`, then `Hello <name>`, each in a
`role="status"` paragraph; a rejection shows its message in a `role="alert"`
instead. The button is disabled while the request is in flight, and the form
disappears once somebody is signed in.

```
uv run dojo test react d18_context_reducer_apps ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — load once, save changes

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. `DraftProvider({ store, label, children })` where
`store` is `{ load(), save(text) }`, plus `DraftEditor()` — a textarea labelled
`Draft` — and `DraftCount()`, a `role="status"` paragraph reading
`<n> characters`. `store.load()` is called **exactly once**; `store.save()` is
called for every edit and **never** for a draft that has only been loaded.

```
uv run dojo test react d18_context_reducer_apps ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — undo that knows when it cannot

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. `NotesProvider({ children })`, `NotesEditor()` — an
input labelled `New note`, an `Add` button that adds it and clears the box, and
a `<ul>` of the notes — and `HistoryBar()`, with `Undo` and `Redo` buttons.
Each button is disabled when there is nothing for it to do, and adding a note
after an undo throws the redo branch away.

```
uv run dojo test react d18_context_reducer_apps ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — the basket

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. `BasketProvider({ children })`,
`AddToBasket({ product, onRender })` — a button reading `Add <name>` —
`BasketLines()`, a `<ul>` with one `<li>` per line containing `<name> x<qty>`
and buttons `More <name>` and `Fewer <name>`, and `BasketTotal()`, a
`role="status"` paragraph reading `Total: <sum of price times qty>`.

Adding a product already in the basket raises its quantity; taking the last one
away removes the line entirely. And the `Add` buttons must render **once each**,
no matter how much the basket changes. Leave the `onRender()` call where the
stub has it.

```
uv run dojo test react d18_context_reducer_apps ex8
```
