# Reading — react/d18_context_reducer_apps

## Notes

Context and a reducer together are the smallest thing that deserves the word
"architecture" in a React app: one reducer that owns the rules, one provider
that publishes the state and the way to change it, and consumers that are
almost stupid. The reason it works is that it removes choices from the
consumers, and almost every bug in this set is a consumer that took one back —
a toggle that remembered whether it was on, a button that decided for itself
whether it should be enabled, a component that stored a total it could have
added up. The provider's other job is derivation: `canNext`, `canUndo`,
`indeterminate` and the basket total are all questions the state can answer, and
answering them once in the provider is what lets a button in one branch depend
on a field in another without either knowing the other exists. Everything else
here is the machinery from the two previous sets showing up in a real shape:
lazy initialisers, stable dispatch, split contexts, and ids that have to stay
unique for longer than the list is long.

## ex1

Tests identity in a list that shrinks. The classic mistake is deriving an id
from `toasts.length`, which is the same as "how many have ever existed" only
until the first dismissal — after that the next toast collides with one already
on screen, and dismissing either takes both. The model answer keeps a counter in
the reducer's state, because "which numbers have been handed out" is a fact
about the list that no other field records, and only the reducer may advance it.

## ex2

Tests single source of truth. The classic mistake is a consumer that keeps its
own `useState` mirror of something the provider already knows: it works
perfectly until the same item appears twice, at which point the two copies
disagree and the count drifts away from the buttons. The model answer derives
the label from the shared list with `items.includes(item)`, which makes
disagreement unrepresentable.

## ex3

Tests deriving a guard in the provider. The classic mistake is a `Next` button
that only knows about the step number, because the email lives in a different
branch of the tree and passing it across would mean prop-drilling; the result is
a wizard that walks to a confirmation page with nothing to confirm. The model
answer computes `canNext` from the whole state where the whole state is, and
puts the same check inside the reducer — a disabled button is a courtesy, the
reducer is the guarantee.

## ex4

Tests the third state of a checkbox. The classic mistake is treating selection
as a boolean, so "some rows" renders as "no rows" and the user cannot tell a
fresh table from a half-selected one. `indeterminate` is a property of the DOM
node with no JSX attribute, so the model answer reaches for a ref and an effect
keyed on whether the selection is partial — and derives `all` and `some` rather
than storing them.

## ex5

Tests modelling a request as states. The classic mistakes are dispatching only
on success — so the moment the button is pressed is invisible and the user
presses it again — and having no failure branch at all, which leaves a disabled
button and a spinner for ever. The model answer dispatches three times for one
request, and types the state as a union so that "pending and also failed" cannot
be written down, let alone rendered.

## ex6

Tests the two ends of persistence. The classic mistakes are reading the store as
an ordinary expression in the provider's body, which runs on every render, and
writing from an effect with no guard, which saves the draft it has just loaded
every time the app opens. The model answer uses `useReducer`'s initialiser
argument for the read and a ref flag for the write, so the first run of the
effect is recognised and skipped.

## ex7

Tests deriving affordances from history. The classic mistake is offering `Undo`
and `Redo` unconditionally: a button that does nothing is worse than no button,
and a reducer that undoes an empty past sets `present` to `undefined` and takes
the app down. The model answer derives both flags from the two stacks in the
provider, guards both cases in the reducer, and clears `future` whenever a new
note is added — the redo branch is not reachable once you have gone somewhere
else.

## ex8

Tests everything at once. Three separate ideas have to be right: quantities are
one operation with a different sign, a line at zero is a line that no longer
exists, and the total is derived rather than stored. The one that catches people
is the render count — reading a context is a subscription, so a value bundling
`{ lines, dispatch }` subscribes the Add buttons to the basket even though they
only ever dispatch. The model answer publishes the lines and the dispatch as two
contexts, which costs nothing because `dispatch` is guaranteed stable and its
context value therefore never changes at all.

## Further reading

- [Scaling up with reducer and context](https://react.dev/learn/scaling-up-with-reducer-and-context)
- [`useReducer` reference](https://react.dev/reference/react/useReducer)
- [`useContext` reference](https://react.dev/reference/react/useContext)
- [Choosing the state structure](https://react.dev/learn/choosing-the-state-structure)
- [MDN: the checkbox `indeterminate` property](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/HTMLInputElement/indeterminate)
- [WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices: checkbox with three states](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/checkbox/)

## Exercise 1 — an id that stays unique

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `ToastProvider({ children })`,
`ToastTrigger({ message })` — a button reading `Notify <message>` that adds a
toast — and `ToastList()`, a `<ul>` with one `<li>` per toast containing the
message and a button reading `Dismiss <message>`. Dismissing a toast removes
that toast and no other, however many have come and gone.

```
uv run dojo test react d18_context_reducer_apps ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Work through the gate's sequence on paper, writing the id beside each toast.
Three toasts get 0, 1 and 2. Dismiss the middle one and add a fourth — what id
does it get, and who already has it?

## Hint 2

`toasts.length` describes how many toasts are on screen, which stops being the
same thing as "how many have ever existed" the first time one is dismissed. An
id has to be unique for the life of the list, so the number that produces it
has to only ever go up.

## Hint 3

That counter is part of the state: it is a fact about the list that no other
field records, and the reducer is the only thing allowed to advance it.

`FlowNav()`. The flow has three steps: an input labelled `Email`, then a

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`canNext` currently means "there is a step after this one". It also has to mean
"this step is finished" — and what finished means depends on which step you are
on. Step one is finished when the email is not empty.

## Hint 2

Write that as one small function of the state and call it from the provider, so
the derived flag reaches `FlowNav` through the context. The email field and the
button never have to know about each other.

## Hint 3

Put the same check inside the reducer's `next` case as well. A disabled button
is a courtesy to the user; the reducer is the thing that actually guarantees
nobody reaches step two without an email.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`canNext` currently means "there is a step after this one". It also has to mean
"this step is finished" — and what finished means depends on which step you are
on. Step one is finished when the email is not empty.

## Hint 2

Write that as one small function of the state and call it from the provider, so
the derived flag reaches `FlowNav` through the context. The email field and the
button never have to know about each other.

## Hint 3

Put the same check inside the reducer's `next` case as well. A disabled button
is a courtesy to the user; the reducer is the thing that actually guarantees
nobody reaches step two without an email.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — none, some, all

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `SelectionProvider({ ids, children })`,
`RowBox({ id })` — a checkbox labelled with the id — and `SelectAllBox()`, a
checkbox labelled `All`. `All` is checked when every row is, **partially
checked** when some but not all are, and unchecked otherwise. Clicking it when
it is fully checked clears the selection; clicking it in either other state
selects everything.

```
uv run dojo test react d18_context_reducer_apps ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Select one row of three and look at the All box: it says "no rows are
selected", which is a lie. A checkbox has three states, and the third one has
no JSX attribute — which is the whole difficulty.

## Hint 2

`indeterminate` is a property you set on the DOM node itself. Get a ref onto
the input and write to it from an effect, keyed on whether the selection is
currently partial.

## Hint 3

Work out `all` and `some` from the ids the provider knows about and the ids
that are selected — neither belongs in state. And decide what clicking a
partial box should do: finishing the selection is kinder than clearing it.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two separate bugs, one on each side of the store. The read happens as an
ordinary expression in the provider's body, which means every render. The write
happens in an effect with no guard, which means the very first render too — so

run. A ref is memory that survives a render without causing one, and consuming
it inside the effect keeps the dependency array honest.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two separate bugs, one on each side of the store. The read happens as an
ordinary expression in the provider's body, which means every render. The write
happens in an effect with no guard, which means the very first render too — so
opening the app immediately saves the draft it has just loaded.

## Hint 2

`useReducer` takes a third argument for the first problem: the value to start
from, and a function to turn it into state. React calls that once.

## Hint 3

For the second, the effect needs to know whether this is the first time it has
run. A ref is memory that survives a render without causing one, and consuming
it inside the effect keeps the dependency array honest.

## Exercise 7 — undo that knows when it cannot

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. `NotesProvider({ children })`, `NotesEditor()` — an
input labelled `New note`, an `Add` button that adds it and clears the box, and
a `<ul>` of the notes — and `HistoryBar()`, with `Undo` and `Redo` buttons.
Each button is disabled when there is nothing for it to do, and adding a note
after an undo throws the redo branch away.

```
uv run dojo test react d18_context_reducer_apps ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`canUndo: true, canRedo: true` is a placeholder, and the state already contains
the real answer. There is something to undo exactly when one of the two stacks
is not empty.

## Hint 2

Derive both flags in the provider so `HistoryBar` gets them through the
context — it never needs to know that a past or a future exists. And make the
reducer safe on its own: undo with an empty past should change nothing rather
than set `present` to `undefined`.

## Hint 3

One case is easy to miss. After undoing twice and then adding a note, the two
notes you had undone your way out of are not reachable any more, so redo must
have nowhere to go.

`canUndo: true, canRedo: true` is a placeholder, and the state already contains
the real answer. There is something to undo exactly when one of the two stacks
is not empty.

## Hint 2

Derive both flags in the provider so `HistoryBar` gets them through the
context — it never needs to know that a past or a future exists. And make the
reducer safe on its own: undo with an empty past should change nothing rather
than set `present` to `undefined`.

## Hint 3

One case is easy to miss. After undoing twice and then adding a note, the two
notes you had undone your way out of are not reachable any more, so redo must
have nowhere to go.

## Exercise 8 — the basket

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. `BasketProvider({ children })`,
`AddToBasket({ product, onRender })` — a button reading `Add <name>` —
`BasketLines()`, a `<ul>` with one `<li>` per line containing `<name> x<qty>`
and buttons `More <name>` and `Fewer <name>`, and `BasketTotal()`, a
`role="status"` paragraph reading `Total: <sum of price times qty>`.

Adding a product already in the basket raises its quantity; taking the last one
away removes the line entirely. And the `Add` buttons must render **once each**,
no matter how much the basket changes. Leave the `onRender()` call where the
stub has it.

uv run dojo test react d18_context_reducer_apps ex8
```

lessons.briefing:
# d19 — Custom hooks, part 1 (drill set)

Eight problems on writing a hook other people can use. It drills
`10_custom_hooks`, and the sentence that lesson opens with is the one to hold
on to: extracting a hook moves lines, it does not move state — the state still
belongs to whichever component called the hook.

Everything here is about the **shape of what a hook hands back**. Values that
should be derived rather than stored, functions that must be the same object
next render, an API object that must not be rebuilt for nothing, and work that
should not run again just because the component redrew. Two of the eight are
about the rules rather than the shape.

Where a hook's return value is the whole API, the gate drives it with
`renderHook`. Where a hook only makes sense wired to markup, the gate writes its
own little component and asserts on the accessible DOM.

## Exercise 1 — the same functions next render

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `useCarousel(count)` returns
`{ index, next, prev, atStart, atEnd }`. `next` and `prev` move the index one
place and stop at both ends; `atStart` and `atEnd` say where it is. The gate
holds on to `next` and `prev` and checks they are still the same function
objects several renders later.

```
uv run dojo test react d19_custom_hooks_1 ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — edited, and un-edited

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `useTextField(initial)` returns
`{ value, onChange, dirty, reset }`, where `onChange` goes straight onto an
`<input>` and `reset` puts `initial` back. `dirty` is true exactly when the
current value differs from the one the field started with — so typing something
and typing it back leaves it false.

```
uv run dojo test react d19_custom_hooks_1 ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — one tally each

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `useTally()` returns `{ count, add }`. The gate puts
two components using it on screen at once and adds to one of them; the other
must not move.

```
uv run dojo test react d19_custom_hooks_1 ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — a hook in a loop

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `PriceRows({ rows })` renders a `<ul>` with one `<li>`
per row containing `<label>: marked` or `<label>: unmarked` and a button reading
`Mark <label>` that marks that row. The gate marks a row and then rerenders with
a **shorter** list, which the stub does not survive. A row's mark stays with its
row.

```
uv run dojo test react d19_custom_hooks_1 ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — a timer that stops

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. `useCountdown(from)` returns
`{ remaining, running, start, pause, reset }`. It counts down one per second
only while it is running, stops at `0`, and leaves **no timer running** once it
has finished, once it is paused, or once the component has gone.

```
uv run dojo test react d19_custom_hooks_1 ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — filter when the question changes

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. `useFilteredList(items, query, onFilter)` returns
`{ matches, count }`, where `matches` are the items containing `query`,
case-insensitively. The filtering pass — including the `onFilter()` call, which
you should leave where it is — must run only when `items` or `query` change,
not on every render of the component that called the hook.

```
uv run dojo test react d19_custom_hooks_1 ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — one API object

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. `useCollection(initial)` returns
`{ items, add, remove, clear }`. The three functions must be the same objects
for the whole life of the hook, and the object holding them must be the same
object until `items` actually changes — which removing something that was never
there does not do.

```
uv run dojo test react d19_custom_hooks_1 ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — errors that cannot go stale

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. `useForm(initial, validate)` returns
`{ values, errors, isValid, setField, reset }`. `errors` is whatever
`validate(values)` says about the values as they are now, `isValid` is true when
there are none, `setField(name, value)` changes one field and `reset()` goes back
to the values the form started with. `validate` must not be called again on a
render where nothing changed.

```
uv run dojo test react d19_custom_hooks_1 ex8
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading — react/d19_custom_hooks_1

## Notes

A custom hook is a function that follows the rules of hooks, and that is the
whole definition — which is why the two things people get wrong are the two
things the definition implies. It is a *function*, so its body runs on every
render of every component that calls it, and everything it builds is built
again: work that should be conditional needs `useMemo`, functions that consumers
will compare need `useCallback`, and the object wrapping them needs memoizing
too or all that care is thrown away at the last step. And it follows *the rules
of hooks*, which exist because React matches each hook call to a slot by call
order — so a hook in a loop or behind a condition is not a style violation, it
is a component whose state list stops lining up. Threaded through the set is the
same reflex the whole track keeps returning to: a value you can compute from
what you already have is not state. A dirty flag, an `atEnd`, an `isValid`, a
set of validation errors — every one of those is a question, and storing the
answer means owning the job of keeping it true.

## ex1

Tests returning stable functions. The classic mistake is defining the callbacks
in the hook body, which is correct in every way except identity: consumers who
put them in a dependency array re-run their effects on every render, and a
memoized child taking one as a prop is never actually skipped. The model answer
wraps both in `useCallback` and uses the updater form of `setIndex`, so neither
needs to read the current index and the dependency lists stay nearly empty.

## ex2

Tests derived state inside a hook. The classic mistake is a `dirty` boolean set
to `true` on change and cleared nowhere — so a field typed back to its original
value still claims to be edited, and so does one that has just been reset. The
model answer compares the current value with the initial one during render,
which is a question that cannot be forgotten the way a setter can.

## ex3

Tests what a hook actually is. The classic mistake is thinking of a hook as a
place where state lives and putting the value at module scope, which works
perfectly until a second component calls the hook and starts sharing a number
with the first. The model answer keeps the count in the `useState` the hook
already had — a recipe each caller follows separately, getting a slot of its own.

## ex4

Tests the rules of hooks with a loop rather than the usual `if`. The classic
mistake is one `useState` per row inside `.map`, which is fine right up until
the list gets shorter and React finds fewer hooks than it stored. The model
answer notices whose state it is: a row's mark belongs to a component that is
one row, called unconditionally, with a `key` so React keeps the state attached
to the right row when the list around it moves.

## ex5

Tests cleanup inside a hook. The classic mistake is starting an interval and
returning nothing, so pausing flips a flag the running interval has never heard
of and unmounting leaves it ticking for the life of the page. The model answer
clears the interval from the effect's cleanup — which covers pausing, resetting
and unmounting at once — and lists `remaining` in the dependencies so reaching
zero stops the timer rather than merely clamping the number.

## ex6

Tests that a hook body is part of a render. The classic mistake is doing the
work in the hook body, where it runs for every render of the calling component
whatever the render was for — a click on an unrelated button re-filters the
whole list. The model answer moves the pass into `useMemo` keyed on the list and
the query, which also keeps `matches` identity-stable between renders, worth as
much as the saved work.

## ex7

Tests identity at two levels. The classic mistake is memoizing the functions and
then returning them in a fresh object literal, which changes on every render
anyway and defeats every consumer that was relying on the care you took. The
model answer wraps the functions in `useCallback` with empty dependency arrays
— possible because they all use the updater form — and the result object in
`useMemo`; and it has each updater return the state unchanged when nothing
happened, so a no-op removal does not even cause a render.

## ex8

Tests derived state in its most valuable form. The classic mistake is keeping
`errors` in state: something has to recompute them after every change, that
something is a line in every action, and the one that gets forgotten leaves a
complaint on screen next to a field that is now correct. The model answer
computes the errors from the values with `useMemo`, so they cannot be stale, and
captures the original values in a ref so `reset` goes back to the form's real
starting point rather than to whatever object the caller passed this render.

## Further reading

- [Reusing logic with custom hooks](https://react.dev/learn/reusing-logic-with-custom-hooks)
- [Rules of hooks](https://react.dev/reference/rules/rules-of-hooks)
- [`useCallback` reference](https://react.dev/reference/react/useCallback)

# Reading — react/d19_custom_hooks_1

## Notes

A custom hook is a function that follows the rules of hooks, and that is the
whole definition — which is why the two things people get wrong are the two
things the definition implies. It is a *function*, so its body runs on every
render of every component that calls it, and everything it builds is built
again: work that should be conditional needs `useMemo`, functions that consumers
will compare need `useCallback`, and the object wrapping them needs memoizing
too or all that care is thrown away at the last step. And it follows *the rules
of hooks*, which exist because React matches each hook call to a slot by call
order — so a hook in a loop or behind a condition is not a style violation, it
is a component whose state list stops lining up. Threaded through the set is the
same reflex the whole track keeps returning to: a value you can compute from
what you already have is not state. A dirty flag, an `atEnd`, an `isValid`, a
set of validation errors — every one of those is a question, and storing the
answer means owning the job of keeping it true.

## ex1

Tests returning stable functions. The classic mistake is defining the callbacks
in the hook body, which is correct in every way except identity: consumers who
put them in a dependency array re-run their effects on every render, and a
memoized child taking one as a prop is never actually skipped. The model answer
wraps both in `useCallback` and uses the updater form of `setIndex`, so neither
needs to read the current index and the dependency lists stay nearly empty.

## ex2

Tests derived state inside a hook. The classic mistake is a `dirty` boolean set
to `true` on change and cleared nowhere — so a field typed back to its original
value still claims to be edited, and so does one that has just been reset. The
model answer compares the current value with the initial one during render,
which is a question that cannot be forgotten the way a setter can.

## ex3

Tests what a hook actually is. The classic mistake is thinking of a hook as a
place where state lives and putting the value at module scope, which works
perfectly until a second component calls the hook and starts sharing a number
with the first. The model answer keeps the count in the `useState` the hook
already had — a recipe each caller follows separately, getting a slot of its own.

## ex4

Tests the rules of hooks with a loop rather than the usual `if`. The classic
mistake is one `useState` per row inside `.map`, which is fine right up until
the list gets shorter and React finds fewer hooks than it stored. The model
answer notices whose state it is: a row's mark belongs to a component that is
one row, called unconditionally, with a `key` so React keeps the state attached
to the right row when the list around it moves.

## ex5

Tests cleanup inside a hook. The classic mistake is starting an interval and
returning nothing, so pausing flips a flag the running interval has never heard
of and unmounting leaves it ticking for the life of the page. The model answer
clears the interval from the effect's cleanup — which covers pausing, resetting
and unmounting at once — and lists `remaining` in the dependencies so reaching
zero stops the timer rather than merely clamping the number.

## ex6

Tests that a hook body is part of a render. The classic mistake is doing the
work in the hook body, where it runs for every render of the calling component
whatever the render was for — a click on an unrelated button re-filters the
whole list. The model answer moves the pass into `useMemo` keyed on the list and
the query, which also keeps `matches` identity-stable between renders, worth as
much as the saved work.

## ex7

Tests identity at two levels. The classic mistake is memoizing the functions and
then returning them in a fresh object literal, which changes on every render
anyway and defeats every consumer that was relying on the care you took. The
model answer wraps the functions in `useCallback` with empty dependency arrays
— possible because they all use the updater form — and the result object in
`useMemo`; and it has each updater return the state unchanged when nothing
happened, so a no-op removal does not even cause a render.

## ex8

Tests derived state in its most valuable form. The classic mistake is keeping
`errors` in state: something has to recompute them after every change, that
something is a line in every action, and the one that gets forgotten leaves a
complaint on screen next to a field that is now correct. The model answer
computes the errors from the values with `useMemo`, so they cannot be stale, and
captures the original values in a ref so `reset` goes back to the form's real
starting point rather than to whatever object the caller passed this render.

## Exercise 1 — the same functions next render

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `useCarousel(count)` returns
`{ index, next, prev, atStart, atEnd }`. `next` and `prev` move the index one
place and stop at both ends; `atStart` and `atEnd` say where it is. The gate
holds on to `next` and `prev` and checks they are still the same function
objects several renders later.

uv run dojo test react d19_custom_hooks_1 ex1

## Hint 1

Everything the hook computes is already right. What is wrong is that `next` and
`prev` are built again from scratch on every render, so no two renders hand back
the same function object.

`useCallback(fn, deps)` returns the same function until one of its dependencies
changes. Look at what each of these two actually reads: because they use the
updater form of `setIndex`, neither needs the current index, and one of them
needs nothing at all.

## Hint 1

Everything the hook computes is already right. What is wrong is that `next` and
`prev` are built again from scratch on every render, so no two renders hand back
the same function object.

## Hint 2

`useCallback(fn, deps)` returns the same function until one of its dependencies
changes. Look at what each of these two actually reads: because they use the
updater form of `setIndex`, neither needs the current index, and one of them
needs nothing at all.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — edited, and un-edited

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `useTextField(initial)` returns
`{ value, onChange, dirty, reset }`, where `onChange` goes straight onto an
`<input>` and `reset` puts `initial` back. `dirty` is true exactly when the
current value differs from the one the field started with — so typing something
and typing it back leaves it false.

```
uv run dojo test react d19_custom_hooks_1 ex2

per row containing `<label>: marked` or `<label>: unmarked` and a button reading

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Run the gate and read React's error before you change anything. React stores
hook state in a list per component and matches each call to a slot by call
order — so a component that calls `useState` three times on one render and
twice on the next has nothing to match the third slot against.

## Hint 2

The rule is "only call hooks at the top level", and a `.map` callback is not
the top level. The fix is not to move the loop; it is to notice whose state
this is. Each row's mark belongs to that row.

## Hint 3

Give the row a component of its own, with its own `useState` called
unconditionally. Then keep the `key` on it, so React knows which row is which
when the list changes and the state stays where it belongs.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Run the gate and read React's error before you change anything. React stores
hook state in a list per component and matches each call to a slot by call
order — so a component that calls `useState` three times on one render and
twice on the next has nothing to match the third slot against.

## Hint 2

The rule is "only call hooks at the top level", and a `.map` callback is not
the top level. The fix is not to move the loop; it is to notice whose state
this is. Each row's mark belongs to that row.

## Hint 3

Give the row a component of its own, with its own `useState` called
unconditionally. Then keep the `key` on it, so React knows which row is which
when the list changes and the state stays where it belongs.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The effect starts an interval and returns nothing. Pausing flips a flag that
the already-running interval has never heard of, so the countdown keeps going —
and unmounting the component leaves it going for the life of the page.

## Hint 2

Keep the id `setInterval` gives you and clear it from the effect's cleanup.
That one function covers pausing, resetting and unmounting, because React runs
the cleanup before every re-run of the effect and once more on the way out.

## Hint 3

The last check is that a finished countdown has no timer at all. Reaching zero
is a second reason not to be ticking, and the effect can only notice it if the
dependency array mentions what it is watching.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A custom hook's body is part of the component's render. Anything you write
there runs every time that component renders, for whatever reason — including a
click on a button that has nothing to do with the list.

## Hint 2

`useMemo(factory, deps)` runs the factory again only when a dependency changes.
Move the whole filtering pass inside it, `onFilter()` included, and name the
inputs the answer really depends on.

## Hint 3

Be honest in the array: the list and the query are obvious, and the callback is
a dependency too. Note that this also keeps `matches` identity-stable between
renders, which is worth as much as skipping the work.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — one API object

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. `useCollection(initial)` returns
`{ items, add, remove, clear }`. The three functions must be the same objects
for the whole life of the hook, and the object holding them must be the same
object until `items` actually changes — which removing something that was never
there does not do.

```
uv run dojo test react d19_custom_hooks_1 ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two layers of identity have to hold. The three functions must survive a render
unchanged, and so must the object they are handed back in — a stable set of
functions inside a fresh wrapper is still a changed value to everybody
consuming it.

## Hint 2

`useCallback` for the functions, `useMemo` for the object. Write each function
with the updater form of `setItems` so that none of them needs to read the
current items, which leaves all three with empty dependency arrays.

## Hint 3

One check is about something else: removing an item that is not in the
collection must leave everything looking untouched. A setter that is handed
back the state it was given is a change React does not make — which means the
memoized object survives too, for free.

## Hint 1

Two layers of identity have to hold. The three functions must survive a render
unchanged, and so must the object they are handed back in — a stable set of
functions inside a fresh wrapper is still a changed value to everybody
consuming it.

## Hint 2

`useCallback` for the functions, `useMemo` for the object. Write each function
with the updater form of `setItems` so that none of them needs to read the
current items, which leaves all three with empty dependency arrays.

## Hint 3

One check is about something else: removing an item that is not in the
collection must leave everything looking untouched. A setter that is handed
back the state it was given is a change React does not make — which means the
memoized object survives too, for free.

lessons.briefing:
# d20 — Custom hooks, part 2 (drill set)

Eight hooks that talk to something outside React: a document listener, a
subscription, a store, a clock, a server. It drills `10_custom_hooks` again,
and leans on everything the effects and refs sets taught — because a hook that
owns an effect owns its cleanup, and a hook whose caller writes a callback
inline has to cope with that callback being a new function every render.

Everything outside React is **injected**: subscriptions, stores and loaders are
all functions the gate hands in, so nothing here touches the real network or
the real clock. Anything timed uses fake timers.

Two questions come up again and again. What does this effect really depend on —
and where does a value live if it must be readable *now*, before the next
render?

## Exercise 1 — the newest handler

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `useKeyPress(key, handler)` calls `handler()` whenever
that key is pressed on the document, and nothing on any other key. The listener
must be removed when the component goes — and the handler that runs must be the
one the component has now, even though the caller passes a new function on
every render.

```
uv run dojo test react d20_custom_hooks_2 ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — close what you opened

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `useSubscription(subscribe, initial)` returns the most
recent value pushed by `subscribe(onValue)`, starting at `initial`. It
subscribes once per distinct `subscribe` function, and whenever it drops one —
because the source changed, or the component unmounted — it calls the
unsubscribe function that source gave it.

```
uv run dojo test react d20_custom_hooks_2 ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — the page that stopped existing

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `usePaged(items, pageSize)` returns
`{ page, pageItems, totalPages, hasNext, hasPrev, next, prev }`, with `page`
counting from 1. `next` and `prev` stop at the ends — and when `items` gets
shorter, the page shown must come back inside the list rather than pointing at
nothing.

```
uv run dojo test react d20_custom_hooks_2 ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — a real debounce

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `useDebouncedCallback(fn, delay)` returns a function
that calls `fn` `delay` milliseconds after the **last** time it was called —
each call cancelling the one before. The returned function is the same object
for the life of the hook, it always calls the newest `fn`, and a call still
pending when the component unmounts never happens.

```
uv run dojo test react d20_custom_hooks_2 ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — a key that can change

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. `useStorageState(key, initial, storage)` returns
`[value, setValue]`. The value comes from `storage.getItem(key)` — parsed as
JSON — on the **first render**, or `initial` when there is nothing stored.
`setValue` updates React and writes JSON back under the current key. When `key`
changes, the value must become whatever is stored under the new key.

```
uv run dojo test react d20_custom_hooks_2 ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — polling that waits its turn

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. `useIntervalPoll(load, everyMs)` returns `{ data }`.
It calls `load()` immediately, then every `everyMs` — **skipping** any tick
that arrives while a previous call is still unresolved — and shows the newest
resolved value. Unmounting stops the polling entirely.

```
uv run dojo test react d20_custom_hooks_2 ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — a reducer that keeps a log

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. `useLoggedReducer(reducer, initial, log)` returns
`[state, dispatch]` and behaves exactly like `useReducer`, except that every
dispatch also calls `log(action, next)` with the state that action **produced**.
`dispatch` must be the same function for the life of the hook, and must use the
newest `log` it was given.

```
uv run dojo test react d20_custom_hooks_2 ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — controlled, or not

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. `useControllableState({ value, defaultValue, onChange })`
returns `[value, setValue]`. When `value` is given the hook is **controlled**:
the returned value is always the prop, and `setValue` only calls `onChange`.
When it is not, the hook keeps the value itself, starting at `defaultValue`,
and calls `onChange` as well. Which of the two it is must be decided on the
first render and never change.

```
uv run dojo test react d20_custom_hooks_2 ex8
```

# Reading — react/d20_custom_hooks_2

## Notes

Once a hook owns something outside React — a listener, a socket, a timer, a
poll — it owns the whole life of that thing, and two questions decide almost
every line. The first is what the effect really depends on. Callers write
handlers and loaders inline, so those arrive as new functions on every render;
listing them in a dependency array is honest and tears the subscription down
several times a second, while leaving them out is a lie that shows up as a
stale closure calling last week's callback. The way out, three times in this
set, is a ref holding the newest function, updated by its own tiny effect, read
at the moment the event happens — the pattern `useEffectEvent` is being designed
to replace. The second question is *when* a value has to be readable. State is
a value between renders; a ref is a value now. Whether a request is in flight,
which timeout is pending, what the state became a microsecond ago — none of
those can wait for a render, and all of them are refs. The rest of the set is
the recurring lesson that a hook's return value is an API: it must survive
renders unchanged, and it must not quietly stop tracking a prop that changed.

## ex1

Tests the latest-value ref in its smallest form. The classic mistake is the
empty dependency array, which promises the effect reads nothing that can change
while it reads two things that can — so the shortcut goes on calling the
handler from the first render. Adding `handler` to the array is the other
mistake: it is honest and it removes and re-adds a document listener on every
render. The model answer depends on `key` alone and reads the handler out of a
ref when the key is actually pressed.

## ex2

Tests cleanup, and rewards reading the API you were given. The classic mistake
is calling `subscribe` and dropping what it returns, which leaks one live
connection per change of source — all of them still pushing into a component
that has moved on. The model answer notices that an unsubscribe function and an
effect's cleanup are the same shape, and returns it directly.

## ex3

Tests derived state at the boundary. The classic mistake is treating the page
number as the truth: clamping it when the reader moves is easy, and nothing
clamps it when the *list* moves, so a filter that removes rows leaves somebody
staring at an empty page. The model answer keeps the page that was asked for in
state and computes the page that is shown during render, which also avoids the
frame of empty list that a correcting effect would commit.

## ex4

Tests what makes a debounce a debounce. The classic mistake is scheduling a
timeout per call and cancelling none, which delays every call instead of
replacing it. Two refs solve it: the pending timeout id, which must be readable
the instant the next call arrives, and the newest `fn`, which lets the returned
function keep its identity — and that identity matters, because whatever is
holding the debounced function would otherwise be holding a different debounce
with its own pending timeout.

## ex5

Tests initialisation against a moving target. The classic mistake is a lazy
`useState` initialiser, which is exactly right for the value and blind to the
key changing under it — the hook then shows one document's draft under another
document's name. The model answer stores the key beside the value so staleness
is a question it can ask, and adjusts the state during render rather than in an
effect, so no wrong pairing is ever committed.

## ex6

Tests overlapping work. The classic mistakes are the interval that is never
cleared and the tick that fires regardless — on a slow connection the second
turns one poll a second into a growing queue of requests, each answering later
than the last. The model answer keeps an in-flight flag in a ref, because it
must be true the instant the request goes out rather than after the next
render, and clears it on both the success and the failure path.

## ex7

Tests wrapping a hook without breaking its contract. The classic mistake is
reading `state` inside the wrapper, which is the render's value — the state
*before* the action — so every line of the log is one step behind. The model
answer calls the reducer itself, which is free because a reducer is pure, and
keeps the current state, the reducer and the log in refs so `dispatch` can have
an empty dependency array and stay as stable as the one React handed over.

## ex8

Tests the controlled/uncontrolled contract every component library implements.
The classic mistake is seeding internal state from the `value` prop and then
ignoring the prop, which produces a component that claims to be controlled and
shows something its parent does not believe. The model answer decides the mode
once, on the first render, keeps it in a ref, and always calls `useState` — the
number of hooks a component calls may not depend on a prop, even one it will
never use.

- [Separating events from effects](https://react.dev/learn/separating-events-from-effects)
- [You might not need an effect](https://react.dev/learn/you-might-not-need-an-effect)

## Exercise 1 — the newest handler

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `useKeyPress(key, handler)` calls `handler()` whenever
that key is pressed on the document, and nothing on any other key. The listener
must be removed when the component goes — and the handler that runs must be the
one the component has now, even though the caller passes a new function on
every render.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The empty dependency array is a promise that the effect reads nothing that can
change, and it reads two things that can: `key` and `handler`. The listener
goes on calling the handler from the first render for ever.

## Hint 2

Adding `handler` to the array would be honest and would also remove and re-add
a document listener on every render, since the caller almost certainly writes
the handler inline. Keep the newest one in a ref updated by its own tiny
effect, and let the listener read `ref.current` when the key is actually
pressed.

## Exercise 2 — close what you opened

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `useSubscription(subscribe, initial)` returns the most
recent value pushed by `subscribe(onValue)`, starting at `initial`. It
subscribes once per distinct `subscribe` function, and whenever it drops one —
because the source changed, or the component unmounted — it calls the
unsubscribe function that source gave it.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`subscribe` returns something, and the stub throws it away. Look at what it
returns and at what an effect is allowed to return, and notice that they are
the same shape.

## Hint 2

React runs the previous cleanup before the next effect and once more on the way
out, so returning the unsubscribe function covers both cases the gate checks:
swapping the source, and unmounting. Note that `setValue` from `useState` is
stable, which is why it does not belong in the dependency array.

## Exercise 4 — a real debounce

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `useDebouncedCallback(fn, delay)` returns a function
that calls `fn` `delay` milliseconds after the **last** time it was called —
each call cancelling the one before. The returned function is the same object
for the life of the hook, it always calls the newest `fn`, and a call still
pending when the component unmounts never happens.

```
uv run dojo test react d20_custom_hooks_2 ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The stub delays every call by 500ms and sends all of them. A debounce sends
one — which means each call has to cancel whatever was already scheduled, and
that means keeping the id `setTimeout` handed back.

## Hint 2

The id has to survive renders without causing them, so it belongs in a ref, not
in state. While you are there, note the second thing a ref gives you: the
cleanup that clears a pending timeout when the component unmounts.

## Hint 3

The returned function must be the same object every render, so `fn` cannot be
in its dependency array — and it still has to call the newest `fn`. That is the
same latest-in-a-ref trick as exercise 1, applied to the function instead of
the handler.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The stub delays every call by 500ms and sends all of them. A debounce sends
one — which means each call has to cancel whatever was already scheduled, and
that means keeping the id `setTimeout` handed back.

## Hint 2

The id has to survive renders without causing them, so it belongs in a ref, not
in state. While you are there, note the second thing a ref gives you: the
cleanup that clears a pending timeout when the component unmounts.

## Hint 3

The returned function must be the same object every render, so `fn` cannot be
in its dependency array — and it still has to call the newest `fn`. That is the
same latest-in-a-ref trick as exercise 1, applied to the function instead of
the handler.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — a key that can change

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. `useStorageState(key, initial, storage)` returns
`[value, setValue]`. The value comes from `storage.getItem(key)` — parsed as
JSON — on the **first render**, or `initial` when there is nothing stored.
`setValue` updates React and writes JSON back under the current key. When `key`
changes, the value must become whatever is stored under the new key.

```
uv run dojo test react d20_custom_hooks_2 ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The initialiser passed to `useState` runs once, on the first render, and never
again — which is exactly right for the value and exactly wrong for a key that
can change underneath it.

## Hint 2

Store the key alongside the value, so the hook can compare the key its state
was built for against the key it has been given this render. When they differ,
the state is stale and has to be replaced.

## Hint 3

Do that replacement **during render**, not in an effect: set the new state and
use the new value in the same pass. React notices a component setting its own
state while rendering, throws that render away and runs it again — so nothing
is ever committed showing one key's value under another's name.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The initialiser passed to `useState` runs once, on the first render, and never
again — which is exactly right for the value and exactly wrong for a key that
can change underneath it.

## Hint 2

Store the key alongside the value, so the hook can compare the key its state
was built for against the key it has been given this render. When they differ,
the state is stale and has to be replaced.

## Hint 3

Do that replacement **during render**, not in an effect: set the new state and
use the new value in the same pass. React notices a component setting its own
state while rendering, throws that render away and runs it again — so nothing
is ever committed showing one key's value under another's name.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — a reducer that keeps a log

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. `useLoggedReducer(reducer, initial, log)` returns
`[state, dispatch]` and behaves exactly like `useReducer`, except that every
dispatch also calls `log(action, next)` with the state that action **produced**.
`dispatch` must be the same function for the life of the hook, and must use the
newest `log` it was given.

```
uv run dojo test react d20_custom_hooks_2 ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`state` inside `dispatch` is the value from the render that created that
`dispatch` — the state *before* this action. The log is supposed to say what the
action produced, which is a value nobody has computed yet.

## Hint 2

You have the reducer, and a reducer is a pure function: calling it yourself to
find out what the next state will be is free and has no side effects. You need
the current state to call it with, though, and that has to be readable
synchronously — which is a ref rather than the render's variable.

## Hint 3

The other half is identity. `dispatch` from `useReducer` never changes, and a
wrapper that changes on every render breaks every consumer relying on that. Put
whatever can change — the reducer, the log function — in refs, and the wrapper
can have an empty dependency array.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`state` inside `dispatch` is the value from the render that created that
`dispatch` — the state *before* this action. The log is supposed to say what the
action produced, which is a value nobody has computed yet.

## Hint 2

You have the reducer, and a reducer is a pure function: calling it yourself to
find out what the next state will be is free and has no side effects. You need
the current state to call it with, though, and that has to be readable
synchronously — which is a ref rather than the render's variable.

## Hint 3

The other half is identity. `dispatch` from `useReducer` never changes, and a
wrapper that changes on every render breaks every consumer relying on that. Put
whatever can change — the reducer, the log function — in refs, and the wrapper
can have an empty dependency array.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — controlled, or not

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. `useControllableState({ value, defaultValue, onChange })`
returns `[value, setValue]`. When `value` is given the hook is **controlled**:
the returned value is always the prop, and `setValue` only calls `onChange`.
When it is not, the hook keeps the value itself, starting at `defaultValue`,
and calls `onChange` as well. Which of the two it is must be decided on the
first render and never change.

```
uv run dojo test react d20_custom_hooks_2 ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The stub reads the `value` prop once, to seed its own state, and then ignores
it for ever. A controlled value is not a starting point — it is the answer,
every render.

## Hint 2

Two modes. When `value` is given, return it and let the setter do nothing but
call `onChange`; when it is not, keep the value in state as the stub does and
call `onChange` as well. Which mode you are in is decided by whether `value`
was supplied.

## Hint 3

Decide that **once** and remember it — a component that switches modes halfway
through its life makes its value appear to jump, and the warning React's own
inputs print about exactly this is worth reading. And call `useState`
unconditionally either way: the number of hooks a component calls may not
depend on a prop.

call `onChange`; when it is not, keep the value in state as the stub does and
call `onChange` as well. Which mode you are in is decided by whether `value`
was supplied.

## Hint 3

Decide that **once** and remember it — a component that switches modes halfway
through its life makes its value appear to jump, and the warning React's own
inputs print about exactly this is worth reading. And call `useState`
unconditionally either way: the number of hooks a component calls may not
depend on a prop.

# d21 — Memoization (drill set)

Eight problems on `memo`, `useMemo` and `useCallback` — what they compare, what
defeats them, and the one way they can make a component wrong rather than
slow. It drills `11_performance_patterns`; the sentence to have in mind is that
`memo` compares each prop with `Object.is`, so **objects, arrays and functions
are compared by identity**.

Nothing here is described, everything is measured. Injected `onRender` spies
count how often a component ran and injected work functions count how often the
expensive thing happened, so a memo that "looks right" and does nothing fails
the same way a missing one does. Leave those calls where the stubs have them.

Six of the eight are a memoized component that never skips a render. The cause
is different every time.

## Exercise 1 — the object in the JSX

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `MetricBoard({ onTileRender })` renders `Ticks: <n>` in
a `role="status"` paragraph, a `Tick` button, and a memoized `MetricTile`
showing `Revenue: 1200 EUR`. Ticking must not re-render the tile.

```
uv run dojo test react d21_memoization ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — the function in the JSX

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `ColumnBoard({ onFilterRender })` renders an input
labelled `Board name`, `Board: <name>`, a `role="status"` paragraph reading
`Status toggled <n> times` — `1 time` in the singular — and a memoized
`ColumnFilter` whose button reads `Toggle Status`. Typing must not re-render
the filter, and the button must still work.

```
uv run dojo test react d21_memoization ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — the array that lies

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `SlugPreview({ title, onCompute })` renders the title
slugified — lower case, non-alphanumerics collapsed to `-`, no leading or
trailing `-` — in a `role="status"` paragraph. The slug follows the title, and
the work is done again only when the title actually changes.

```
uv run dojo test react d21_memoization ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — identity, not speed

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `TagPanel({ tags, onTagsRender })` renders an input
labelled `Search`, `Ticks: <n>` in a `role="status"` paragraph, a `Tick`
button, and a memoized `VisibleTags` listing the tags containing the search
text. Ticking must not re-render the list; searching must.

```
uv run dojo test react d21_memoization ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — the callback that rebuilds itself

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. `ZoomPanel({ onControlsRender })` renders
`Zoom: <n>` in a `role="status"` paragraph and a memoized `ZoomControls` with
`Zoom in` and `Reset zoom` buttons. Zooming changes the number and must never
re-render the controls, which do not show it.

```
uv run dojo test react d21_memoization ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — the prop you did not write

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. `FrameBoard({ onFrameRender, onBodyRender })` renders
`Ticks: <n>` in a `role="status"` paragraph, a `Tick` button, and a memoized
`Frame` with a `Summary` heading containing a `Body` that reads
`Nothing to report`. Ticking must re-render neither the frame nor the body.

```
uv run dojo test react d21_memoization ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — one row, one render

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. `ChecklistRows({ items, onRowRender })` renders a
memoized row per item, each with `<label>: done` or `<label>: to do` and a
button reading `Toggle <label>`. Toggling one row must re-render that row and
no other. `onRowRender` is called with the row's id, so the gate can tell which
rendered.

```
uv run dojo test react d21_memoization ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — all three at once

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. `ChartPanel({ points, buildSeries, onLegendRender })`
renders `Theme: <theme>` in a `role="status"` paragraph, a `Switch theme`
button, a memoized `Legend` listing `buildSeries(points)` as buttons, and
`Picked: <label>` once one has been clicked. Switching the theme must neither
call `buildSeries` again nor re-render the legend; picking a label must not
re-render the legend either; new `points` must do both.

```
uv run dojo test react d21_memoization ex8
```

# Reading — react/d21_memoization

## Notes

`memo` compares each prop with `Object.is`. Everything in this set follows from
that one line. Strings and numbers behave the way people expect; objects,
arrays and functions do not, because two structurally identical values written
in two renders are two different values — so the memo comparison fails, the
child renders anyway, and you have paid for a comparison as well. That is why
six of these eight problems are the same bug wearing different clothes: an
object literal in the JSX, an arrow function in the JSX, an array from
`filter`, a callback whose dependency array names the state it is about to
replace, the `children` prop nobody thinks of as a prop, and a handler built
per row inside a `map`. The other two are about `useMemo` itself: its dependency
array is a **claim** about what the value is made of, and getting it wrong does
not make a component slow, it makes it wrong — which is the failure mode worth
fearing, because the other kind only costs milliseconds. Interviewers like this
material because "I added memo and nothing happened" is an experience every
candidate has had, and the ones who can say why have understood identity.

## ex1

Tests the shallow comparison against an object literal. The classic mistake is
writing `format={{ currency: "EUR", decimals: 0 }}` in the JSX, which builds a
new object on every render of the parent, so the memoized tile's comparison
fails every time and the memo is pure overhead. The model answer notices that
the object depends on nothing at all and hoists it to module scope — no hook
needed, and nothing left to keep in step.

## ex2

Tests the same comparison against a function. The classic mistake is an inline
arrow as a prop: it is the commonest single reason `memo` "does nothing", and
it is invisible in a diff because the code looks like every other handler. The
model answer wraps it in `useCallback` with an empty dependency array, which is
possible because the updater form of the setter means the function never has to
read the count it increments.

## ex3

Tests the dependency array as a correctness tool. The classic mistake is `[]` —
often left behind while "making it fast" — which computes the value once and
shows it for ever, so the component silently displays an answer to a question
nobody is asking any more. The model answer lists everything the factory reads,
which turns the memo back into an optimisation instead of a bug.

## ex4

Tests `useMemo`'s second job. Filtering four strings is free, so nothing here is
about saving time: `filter` returns a new array on every render, and a new array
is a changed prop however identical its contents. The model answer memoizes the
derived list keyed on the source and the query, which is the same technique as
exercise 1 applied to a value that genuinely does change sometimes.

## ex5

Tests a `useCallback` that undoes itself. The classic mistake is
`useCallback(() => setZoom(zoom + 1), [zoom])`: it is honest about what it
reads and therefore rebuilt every time the zoom moves, which is every time the
callback is used — so the memoized child re-renders on exactly the event the
memo was meant to survive. The model answer removes the read rather than the
dependency, by using the updater form.

## ex6

Tests the prop that is not written like one. The classic mistake is assuming
`memo` will protect a wrapper component: `children` is an ordinary prop, and
the JSX between the tags is an element object rebuilt on every render of the
parent, so the comparison always fails. The model answer memoizes the element
itself — and the wider lesson is that wrapping a component that takes children
in `memo` usually buys nothing on its own.

## ex7

Tests memoized rows in a list. The classic mistake is `onToggle={() =>
toggle(item.id)}` inside the `map`, which gives every row a fresh function on
every render of the list, so toggling one row redraws all of them — the exact
cost the memo was added to avoid, at scale. The model answer passes one
`useCallback` handler to every row and lets the row say which row it is when it
calls back.

## ex8

Tests the three tools together, and the order to reach for them in. One
`useMemo` does two jobs at once here — it skips the expensive `buildSeries` and
it keeps the array identity the memoized legend compares against — while a
`useCallback` covers the handler. The check that proves it is the last one:
after picking a label the panel re-renders, and the legend still must not,
because nothing it is given has changed.

## Further reading

- [`memo` reference](https://react.dev/reference/react/memo)
- [`useMemo` reference](https://react.dev/reference/react/useMemo)
- [`useCallback` reference](https://react.dev/reference/react/useCallback)
- [Passing JSX as children](https://react.dev/learn/passing-props-to-a-component#passing-jsx-as-children)
- [MDN: `Object.is()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Object/is)
- [React Compiler](https://react.dev/learn/react-compiler)

Filtering four strings is free, so this is not about saving work. `filter`

identity stable so that a memoized child, or a dependency array, sees it as
unchanged. Name the two things the filtered list is made of.

## Hint 1

Filtering four strings is free, so this is not about saving work. `filter`
returns a **new array** every time it runs, and the memoized child compares its
props by identity — so it sees a different list on every render of the panel,
including the ones caused by a button it knows nothing about.

## Hint 2

`useMemo` has a second job that is not about speed at all: keeping a value's
identity stable so that a memoized child, or a dependency array, sees it as
unchanged. Name the two things the filtered list is made of.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — one row, one render

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. `ChecklistRows({ items, onRowRender })` renders a
memoized row per item, each with `<label>: done` or `<label>: to do` and a
button reading `Toggle <label>`. Toggling one row must re-render that row and
no other. `onRowRender` is called with the row's id, so the gate can tell which
rendered.

```
uv run dojo test react d21_memoization ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Toggling one row re-renders all of them. Three of the row's four props are
fine — the item object comes from the array unchanged, `done` is a boolean,
`onRender` comes from above. The fourth is written inside the `map`.

## Hint 2

`onToggle={() => toggle(item.id)}` creates a function per row on every render
of the list, so every row's props differ from last time. Look at what the row
already does with `onToggle`: it calls it with its own id.

## Hint 3

That means the list can pass **one** function to every row — the same object
for all of them, and the same object next render. `useCallback` with an empty
dependency array works because the updater form of the setter means the
function never has to read the current state.

lessons.briefing:
# d22 — Render performance without memo (drill set)

Eight problems where the answer is to move something rather than to remember
something. It drills the part of `11_performance_patterns` that is easiest to
skip past: **prefer structure**. Moving state down, passing content as
children, and not rendering what nobody is looking at are all free, permanent,
and cannot go stale the way a dependency array can.

Measured exactly as the last set was, with injected `onRender` spies — leave
those calls where the stubs have them. Seven of the eight are solved without
`memo`, `useMemo` or `useCallback` appearing anywhere; the last one needs all
three, which is the point of putting it last.

## Exercise 1 — content from above

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `TickerPage({ onPanelRender })` renders a ticker with
`Ticks: <n>` in a `role="status"` paragraph and a `Tick` button, plus a panel
reading `Panel contents`. Ticking must not re-render the panel — and no
memoization of any kind may be involved.

```
uv run dojo test react d22_render_performance ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — state that belongs lower

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `HelpPanel({ onBodyRender })` renders a button reading
`Show help` or `Hide help`, the paragraph `Read the manual` while help is
showing, and a report reading `Quarterly report`. Opening and closing the help
must never re-render the report.

```
uv run dojo test react d22_render_performance ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — do not build what is not shown

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `ExpandableRows({ rows, onBodyRender })` renders one
`<li>` per row with a button reading `Open <label>` or `Close <label>`, and —
only while that row is open — a body reading `<label> details`. A closed row's
body must never be built at all.

```
uv run dojo test react d22_render_performance ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — a window on a long list

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `WindowedRows({ items, windowSize, onRowRender })`
renders the first `windowSize` items as `<li>`s, a `role="status"` paragraph
reading `Showing <n> of <total>`, and a `Show more` button that reveals another
`windowSize` of them. Rows nobody can see are not rendered.

```
uv run dojo test react d22_render_performance ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — the change that is not one

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. `SelectionBar({ options, onRender })` renders
`Selected: <option>` in a `role="status"` paragraph, starting at the first
option, and a `Pick <option>` button for each. Picking the option that is
already selected must not re-render the component at all.

```
uv run dojo test react d22_render_performance ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — right on the first render

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. `SessionPanel({ readToken, onRender })` renders
`Session <token>` in a `role="status"` paragraph, where the token comes from
`readToken()`. Mounting the panel must produce exactly **one** render, with the
token already in it, and must call `readToken` once.

```
uv run dojo test react d22_render_performance ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — a shell with nothing to render

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. `DashboardShell({ onLeftRender, onRightRender })`
renders `Ticks: <n>` in a `role="status"` paragraph with a `Tick` button, an
input labelled `Search` with `Searching for <text>` beside it, and two panels
reading `Left panel` and `Right panel`. Ticking and typing must leave both
panels alone.

```
uv run dojo test react d22_render_performance ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — the table

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. `SortableTable({ rows, onSort, onRowRender })` renders
an input labelled `Filter`, a `Sort by name` button that flips the direction,
and one `<li>` per visible row containing the name — with ` *` appended once it
is starred — and a button reading `Star <name>`. Rows are sorted by name and
then filtered by the query. Typing must not re-sort, starring must not re-sort,
and starring one row must re-render that row only.

```
uv run dojo test react d22_render_performance ex8
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading — react/d22_render_performance

## Notes

Memoization is the second thing to reach for. The first is structure, and the
reason is worth stating plainly: a memo is a comparison on every render plus a
dependency array somebody has to keep honest for ever, while moving state down
or lifting content up removes the problem outright and cannot rot. Three moves
cover most of this set. State belongs to the smallest component that needs it,
because a render caused by a piece of state reaches everything the component
holding it renders. Content that does not depend on a component's state can be
handed to it as `children`, which arrives as the same element object each time
and lets React skip the subtree. And the cheapest render is the one that never
happens — a closed row, a row below the fold, or a state change that is not a
change at all. The last exercise is the counterweight: when the work really is
derived data and per-row state, memoization is the right tool, and it only pays
once every prop reaching the memoized component is stable.

## ex1

Tests lifting content up as `children`. The classic mistake is not seeing that
there is a problem: the panel is written inside the ticker because that is where
it appears on screen, and so it is re-created every time the ticker's own state
moves. The model answer builds the panel's element in a component with no state
and passes it down, so React compares the same element object against itself and
skips the subtree — no `memo` involved.

# Reading — react/d22_render_performance

## Notes

Memoization is the second thing to reach for. The first is structure, and the
reason is worth stating plainly: a memo is a comparison on every render plus a
dependency array somebody has to keep honest for ever, while moving state down
or lifting content up removes the problem outright and cannot rot. Three moves
cover most of this set. State belongs to the smallest component that needs it,
because a render caused by a piece of state reaches everything the component
holding it renders. Content that does not depend on a component's state can be
handed to it as `children`, which arrives as the same element object each time
and lets React skip the subtree. And the cheapest render is the one that never
happens — a closed row, a row below the fold, or a state change that is not a
change at all. The last exercise is the counterweight: when the work really is
derived data and per-row state, memoization is the right tool, and it only pays
once every prop reaching the memoized component is stable.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The panel is rendered by the component whose state keeps changing, so it is
re-created every time that state moves. Nothing about the panel depends on the
tick count — the only connection between them is where the JSX happens to be
written.

## Hint 2

Move the panel's JSX up into a component that has no state, and hand it to the
ticker as `children`. React compares the children element with the previous one
by identity, and a component that never re-renders keeps handing over the same
element — so the subtree is skipped.

## Hint 3

Note what you did *not* need: `memo`, `useMemo`, or a dependency array. This is
a structural fix, which means there is nothing to keep in step later.

## Hint 1

The panel is rendered by the component whose state keeps changing, so it is
re-created every time that state moves. Nothing about the panel depends on the
tick count — the only connection between them is where the JSX happens to be
written.

## Hint 2

Move the panel's JSX up into a component that has no state, and hand it to the
ticker as `children`. React compares the children element with the previous one
by identity, and a component that never re-renders keeps handing over the same
element — so the subtree is skipped.

## Hint 3

Note what you did *not* need: `memo`, `useMemo`, or a dependency array. This is
a structural fix, which means there is nothing to keep in step later.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Count the renders on mount: one showing `No session`, then the effect runs, sets
state, and a second one shows the token. The user sees the empty state flash
past, and nothing about reading the token needed to wait.

## Hint 2

An effect is for synchronising with something outside React *after* the screen
has been painted. Reading a value you already have is not that. `useState`
accepts a **function** as its initial state and calls it once, before the first
render — note that you pass the function itself rather than calling it.

Once the token can never be missing, the `null` branch of the render has
nothing to describe, and it can go too. A state that cannot hold a value is
simpler than one that can.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Count the renders on mount: one showing `No session`, then the effect runs, sets
state, and a second one shows the token. The user sees the empty state flash
past, and nothing about reading the token needed to wait.

## Hint 2

An effect is for synchronising with something outside React *after* the screen
has been painted. Reading a value you already have is not that. `useState`
accepts a **function** as its initial state and calls it once, before the first
render — note that you pass the function itself rather than calling it.

## Hint 3

Once the token can never be missing, the `null` branch of the render has
nothing to describe, and it can go too. A state that cannot hold a value is
simpler than one that can.

## Exercise 8 — the table

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. `SortableTable({ rows, onSort, onRowRender })` renders
an input labelled `Filter`, a `Sort by name` button that flips the direction,
and one `<li>` per visible row containing the name — with ` *` appended once it
is starred — and a button reading `Star <name>`. Rows are sorted by name and
then filtered by the query. Typing must not re-sort, starring must not re-sort,
and starring one row must re-render that row only.

```
uv run dojo test react d22_render_performance ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three separate things are wrong, and it is worth naming them before touching
anything: the sort runs on every render, the rows are not memoized at all, and
each row is handed a fresh `onStar` built inside the `map`.

## Hint 2

Sorting and filtering are two steps with two different sets of inputs. Give
each its own `useMemo` and be exact about the dependencies — the sort depends
on the rows and the direction, the filter depends on the sorted rows and the
query. Typing then cannot cost a sort.

## Hint 3

lessons.briefing:
# d23 — Component patterns (drill set)

Eight problems on the shape of the API a component offers, drawing on
`02_props_composition`, `10_custom_hooks` and `11_performance_patterns` at
once. Children and slots, compound components that find each other through a
context, render props, and behaviour extracted into a hook so the markup can be
anybody's.

The gate uses these components the way a colleague would — composing the parts
itself, in its own arrangement — and then checks the accessible DOM that comes
out. That is not decoration here: a tab that does not say it is selected and a
popover whose trigger is not wired to its content are the bugs, not the
styling.

## Exercise 1 — content, not a string

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `Callout({ tone, title, children })` renders a
`role="alert"` element when `tone` is `danger` and `role="status"` otherwise,
containing a level-3 heading with the `title` and then whatever it was given
between its tags — including markup.

```
uv run dojo test react d23_component_patterns ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — the behaviour, extracted

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `useDisclosure(initial?)` returns
`{ open, toggle, close }` and actually holds that state. `FaqItem({ question, answer })`
is built on it: a button reading the question, carrying `aria-expanded`, and
the answer in a paragraph while it is open. Two items on a page keep their own
state.

```
uv run dojo test react d23_component_patterns ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — parts that find each other

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `Tabs({ defaultTab, children })` with `Tabs.List`,
`Tabs.Tab` and `Tabs.Panel` attached to it. The list is a `role="tablist"`
named by its `label`; each tab is a `role="tab"` carrying `aria-selected`;
only the selected panel is rendered, as a `role="tabpanel"`. **No part is ever
given the selected tab as a prop** — the gate does not pass one.

```
uv run dojo test react d23_component_patterns ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — named by what is inside it

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `ProductCard` with `ProductCard.Media`, `ProductCard.Body`, `ProductCard.Title`
and `ProductCard.Actions`. The card is an `<article>`, the title a level-3 heading,
the actions a `<footer>` — and the article's **accessible name** is the title
written inside it. Two cards on one page must not collide.

```
uv run dojo test react d23_component_patterns ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — ids handed to the caller

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. `HintedField({ label, hint, children })` where `children` is
a **function** taking `{ id, describedBy }` and returning the control. The
label is bound to that id; the hint, when there is one, is rendered and becomes
the control's accessible description. With no hint, `describedBy` is
`undefined` and the control ends up with no `aria-describedby` at all.

```
uv run dojo test react d23_component_patterns ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — a decision that travels

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. `Toolbar({ label, disabled, children })` renders a
`role="toolbar"` with an accessible name; `ToolbarButton({ onClick, disabled, children })`
renders a button. A disabled toolbar disables every button inside it, however
deep, without anybody passing the flag down by hand — and a button may still be
disabled on its own account.

```
uv run dojo test react d23_component_patterns ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — the caller draws the row

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. `PickerList({ items, renderItem, empty })` renders one
`<li>` per item, each holding a button whose content is
`renderItem(item, picked)`. Clicking a row picks it — one at a time — and an
empty `items` renders the `empty` slot instead of a list.

```
uv run dojo test react d23_component_patterns ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — a trigger and its content

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. `Popover` with `Popover.Trigger` and
`Popover.Content`. The trigger carries `aria-expanded`, and while the popover
is open it carries `aria-controls` pointing at the content's id. The content is
rendered only while open. Opening moves focus to the first focusable element
inside it; `Escape` closes it and returns focus to the trigger.

```
uv run dojo test react d23_component_patterns ex8
```
