# Reading — react/d23_component_patterns

## Notes

Every problem here is the same question asked about a different component: what
does the caller have to know, and what can you decide for them? A `text` prop
decides that the content is a sentence; `children` decides nothing. A `selected`
prop on every tab makes the caller wire up something they should never have to
think about; a context inside the component does it invisibly. A render prop
gives the caller the markup and keeps the state — which only works if you hand
them the state at the moment you ask for the markup. And an extracted hook
splits the two halves cleanly: behaviour that any markup can use, markup that
any behaviour can drive. The accessibility work in this set is not a separate
subject, either. An id linking a label to a control, a trigger to its content,
a card to its title — those are exactly the pieces that a caller writing the
parts separately cannot supply, which is why the component that contains both
halves has to generate them with `useId` and pass them around itself.

## ex1

Tests the difference between a slot and children. The classic mistake is a
`text` prop, which looks fine for weeks and then somebody needs a link in the
message and there is nowhere to put it. The model answer renders `children` for
the body and keeps `title` as a named prop — the rule being that a slot is
right when there is exactly one thing in exactly one place, and children is
right when the answer is "whatever the caller needs".

## ex2

Tests extraction. The classic mistake is writing a hook that describes the
shape of the answer without holding any of it, so callers get a `toggle` that
does nothing — extracting behaviour means moving the `useState`, not
reproducing its signature. The model answer puts the state and the callbacks in
the hook and rebuilds the component on top of it, unchanged on screen, and adds
the `aria-expanded` a disclosure button owes its user.

## ex3

Tests compound components. The classic mistake is trying to pass the selected
tab to each part as a prop, which is exactly the prop-drilling the pattern
exists to avoid, and which the gate makes impossible by never passing one. The
model answer creates a context inside the module, provides it from `Tabs` and
reads it from `Tab` and `Panel`, keeping the context itself private so callers
only ever see the parts.

## ex4

Tests a compound component whose job is an id rather than state. The classic
mistake is leaving an `<article>` with no accessible name, which reads to a
screen reader as an unlabelled region among many. The name has to come from a
heading the caller writes inside, so an id travels down through a context and
the reference comes back up in `aria-labelledby` — and it comes from `useId`,
because two cards on one page with the same id both point at the first heading.

## ex5

Tests a render prop carrying the pieces the caller cannot know. The classic
mistakes are both about ids: a hard-coded one, which makes the second field on
the page steal the first one's label, and an `aria-describedby` handed over
even when there is no hint, which points at an element that does not exist. The
model answer generates the id with `useId`, derives the hint's id from it, and
passes `undefined` when there is nothing to describe — React then omits the
attribute entirely.

## ex6

Tests a decision that has to reach an unknown depth. The classic mistake is
passing `disabled` down by hand, which works for the buttons that exist today
and silently fails for the one somebody nests inside a group tomorrow. The model
answer publishes the flag on a context with a default of `false`, so a button
used outside a toolbar still works, and combines it with the button's own
`disabled` so that either reason is enough.

## ex7

Tests the division of labour a render prop makes possible. The classic mistake
is calling the render function without the information the caller needs — the
list knows which row is picked and hands over `false` anyway, so the caller can
never show it. The second, easy to miss, is accepting an `empty` slot and
rendering an empty `<ul>` instead: the caller has already written the words for
that state.

## ex8

Tests everything at once, which is what a real component library component
looks like. Three things have to travel between two components the caller wrote
separately: the open flag, the id linking trigger to content, and a ref to the
trigger. All three belong to the component containing both, published on a
context. And focus is two distinct moments — into the content when it opens,
back to the trigger when it closes, because the element that had focus is about
to be removed from the document and something has to catch it.

## Further reading

- [Passing props to a component](https://react.dev/learn/passing-props-to-a-component)
- [Passing data deeply with context](https://react.dev/learn/passing-data-deeply-with-context)
- [Reusing logic with custom hooks](https://react.dev/learn/reusing-logic-with-custom-hooks)
- [`useId` reference](https://react.dev/reference/react/useId)
- [WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices: tabs](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/tabs/)
- [MDN: `aria-describedby`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Attributes/aria-describedby)

Tests a decision that has to reach an unknown depth. The classic mistake is
passing `disabled` down by hand, which works for the buttons that exist today
and silently fails for the one somebody nests inside a group tomorrow. The model
answer publishes the flag on a context with a default of `false`, so a button
used outside a toolbar still works, and combines it with the button's own
`disabled` so that either reason is enough.

## ex7

Tests the division of labour a render prop makes possible. The classic mistake
is calling the render function without the information the caller needs — the
list knows which row is picked and hands over `false` anyway, so the caller can
never show it. The second, easy to miss, is accepting an `empty` slot and
rendering an empty `<ul>` instead: the caller has already written the words for
that state.

## ex8

Tests everything at once, which is what a real component library component
looks like. Three things have to travel between two components the caller wrote
separately: the open flag, the id linking trigger to content, and a ref to the
trigger. All three belong to the component containing both, published on a
context. And focus is two distinct moments — into the content when it opens,
back to the trigger when it closes, because the element that had focus is about
to be removed from the document and something has to catch it.

## Exercise 1 — content, not a string

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `Callout({ tone, title, children })` renders a
`role="alert"` element when `tone` is `danger` and `role="status"` otherwise,
containing a level-3 heading with the `title` and then whatever it was given
between its tags — including markup.

uv run dojo test react d23_component_patterns ex1

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The gate writes a whole `<button>` inside the callout. A `text` prop can carry
a sentence and nothing else — no emphasis, no link, no button — which is why
`children` exists in the first place.

## Hint 2

Render the `children` where the text used to go, and drop the `text` prop
entirely. Keep `title` as a prop: it is one specific thing in one specific
place, which is exactly when a named slot beats children.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Look at how the gate uses this: it never passes a `selected` prop to a tab or a
panel, and it never will — that is the deal a compound component offers. So the
parts have to learn which tab is selected from somewhere other than their props.

## Hint 2

A context created in this file, provided by `Tabs`, read by `Tab` and `Panel`.
Put both the selected id and the way to change it in the value, and keep the
context itself private to the module so callers only ever see the parts.

## Hint 3

The rest is ARIA, and it is not decoration: `role="tablist"` with a name,
`role="tab"` with `aria-selected` on every tab, `role="tabpanel"` on the one
panel that is showing — and only that one should be rendered.

## Exercise 4 — named by what is inside it

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `ProductCard` with `ProductCard.Media`, `ProductCard.Body`, `ProductCard.Title`
and `ProductCard.Actions`. The card is an `<article>`, the title a level-3 heading,
the actions a `<footer>` — and the article's **accessible name** is the title
written inside it. Two cards on one page must not collide.

```
uv run dojo test react d23_component_patterns ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Every part renders the right element and the card still has no accessible name.
An `<article>` gets one from `aria-labelledby` pointing at an element's id — and
the element that holds its name is written by the caller, inside it.

## Hint 2

So an id has to travel down from the card to the title, and the reference back
up. `useId` in the card, a context to carry it, and the title puts it on its
heading. The caller writes exactly the same JSX either way.

## Hint 3

The gate puts two cards on one page, which is why the id must come from `useId`
rather than a constant: two identical ids make both `aria-labelledby`
references point at the same heading.

## Exercise 5 — ids handed to the caller

a **function** taking `{ id, describedBy }` and returning the control. The

## Exercise 6 — a decision that travels

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. `Toolbar({ label, disabled, children })` renders a
`role="toolbar"` with an accessible name; `ToolbarButton({ onClick, disabled, children })`
renders a button. A disabled toolbar disables every button inside it, however
deep, without anybody passing the flag down by hand — and a button may still be
disabled on its own account.

```
uv run dojo test react d23_component_patterns ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The toolbar takes a `disabled` prop and does nothing with it. Passing it to
each button by hand would work here and would mean every future button — and
every button nested a level deeper — has to remember to accept and forward it.

## Hint 2

A context published by the toolbar and read by the button reaches any depth
without anybody passing anything. Give it a default of `false`, so a button
used outside a toolbar still works.

## Hint 3

A button can also be disabled on its own account. Both reasons count, and
neither should be able to turn the other off — which is one boolean expression
in the `disabled` attribute.

## Hint 1

The toolbar takes a `disabled` prop and does nothing with it. Passing it to
each button by hand would work here and would mean every future button — and
every button nested a level deeper — has to remember to accept and forward it.

## Hint 2

A context published by the toolbar and read by the button reaches any depth
without anybody passing anything. Give it a default of `false`, so a button
used outside a toolbar still works.

A button can also be disabled on its own account. Both reasons count, and
neither should be able to turn the other off — which is one boolean expression
in the `disabled` attribute.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — a trigger and its content

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. `Popover` with `Popover.Trigger` and
`Popover.Content`. The trigger carries `aria-expanded`, and while the popover
is open it carries `aria-controls` pointing at the content's id. The content is
rendered only while open. Opening moves focus to the first focusable element
inside it; `Escape` closes it and returns focus to the trigger.

```
uv run dojo test react d23_component_patterns ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Everything this exercise wants is a connection between two components the
caller wrote separately: the open flag, the id linking them, and a ref to the
trigger so focus can come back. All three belong to the one component that
contains them both, published through a context.

## Hint 2

The trigger needs `aria-expanded` and, while the content exists,
`aria-controls` pointing at the content's id — `useId` in `Popover` is where
that id comes from. Set `aria-controls` only while it is open, or it points at
nothing.

## Hint 3

Focus is the hard half, and it is two separate moments. Opening: an effect
keyed on `open` finds the first focusable element inside the content and
focuses it. Closing: the element that had focus is about to be removed, so the
close handler sends focus back to the trigger — which is why `Popover` keeps a
ref to it rather than the trigger keeping one for itself.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Everything this exercise wants is a connection between two components the
caller wrote separately: the open flag, the id linking them, and a ref to the
trigger so focus can come back. All three belong to the one component that
contains them both, published through a context.

## Hint 2

The trigger needs `aria-expanded` and, while the content exists,
`aria-controls` pointing at the content's id — `useId` in `Popover` is where
that id comes from. Set `aria-controls` only while it is open, or it points at
nothing.

## Hint 3

Focus is the hard half, and it is two separate moments. Opening: an effect
keyed on `open` finds the first focusable element inside the content and
focuses it. Closing: the element that had focus is about to be removed, so the
close handler sends focus back to the trigger — which is why `Popover` keeps a
ref to it rather than the trigger keeping one for itself.

lessons.briefing:
# d24 — The mixed gauntlet (drill set)

The last set. Every problem here is two or three of the track's ideas at once,
and none of them announces which — that is the whole exercise. A controlled
input whose validity is derived; a list whose order is derived; a timer that
has to restart and a callback that has to be current; a context feeding a
request that can be overtaken; a hook with a reducer inside it; a queue where
every item has its own clock; a debounce that still needs a race guard; a
compound component that also has to manage focus.

The instruments are the ones used all the way through Volume 2: requests are
injected and resolved by hand, anything timed uses fake timers with
`fireEvent`, and every assertion is about something a user could see, hear, or
tab to.

If a problem stalls, the honest move is to name the ideas in it before writing
anything — the reading notes for this set are written the same way.

## Exercise 1 — the code, not the keystrokes

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `VoucherBox({ onRedeem })` renders an input labelled
`Voucher` showing exactly what was typed, a `role="status"` paragraph reading
`Ready` or `Keep typing`, and a `Redeem` button. The **code** is the typed
value trimmed and upper-cased; it is ready at five characters or more, and that
is what `Redeem` sends.

```
uv run dojo test react d24_mixed_gauntlet ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — one lead at a time

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. `RosterBoard({ people })` renders one `<li>` per
person containing their name — with ` (lead)` appended for the lead — and a
button reading `Promote <name>`. The lead is shown first and everybody else
keeps the order they arrived in; promoting somebody else moves the title; a
`Reset` button clears it. An empty roster renders `Nobody on the roster` in a
`role="status"` paragraph and no list.

```
uv run dojo test react d24_mixed_gauntlet ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — the clock that restarts

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `IdleWatcher({ timeoutMs, onIdle })` renders
`Active` or `Idle` in a `role="status"` paragraph and an `Activity` button.
`timeoutMs` after the last activity — not after mounting — it goes idle and
calls `onIdle` once. It uses whichever `onIdle` it has at that moment, and it
leaves no timer running once it is idle or once it is gone.

```
uv run dojo test react d24_mixed_gauntlet ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — the profile for this session

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `SessionProvider({ userId, children })` publishes the
current user id. `ProfilePane({ loadProfile })` takes **no** id as a prop: it
reads it from the session, calls `loadProfile(userId)`, shows
`Loading profile` in a `role="status"` paragraph until the answer arrives and
the name in a level-2 heading afterwards. When the session changes, the answer
to the old one must change nothing, whenever it turns up.

```
uv run dojo test react d24_mixed_gauntlet ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — the cart is the hook

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. `useCart()` returns `{ lines, total, add, remove }`,
with a reducer inside it: `add` raises an existing line's quantity or starts a
new one, `remove` lowers it and drops the line at zero, `total` is the sum of
price times quantity, and `add` and `remove` are the same functions for the
life of the hook. `CartPanel({ products })` is only the markup — `Add <name>`
buttons, `<name> x<qty>` in `<li>`s, and `Total: <n>` in a `role="status"`
paragraph.

```
uv run dojo test react d24_mixed_gauntlet ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — every toast on its own clock

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. `ToastQueue({ autoDismissMs })` renders a `Notify`
button which adds a toast reading `Message <n>`, numbered from 1 and never
reusing a number, each with a `Dismiss <message>` button. A toast disappears
`autoDismissMs` after **it** appeared — not after the queue last changed — and
dismissing one by hand or leaving the page cancels its timer.

```
uv run dojo test react d24_mixed_gauntlet ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — quiet, then ask

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. `SearchWorkbench({ search })` renders an input
labelled `Query`, a `role="status"` paragraph reading `Idle`, `Searching` or
`<n> results`, and the results as `<li>`s. `search(query)` is called 300ms
after the **last** keystroke and not before — and the answer to a query the
user has moved on from must never reach the screen.

```
uv run dojo test react d24_mixed_gauntlet ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — one step at a time

Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. `Wizard` with `Wizard.Step({ title, children })` and
`Wizard.Nav()`. Only the current step is rendered, its `title` as a level-2
heading. `Nav` renders `Step <n> of <total>` in a `role="status"` paragraph and
`Back` and `Next` buttons, each disabled at its end — and it is never told the
step or the total by the caller. When the step changes, focus moves to the new
step's heading.

```
uv run dojo test react d24_mixed_gauntlet ex8
```

# Reading — react/d24_mixed_gauntlet

## Notes

The point of a cumulative set is that nothing tells you which idea is being
tested, which is the only condition under which you find out whether you have
learned them. Read back over the eight and the same three questions decide most
of the code. **What is really state?** — not the code, not the order of the
roster, not the total of a cart, not the validity of a form; those are all
questions you can answer from something smaller. **What does this effect
depend on, and what does it own?** — a timer that restarts, a subscription that
must not, a request that can be overtaken, a toast with a deadline of its own.
And **who needs to know?** — the id linking a trigger to its content, the
session a request belongs to, the step a nav is looking at, none of which the
caller should have to pass by hand. Almost every bug in Volume 2 has been one
of those three answered wrongly, which is worth more than any individual API.

## ex1

Controlled inputs, normalisation and derived state at once. The classic mistake
is normalising in the change handler and storing the result, which means the
user cannot type a space and watches their cursor jump; the second is judging
the raw string, so `"  ab  "` looks like six characters of voucher code. The
model answer keeps the typed value in state exactly as typed and derives the
code — and everything downstream, the message and the disabled button, is a
question about the derived value rather than about the box.

## ex2

List state, immutable updates and the empty case. The classic mistakes are a
list of leads that only ever grows, so two people are lead at once, and an
order kept in state that goes stale when the roster prop changes. The model
answer stores one thing — who leads — and derives the order from it, which
makes both problems unrepresentable, and remembers that an empty list is a
state with something to say rather than an empty `<ul>`.

## ex3

Timers, cleanup and the latest-callback ref. The classic mistake is an effect
with an empty dependency array, which starts the countdown once and never hears
about the activity that should restart it — the version of this bug in
production logs people out while they are typing. The model answer makes the
activity counter a dependency, so React's cleanup cancels the old timer for
free, stops counting once it is idle, and reads `onIdle` from a ref so the
countdown does not restart every time the parent re-renders.

## ex4

Context and a race. The classic mistake is fetching from a value that arrives
by context and forgetting that context values change like any other prop: two
requests end up in flight, and the slow answer to the previous session paints
one user's name over another's. The model answer keeps the guard where it
belongs — a `let` inside the effect body, flipped by the cleanup — and puts the
throw for a missing provider after every hook has been called.

## ex5

A hook, a reducer inside it, and derived state. The classic mistakes are a
total kept in state that nothing updates, and a hook that hands out new
functions on every render so every consumer of it re-renders for nothing. The
model answer computes the total from the lines while rendering and wraps the
two actions in `useCallback` with empty dependency arrays — possible because
`dispatch` is guaranteed stable — leaving the panel as pure markup that the
gate does not even need in order to test the cart.

## ex6

Per-item lifetimes. The classic mistake is one timer for the whole queue, which
cannot express "a second after *it* appeared" and cuts short every toast that
arrived late. The model answer gives each toast a component with its own effect
and its own timeout, which also makes dismissing by hand and unmounting fall
out of the same cleanup — and it keeps ids in a counter that only goes up, so a
number is never reused by a toast that arrives after one was dismissed.

## ex7

Debounce and race together, which is the pairing people get half right. The
classic mistake is a `setTimeout` with no cleanup: it delays every keystroke
rather than replacing it, so the requests all still go out, just late. The
second is assuming the debounce removed the race — it made it rarer, and a slow
answer to an abandoned query still arrives after a fast answer to the current
one. Two effects, two cleanups, and each one does exactly one job.

## ex8

A compound component that also has to manage focus. The parts have to find the
current step, the total and the two moves without the caller passing anything,
which is a context; only one step may render, which means the wizard has to
separate the steps from the rest of what it was handed. And the piece that is
invisible until somebody uses a keyboard: changing step removes the element
that had focus, so the new step's heading catches it — with `tabIndex={-1}`,
because a heading is not focusable otherwise.

## Further reading

- [You might not need an effect](https://react.dev/learn/you-might-not-need-an-effect)
- [Synchronizing with effects](https://react.dev/learn/synchronizing-with-effects)
- [Choosing the state structure](https://react.dev/learn/choosing-the-state-structure)
- [Scaling up with reducer and context](https://react.dev/learn/scaling-up-with-reducer-and-context)
- [Reusing logic with custom hooks](https://react.dev/learn/reusing-logic-with-custom-hooks)
- [MDN: `HTMLElement.focus()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/HTMLElement/focus)

rather than replacing it, so the requests all still go out, just late. The
second is assuming the debounce removed the race — it made it rarer, and a slow
answer to an abandoned query still arrives after a fast answer to the current
one. Two effects, two cleanups, and each one does exactly one job.

## ex8

A compound component that also has to manage focus. The parts have to find the
current step, the total and the two moves without the caller passing anything,
which is a context; only one step may render, which means the wizard has to
separate the steps from the rest of what it was handed. And the piece that is
invisible until somebody uses a keyboard: changing step removes the element
that had focus, so the new step's heading catches it — with `tabIndex={-1}`,
because a heading is not focusable otherwise.

## Exercise 1 — the code, not the keystrokes

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. `VoucherBox({ onRedeem })` renders an input labelled
`Voucher` showing exactly what was typed, a `role="status"` paragraph reading
`Ready` or `Keep typing`, and a `Redeem` button. The **code** is the typed
value trimmed and upper-cased; it is ready at five characters or more, and that
is what `Redeem` sends.

```
uv run dojo test react d24_mixed_gauntlet ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

There are two strings here and the stub only has one. What the user typed
belongs in the box exactly as they typed it; what the server is going to be
sent is that string trimmed and upper-cased. Everything else — the message, the
disabled button — is a question about the second one.

## Hint 2

Normalising inside `onChange` and storing that is the tempting shortcut, and it
means the user cannot type a space at all. Keep the raw value in state and
derive the code during render.

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `IdleWatcher({ timeoutMs, onIdle })` renders
`Active` or `Idle` in a `role="status"` paragraph and an `Activity` button.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The button already records that something happened — and the effect's empty
dependency array means the countdown never hears about it. React runs the
previous cleanup before re-running an effect, so a dependency that changes on
every activity is exactly "cancel the old timer and start a new one".

## Hint 2

Once it has gone idle there is nothing left to count, and saying so in the
effect is what leaves no timer running at the end. That means the idle flag is
a dependency too.

## Hint 3

The last piece: the parent may hand over a different `onIdle` between one
activity and the next, and the timer that eventually fires has to call the
current one. Listing it in the array would restart the countdown on every
render — a ref updated by its own effect will not.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The button already records that something happened — and the effect's empty
dependency array means the countdown never hears about it. React runs the
previous cleanup before re-running an effect, so a dependency that changes on
every activity is exactly "cancel the old timer and start a new one".

## Hint 2

Once it has gone idle there is nothing left to count, and saying so in the
effect is what leaves no timer running at the end. That means the idle flag is
a dependency too.

## Hint 3

The last piece: the parent may hand over a different `onIdle` between one
activity and the next, and the timer that eventually fires has to call the
current one. Listing it in the array would restart the countdown on every
render — a ref updated by its own effect will not.

## Exercise 4 — the profile for this session

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. `SessionProvider({ userId, children })` publishes the
current user id. `ProfilePane({ loadProfile })` takes **no** id as a prop: it
reads it from the session, calls `loadProfile(userId)`, shows
`Loading profile` in a `role="status"` paragraph until the answer arrives and
the name in a level-2 heading afterwards. When the session changes, the answer
to the old one must change nothing, whenever it turns up.

```
uv run dojo test react d24_mixed_gauntlet ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The context part already works: the pane takes no id as a prop and asks the
session for it. What is missing is what happens when the session changes while
a request for the old one is still out.

## Hint 2

Two requests, and the first one answers last. The effect that started it is
long retired, but its `.then` closure is not — promises have no cancel button,
so the callback has to be able to tell that nobody wants its answer.

## Hint 3

A `let` declared inside the effect body, flipped by the cleanup, checked before
`setProfile`. One flag per run, which is why it cannot be a ref: a ref would be
one flag shared by every session this component ever shows.

One effect in the queue can only ever express one deadline, and it currently
clears everything at once — so a toast that arrived half a second later gets
half a second less. Say the requirement out loud: each toast disappears a

unmounting the queue.

Watch the row's dependency array. The callback it uses to remove itself comes
from the queue, and if that is a new function on every render the row will
re-arm its timer every render and never expire. `useCallback` in the queue
fixes it.

## Hint 1

One effect in the queue can only ever express one deadline, and it currently
clears everything at once — so a toast that arrived half a second later gets
half a second less. Say the requirement out loud: each toast disappears a
second after **it** appeared.

## Hint 2

That is a per-toast lifetime, so it wants a per-toast component with a
per-toast effect. Give the row its own `useEffect` with its own `setTimeout`,
and a cleanup that clears it — which then also covers dismissing by hand and
unmounting the queue.

## Hint 3

Watch the row's dependency array. The callback it uses to remove itself comes
from the queue, and if that is a new function on every render the row will
re-arm its timer every render and never expire. `useCallback` in the queue
fixes it.

uv run dojo test react d24_mixed_gauntlet ex7

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The two-state split — what is in the box, what has been asked — is already
right, and the debounce is not a debounce. A `setTimeout` with nothing to
cancel it delays every keystroke by 300ms and sends all of them.

## Hint 2

Return a cleanup that clears the pending timeout. React runs it before the next
run of the effect, so each keystroke cancels the request the previous one was
about to make.

## Hint 3

Then the second effect. Debouncing makes a race rarer and cannot remove it: a
slow answer to an old query still arrives after a fast answer to a new one.
That needs the flag-in-a-cleanup guard, in the effect that does the searching.

lessons.briefing:
# i1 — Interview concepts

The main course is behind you. This part is about being able to *say* what you
know, under time pressure, to somebody who is deciding whether to hire you.

Those are different skills. You can fix a stale closure and still fumble the
sentence that explains it. Interviewers are listening for the mechanism —
"the callback was created during one render and captured that render's
`count`" — and a candidate who says it plainly reads as senior even when the
code takes them two minutes.

So this lesson is mostly `reading.md`, which carries **a bank of 55 questions
with model answers**, grouped by topic, each tagged by how often it actually
gets asked:

| tag | meaning |
|---|---|
| ⭐⭐⭐ | expect it in most React interviews. Know it cold. |
| ⭐⭐ | common, especially for mid-level and above. |
| ⭐ | asked when the conversation goes deep, or by a specialist. |

Each answer is written the way a strong candidate would actually say it — three
to six sentences, one concrete example, and the **follow-up** the interviewer
will reach for next. Every question names the lesson that teaches it, so a
question you cannot answer turns straight into "redo `06_effects`".

The five graded exercises here are the concepts that can be checked in code:
four bugs of the kind interviewers put in front of you, and one code review.
Each one compiles and is wrong, and none of them takes more than a few lines to
fix — because the point is the diagnosis.

## How to use the question bank

Do not read it like a document. Work it like flashcards:

1. Open `reading.md` — `uv run dojo read react i1_interview_concepts` — and
   cover everything below a question.
2. **Say the answer out loud.** Not in your head. The gap between "I know this"
   and "I can say this" is the entire reason people fail interviews they were
   qualified for, and it only closes by talking.
3. Uncover, and compare. Did you name the mechanism, or only the fix? Did you
   have an example ready? Could you answer the follow-up?
4. Mark the ⭐⭐⭐ questions you fumbled and come back to them tomorrow. The
   review ladder does this for the exercises; do it yourself for the prose.

A pass through all 55 takes about an hour. A pass through the ⭐⭐⭐ subset
takes fifteen minutes, and is the thing to do the morning of an interview.

## Exercise 1 — the stale-closure counter

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`.

> *"This counter is supposed to tick up every second. It stops at 1. Talk me
> through why, then fix it."*

Answer the "why" out loud before you edit anything — that is what is being
marked. Then make it count 3 after three seconds, and keep going.

```
uv run dojo test react i1_interview_concepts ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — index keys

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`.

> *"Type something into the Zebra row, then hit Sort. Where did your text go,
> and why?"*

Each row has an uncontrolled text box. Sorting must not move what the user
typed into a different row.

```
uv run dojo test react i1_interview_concepts ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — controlled vs uncontrolled

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`.

> *"Reset does nothing. React clearly knows the value — the character count is
> right. So who is deciding what the box displays?"*

After Reset, the field must be empty and the counter must read `0 characters`.

```
uv run dojo test react i1_interview_concepts ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — the effect that should not exist

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`.

> *"What's wrong with this component? It works."*

It does work, and it renders twice for every change, showing `Total: 0` for a
frame. The gate counts renders and requires exactly one per change.

```
uv run dojo test react i1_interview_concepts ex4
```

## Review — read this effect back to me

`review1/solution.tsx`.

> *"Code review this for me. Anything you'd change?"*

There are two defects and they compound. The gate re-renders the component and
then unmounts it, checking how many times one keystroke fires the handler.

```
uv run dojo test react i1_interview_concepts review1
```

# Reading — react/i1_interview_concepts ## Notes This page is a bank of 55 questions with model answers, grouped by topic and tagged ⭐ to ⭐⭐⭐ by how often they actually come up. Work it out loud, with the answers covered, rather than reading it through — the skill being practised is speaking, not recognising. Every question names the lesson that teaches it, so anything you fumble converts directly into a lesson to redo. The ⭐⭐⭐ subset is about fifteen minutes and is the right thing to run through on the morning of an interview. ## The question bank ### Rendering, JSX and reconciliation **1. What is JSX, really?** ⭐⭐⭐ *(01_components_jsx)* JSX is syntax sugar that a compiler rewrites into function calls — `

hi

` becomes roughly `jsx("p", { id: "x", children: "hi" })`, which returns a plain object describing an element. Nothing is parsed at runtime and no DOM is created until React commits. That is why JSX can be stored in a variable, returned from a function or passed as a prop, and why attributes are camelCase JavaScript property names (`className`, `htmlFor`). *Follow-up: "so what is the difference between an element and a component?" — a component is the function; an element is one object describing one invocation of it, with particular props.* **2. What is the virtual DOM?** ⭐⭐⭐ *(04_lists_conditional)* It is the tree of those lightweight element objects. On a re-render React builds a new tree, compares it with the previous one, and applies the minimal set of real DOM operations. The value is not that it is faster than hand-written DOM code — it is not — but that you get to describe the UI declaratively and let React work out the transitions. Be careful not to oversell it: "the virtual DOM is fast" is a red flag answer. *Follow-up: "is it always faster than direct DOM manipulation?" — no; it is usually fast enough, and the win is in maintainability.* **3. What does reconciliation actually do?** ⭐⭐⭐ *(04_lists_conditional)* It walks the old and new trees together, position by position. Two rules do most of the work: if the element *type* at a position changed, the whole subtree is thrown away and rebuilt from scratch — state and all; and within a list of children, items are matched by `key`. Everything surprising about React state disappearing or persisting comes from one of those two rules. *Follow-up: "what happens to state when a component's type changes?" — it is destroyed, because React unmounts the old instance.* **4. Why does React re-render children when a parent re-renders?** ⭐⭐ *(11_performance_patterns)* Because comparing props costs time and memory, and for most components the comparison is more expensive than just re-running the function. React chose the default that is right most of the time and made the opt-out explicit with `memo`. Re-rendering is not repainting either — React still only touches the DOM nodes that actually differ. *Follow-up: "when is that default a problem?" — when render does expensive work, or when a big subtree re-renders because of unrelated state.* **5. Why must a component return a single root element?** ⭐ *(01_components_jsx)* Because it is a function and a function returns one value. When you genuinely need siblings with no wrapper — inside a `
`, a ``, or a CSS grid — use a fragment, `<>…`, which groups children and renders nothing itself. *Follow-up: "how do you put a key on a fragment?" — use the long form, ``; the shorthand cannot take one.* **6. What does it mean that a component must be pure?** ⭐⭐ *(11_performance_patterns)* Given the same props and state it must produce the same JSX, and it must not do anything observable while rendering — no mutating props, no writing to variables outside itself, no network calls, no DOM writes. Every optimisation React ships is licensed by that purity: bailouts, memoization, concurrent rendering, and Strict Mode's deliberate double-render in development. *Follow-up: "why does React call my component twice in dev?" — to surface impure renders.* **7. Why do component names have to be capitalised?** ⭐ *(01_components_jsx)* The compiler decides between "HTML tag" and "your component" by the first character. `
` compiles to the string `"header"`; `
` compiles to a reference to the variable. A lowercase component name therefore fails silently — React renders an unknown element and nothing appears. *Follow-up: "what if the component is a property, like `obj.Thing`?" — dotted names are always treated as components regardless of case.* ### State **8. Why does calling `setCount(count + 1)` twice only add one?** ⭐⭐⭐ *(03_state_events)* Because `count` is a snapshot of the render that created the handler; it does not change while the handler runs. Both calls therefore enqueue "become 1", and the second is identical to the first. Passing a function instead — `setCount(c => c + 1)` — enqueues a *recipe*, and React applies the recipes in order against the accumulating result. *Follow-up: "when should you always use the updater form?" — whenever the next state is computed from the current state.* **9. What is batching, and what changed in React 18?** ⭐⭐ *(03_state_events)* React collects every state update produced by one event and applies them together, rendering once. Before React 18 that only applied inside React's own event handlers, so updates inside `setTimeout` or a `.then` rendered immediately and separately; React 18 made batching automatic everywhere. *Follow-up: "how do you opt out?" — `flushSync`, which forces a synchronous render and should be rare.* **10. Why can't you mutate state directly?** ⭐⭐⭐ *(03_state_events)* React decides whether anything changed by comparing the new value with the old using `Object.is`. `items.push(x)` returns a length and leaves the reference unchanged, so React concludes nothing happened and renders nothing. Replace instead: `setItems(prev => [...prev, x])`. *Follow-up: "what's the symptom of getting this wrong?" — a UI that only updates when something else forces a render.* **11. `useState` vs `useReducer` — how do you choose?** ⭐⭐ *(09_context_reducer)* Not by how many fields. Reach for a reducer when the *transitions have rules* — when one action changes several things together, when the same change is triggered from several places, or when the logic is worth testing on its own. A reducer is a pure function you can call directly in a test, and `dispatch` is guaranteed stable, so it never needs to appear in a dependency array. *Follow-up: "is `useReducer` faster?" — no; it is a structural choice, not a performance one.* **12. What is the lazy initialiser and when do you need it?** ⭐⭐ *(10_custom_hooks)* `useState(() => expensive())` runs the function only on the first render; `useState(expensive())` evaluates on every render and throws the result away. Use it whenever the initial value costs something — parsing JSON out of `localStorage`, building a large structure. *Follow-up: "does the same apply to `useRef`?" — `useRef` has no lazy form, so the usual trick is `if (ref.current === null) ref.current = create()`.* **13. How do you reset a component's state when a prop changes?** ⭐⭐ *(04_lists_conditional)* Give it a different `key`. Changing the key makes React unmount the old instance and mount a fresh one, which is a complete, honest reset. The alternative people reach for — an effect that watches the prop and calls setters — renders twice and is easy to get subtly wrong. *Follow-up: "when is the effect version right?" — when only part of the state should reset.* **14. What state should you not store?** ⭐⭐ *(03_state_events)* Anything you can compute during render from props or other state: a filtered list, a total, whether the form is valid. Every derived value you store is a second copy that can go stale, and keeping it in step is work you took on for nothing. Store the source; derive the view. *Follow-up: "what about expensive derivations?" — compute them during render and wrap in `useMemo` if profiling says so.* **15. What is "lifting state up"?** ⭐⭐ *(11_performance_patterns)* Moving a piece of state to the nearest common ancestor of the components that need it, then passing the value down and a callback up. It is the standard fix for two siblings that must agree. The counter-move matters just as much: state that only one subtree uses should be pushed *down* into it, so unrelated siblings stop re-rendering. *Follow-up: "what's the cost of lifting?" — everything under the new owner re-renders on every change.* ### Props, composition and structure **16. What is prop drilling and what are the fixes, in order?** ⭐⭐ *(09_context_reducer)* Passing a prop through components that do not use it. In order of preference: restructure so the data is nearer its consumer; pass JSX down as `children`, which frequently deletes the problem entirely; then context; then a store. The common mistake is jumping to a global store first. *Follow-up: "is two levels of drilling a problem?" — no; it is normal and explicit.* **17. Composition versus configuration — what's the difference?** ⭐⭐ *(02_props_composition)* Configuration is ``; composition is `Save} />`. Configuration works until somebody wants two buttons and an icon, at which point you are in the business of predicting everything callers might want. Composition never has that problem because the component was never describing the content. *Follow-up: "when is a config prop right?" — when it is a decision the component owns, like `max` or `variant`.* **18. Why should a wrapper component spread `...rest`?** ⭐ *(02_props_composition)* Because swallowing props people expect — `className`, `aria-*`, `data-*`, `onBlur`, `ref` — is how design-system components get forked. `...rest` is a one-line insurance policy, and spread order decides whether callers can override your defaults. *Follow-up: "what breaks if you spread unknown props onto a DOM element?" — React warns about unrecognised attributes.* **19. Why are props read-only?** ⭐⭐ *(02_props_composition)* Because data flows one way: a child cannot rewrite its parent's variables any more than a function can rewrite its caller's. Mutating a prop object often appears to work and then fails invisibly — another holder of the same object sees the change with no re-render, or a memoized child skips an update because the reference did not change. *Follow-up: "how does a child change something above it?" — the parent passes a function down.* **20. What is `children` and is it special?** ⭐⭐ *(02_props_composition)* It is an ordinary prop with syntax: whatever sits between a component's tags is put on the props object under that name. `} />` is legal and identical. It is typed `ReactNode`, which covers elements, strings, numbers, arrays, `null`, `undefined` and `false`. *Follow-up: "what about `React.Children` and `cloneElement`?" — legacy; they couple you to the exact shape callers pass.* ### Lists and keys **21. Why do lists need keys?** ⭐⭐⭐ *(04_lists_conditional)* So React can tell which item is which between renders. Keys decide which DOM nodes and component instances are reused, moved, created or destroyed — and therefore which pieces of state, focus and uncontrolled input values survive a reorder. Without them React falls back to position and warns. *Follow-up: "unique where?" — among siblings, not globally.* **22. Why is the array index a bad key?** ⭐⭐⭐ *(04_lists_conditional)* Because position is not identity. Prepend an item and every index now points at a different thing, so React concludes row 0 is the same row with new text and *reuses its DOM node* — updating what it manages (text, attributes) and leaving what the DOM manages (an uncontrolled input's value, focus, scroll) attached to the wrong item. The correct answer names that mechanism rather than saying "it's bad practice". *Follow-up: "when is an index key fine?" — a list that never reorders, filters or inserts except at the end, whose items hold no state.* **23. Why not `key={Math.random()}`?** ⭐⭐ *(04_lists_conditional)* It is unique but not stable, so every render looks like a completely new set of items. React destroys and rebuilds the entire list every time, losing state and focus and doing the maximum possible work. *Follow-up: "where should an id come from when the data has none?" — generate it where the item is created, not during render.* **24. Is `key` a prop?** ⭐ *(04_lists_conditional)* No. React consumes it and it never appears in `props`. If the component also needs the identifier, pass it twice: ``. *Follow-up: "what else is like that?" — `ref` was, until React 19 made it a normal prop for function components.* **25. Why does `{count && }` sometimes render a `0`?** ⭐⭐⭐ *(04_lists_conditional)* Because `&&` returns its left operand when that operand is falsy, and React renders `0` — it only skips `false`, `null` and `undefined`. `0`, `""` and `NaN` are falsy but perfectly renderable. Fix by making the left side a real boolean: `count > 0 && …`. *Follow-up: "what about `items.length &&`?" — same bug, more common.* ### Effects **26. What is `useEffect` for?** ⭐⭐⭐ *(06_effects)* Synchronising your component with something outside React — the document, a subscription, a timer, a server. The framing matters, because it answers most "should this be an effect" questions on its own: if there is no external system, there is probably no effect. *Follow-up: "name three things people put in effects that shouldn't be" — deriving data for rendering, resetting state on a prop change, and reacting to a user event.* **27. Explain the dependency array honestly.** ⭐⭐⭐ *(06_effects)* It is a claim: "this effect reads exactly these values, and if none of them changed, running it again would produce the same result." Omitted means run after every render; `[]` means run once on mount; `[a, b]` means re-run when `a` or `b` changes by `Object.is`. Every value from inside the component that the effect reads belongs in it. *Follow-up: "what happens if you lie?" — either a stale closure or an infinite loop.* **28. What is a stale closure?** ⭐⭐⭐ *(06_effects)* A function created during one render that keeps reading that render's props and state forever. The classic is `setInterval(() => setCount(count + 1), 1000)` with `[]` deps: the callback captured `count` at `0`, so every tick computes `0 + 1` and the counter freezes at 1. The fix is usually to stop reading the value — `setCount(c => c + 1)` describes a change instead of capturing a value. *Follow-up: "what would adding `count` to the deps cost?" — the interval is destroyed and recreated every second, so the cadence drifts.* **29. When does a cleanup function run?** ⭐⭐ *(06_effects)* Before every re-run of the effect, and once more on unmount. The cleanup belongs to the render that created it, so it closes over that render's values — which is why the cleanup for a `Saved` message clears `Saved`, not the new one. *Follow-up: "so is it the unmount handler?" — no; it is the undo for one particular run.* **30. Why does React run effects twice in development?** ⭐⭐ *(06_effects)* Strict Mode mounts, runs effects, runs cleanups, and runs effects again, to prove your effect can be run twice safely. An effect that opens something and never closes it fails that test — which is exactly the bug it is designed to surface. *Follow-up: "how do you fix a double-fetch on mount?" — write the cleanup that ignores or aborts the first request; do not add a ref guard.* **31. `useEffect` vs `useLayoutEffect`?** ⭐⭐ *(06_effects)* Both run after the commit; `useLayoutEffect` runs *before* the browser paints and blocks it. Use it only when you must measure and adjust the DOM without the user seeing an intermediate state — positioning a tooltip, preventing a scroll jump. Default to `useEffect`; a visible flicker is the signal to switch. *Follow-up: "what's the downside?" — it blocks painting, and it does not run on the server.* **32. Should this go in an effect or an event handler?** ⭐⭐⭐ *(06_effects)* If it happened *because the user did a specific thing*, it belongs in the handler — sending analytics, POSTing a form, showing a toast. If it is about keeping something in sync with the current state, whoever caused it, it is an effect. Putting event logic in an effect makes it fire in situations you did not intend, such as a remount. *Follow-up: "where does 'fetch when the id changes' go?" — an effect, because the id can change for reasons other than a click.* **33. What is the exhaustive-deps lint rule and should you disable it?** ⭐⭐ *(06_effects)* It statically works out what your effect reads and requires those values in the array. It is essentially never wrong about what is read, though it can be wrong about what you *want* — and the right response then is to change the code, not to silence the rule. Every codebase littered with disable comments has an undiscovered stale-closure bug. *Follow-up: "how do you avoid needing a dependency?" — updater functions, refs, or moving the value out of the component.* ### Data fetching **34. Walk me through fetching data in a component.** ⭐⭐⭐ *(07_data_fetching)* Three states, not one: loading, success and error, all of which the user must be able to see. Kick the request off in an effect keyed on whatever identifies it, store the result in state, and stop the spinner on both paths — `.finally` makes that hard to forget. A component that renders only its happy path shows a blank box on a slow connection and forever on a 500. *Follow-up: "what's missing from that?" — cancellation and races.* **35. What is the race condition in data fetching?** ⭐⭐⭐ *(07_data_fetching)* Two requests in flight, and the slower one answers last. Nothing about React is wrong — the `.then` was scheduled before the effect was cleaned up, and promises cannot be un-started. *Follow-up: "how do you fix it?" — see the next question.* **36. What is context, and what is it not?** ⭐⭐⭐ *(09_context_reducer)* It is a lookup: `useContext(C)` walks up the tree and returns the value of the nearest provider. It holds nothing itself — the state lives in whatever component renders the provider. It is not a state manager: no selectors, no caching, no devtools, and every consumer re-renders when the value changes. *Follow-up: "so when is it right?" — values that are tree-wide and change rarely: theme, locale, current user, dispatch.* **47. Why is `value={{ user, logout }}` a bug?** ⭐⭐ *(09_context_reducer)* It is a new object on every render of the provider, so `Object.is` always fails and every consumer re-renders even when nothing changed. `useMemo` it, or split into two contexts — one for the value and one for the stable `dispatch`, so components that only dispatch never re-render at all. *Follow-up: "does `memo` on the consumer help?" — no; memo compares props, and context is not a prop.* **48. How do you make a context impossible to misuse?** ⭐⭐ *(09_context_reducer)* Default it to `null`, export a `useThing()` hook that throws a named error when the value is `null`, and do not export the context object. A missing provider becomes a loud error naming what to add, instead of a component that silently renders a plausible default — and TypeScript narrows the value for every consumer for free. *Follow-up: "what does the default argument to `createContext` actually mean?" — the value when there is no provider, not an initial value.* **49. When do you reach for Redux/Zustand/Jotai?** ⭐⭐ *(09_context_reducer)* When client state is large, frequently changing, and read by many components in different parts of the tree — because those libraries let a component subscribe to a *slice*, which context cannot do. If the state in question is really server data, a data-fetching library is the better answer. *Follow-up: "could you build a simple store yourself?" — yes, with `useSyncExternalStore`.* ### Performance **50. What does `memo` compare, and when does it do nothing?** ⭐⭐⭐ *(11_performance_patterns)* It compares props shallowly, each with `Object.is`, and skips the render when they all match. It does nothing when a prop is rebuilt every render — an inline arrow, an object literal, an array literal — because those are new references every time. It also does not prevent re-renders caused by the component's own state or by a context it reads. *Follow-up: "so what does memo cost when it fails?" — a comparison on every render plus the render you did not avoid.* **51. `useMemo` and `useCallback` — when are they worth it?** ⭐⭐⭐ *(11_performance_patterns)* When the computation is genuinely expensive, or when the identity matters to something else — a memoized child's props, an effect's dependency array, a custom hook's return value. `useCallback(fn, deps)` is exactly `useMemo(() => fn, deps)`. Why do lists need keys?** ⭐⭐⭐ *(04_lists_conditional)* So React can tell which item is which between renders. Keys decide which DOM nodes and component instances are reused, moved, created or destroyed — and therefore which pieces of state, focus and uncontrolled input values survive a reorder. Without them React falls back to position and warns. *Follow-up: "unique where?" — among siblings, not globally.* **22. Why is the array index a bad key?** ⭐⭐⭐ *(04_lists_conditional)* Because position is not identity. Prepend an item and every index now points at a different thing, so React concludes row 0 is the same row with new text and *reuses its DOM node* — updating what it manages (text, attributes) and leaving what the DOM manages (an uncontrolled input's value, focus, scroll) attached to the wrong item. The correct answer names that mechanism rather than saying "it's bad practice". *Follow-up: "when is an index key fine?" — a list that never reorders, filters or inserts except at the end, whose items hold no state.* **23. Why not `key={Math.random()}`?** ⭐⭐ *(04_lists_conditional)* It is unique but not stable, so every render looks like a completely new set of items. React destroys and rebuilds the entire list every time, losing state and focus and doing the maximum possible work. *Follow-up: "where should an id come from when the data has none?" — generate it where the item is created, not during render.* **24. Is `key` a prop?** ⭐ *(04_lists_conditional)* No. React consumes it and it never appears in `props`. If the component also needs the identifier, pass it twice: ``. *Follow-up: "what else is like that?" — `ref` was, until React 19 made it a normal prop for function components.* **25. Why does `{count && }` sometimes render a `0`?** ⭐⭐⭐ *(04_lists_conditional)* Because `&&` returns its left operand when that operand is falsy, and React renders `0` — it only skips `false`, `null` and `undefined`. `0`, `""` and `NaN` are falsy but perfectly renderable. Fix by making the left side a real boolean: `count > 0 && …`. *Follow-up: "what about `items.length &&`?" — same bug, more common.* ### Effects **26. What is `useEffect` for?** ⭐⭐⭐ *(06_effects)* Synchronising your component with something outside React — the document, a subscription, a timer, a server. The framing matters, because it answers most "should this be an effect" questions on its own: if there is no external system, there is probably no effect. *Follow-up: "name three things people put in effects that shouldn't be" — deriving data for rendering, resetting state on a prop change, and reacting to a user event.* **27. Explain the dependency array honestly.** ⭐⭐⭐ *(06_effects)* It is a claim: "this effect reads exactly these values, and if none of them changed, running it again would produce the same result." Omitted means run after every render; `[]` means run once on mount; `[a, b]` means re-run when `a` or `b` changes by `Object.is`. Every value from inside the component that the effect reads belongs in it. *Follow-up: "what happens if you lie?" — either a stale closure or an infinite loop.* **28. What is a stale closure?** ⭐⭐⭐ *(06_effects)* A function created during one render that keeps reading that render's props and state forever. The classic is `setInterval(() => setCount(count + 1), 1000)` with `[]` deps: the callback captured `count` at `0`, so every tick computes `0 + 1` and the counter freezes at 1. The fix is usually to stop reading the value — `setCount(c => c + 1)` describes a change instead of capturing a value. *Follow-up: "what would adding `count` to the deps cost?" — the interval is destroyed and recreated every second, so the cadence drifts.* **29. When does a cleanup function run?** ⭐⭐ *(06_effects)* Before every re-run of the effect, and once more on unmount. The cleanup belongs to the render that created it, so it closes over that render's values — which is why the cleanup for a `Saved` message clears `Saved`, not the new one. *Follow-up: "so is it the unmount handler?" — no; it is the undo for one particular run.* **30. Why does React run effects twice in development?** ⭐⭐ *(06_effects)* Strict Mode mounts, runs effects, runs cleanups, and runs effects again, to prove your effect can be run twice safely. An effect that opens something and never closes it fails that test — which is exactly the bug it is designed to surface. *Follow-up: "how do you fix a double-fetch on mount?" — write the cleanup that ignores or aborts the first request; do not add a ref guard.* **31. `useEffect` vs `useLayoutEffect`?** ⭐⭐ *(06_effects)* Both run after the commit; `useLayoutEffect` runs *before* the browser paints and blocks it. Use it only when you must measure and adjust the DOM without the user seeing an intermediate state — positioning a tooltip, preventing a scroll jump. Default to `useEffect`; a visible flicker is the signal to switch. *Follow-up: "what's the downside?" — it blocks painting, and it does not run on the server.* **32. Should this go in an effect or an event handler?** ⭐⭐⭐ *(06_effects)* If it happened *because the user did a specific thing*, it belongs in the handler — sending analytics, POSTing a form, showing a toast. If it is about keeping something in sync with the current state, whoever caused it, it is an effect. Putting event logic in an effect makes it fire in situations you did not intend, such as a remount. *Follow-up: "where does 'fetch when the id changes' go?" — an effect, because the id can change for reasons other than a click.* **33. What is the exhaustive-deps lint rule and should you disable it?** ⭐⭐ *(06_effects)* It statically works out what your effect reads and requires those values in the array. It is essentially never wrong about what is read, though it can be wrong about what you *want* — and the right response then is to change the code, not to silence the rule. Every codebase littered with disable comments has an undiscovered stale-closure bug. *Follow-up: "how do you avoid needing a dependency?" — updater functions, refs, or moving the value out of the component.* ### Data fetching **34. Walk me through fetching data in a component.** ⭐⭐⭐ *(07_data_fetching)* Three states, not one: loading, success and error, all of which the user must be able to see. Kick the request off in an effect keyed on whatever identifies it, store the result in state, and stop the spinner on both paths — `.finally` makes that hard to forget. A component that renders only its happy path shows a blank box on a slow connection and forever on a 500. *Follow-up: "what's missing from that?" — cancellation and races.* **35. What is the race condition in data fetching?** ⭐⭐⭐ *(07_data_fetching)* Two requests in flight, and the slower one answers last. Render with id 1, then id 2; request 2 resolves and shows the right thing; request 1 resolves later and overwrites it with data nobody asked for. Nothing about React is wrong — the `.then` was scheduled before the effect was cleaned up, and promises cannot be un-started. *Follow-up: "how do you fix it?" — see the next question.* **36. How do you fix it?** ⭐⭐⭐ *(07_data_fetching)* A flag declared *inside* the effect body, checked before setting state, flipped by the cleanup — so each effect run retires only its own request. Where the transport supports it, `AbortController` is better because it actually stops the work and frees the connection. The two compose: abort what you can, ignore what you cannot. *Follow-up: "why not a `useRef` for the flag?" — one ref is shared by every effect run, so retiring the old request would retire the new one too.* **37. Why is it better to inject the fetcher than to import it?** ⭐ *(07_data_fetching)* Because the component then states what it needs — "something that turns an id into a promise of a user" — rather than naming an implementation. It becomes testable with no network and no mocking library, and reusable against a cache, a different backend or a fixture. *Follow-up: "how do you keep the injected function stable?" — define it outside the component or wrap it in `useCallback`.* **38. Why would you use TanStack Query or SWR instead?** ⭐⭐ *(10_custom_hooks)* Because hand-rolled fetching gives you loading, error and data, and nothing else. Those libraries add caching by key, request deduplication, retries, revalidation on focus and reconnect, pagination and optimistic updates — all of which you would otherwise reimplement badly. The decision is an engineering one: you should be able to name exactly which of those you need. *Follow-up: "is that state management?" — it is *server* state, which has different rules from client state and is why the split exists.* **39. What does `AbortController` actually do?** ⭐ *(07_data_fetching)* It signals the underlying operation to stop. `fetch` opts into it and rejects the promise with an `AbortError` — so the promise is not "cancelled", it is rejected, and you have to remember not to display that rejection as an error. *Follow-up: "does it work with any promise?" — no, only with APIs that accept a signal.* ### Hooks: rules and custom hooks **40. State the rules of hooks and say why they exist.** ⭐⭐⭐ *(10_custom_hooks)* Call hooks only at the top level — never in a condition, a loop, a callback, or after an early return — and only from components or other hooks. The reason is mechanical: React stores hook state in a list per component instance and matches each call to a slot by call order, so a render that skips a hook shifts every later hook by one. *Follow-up: "how do you do something conditionally, then?" — put the condition inside the hook, or split into two components.* **41. What is a custom hook?** ⭐⭐⭐ *(10_custom_hooks)* A function whose name starts with `use` and which calls other hooks. There is no machinery: the state it creates belongs to the calling component's hook list, so two components calling `useToggle()` get two independent toggles. It shares *logic*, never a value. *Follow-up: "how would you share a value?" — context, or a store.* **42. Why does the `use` prefix matter?** ⭐⭐ *(10_custom_hooks)* It is how the lint rules decide which functions may contain hooks and which call sites are legal. Naming a hook `getSomething` silently turns off all of that checking. *Follow-up: "what about React 19's `use()`?" — a built-in for reading promises and context that, unusually, may be called conditionally.* **43. Why should a custom hook return stable functions?** ⭐⭐ *(10_custom_hooks)* Because a consumer who correctly puts your returned function in a dependency array cannot fix its identity from the outside. If it is new on every render, their effect runs on every render forever. Wrap returned callbacks in `useCallback`; setters and `dispatch` are already stable. *Follow-up: "how do you test a hook?" — `renderHook`, asserting on the return value, which is its public API.* **44. Explain a debounce, and how it differs from a throttle.** ⭐⭐ *(10_custom_hooks)* Debounce waits for a pause and fires once at the end — right for search-as-you-type, autosave and validation. Throttle fires at most once per interval regardless of pauses — right for scroll and resize. In React, a debounce is an effect that `setTimeout`s the new value and whose cleanup clears the pending timer; the cleanup *is* the debounce. *Follow-up: "does debouncing fix the race condition?" — no, it reduces how often it happens; you still need the guard.* **45. What is `useRef` for?** ⭐⭐⭐ *(08_refs_dom)* Two jobs. A ref attached to a JSX element gives you the DOM node, for the imperative things you cannot describe — focus, scroll, measure, play. And a ref is a box that survives re-renders without causing them, for values nothing renders from: timer ids, the previous value of a prop, an instance of a non-React library. The rule: if changing it should change the screen, it is state. *Follow-up: "why shouldn't you read a ref during render?" — React may render without committing, so the value may be from a render that never happened.* ### Context and state management **46. What is context, and what is it not?** ⭐⭐⭐ *(09_context_reducer)* It is a lookup: `useContext(C)` walks up the tree and returns the value of the nearest provider. It holds nothing itself — the state lives in whatever component renders the provider. It is not a state manager: no selectors, no caching, no devtools, and every consumer re-renders when the value changes. *Follow-up: "so when is it right?" — values that are tree-wide and change rarely: theme, locale, current user, dispatch.* **47. Why is `value={{ user, logout }}` a bug?** ⭐⭐ *(09_context_reducer)* It is a new object on every render of the provider, so `Object.is` always fails and every consumer re-renders even when nothing changed. `useMemo` it, or split into two contexts — one for the value and one for the stable `dispatch`, so components that only dispatch never re-render at all. *Follow-up: "does `memo` on the consumer help?" — no; memo compares props, and context is not a prop.* **48. How do you make a context impossible to misuse?** ⭐⭐ *(09_context_reducer)* Default it to `null`, export a `useThing()` hook that throws a named error when the value is `null`, and do not export the context object. A missing provider becomes a loud error naming what to add, instead of a component that silently renders a plausible default — and TypeScript narrows the value for every consumer for free. *Follow-up: "what does the default argument to `createContext` actually mean?" — the value when there is no provider, not an initial value.* **49. When do you reach for Redux/Zustand/Jotai?** ⭐⭐ *(09_context_reducer)* When client state is large, frequently changing, and read by many components in different parts of the tree — because those libraries let a component subscribe to a *slice*, which context cannot do. If the state in question is really server data, a data-fetching library is the better answer. *Follow-up: "could you build a simple store yourself?" — yes, with `useSyncExternalStore`.* ### Performance **50. What does `memo` compare, and when does it do nothing?** ⭐⭐⭐ *(11_performance_patterns)* It compares props shallowly, each with `Object.is`, and skips the render when they all match. It does nothing when a prop is rebuilt every render — an inline arrow, an object literal, an array literal — because those are new references every time. It also does not prevent re-renders caused by the component's own state or by a context it reads. *Follow-up: "so what does memo cost when it fails?" — a comparison on every render plus the render you did not avoid.* **51. `useMemo` and `useCallback` — when are they worth it?** ⭐⭐⭐ *(11_performance_patterns)* When the computation is genuinely expensive, or when the identity matters to something else — a memoized child's props, an effect's dependency array, a custom hook's return value. `useCallback(fn, deps)` is exactly `useMemo(() => fn, deps)`. ## Exercise 1 — the stale-closure counter

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`.

> *"This counter is supposed to tick up every second. It stops at 1. Talk me
> through why, then fix it."*

Answer the "why" out loud before you edit anything — that is what is being
marked. Then make it count 3 after three seconds, and keep going.

```
uv run dojo test react i1_interview_concepts ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Before you touch anything, be able to say what is wrong. The interval is
created once, on mount. The function it was given was created during that same
render. What is `count` worth inside that function, on the tenth tick?

## Hint 2
Still `0` — it was baked in when the closure was created, and the effect never
re-runs to make a new one. So every tick calls `setCount(0 + 1)`, state goes to
`1`, and React bails out of the next identical update. That is a **stale
closure**.

## Hint 3
Two fixes exist and only one is good. Adding `count` to the dependency array
gives the effect a fresh closure each second, at the cost of tearing down and
recreating the timer every tick, which drifts. The better fix stops the callback
reading `count` at all — it describes the change instead of computing from a
captured value — and it is one word long.

## Hint 1
Before you touch anything, be able to say what is wrong. The interval is
created once, on mount. The function it was given was created during that same
render. What is `count` worth inside that function, on the tenth tick?

## Hint 2
Still `0` — it was baked in when the closure was created, and the effect never
re-runs to make a new one. So every tick calls `setCount(0 + 1)`, state goes to
`1`, and React bails out of the next identical update. That is a **stale
closure**.

## Hint 3
Two fixes exist and only one is good. Adding `count` to the dependency array
gives the effect a fresh closure each second, at the cost of tearing down and
recreating the timer every tick, which drifts. The better fix stops the callback
reading `count` at all — it describes the change instead of computing from a
captured value — and it is one word long.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Typing works, the counter updates, Save hands over the right string — so React
clearly knows what is in the box. And yet setting the state back to `""` leaves
the text on screen. Which of the two of them is actually deciding what the input
displays?

## Hint 2
`defaultValue` is read exactly once, when React creates the DOM node. From that
moment the browser owns the value, React never writes to it again, and the state
is a *copy* that happens to be kept in step by the change handler. Copies can be
updated independently, which is precisely what Reset did.

## Hint 3
The fix is a one-word rename that changes who is in charge: the input renders
the state on every render, so setting the state is the only way the box ever
changes. Be ready for the follow-up, because it is always asked — when *would*
you deliberately choose an uncontrolled input, and how would you read its value
on submit?

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Typing works, the counter updates, Save hands over the right string — so React
clearly knows what is in the box. And yet setting the state back to `""` leaves
the text on screen. Which of the two of them is actually deciding what the input
displays?

## Hint 2
`defaultValue` is read exactly once, when React creates the DOM node. From that
moment the browser owns the value, React never writes to it again, and the state
is a *copy* that happens to be kept in step by the change handler. Copies can be
updated independently, which is precisely what Reset did.

## Hint 3
The fix is a one-word rename that changes who is in charge: the input renders
the state on every render, so setting the state is the only way the box ever
changes. Be ready for the follow-up, because it is always asked — when *would*
you deliberately choose an uncontrolled input, and how would you read its value
on submit?

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Trace what a user sees on the first render. The component renders with
`total` at its initial value, the DOM is committed, *then* the effect runs and
sets the real total, and the component renders again. For one frame the page
said `Total: 0`.

## Hint 2
Ask the question that deletes most effects: **is this synchronising with
something outside React?** Adding up numbers you were handed is not. It is a
calculation, and calculations belong in the render body where they cannot be
out of date.

## Hint 3
So the state and the effect both go, and `total` becomes a plain `const`
computed from `items`. Nothing can then show a stale or half-updated total,
because there is nothing to keep in step. The follow-up to have ready: at what
point *would* you wrap that calculation in `useMemo`, and how would you decide?
