lessons.briefing:
# i2 — Interview drills

These are the tasks. Not questions about React — things an interviewer hands you
a blank editor and forty minutes for, or pairs with you on while watching how
you work.

Each drill is written the way it would be said to you, with a **time-box**. The
time-box is not a target to beat; it is there so you find out where you actually
are. A drill you cannot finish in twice its box is a lesson to redo, and each
one names which.

Two things are being assessed in a live version of these, and only one of them is
the code. The other is how you work: whether you restate the problem before
typing, whether you name the state out loud, whether you say "I'd normally reach
for TanStack Query here, but let me show you the manual version", whether you
notice the accessibility requirement without being prompted. Practise the
narration along with the code — talk to the empty room. It feels ridiculous and
it is the highest-value thing on this page.

Every drill takes its data source as a **prop**, as always, so nothing here
touches the network.

A note on the gates. Drills with timers are driven with `fireEvent.change`
rather than `user-event`, because `user-event` waits on real timers and mixing
that with fake ones produces a test that passes on your machine and fails on a
slow one. Where there are no timers, it is `user-event` as usual.

## Drill 1 — the debounced search box · ~12 minutes

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`.

> *"Here's a `search` function that returns a promise of results. Build me a
> search box. Don't fire a request on every keystroke."*

`DebouncedSearch({ search })` renders an input labelled `Search` and a list of
results, and:

- waits **300ms after the typing stops** before calling `search`;
- calls it **once** for a burst of typing, with the final value;
- does not call it at all for an empty box, and shows no results then;
- never lets an older response replace a newer one.

That last requirement is not in the prompt. Interviewers leave it out on
purpose. *(Weak here → redo `10_custom_hooks` and `07_data_fetching`.)*

```
uv run dojo test react i2_interview_drills ex1
```

## Drill 2 — the paginated list · ~15 minutes

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`.

> *"`fetchPage(n)` gives you `{ items, total }`. Page through it, two at a
> time."*

`PagedList({ fetchPage, pageSize })`:

- loads page 1 on mount and lists the items;
- a live region reads `Page 1 of 3` — the page count comes from `total` and
  `pageSize`;
- `Previous` and `Next` move one page and are disabled at the ends;
- only the current page's items are on screen.

*(Weak here → redo `07_data_fetching`.)*

```
uv run dojo test react i2_interview_drills ex2
```

## Drill 3 — the validated form · ~15 minutes

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`.

> *"Two fields, display name and email. Don't let a bad one through, and tell
> the user what's wrong — properly, not just red borders."*

`ProfileForm({ onSubmit })`:

- display name must be at least 2 characters, message
  `Display name must be at least 2 characters`;
- email must contain an `@`, message `Enter a valid email address`;
- **no errors before the first submit attempt**; after one, each broken field
  carries `aria-invalid="true"` and has its message as its accessible
  description, and each valid field carries `aria-invalid="false"`;
- once a submit has been attempted, fixing a field clears its error **as the
  user types**;
- `onSubmit` gets `{ displayName, email }` only when everything is valid.

*(Weak here → redo `05_forms`.)*

```
uv run dojo test react i2_interview_drills ex3
```

## Drill 4 — the accessible accordion · ~12 minutes

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`.

> *"An FAQ accordion. One open at a time. Assume a screen-reader user."*

`Accordion({ sections })` where each section is `{ id, title, body }`:

- each header is a `<button>` with `aria-expanded` (present and `"false"` when
  closed) and `aria-controls` pointing at its panel;
- the open panel has `role="region"` and takes its accessible name from its
  header via `aria-labelledby`;
- opening one closes the other; clicking an open header closes it.

*(Weak here → redo `03_state_events` and `01_components_jsx`.)*

```
uv run dojo test react i2_interview_drills ex4
```

## Drill 5 — the cart editor · ~12 minutes

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`.

> *"Quantities up and down, remove a line, keep the total right."*

`CartEditor({ initialItems })` over `{ id, name, price, quantity }`:

- one `<li>` per line showing `Apple x2`;
- buttons named `Increase Apple`, `Decrease Apple` and `Remove Apple` — the
  name matters, an unlabelled `+` is a column of identical controls to a screen
  reader;
- decreasing to zero removes the line;
- a live region reads `Total: 5.50`, two decimal places, derived not stored.

*(Weak here → redo `04_lists_conditional` and `09_context_reducer`.)*

```
uv run dojo test react i2_interview_drills ex5
```

## Drill 6 — the confirm dialog · ~15 minutes

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`.

> *"A delete button that asks first. Try it with the keyboard."*

`DeleteButton({ onConfirm })`. The markup is already correct; the keyboard
behaviour is missing:

- clicking `Delete` opens a `role="dialog"` named `Delete item?`;
- **focus moves to `Cancel`** when it opens;
- `Escape` closes it, and `Cancel` closes it, without confirming;
- `Confirm` calls `onConfirm` once and closes;
- every close **returns focus to the `Delete` button**.

*(Weak here → redo `08_refs_dom` and `06_effects`.)*

```
uv run dojo test react i2_interview_drills ex6
```

## Challenge — the typeahead · ~45 minutes

Edit `challenge/solution.tsx`. This is the real take-home-sized one, and it
combines every drill above.

> *"Build an autocomplete. Debounced. Keyboard-navigable. It should be a proper
> combobox, not a text box with a menu under it."*

`Typeahead({ search, onSelect })`:

- an input labelled `Search products` with `role="combobox"`, `aria-expanded`
  and `aria-controls`;
- suggestions after a **300ms** pause, one request per pause;
- suggestions render as `role="option"` inside a `role="listbox"`;
- `ArrowDown` / `ArrowUp` move a highlighted option — **focus stays in the
  input**, and the input's `aria-activedescendant` holds the highlighted
  option's `id`;
- `Enter` selects the highlighted option: calls `onSelect`, puts the value in
  the box, closes the list. `Escape` closes it;
- a response for a query the user has moved on from is ignored.

Honest difficulty note: this is genuinely a 45-minute task, and the
`aria-activedescendant` pattern is the part most candidates have never
implemented. Enumerate the state before you type anything — hint 1 tells you how
many pieces there are.

```
uv run dojo test react i2_interview_drills challenge
```

## Review — the live filter

`review1/solution.tsx`. `LiveFilter({ fetchMatches })`: an input labelled
`Filter`, a **200ms** debounce, results in a list, and no stale answer allowed
to win. Drill 1 in miniature, resurfaced by the review ladder.

```
uv run dojo test react i2_interview_drills review1
```

# Reading — react/i2_interview_drills

## Notes

A live coding round is scored on more than the code. Interviewers are watching
for a repeatable process: restate the task, enumerate the state out loud, build
the simplest version that renders, then layer on the requirements one at a time,
running as you go. Candidates who type in silence read as guessing even when
they are right, and candidates who name the trade-off they are not implementing
("I'd debounce this and I'd also want the stale-response guard") read as senior
even when they run out of time. Every drill on this page has at least one
requirement that was deliberately left out of the prompt — noticing it unasked
is the whole test.

## ex1 — the debounced search box

This is the most-given React drill in existence, because it touches state,
effects, cleanup, async and API etiquette in about twenty lines.

The mechanism worth being able to narrate: the effect schedules the request with
`setTimeout` and returns a cleanup that clears it. Because React runs the
previous cleanup before the next effect, a keystroke arriving inside the window
cancels the request that was about to go out. You are not writing a queue or
comparing timestamps — the effect lifecycle already has debounce semantics, and
saying that out loud is worth more than the code.

The unasked requirement is the stale-response guard. Debouncing reduces how
often two requests overlap; it does not prevent it. Pause, type, pause, and two
requests are in flight, and the first can still answer last. The `let current`
flag inside the effect body handles it. If the interviewer does not raise it,
you should.

The empty-query case is the other thing candidates skip. An empty box that still
shows the last search's results is a small bug with a big smell, and firing a
request for `""` is worse — many APIs interpret it as "everything".

Two follow-ups to have ready. *"Would you extract this?"* — yes, into
`useDebouncedValue` (you wrote it in lesson 10), which separates "when to ask"
from "what to do with the answer". *"What would you use in production?"* —
TanStack Query or SWR, which give you the debounce-adjacent parts you have not
built: caching by key, deduplication, retries and revalidation.

## ex2 — the paginated list

The design pressure is what counts as state. The user changes exactly one thing
— the page number — and everything else either arrives from the server as a unit
or is computed during render. Candidates who store `items`, `page`, `hasNext`,
`pageCount` and `loading` as five independent pieces of state spend the rest of
the drill keeping them in step, and an interviewer watching that happen has
already made their assessment.

Two details separate a working answer from a good one. Replacing the items
rather than appending them is what distinguishes pagination from infinite
scroll, and the bug where a "load more" implementation is reused for pages is
common enough to be worth mentioning unprompted. And the race applies here as
much as in drill 1: two quick clicks on Next put two page requests in flight, and

## Challenge — the typeahead · ~45 minutes

Edit `challenge/solution.tsx`. This is the real take-home-sized one, and it
combines every drill above.

> *"Build an autocomplete. Debounced. Keyboard-navigable. It should be a proper
> combobox, not a text box with a menu under it."*

`Typeahead({ search, onSelect })`:

- an input labelled `Search products` with `role="combobox"`, `aria-expanded`
  and `aria-controls`;
- suggestions after a **300ms** pause, one request per pause;
- suggestions render as `role="option"` inside a `role="listbox"`;
- `ArrowDown` / `ArrowUp` move a highlighted option — **focus stays in the
  input**, and the input's `aria-activedescendant` holds the highlighted
  option's `id`;
- `Enter` selects the highlighted option: calls `onSelect`, puts the value in
  the box, closes the list. `Escape` closes it;
- a response for a query the user has moved on from is ignored.

Honest difficulty note: this is genuinely a 45-minute task, and the
`aria-activedescendant` pattern is the part most candidates have never
implemented. Enumerate the state before you type anything — hint 1 tells you how
many pieces there are.

```
uv run dojo test react i2_interview_drills challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Do not start typing. Enumerate the state out loud first — there are exactly
three things: what is in the box, the suggestions currently on screen, and which
one is highlighted. Whether the list is open is *derived* from the second, not
stored. Getting that list right in the first two minutes is most of what an
interviewer is measuring.

## Hint 2
The fetching half is drill 1 again: an effect on `query`, a `setTimeout`, a
cleanup that clears the timer and flips a `current` flag before any state is
set. Reset the highlight to "none" whenever new suggestions arrive.

The keyboard half is an `onKeyDown` on the input, not on the list, with four
cases: ArrowDown and ArrowUp move the index (clamped, not wrapped, unless you
decide otherwise), Enter selects when something is highlighted, Escape closes.
Call `preventDefault()` on the arrows or the caret jumps to the end of the text.

## Hint 3
The accessibility wiring is what makes this a combobox rather than a text box
with a menu under it. **Focus never leaves the input.** Instead the input
carries `aria-activedescendant` holding the `id` of the highlighted option, so a
screen reader announces it while the user is still typing. The list is
`role="listbox"`, each item is `role="option"` with `aria-selected`, and
`aria-expanded` on the input says whether it is showing. Every option therefore
needs a stable id you can build from an index — and selecting has to do four
things at once, so put it in one function that both Enter and a click can call.

## Drill 1 — the debounced search box · ~12 minutes

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`.

> *"Here's a `search` function that returns a promise of results. Build me a
> search box. Don't fire a request on every keystroke."*

`DebouncedSearch({ search })` renders an input labelled `Search` and a list of
results, and:

- waits **300ms after the typing stops** before calling `search`;
- calls it **once** for a burst of typing, with the final value;
- does not call it at all for an empty box, and shows no results then;
- never lets an older response replace a newer one.

That last requirement is not in the prompt. Interviewers leave it out on
purpose. *(Weak here → redo `10_custom_hooks` and `07_data_fetching`.)*

```
uv run dojo test react i2_interview_drills ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Three requirements hide in the prompt: do not ask until the typing pauses, do
not ask at all for an empty box, and do not let an old answer overwrite a new
one. Work through them in that order and rerun the gate after each.

## Hint 2
The debounce is an effect whose cleanup cancels the pending timer:

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  const timer = setTimeout(() => { /* … */ }, 300);
  return () => clearTimeout(timer);
}, [query, search]);
```

## Hint 1
Say what the state is before you write anything — interviewers ask. Exactly one
thing here changes because the user did something: the page number. The items
and the total are the *answer* for that page, and both arrive together.

## Hint 2
```tsx
const [page, setPage] = useState(1);
const [data, setData] = useState<Page | null>(null);

useEffect(() => { /* fetch this page, store the result */ }, [page, fetchPage]);
```

The buttons do not fetch. They move `page`, and the effect notices.

## Hint 3
The page count comes from the server's `total` and the `pageSize` you were
given — `Math.ceil` — and both `disabled` values are derived during render
rather than stored. Two things worth getting right because they are the ones
that get probed: replace the items instead of appending them, and carry the
cleanup guard across, because two quick clicks on Next put two requests in
flight.

## Hint 1
Validation is a pure function of the two values, so write it outside the
component and have it return an object keyed by field name. That keeps the
component to three jobs: run it, decide whether to show the results, and decide
whether to submit.

## Hint 2
The timing requirement is the interesting one. Errors must not appear before the
first submit, and after that they must clear *as the user types*. One extra
boolean gets you both:

```tsx
const errors = validate(displayName, email);      // recomputed every render
const shown = attempted ? errors : {};
```

Because `errors` is derived rather than stored, it is never stale.

## Hint 3
Each input then needs `aria-invalid` — which must be `"false"`, not absent, when
the field is fine — and `aria-describedby` pointing at the id of that field's
message, or nothing when there is no message. Rendering `aria-describedby` as
`undefined` omits the attribute. The judgement call worth naming out loud: is
per-field wiring enough, or would you also add a summary at the top, and where
should focus go after a failed submit?

The total is not state — it is the lines, added up. Compute it during render and
it can never disagree with what is on screen. Storing it means updating it in
three handlers and forgetting one.

## Hint 2
Increase and Decrease are the same operation with a different sign, so write one
function taking the id and the step. Inside it, `map` to change the matching
line and `filter` to drop anything that has reached zero — both return new
arrays, which is what React needs to see a change:

```tsx
setItems((previous) =>
  previous.map(…).filter(…),
);
```

## Hint 3
Every button must say *which* line it belongs to in its accessible name —
`Increase Apple`, not a bare `+` — or a screen-reader user hears a column of
identical controls. The remaining decisions: `toFixed(2)` is fine for a drill
but ask yourself what you would really do about money and floating point, and
what should happen to the list when it empties.

exercises.prompt:
## Drill 6 — the confirm dialog · ~15 minutes

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`.

> *"A delete button that asks first. Try it with the keyboard."*

`DeleteButton({ onConfirm })`. The markup is already correct; the keyboard
behaviour is missing:

- clicking `Delete` opens a `role="dialog"` named `Delete item?`;
- **focus moves to `Cancel`** when it opens;
- `Escape` closes it, and `Cancel` closes it, without confirming;
- `Confirm` calls `onConfirm` once and closes;
- every close **returns focus to the `Delete` button**.

*(Weak here → redo `08_refs_dom` and `06_effects`.)*

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The markup is already right — dialog role, modal flag, named by its heading.
What is missing is everything to do with the keyboard: focus does not move in,
Escape does nothing, and focus is not handed back on close. Those three are what
an interviewer is checking for.

## Hint 2
Two refs, one for each end of the journey. Focusing the Cancel button cannot
happen in the click handler that opens the dialog — the button does not exist
yet — so it goes in an effect keyed on `open`. Restoring focus to the trigger
*can* happen directly in a handler, because that button never left the page.

```tsx
useEffect(() => { if (open) cancel.current?.focus(); }, [open]);
```

## Hint 3
Escape is a document-level `keydown` listener, subscribed only while the dialog
is open and removed by the effect's cleanup. Route every way of closing —
Cancel, Escape, Confirm — through one `close()` function, so the focus
restoration cannot be forgotten in one of them. What a real modal still owes its
users after this: trapping Tab inside it, and making the rest of the page inert.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
The markup is already right — dialog role, modal flag, named by its heading.
What is missing is everything to do with the keyboard: focus does not move in,
Escape does nothing, and focus is not handed back on close. Those three are what
an interviewer is checking for.

## Hint 2
Two refs, one for each end of the journey. Focusing the Cancel button cannot
happen in the click handler that opens the dialog — the button does not exist
yet — so it goes in an effect keyed on `open`. Restoring focus to the trigger
*can* happen directly in a handler, because that button never left the page.

```tsx
useEffect(() => { if (open) cancel.current?.focus(); }, [open]);
```

## Hint 3
Escape is a document-level `keydown` listener, subscribed only while the dialog
is open and removed by the effect's cleanup. Route every way of closing —
Cancel, Escape, Confirm — through one `close()` function, so the focus
restoration cannot be forgotten in one of them. What a real modal still owes its
users after this: trapping Tab inside it, and making the rest of the page inert.

## Hint 1
Two defences, and they are not the same defence. The debounce decides *how
often* you ask. The guard decides *whether you listen* to an answer that
arrives after you have moved on. A component with only the first still shows the
wrong results when the network is uneven.

## Hint 2
Both live in one effect. Schedule the request with `setTimeout`; declare a
`let current = true` beside it; check that flag before setting state; and have
the cleanup clear the timer *and* flip the flag. The delay here is 200ms.

Remember the empty-query case — an empty filter box should show nothing rather
than the last search's leftovers, and should not send a request at all. Then
answer the follow-up in your head: if debouncing already reduces the number of
requests, why is the guard still necessary?

lessons.briefing:
# i3 — Rapid fire

Five short rounds. Every one of them is a ⭐⭐⭐ concept from the question bank,
in a shape you have not seen it in — because the thing that fails in an
interview is never the concept you studied, it is the concept you studied
*wearing different clothes*.

None of these needs more than a few minutes. That is the point: this is the
lesson you run when you have twenty minutes and an interview on Thursday. Aim
to diagnose each one **before** you run the gate — read the component, predict
the failure, then check whether you were right. Being able to spot the bug by
reading is a different skill from being able to fix it once a test has told you
where it is, and it is the one that transfers.

Every exercise here, including the four core ones, is marked for **spaced
review**. `dojo review` will bring them back at 3, 7, 21 and 60 days, which is
the mechanism that stops this material fading between now and whenever you
actually need it. Run `uv run dojo review run` when it tells you something is
due.

## Round 1 — keys, with state inside the row

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`.

`ScoreBoard` renders one `PlayerRow` per player, and each row keeps **its own
score in its own `useState`**. Score Ada twice, add a player to the front, and
Ada's two points must still be Ada's.

Lesson 04 made this happen to an uncontrolled input. Notice what is different
here, and what that tells you about what keys really control.

```
uv run dojo test react i3_interview_rapidfire ex1
```

## Round 2 — dependencies and cleanup, on a subscription

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`.

`ChannelIndicator({ channel, label, onSubscribe, onUnsubscribe })` must:

- subscribe once on mount;
- do **nothing** when only `label` changes;
- on a channel change, unsubscribe from the **old** channel and then subscribe
  to the new one;
- unsubscribe on unmount.

Four requirements, one effect, and three of them are currently wrong.

```
uv run dojo test react i3_interview_rapidfire ex2
```

## Round 3 — the update queue

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`.

`TripleBump` has one button, `Add three`, whose handler calls the setter three
times — and moves the counter by one. Make it three, keeping all three calls,
and note the second assertion: it must still be a **single** render.

```
uv run dojo test react i3_interview_rapidfire ex3
```

## Round 4 — memo, defeated by one prop

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`.

`Body` is wrapped in `memo` and you may not change it. `Panel` re-renders it on
every toggle anyway. Find the prop that makes the comparison impossible and fix
it in `Panel`.


# Reading — react/i3_interview_rapidfire

## Notes

The five rounds here are the ⭐⭐⭐ concepts from `i1_interview_concepts`
re-dressed, and re-dressing is the whole design. A concept you can only
recognise in the example you first met it in has not been learned; it has been
memorised. Every round is marked for the spaced-review ladder, so `dojo review`
brings them back at 3, 7, 21 and 60 days — which is the mechanism that turns
this from a course you finished into knowledge you still have in October. Aim to
diagnose each one by reading before you run the gate.

## ex1 — keys control component instances, not just DOM nodes

Lesson 04 demonstrated index keys with an uncontrolled `<input>`, and it is easy
to come away thinking the problem is about the DOM: React reuses a node, the
browser-owned value stays behind. This round moves the state into a `useState`
inside the row component and the bug is identical — which tells you the rule is
one level up. Keys decide which **component instances** React considers to be
the same thing across renders, and an instance carries its whole hook list with
it.

So the list of things that go to the wrong row with a bad key is longer than
people expect: `useState` and `useReducer` values, refs, running effects and
their cleanups, uncontrolled input values, focus, selection, scroll position,
in-flight CSS transitions, and playing media. Any of those is a symptom.

The follow-up in hint 3 is worth rehearsing because it inverts the lesson.
Everything above describes keys *preserving* state you wanted preserved. The
same mechanism is the cleanest way to **destroy** state you want destroyed:
`<Editor key={documentId} />` gives every document a fresh editor, with no
effect watching a prop and calling setters. React's own documentation
recommends it, and candidates who reach for it unprompted stand out.

## ex2 — the four things an effect owes a subscription

This is the effect lifecycle with nowhere to hide. Subscribe on mount;
unsubscribe and resubscribe when the identity of the thing you are subscribed to
changes; unsubscribe on unmount; and do nothing at all when something unrelated
re-renders. A missing dependency array breaks the fourth, a missing cleanup
breaks the second and third.

The assertion that repays study is the one checking *which* channel is
unsubscribed. When the channel goes from `news` to `sport`, React runs the
cleanup created by the `news` render — which closed over `news` — before running
the new effect. You do not have to arrange that; it falls out of the cleanup and
its effect belonging to the same render. Once that clicks, a lot of effect code
stops being surprising: a cleanup closes *its own* socket, cancels *its own*
request, clears *its own* timer.

The dependency array here is `[channel, onSubscribe, onUnsubscribe]`, and the
two function props are where an interviewer will push. Including them is
correct: if the parent passed different functions and you had omitted them, the
effect would keep calling the old ones forever. The cost is that a parent
defining those inline re-subscribes on every render — cheap for a fake, ruinous
for a WebSocket — and the fix belongs in the parent (`useCallback`, or hoisting
the function), not in a shortened array. Being able to describe both sides of
that trade is the answer they are listening for.

## ex3 — one queue, one render

Two ⭐⭐⭐ ideas in eight lines. The first is that `count` is a `const` belonging
to the render that created the handler, so three calls to `setCount(count + 1)`
are the same instruction three times. Passing a function enqueues a recipe
instead of a value, and React applies the recipes in order against the
accumulating result.

The second is the render count, which is not something you fix — it is something
to notice. Three state updates inside one event produce **one** render, because
React collects everything the event produced and applies it in a single pass.
That guarantee is why splitting state into several `useState` calls is free, and
why you cannot observe a half-updated component.

Two follow-ups worth having. *"Was that always true?"* No — before React 18,
batching applied only inside React's own event handlers, so two updates inside a
`setTimeout` or a `.then` rendered twice; React 18 made it automatic everywhere.
*"How would you opt out?"* `flushSync`, which forces a synchronous render and is
a last resort for things like measuring the DOM between two updates.

## ex4 — the prop that makes memo impossible

`memo` compares props shallowly with `Object.is`. `{ padding: 8 }` written in
the render body allocates a new object every render: same contents, different
identity, comparison fails, child renders — and you have paid for a comparison
on top of the render you did not avoid. That is strictly worse than not
memoizing at all, which is the sentence to say out loud.

The family of props that do this is worth being able to list on demand:
`style={{…}}`, `items={[…]}`, `onClick={() => …}`, `config={{…}}`, and anything
built by a `.map()` or a `.filter()` in the render body. Each is a new reference
every time.

The fixes, in order of preference. If the value never varies, hoist it out of
the component so it is created once for the module — that is what the reference
does, and it costs nothing. If it depends on props or state, `useMemo` for
values and `useCallback` for functions. If the object is only ever passed to a
DOM element rather than a memoized component, do nothing at all: DOM elements
do not compare props, so the allocation is trivial and the memoization would be
pure ceremony.

The senior-level observation: a memoized component's effectiveness depends on
callers it cannot control, which means `memo` is a contract between two files.
That is a real argument for measuring with the Profiler rather than sprinkling,
and for the React Compiler, which does this bookkeeping mechanically.

## review1 — the two conditional-rendering mistakes

The stray zero is one of the most-reported React bugs in existence, and the
explanation is one sentence: `&&` returns its left operand when that operand is
falsy, and React renders `0` because it only skips `false`, `null` and
`undefined`. `0`, `""` and `NaN` are falsy in JavaScript and perfectly
renderable. `items.length && <List/>` is the same bug and is even more common.

Three fixes exist and they are not equal. `count > 0 && …` is the clearest
because it says what you meant. `Boolean(count) && …` works and reads like an
apology. `count ? <Badge/> : null` sidesteps the operator entirely and is the
safer default when the condition is not obviously boolean — which is why some
teams ban `&&` in JSX outright.

The empty state is the other half, and it is a product requirement rather than a
React one. An empty `<ul>` is technically correct and tells the user nothing:
did it load, is it broken, is there a filter on? An empty state says what
happened and, ideally, what to do next. Interviewers who have shipped products
notice when a candidate adds one without being asked, and notice when they do
not.

## Further reading

- [react.dev — Preserving and Resetting State](https://react.dev/learn/preserving-and-resetting-state) — ex1, including resetting state deliberately with a key.
- [react.dev — Lifecycle of Reactive Effects](https://react.dev/learn/lifecycle-of-reactive-effects) — ex2, subscription by subscription.
- [react.dev — Queueing a Series of State Updates](https://react.dev/learn/queueing-a-series-of-state-updates) — ex3, with the queue drawn out.
- [react.dev — `memo`](https://react.dev/reference/react/memo) — ex4, including "should you add memo everywhere?".
- [react.dev — Conditional Rendering](https://react.dev/learn/conditional-rendering) — the `&&` trap, in the official words.
- [MDN — Logical AND (`&&`)](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/Logical_AND) — why it returns an operand rather than a boolean.

## Round 1 — keys, with state inside the row

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`.

`ScoreBoard` renders one `PlayerRow` per player, and each row keeps **its own
score in its own `useState`**. Score Ada twice, add a player to the front, and
Ada's two points must still be Ada's.

here, and what that tells you about what keys really control.


exercises.prompt:
## Round 2 — dependencies and cleanup, on a subscription

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`.

`ChannelIndicator({ channel, label, onSubscribe, onUnsubscribe })` must:

- subscribe once on mount;
- do **nothing** when only `label` changes;
- on a channel change, unsubscribe from the **old** channel and then subscribe
  to the new one;
- unsubscribe on unmount.

Four requirements, one effect, and three of them are currently wrong.

```
uv run dojo test react i3_interview_rapidfire ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Say the lifecycle out loud before editing: subscribe when the component
appears, unsubscribe and resubscribe when the channel changes, unsubscribe when
it goes away — and do nothing at all when something unrelated re-renders. Three
of those four are currently wrong.

## Hint 2
The cleanup is the unsubscribe, and the dependency array is what stops the
effect running when only `label` changed:

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  onSubscribe(channel);
  return () => { /* … */ };
}, [/* … */]);
```

## Hint 3
The gate checks *which* channel is unsubscribed when it changes, and expects the
old one — that falls out for free, because each cleanup closes over the same
`channel` its own effect run saw. List everything the effect and its cleanup
read between them; there are three, not one, and being able to justify the two
function props is the part an interviewer will push on.

## Hint 1
Say the lifecycle out loud before editing: subscribe when the component
appears, unsubscribe and resubscribe when the channel changes, unsubscribe when
it goes away — and do nothing at all when something unrelated re-renders. Three
of those four are currently wrong.

## Hint 2
The cleanup is the unsubscribe, and the dependency array is what stops the
effect running when only `label` changed:

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  onSubscribe(channel);
  return () => { /* … */ };
}, [/* … */]);
```

## Hint 3
The gate checks *which* channel is unsubscribed when it changes, and expects the
old one — that falls out for free, because each cleanup closes over the same
`channel` its own effect run saw. List everything the effect and its cleanup
read between them; there are three, not one, and being able to justify the two
function props is the part an interviewer will push on.

## Round 3 — the update queue

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`.

`TripleBump` has one button, `Add three`, whose handler calls the setter three
times — and moves the counter by one. Make it three, keeping all three calls,
and note the second assertion: it must still be a **single** render.

```
uv run dojo test react i3_interview_rapidfire ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
`count` is a `const` belonging to the render that created this handler, and
nothing that happens inside the handler changes it. So all three calls are the
same instruction sent three times.

## Hint 2
Pass a function instead of a value. React applies the queued functions in order
against the accumulating result, so "add one" three times composes where "become
1" three times does not.

## Hint 3
The second assertion is the one to think about rather than fix. Three updates in
one handler produce **one** render, because React collects everything an event
produces and applies it in a single pass. Be ready to say when that was not true
— and what `flushSync` is for.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Two independent problems. One is that an empty inbox renders an empty list
instead of saying anything. The other is a single character on the page that
should not be there — run the gate and read which.

## Hint 2
`&&` returns its **left operand** when that operand is falsy, so
`{unread && <span/>}` evaluates to the number `0`, and React renders `0`. It
skips `false`, `null` and `undefined` only; `0`, `""` and `NaN` are falsy in
JavaScript and perfectly renderable. Make the left side a real boolean.

## Hint 3
For the empty state, an early return keeps the main path un-nested. Note that
`items.length && <List/>` is the same bug wearing different clothes, and is even
more common — being able to name both on sight is what this round is for.

## Hint 1
Two independent problems. One is that an empty inbox renders an empty list
instead of saying anything. The other is a single character on the page that
should not be there — run the gate and read which.

## Hint 2
`&&` returns its **left operand** when that operand is falsy, so
`{unread && <span/>}` evaluates to the number `0`, and React renders `0`. It
skips `false`, `null` and `undefined` only; `0`, `""` and `NaN` are falsy in
JavaScript and perfectly renderable. Make the left side a real boolean.

## Hint 3
For the empty state, an early return keeps the main path un-nested. Note that
`items.length && <List/>` is the same bug wearing different clothes, and is even
more common — being able to name both on sight is what this round is for.
